# ChatGPT vs Copilot: the difference, and how to use Copilot in Teams
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/chatgpt-vs-copilot-teams/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot are both AI assistants, and Copilot runs largely on OpenAI's GPT models, but they are different products: ChatGPT is OpenAI's standalone app with its own tools, while Copilot is Microsoft's assistant built into Windows, Edge, Bing and Microsoft 365. The right choice depends on where your work lives. This page compares them, explains why Copilot sometimes seems weaker, and covers Copilot in Microsoft Teams: where to find it, how it works in chats and meetings, and where meeting transcripts are stored.

## ChatGPT vs Copilot: which should I use?

Use Copilot when your work is in Microsoft 365, such as Outlook, Word, Excel and Teams, or your organisation provides it with data protection. Use ChatGPT as a broad assistant with custom GPTs, projects, memory, strong image generation and coding agents.

For a student, ChatGPT is often the more flexible learning and side-project companion, while Copilot is the natural choice inside a college or company Microsoft 365 account, where it can see your documents and meetings with your permissions. Many people use both: Copilot for work documents and meetings, ChatGPT for exploration and personal projects. Test both on three of your real tasks before deciding.

## Is Copilot the same as ChatGPT?

No. They share technology, since Microsoft builds Copilot largely on OpenAI's models, but they are separate products from different companies, with different apps, features, integrations, accounts and privacy terms.

Copilot adds Microsoft's own layers: grounding with Bing search, access to your Microsoft 365 data through Microsoft Graph for work accounts, enterprise data protection, and integration into Windows and Office. ChatGPT adds OpenAI's layers: custom GPTs, projects, memory, canvas, Codex and its app ecosystem. The same underlying model can therefore behave differently in each, because the instructions, tools and context around it differ.

## Do Copilot and ChatGPT use the same model?

Often from the same family, but not necessarily the same version at the same time. Copilot uses OpenAI's GPT models hosted by Microsoft, along with Microsoft's own models and, in some features, models from other providers. ChatGPT uses OpenAI's latest models directly.

Microsoft decides which model serves each Copilot request and does not always show it, while ChatGPT lets you choose between modes in many plans. New OpenAI models usually reach ChatGPT first or at the same time, and Microsoft adopts them on its own schedule after testing. In practice, differences in answers come as much from system instructions, safety settings and grounding as from the model version.

## When should I use Copilot vs ChatGPT?

Use Copilot for tasks tied to Microsoft 365 content and Windows: summarising a Teams meeting, drafting a reply in Outlook, analysing an Excel table, or asking about your organisation's files. Use ChatGPT for open-ended learning, writing, coding, image work and anything outside Microsoft 365.

Examples:

- "What did we decide in yesterday's project meeting?": Copilot in Teams.
- "Turn this Word report into a ten-slide deck": Copilot in PowerPoint.
- "Teach me recursion and quiz me": ChatGPT or Copilot both work.
- "Build a small web app with tests in my repository": ChatGPT's Codex or GitHub Copilot.
- "Generate and edit an illustration": ChatGPT.

When company data is involved, use the tool your organisation has approved.

## Why is Copilot worse than ChatGPT?

Copilot is not inherently worse, but it can feel that way because it may use faster models for some requests, applies more conservative instructions, and often lacks the context you assumed it had. Precise prompts and attached context close most of the gap.

Common reasons and fixes:

- **Missing context**: open the document or attach the file before asking.
- **Vague request**: state the goal, audience, format and length.
- **Wrong product**: Microsoft 365 Copilot needs a licence for work data; free Copilot cannot see your work files.
- **Search-heavy answers**: Copilot often grounds in web results, which can make answers shorter and more cautious.

For deep reasoning tasks, choose Copilot's deeper or thinking mode if available.

## Where do I find Copilot in Teams?

In Microsoft Teams, Copilot appears in the left app bar or as Copilot Chat, in chats and channels as a Copilot button, and in meetings as a Copilot button in the meeting controls. Which ones you see depends on your licence and your organisation's settings.

Copilot Chat, available to many work and school accounts, is a general assistant grounded in the web and your uploaded files. The full Microsoft 365 Copilot licence adds Copilot inside chats, channels and meetings, with access to your Teams messages, files and meeting transcripts within your permissions. If you see no Copilot at all, check that Teams is updated and ask your IT team whether Copilot is enabled for your account.

## How does Copilot work in Teams?

In Teams, Copilot uses a language model with access to the content you are allowed to see: chat and channel messages, files and meeting transcripts. It summarises conversations, answers questions about them and drafts messages.

In a chat or channel, ask "summarise the last week of this conversation" or "what decisions were made about the launch date?", and Copilot answers with references to the messages. In meetings, it works from the live transcript. It respects permissions, so it will not reveal content from chats you are not part of. Like any assistant, it can misattribute who said what or miss nuance, so check important points against the transcript before acting on them.

## How do I use Copilot in Teams?

Open a chat, channel or meeting and select the Copilot button, then ask in plain language: summarise, list action items, find what someone said, or draft a reply. You can also use Copilot Chat from the app bar for questions across your work content.

Useful prompts:

- "Summarise the unread messages in this channel and highlight anything that needs my reply."
- "List the action items from this chat with owners and deadlines."
- "Draft a polite reply asking for the report by Friday."
- "What files were shared in this chat about the hackathon?"

Be specific about time ranges and people. Copilot's drafts are starting points; edit them so they sound like you and contain only facts you can stand behind.

## How do I use Copilot in a Teams meeting?

Turn on transcription when the meeting starts, then open Copilot from the meeting controls. During the meeting you can ask for a recap, open questions or action items; afterwards, the meeting recap shows notes and tasks generated from the transcript.

Organisers can also allow Copilot to work only during the meeting without keeping a transcript, depending on organisation settings, in which case after-meeting recaps are limited. Good prompts: "What have I missed in the last ten minutes?", "What are the unresolved questions?", and "Draft a follow-up email with decisions and owners." Tell participants when transcription is on; many organisations require it. Review the recap before sharing, because summaries can drop qualifications or merge points.

## Where are Copilot Teams transcripts stored?

Meeting recordings and transcripts are stored in Microsoft 365 within your organisation's tenant, typically in the meeting organiser's OneDrive for regular meetings and in the channel's SharePoint site for channel meetings, governed by retention and access policies.

Who can see a transcript depends on meeting settings and permissions, usually the organiser and attendees. Copilot reads the transcript to answer questions and build recaps, and Copilot interactions themselves are stored under the organisation's compliance settings. Admins control whether transcription is allowed, how long recordings and transcripts are kept, and who can download them. For sensitive meetings, check with the organiser before turning transcription on, and follow your organisation's data policy.

# ChatGPT vs Gemini: the difference, which is better, and when to use each
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/chatgpt-vs-gemini/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


ChatGPT and Gemini are both AI assistants that chat, answer questions, write, code and work with images and files. ChatGPT is made by OpenAI and runs on its GPT models; Gemini is made by Google and runs on its Gemini models. They are close in capability, and the better choice depends mostly on the task and on which ecosystem you already use. This page explains what each is, how they differ, which is better for what, when to use Claude instead, what this kind of tool is called, and why opinions online disagree so much.

## What are ChatGPT and Gemini?

ChatGPT is OpenAI's AI assistant, launched in November 2022. Gemini is Google's AI assistant, launched as Bard in 2023 and renamed Gemini in early 2024. Both are chat interfaces built on large language models.

You talk to either in plain language by typing or speaking, and they respond with text, code, images or actions such as searching the web. Both have free tiers and paid plans, apps for phones and the web, and developer APIs. Under the hood, both are transformer-based models trained on large amounts of text, code, images and audio, then tuned to follow instructions and behave safely. They make similar kinds of mistakes, so the same verification habits apply to both.

## Are ChatGPT and Gemini the same?

No. They are different products from different companies, built on different model families: GPT models from OpenAI and Gemini models from Google. They overlap heavily in what they do, but differ in strengths, features and integrations.

The overlap is why people treat them as interchangeable for everyday tasks such as explanations, summaries and drafts, where both perform well. The differences show in the details: which tools each can use, how each connects to your other apps, how each handles very long documents or video, and how each phrases and structures answers. Your data also goes to different companies under different privacy terms, which matters for work and personal information.

## What is the difference between ChatGPT and Gemini?

The biggest differences are ecosystem and features. Gemini is built into Google's products, such as Gmail, Docs, Drive, Android, Maps and YouTube. ChatGPT is a standalone assistant with its own ecosystem of custom GPTs, apps, projects, memory and coding tools.

Practical differences that matter:

- **Integration**: Gemini works naturally with Google Workspace; ChatGPT connects to many services through connectors and apps.
- **Media**: Gemini handles video input natively through its API; ChatGPT offers strong image generation and voice.
- **Coding**: ChatGPT has Codex; Google has Gemini Code Assist and Antigravity.
- **Plans**: both have free tiers and paid plans with different bundles, such as Google's plans including cloud storage.

Both change features often, so compare current versions.

## How is Gemini different from ChatGPT under the hood?

Gemini models were designed from the start to handle text, images, audio and video together, and support very long context windows. GPT models also handle multiple types of input, with OpenAI pairing them with separate models for images, video and speech.

Both families come in tiers: fast, cheaper models for everyday use and larger reasoning models for hard problems, and both apps route requests between them. Google grounds Gemini answers with Google Search, while ChatGPT uses its own search integration. The training data, model sizes and exact architectures are not public for either. For most users these differences show up indirectly, as speed, how well long files are handled, and how current the answers are.

## ChatGPT vs Gemini: which is better?

Neither is better at everything. Both are top-tier assistants, and benchmark leadership changes with each model release. The better one for you is the one that gives better results on your actual tasks, in the apps you already use.

A fair test takes twenty minutes: pick five tasks you do often, such as explaining a concept, summarising a PDF, debugging code, drafting an email and planning a week, and run the same prompts in both. Judge accuracy, clarity and how much editing each answer needs. Many people end up using both: Gemini for anything inside Google Workspace and Android, ChatGPT for general work and its tool ecosystem. Public leaderboards, such as LMArena's community rankings, give a broad signal but not a verdict on your use case.

## When should I use ChatGPT vs Gemini?

Use Gemini when your work lives in Google's ecosystem: Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Drive, YouTube, Maps or an Android phone. Use ChatGPT for a broad standalone assistant with custom GPTs, projects, memory, image generation and coding agents.

Examples:

- Summarise a long Gmail thread or a Drive folder: Gemini.
- Ask about a YouTube lecture or analyse a video file: Gemini.
- Build a reusable assistant for a repeated task: either, through custom GPTs or Gems.
- Generate and edit images in conversation: ChatGPT is very strong here.
- Work on a code repository with an agent: ChatGPT's Codex, or Google's coding tools.

If your college uses Google Workspace, Gemini in your student account may be the most convenient.

## When should I use ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini?

Use ChatGPT as a broad all-rounder, Gemini inside Google's ecosystem and for video and very long multimodal inputs, and Claude for long documents, careful writing and coding work, including Claude Code for real repositories.

This is a starting point, not a rule. All three are close enough that the prompt and the context you provide often matter more than the brand. For developers, the choice also depends on the API: pricing, rate limits, latency and features such as tool use or batch processing. In RAG.NextUpgrad I built multi-provider fallback, so the product keeps working when one provider is slow or down; that design also lets you switch models when one improves. Students can use the free tiers of all three and keep whichever helps most.

## How does Gemini AI compare to ChatGPT for students?

For students, both are excellent and free tiers go a long way. Gemini is especially convenient with a Google account, Google Docs and YouTube lectures, and Google has run free plan offers for students. ChatGPT is strong as a tutor, writing coach and coding helper.

Study tasks where each shines:

- Turning a recorded or YouTube lecture into notes: Gemini.
- Step-by-step tutoring and quizzes: both, with ChatGPT's study-style prompting a popular choice.
- Studying from your own notes and papers: Google's NotebookLM is excellent and free.
- Debugging programming assignments: both; check by running the code.

Whatever you use, follow your college's rules on AI in assignments.

## What are ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude called?

They are called AI chatbots or AI assistants, and more technically, applications built on large language models, or LLMs. Because they also handle images, audio and video, they are sometimes called multimodal AI assistants.

When they can take actions, such as browsing, running code or using apps to complete tasks, they are described as AI agents. The broader field is generative AI, since they generate new text, images, audio and code. Microsoft Copilot, Meta AI, Perplexity, DeepSeek and Mistral's Le Chat belong to the same category. In job descriptions, building products with these models is usually called GenAI engineering or AI engineering.

## Why do Reddit opinions on Gemini vs ChatGPT differ so much?

Because people test different tasks, different model versions and different plans at different times. A comparison from a few months ago may describe models that have since been replaced, and one person's coding task says little about another's essay.

Online threads are also shaped by strong feelings about companies, by free-tier users comparing against paid-tier users, and by single memorable failures. Treat them as a source of ideas for what to test, not as a verdict. Look for posts that state the exact model, plan, date and prompt, and ideally share the outputs. Then run your own small test: your tasks, your prompts, both tools, side by side. That answer is the only one that applies to you.

# Chroma vs ChromaDB: what Chroma does in Python, examples and common errors
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/chroma-vector-database-python/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Chroma, often called ChromaDB, is an open-source vector database for AI applications: it stores text chunks, their embeddings and metadata, and returns the most similar chunks for a query, which is the retrieval step in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It is popular for prototypes because it runs inside Python with a few lines of code. This page covers the name, its role in LLM apps, Python usage and examples, avoiding repeated embedding costs, in-memory versus persistent storage, a common Docker crash, testing RAG with Chroma, and the unrelated colour term.

## What is the difference between Chroma and ChromaDB?

There is no difference: Chroma is the project and company name, and ChromaDB is the common name for the database and its Python package, installed with `pip install chromadb`.

Chroma runs in several modes: embedded inside your Python process, as a client-server setup with a separate Chroma server, or as a hosted cloud service. Tutorials use "Chroma", "ChromaDB" and "Chroma DB" interchangeably. In LangChain and LlamaIndex, the integration is usually called Chroma. If you see "Chroma" in a photography or colour context, that is an unrelated meaning covered at the end of this page.

## What is ChromaDB in LLM applications?

In LLM applications, ChromaDB is the vector store that holds your knowledge: document chunks with their embeddings. When a user asks a question, the app searches Chroma for similar chunks and passes them to the LLM so it can answer from your documents.

Chroma provides collections, which are like tables, with documents, embeddings, metadata and IDs. It can compute embeddings for you with a default or chosen embedding function, or accept embeddings you compute yourself. Metadata filters let you restrict search, for example to one course or date range. It uses an approximate nearest-neighbour index, HNSW, for fast search. For many student projects and internal tools, Chroma is all the vector database you need.

## What does Chroma do in Python?

In Python, Chroma lets you create collections, add documents with IDs and metadata, and query them by text or embedding to get the most similar items, all from a simple API that can run in-process without a separate server.

Typical operations:

- `client.get_or_create_collection(name)` to create or open a collection.
- `collection.add(ids=..., documents=..., metadatas=...)` to index chunks.
- `collection.query(query_texts=[...], n_results=5, where={...})` to search with filters.
- `collection.update`, `upsert` and `delete` to keep data current.

Results include IDs, documents, metadata and distances, which you pass to your LLM prompt with IDs for citations.

## How do I use ChromaDB in Python?

Install `chromadb`, create a persistent client, create a collection, add documents with unique IDs, and query it.

```python
import chromadb

client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_store")
col = client.get_or_create_collection("notes")
col.upsert(
    ids=["os-1", "os-2"],
    documents=["A process is a program in execution.", "Paging divides memory into fixed-size pages."],
    metadatas=[{"subject": "os", "page": 3}, {"subject": "os", "page": 7}],
)
res = col.query(query_texts=["what is paging?"], n_results=1, where={"subject": "os"})
print(res["documents"][0], res["metadatas"][0])
```

The default embedding function downloads a small model on first use; for production, choose your embedding model explicitly and use it consistently.

## What are some Chroma examples?

Common Chroma examples are a chatbot over your PDFs, semantic search over notes or support tickets, a FAQ assistant for a college or product, and memory for an AI agent that stores past conversation summaries.

Project ideas to practise:

- **Study assistant**: index lecture notes by page and answer questions with page citations.
- **Support search**: index past tickets and suggest similar resolved issues.
- **Code search**: embed function docstrings and search your codebase in plain language.
- **Agent memory**: store summaries of past tasks and retrieve them when relevant.

Pair Chroma with keyword search for exact terms such as error codes, which embeddings often miss, and add a reranker when results look plausible but wrong.

## How do I avoid recomputing embeddings with Chroma?

Use a persistent client so embeddings survive restarts, give each chunk a stable ID, and upsert only new or changed chunks, tracking a hash of each document to detect changes. Never rebuild the whole collection when one file changes.

A simple pattern: compute an ID such as `docname#chunkindex` and a content hash; before indexing, check which IDs already exist with the same hash; embed and upsert only those that are new or changed; delete IDs for removed content. If you compute embeddings yourself, cache them on disk keyed by content hash. Remember that changing the embedding model requires re-embedding everything, because vectors from different models are not comparable.

## Is it a problem to store a vector database in memory?

For prototypes, tests and small datasets, in-memory storage is fine and fast. For anything users depend on, it is a problem: data disappears when the process restarts, memory limits cap your dataset, and multiple app instances cannot share it.

Use in-memory clients for unit tests and notebooks, and persistent storage in development and production, with backups. If you run several app instances, use a client-server Chroma or a database such as PostgreSQL with pgvector, so all instances see the same data. Also keep your source documents as the true record: the vector index should be rebuildable from them, which makes recovery and model changes straightforward.

## Why does ChromaDB crash with "illegal instruction" in a Docker container?

"Illegal instruction" usually means a compiled dependency, such as the HNSW index library or an ML runtime, was built for CPU instructions your machine or emulator does not support. It often happens when running an image built for a different CPU architecture, such as amd64 under emulation on an ARM Mac.

Fixes to try:

- Run an image that matches your machine's architecture, or build the image natively on it.
- Avoid emulation for this workload where possible.
- Use the official Chroma server image and connect from your app as a client.
- Rebuild the dependency from source without CPU-specific optimisations, following Chroma's troubleshooting docs.
- Pin versions known to work on your platform.

Check Chroma's GitHub issues for your exact error and platform; others usually hit it first.

## How do you test RAG memory with ChromaDB?

Treat retrieval as testable code: create a fresh in-memory or temporary Chroma collection in each test, load a fixed set of documents, run known queries and assert that the expected IDs come back in the top results.

What to test:

- **Retrieval correctness**: expected chunk IDs appear in the top k for each query.
- **Updates**: changed documents replace old chunks; deleted ones disappear.
- **Filters**: metadata filters exclude what they should.
- **Agent memory**: stored summaries are retrieved in later turns and old ones expire as designed.
- **Regressions**: run the suite on every change to chunking or embeddings.

Automated retrieval tests catch silent failures, such as duplicate chunks or broken updates, long before users notice wrong answers.

## What is colour chroma?

In colour theory, chroma is the colourfulness or intensity of a colour relative to a neutral grey of the same brightness: high chroma colours are vivid, low chroma colours are muted or greyish. It is unrelated to the Chroma vector database.

Chroma is one of the three dimensions in colour systems such as Munsell, alongside hue and value or lightness. "High chroma vs low chroma" comparisons appear in painting, design, photography and fashion; for example, a bright red is high chroma, while a dusty rose is low chroma. In photography, "chroma noise" refers to random colour speckles in images. If you came here for databases, the sections above cover ChromaDB.

# What is a Claude API key, and how do you get and set up the Claude API?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/claude-api-key-setup/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A Claude API key is a secret token that lets your own code call Claude models through Anthropic's API; requests made with it are billed to your developer account. You create keys in the Claude Console, store them in an environment variable, and use them with Anthropic's SDKs or plain HTTP. This page covers getting a key, the Console and developer platform, the docs, how the API differs from the claude.ai app, how a request works, setting it up in Python, using Claude in VS Code, and whether the API supports skills.

## What is a Claude API key?

A Claude API key is a long secret string, beginning with `sk-ant-`, that authenticates requests to Anthropic's API. Anyone who has your key can make requests that are charged to your account, so it must be kept private.

Keys belong to a workspace in your organisation in the Claude Console, so you can create separate keys for development and production, set spending limits per workspace, and revoke a key instantly if it leaks. A key is not your claude.ai login and does not give access to your chat history. Common leaks happen when keys are pasted into front-end JavaScript, committed to a public GitHub repository or shared in screenshots. Keep keys in environment variables or a secrets manager, and rotate any key you suspect has been exposed.

## How do I get a Claude AI API key?

Sign up in the Claude Console, set up billing for your organisation, then open the API keys page and create a key. Copy it immediately; the Console shows the full key only once.

The steps:

- Sign in to the Console with your email or Google account.
- Add billing details and purchase credits or set up payment, as the Console prompts.
- Go to API keys and choose "Create key", giving it a clear name such as "college-project-dev".
- Copy the key into a password manager or your project's `.env` file.

A claude.ai Pro or Max subscription does not include API credits; the two are billed separately. Students should set a low spending limit while learning, so a bug in a loop cannot run up a large bill.

## Where is the Claude API Console?

The Claude Console, previously called the Anthropic Console, is Anthropic's web dashboard for developers, linked from the Claude developer documentation. It is where you create keys, manage billing, test prompts and see usage.

Inside the Console you will find a Workbench for trying prompts and model settings before writing code, a prompt generator and improver, usage and cost dashboards, rate-limit information for your tier, and organisation settings for inviting teammates and creating workspaces. It is separate from claude.ai, even though you can use the same email for both. If a link or tutorial points to an old address, start from Anthropic's documentation site and follow the link to the Console from there.

## What is the Claude API platform?

The Claude Developer Platform is Anthropic's set of services for building with Claude: the API itself, the Console, SDKs, documentation and features such as tool use, batch processing, prompt caching, files and agent tooling.

Building blocks you will meet:

- **Messages API**: the core request for a model response.
- **Tool use**: let Claude call your functions and APIs.
- **Message Batches**: process large jobs asynchronously at lower cost.
- **Prompt caching**: reuse long, repeated context cheaply and quickly.
- **Files API** and PDF support: reuse uploaded documents.
- **Agent SDK and MCP**: build agents and connect tools in a standard way.

Claude models are also available through cloud providers such as Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI, which suits teams already on those clouds.

## Where are the Claude API docs?

Anthropic's developer documentation covers getting started, every API endpoint, the SDKs, model details, pricing, rate limits and guides on prompting, tool use, retrieval and agents. It is linked from anthropic.com and the Console.

Read these first: the quickstart, the Messages API reference, the models overview for current model names, the guide to tool use, and the prompt engineering guide. The docs include runnable examples in Python and TypeScript, and an API reference with every parameter. When a blog post or video disagrees with the docs, trust the docs; model names and parameters change, and older tutorials go stale quickly.

## What is the difference between Claude AI and the Claude API?

Claude AI usually means claude.ai, the chat product for people, with a free tier and subscriptions. The Claude API is the developer interface for building Claude into your own software, paid per token used.

The chat app gives you a ready interface, conversation history, projects, file uploads and apps on every device. The API gives you only the model: you send messages and get responses, and you build the interface, storage and logic yourself. Subscriptions and API credits are billed separately; a Pro plan does not cover API usage. Use claude.ai to learn, write and think; use the API when you want Claude inside a website, bot, app or automated workflow.

## How does the Claude API work?

Your code sends an HTTPS request to the Messages endpoint with your API key, a model name, a maximum number of output tokens and a list of messages. Claude returns a response containing content blocks, a stop reason and token usage.

Key ideas:

- **Stateless**: the API does not remember earlier calls; send the conversation history you want it to consider each time.
- **System prompt**: sets the role, rules and context for the whole conversation.
- **Tokens**: you pay for input and output tokens, and limits apply per minute.
- **Streaming**: receive the response as it is generated for a responsive UI.
- **Tools**: describe functions with JSON schemas; Claude replies with a tool call, you run it and send the result back.

Errors come back with clear types, such as rate limits and temporary overload, which you handle with retries.

## How do I set up the Claude API?

Install the SDK, set your key as an environment variable, and make a first request. In Python, that is three steps and about ten lines.

```bash
pip install anthropic
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."     # on Windows PowerShell: $env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
```

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=400,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Give me three RAG project ideas for students."}],
)
print(reply.content[0].text)
```

For projects, keep the key in a `.env` file loaded at startup and add `.env` to `.gitignore`. Check the models overview for the current model names.

## How do I use the Claude API in VS Code?

The simplest route is Claude Code's VS Code extension, which brings Claude's coding agent into the editor. Alternatively, coding extensions that support multiple providers let you paste an Anthropic API key and choose a Claude model.

With Claude Code, you install it, sign in with your Claude account or use an API key, and work with it in the editor: it reads your project, proposes edits shown as diffs and runs commands with your approval. Third-party extensions such as open-source coding assistants also accept Anthropic keys and bill usage to your API account. Whichever you use, set a spending limit in the Console, keep the key out of your settings files that get committed, and review every change before accepting it.

## Can the Claude API use skills?

Yes. Agent Skills, packaged folders of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads when relevant, can be used through the Claude API together with its code execution tool, as well as in Claude Code and the Claude apps.

Anthropic provides some prebuilt skills, for example for working with document formats, and you can upload custom skills for your organisation, such as your report template or data-cleaning procedure. Claude sees a short description of each available skill and loads the full contents only when a task needs it, which keeps context small. Because this feature is newer and its request format may change, follow the current skills guide in the API documentation for the exact parameters, and test custom skills on small tasks first.

# What is the Claude app, the Claude SDK and API, and can Claude apply to jobs?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/claude-app-sdk-api-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The Claude app is Anthropic's assistant on the web at claude.ai, on desktop for macOS and Windows, and on iOS and Android; Claude Code is its coding tool for the terminal and IDEs. Developers reach the same models through the Claude API, usually with Anthropic's official SDKs. This page covers the apps and where your data lives, the API and SDKs and how they differ, what the "overloaded" error means, how to connect Apify's scrapers to Claude, whether that is free, and whether Claude can apply to jobs for you.

## What is the Claude app?

The Claude app is Anthropic's AI assistant, available in a browser at claude.ai and as desktop and mobile apps. You chat with it, upload files and images, create documents and small apps in a side panel, and connect it to tools.

All versions share one account, so conversations and projects appear everywhere you sign in. The desktop app adds conveniences such as a quick-launch shortcut and connecting local tools through the Model Context Protocol. The mobile app is good for voice and quick questions. Claude Code is a separate tool for developers that works directly on code in your terminal or IDE. The same family of Claude models powers all of them, with plans that set your usage limits.

## What are the Claude apps?

The official Claude apps are the web app at claude.ai, desktop apps for macOS and Windows, mobile apps for iOS and Android, and Claude Code for the terminal and IDEs such as VS Code and JetBrains. All are published by Anthropic.

Each suits a different job:

- **Web and desktop**: writing, research, analysing documents and spreadsheets, projects with shared files.
- **Mobile**: voice conversations, photos of notes or whiteboards, quick questions.
- **Claude Code**: reading a codebase, editing files, running tests and commands.

Inside the chat apps, "artifacts" are small documents or apps Claude creates that you can preview, edit and share. Be careful with third-party apps that use the Claude name: unless the publisher is Anthropic or a known IDE vendor, avoid entering your credentials.

## Does the Claude app keep all data locally?

No. The Claude apps store your conversations in your Anthropic account on Anthropic's servers, so they sync across devices. The desktop app is a client, not an offline model; nothing runs fully on your computer.

What stays local depends on what you connect: files on your computer that you expose through a local MCP server are read on your machine and only the parts Claude uses are sent with the conversation. Anthropic's privacy settings let you control whether your chats may be used to improve models, and you can delete conversations. Check the privacy settings once and choose deliberately. If you need data to stay entirely on your own hardware, you need a local open-weight model, not Claude.

## What are the Claude APIs?

The Claude API is Anthropic's HTTP interface for using Claude models in your own software. The core is the Messages API: you send a list of messages and settings, and get Claude's reply, with options for streaming, tool use, images, PDFs and structured outputs.

Around it are supporting APIs: token counting, the Message Batches API for large asynchronous jobs at lower cost, a Files API for reusing uploaded documents, and features such as prompt caching to cut cost on repeated context. You authenticate with an API key from the Anthropic Console and pay per token used, separately from any chat subscription. The API is what you use to build a chatbot into a college project, add document Q&A to an app, or run an agent on a server.

## What is the Claude SDK?

The Claude SDKs are Anthropic's official client libraries for calling the API from code, available for Python, TypeScript and several other languages. There is also the Claude Agent SDK, for building agents on the same foundations as Claude Code.

A minimal Python example:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()   # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=500,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain BM25 in two sentences."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

Install it with `pip install anthropic`. Check the model overview in the docs for the current model names, since new versions replace old ones regularly.

## What is the difference between the Claude API and SDK?

The API is the service: HTTP endpoints that accept requests and return Claude's responses. An SDK is a library in your programming language that calls those endpoints for you, handling authentication, retries, streaming and typed responses.

You can call the API directly with any HTTP client, which is useful for languages without an SDK or for quick tests with `curl`. In practice, the SDK saves effort and prevents mistakes: it retries temporary errors automatically, parses streaming events correctly, and gives editor autocompletion for parameters. Both reach the same models with the same limits and prices. Use the SDK for real projects and raw HTTP only when you have a reason.

## What does "Claude API is overloaded" mean?

It means Anthropic's servers are temporarily under heavy load and could not process your request. The API returns an `overloaded_error`, with HTTP status 529, and the right response is to wait briefly and retry.

It is not a problem with your key, code or account, and it is different from a rate-limit error, which means you exceeded your own limits. Handle it with retries using exponential backoff and a little randomness, so many clients do not retry at the same instant. The official SDKs already retry such errors a couple of times by default, and you can raise the retry count. In production, also add a fallback, such as a smaller model or a different provider, so users see a slower answer rather than an error. RAG.NextUpgrad uses multi-provider fallback for exactly this reason.

## How do I connect Apify to Claude?

Apify provides an MCP server that exposes its scrapers, called Actors, as tools. Add the Apify MCP server to Claude, through the connectors settings or the desktop app's MCP configuration, with your Apify API token, and Claude can run Actors and read their results.

Once connected, you can ask Claude, for example, to collect the titles and links of recent posts from a public page using a suitable Actor, then summarise them. Keep three things in mind: scrape only public data you are allowed to collect and respect each site's terms; store your Apify token like a password; and limit which Actors are exposed so Claude cannot run expensive jobs by accident. Apify's documentation has current setup instructions for its MCP server.

## Is Apify for Claude free?

Connecting Apify to Claude through its MCP server does not need a special paid add-on, but running Apify Actors uses your Apify account's platform usage. Apify has a free plan with a monthly usage allowance, and heavier use needs a paid plan.

Your Claude plan applies on the Claude side as usual. Costs depend on the Actors you run, how many pages they process and how often; some Actors are maintained by third parties and have their own pricing. Start with small test runs and check usage in the Apify console before scheduling anything recurring. Apify's pricing page lists the current free allowance and plans.

## Can Claude apply to jobs for me?

Claude can do most of the work around applying: tailoring your resume to each job description, drafting cover letters and referral messages, and preparing you for interviews. You should still submit applications yourself.

Agent tools that control a browser can technically fill in forms, but automated applications on LinkedIn, Indeed and similar sites can break their terms of service and get accounts restricted. Mass-applying also produces poor matches that recruiters ignore. A better use of Claude: "Here is the job description and my resume. List the gaps, rewrite my project bullets using only facts from my resume, and draft a 100-word note to an engineer at the company." Then read, edit and send it yourself. Quality and a referral beat volume.

# What are Claude artifacts? AI-powered artifacts, limits, terminal use, and Claude vs Aider
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/claude-artifacts-limits-terminal/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Claude artifacts are substantial outputs, such as code, documents, interactive web pages, diagrams and small apps, that Claude creates in a dedicated panel beside the conversation, where you can view, edit, iterate on and share them. Anthropic introduced them in 2024. I build AI products and prototype interfaces with assistants daily, so this page covers how artifacts work, AI-powered artifacts and expiry, Claude in the terminal, Claude versus Aider and Airtable, usage limits, and, for gamers, Claude's best class in Fire Emblem: Three Houses. What are Claude artifacts? Artifacts are self-contained pieces of content Claude creates that appear in a separate window next to the chat: code files, Markdown documents, single-page websites, SVG graphics, Mermaid diagrams and interactive React components. They are meant for content you want to use or keep refining, rather than conversational replies. You can ask Claude to update an artifact, view earlier versions, copy or download it, and publish it to share a link. Typical uses include building calculators, dashboards, landing page drafts, study tools, data visualisations and documentation. They make Claude useful for quick prototyping, since you see working results immediately. How do Claude artifacts work? When you ask for something substantial and standalone, Claude writes it as an artifact, and the app renders it in a sandboxed panel: code is displayed, web pages and React components run live, and diagrams render visually. Each edit creates a new version. You iterate in conversation: "Make the chart a bar chart" or "Add a dark mode toggle", and Claude updates the artifact. Artifacts run in a restricted environment, so they cannot freely access the internet or your files, which keeps them safe to open. You can publish an artifact to get a shareable link, and others can view or remix it. For larger projects, move the code into a real repository and continue with proper tools. What are Claude AI-powered artifacts? AI-powered artifacts are artifacts that call Claude themselves while running, turning them into small AI apps: a flashcard generator, a writing coach or a game with an AI character. When others use a shared AI-powered artifact, usage counts against their own Claude account, not the creator's. Also asked as: what are claude ai powered artifacts You build them by describing the app to Claude, which writes an artifact that sends prompts to Claude through a built-in interface and displays results. This lets non-developers create and share AI tools without managing API keys or hosting. They suit prototypes and personal tools; for production apps with many users, custom data and reliability needs, build with the Claude API in your own application. Do Claude artifacts expire? Artifacts do not have a fixed expiry; they stay within their conversation as long as the conversation exists, and published artifacts remain available at their link until you unpublish them or delete the source, subject to Anthropic's policies. If you delete a conversation, its artifacts go with it. To keep important work safe, download or copy artifact code into your own files or a repository. Artifact features and sharing options change over time, so check Anthropic's help centre for current behaviour. For anything you rely on, such as a tool your team uses daily, keep your own copy rather than depending on a chat history. How do I use Claude in the terminal? Use Claude Code, Anthropic's agentic coding tool: install it, open a terminal in your project folder, and run claude. It can read your codebase, edit files, run commands and tests, and make commits, asking for permission before actions. Also asked as: how to claude in terminal Getting started: Install Claude Code using the instructions in Anthropic's documentation. Run claude inside your project directory and sign in. Ask it to explain the codebase, fix a bug or add a feature. Review proposed changes and approve commands. Add a CLAUDE.md file with project conventions it should follow. It also integrates with editors such as VS Code and JetBrains IDEs, and runs in Anthropic's desktop app. Claude vs Aider: what is the difference? Claude is a family of AI models and Anthropic's apps, including Claude Code for the terminal. Aider is an open-source terminal tool for AI pair programming that works with many models, including Claude, GPT and local models, editing files in your Git repository. The fair comparison is Claude Code versus Aider. Aider is model-agnostic, lightweight and commits each change to Git automatically, which suits developers who want to switch models or use local ones. Claude Code is built by Anthropic for Claude models, with deep agentic features such as running tests, subagents, hooks and integrations. Many developers try both; choose by preferred models, workflow and how much autonomy you want the tool to have. Claude vs Airtable: how do they compare? They are different kinds of tools. Airtable is a cloud database and spreadsheet-style platform for organising records, building views and automations. Claude is an AI assistant that reads, writes, analyses and reasons. They complement rather than compete. Common combinations: use Airtable to store structured data such as leads, content calendars or inventory, and Claude to analyse exports, draft content from records, write formulas or automation scripts, and design base structures. Claude can connect to tools like Airtable through integrations and connectors where available. Airtable also has its own built-in AI features. Pick Airtable for the system of record and Claude for thinking and writing work. How do Claude AI usage limits work? Claude's apps limit how much you can use within a time window, based on factors such as message length, attached files, model choice and conversation length. Limits reset on a rolling session basis, and some paid plans also have weekly limits. Also asked as: how does claude ai limit work Long conversations use more of your limit, because Claude rereads the conversation each turn. To stretch limits: start new chats for new topics, avoid re-uploading large files, use projects for shared context, and choose lighter models for simple tasks. Paid plans offer more usage, and the API is billed separately by tokens. Anthropic's help centre explains current limits for each plan. When does the Claude limit reset? When you reach a limit, the Claude app shows the time your usage resets, typically within a few hours, because limits work on rolling session windows. Weekly limits on some plans reset on a weekly cycle. Also asked as: when claude limit reset If you hit limits often, check whether long conversations or large attachments are using most of your allowance, and consider a plan with higher limits if Claude is central to your work. For developers, the API has separate rate limits by tier. Planning heavy tasks, such as large codebase changes, early in a session window helps avoid interruptions. What is Claude's best class in Fire Emblem: Three Houses? In Fire Emblem: Three Houses, Claude von Riegan, leader of the Golden Deer, is strongest as a flying archer. Wyvern Lord suits him before the timeskip, and his unique Barbarossa class, unlocked later, combines flight, strong stats and his Hero's Relic bow, Failnaught. Also asked as: fe3h claude best class Train his bow and flying skills early, and consider authority and lance for flexibility. Barbarossa is widely regarded as his best class, since flying mobility lets him reach enemies anywhere on the map while avoiding counterattacks. This Claude is unrelated to Anthropic's AI, but the name collision means search results often mix the two.

# How to use Claude Code for AI coding, and what Claude AI is
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/claude-code-ai-coding-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To code with Claude, install Claude Code, open a terminal in your project and run `claude`, then describe the change you want; it reads your files, edits them and runs commands with your approval. Claude itself is the family of AI models made by Anthropic, available on the web, desktop, mobile and through an API. This page covers how to start with Claude Code, what Claude is and how it is built, which version is free, which app to use, what Claude agents are, and how to vibe code without shipping a mess.

## How do I use Claude Code for AI coding?

Install Claude Code, open a terminal in your project folder, run `claude`, and describe a task. It reads the codebase, proposes edits and terminal commands, and applies them when you approve.

A good first session:

```bash
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
cd my-project
claude
```

Then try "explain how this project is structured", followed by a small change such as "add input validation to the signup endpoint and a test for it". Claude Code also runs inside VS Code and JetBrains IDEs. Add a `CLAUDE.md` file at the project root with your build commands, coding style and rules; it is read at the start of every session. Work in small steps, review each diff and commit often so you can roll back. The official documentation lists the current installation options and the plans that include it.

## What is the Claude AI tool?

Claude is an AI assistant from Anthropic. It writes, answers questions, analyses documents and images, and writes and debugs code, through a chat app, a coding tool and an API.

The same model family powers all of these surfaces. On claude.ai you chat, upload PDFs or spreadsheets and create documents or small apps in a side panel. Claude Code is the agentic coding tool for the terminal and IDEs. The Claude API lets developers build Claude into their own products with tool use, structured outputs and long context. Models come in tiers: Opus for the hardest work, Sonnet as the balanced default, and Haiku for fast, low-cost tasks. Students mostly use it for explaining concepts, reviewing code and drafting reports.

## How does Claude AI work?

Claude is a large language model: a transformer neural network that predicts the next piece of text, one token at a time, based on everything earlier in the conversation.

When you send a message, the text is split into tokens and processed together with the conversation history and any files you attached. The model generates a response token by token, and for harder problems it can reason through intermediate steps before answering. Tools extend it: it can search the web, run code or call your functions, and the results come back into its context. It does not look facts up by default and it has a training cutoff, so ask it to cite sources or use search for recent information. The attention mechanism from the 2017 Transformer paper is what lets it relate every part of a long input to every other part.

## How is Claude AI made?

Claude is pretrained on a large body of text and code to predict the next token, then fine-tuned with human feedback and Anthropic's Constitutional AI method to be helpful, honest and harmless.

Pretraining gives the model knowledge and language ability. Fine-tuning shapes behaviour: people rate responses, and the model is trained towards the preferred ones. Constitutional AI, described in Anthropic's 2022 paper, adds a written set of principles; the model critiques and revises its own outputs against them, and that feedback is used for training, which reduces the need for humans to label harmful content. Anthropic also publishes safety research and runs evaluations before release. The training data and exact recipes are not public.

## When was Claude AI created?

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers, and the first Claude model was released to the public in March 2023. New generations have followed regularly since.

The Claude 3 family in March 2024 introduced the Haiku, Sonnet and Opus tiers that the product still uses. Claude Code arrived in early 2025 as a research preview and became generally available later that year. Each generation has improved coding, reasoning and context length, so advice written about an older model can be out of date. If a tutorial names a specific model version, check Anthropic's current model overview before copying its settings.

## Which Claude AI version is free?

Claude has a free plan on claude.ai and in the apps, with a daily usage limit and access to a capable current model. Claude Code and the most capable models need a paid plan or API usage.

The free plan is enough to learn: explaining code, debugging an error, reviewing a project report, or practising interview questions. Paid plans raise the limits, add the strongest models and include Claude Code. The API is billed by usage, separately from the chat plans, and is what you use to build Claude into your own app. Plans and limits change, so check the plans page on claude.ai for what is included today. For a college project, the free plan plus careful prompts goes a long way.

## Which Claude AI app is best?

Use the app that matches the task: claude.ai or the desktop app for writing, research and analysis; Claude Code in the terminal or IDE for changing real code; the mobile app for quick questions and voice.

The desktop app adds conveniences such as connecting local tools through the Model Context Protocol. Claude Code is the right choice once you want changes applied to files, tests run and commits made, rather than code pasted from a chat window. For a developer the usual setup is both: chat for thinking through a design, Claude Code for implementing it. Avoid unofficial third-party apps that ask for your login; use Anthropic's own apps or a known IDE integration.

## Where is the Claude AI website?

Claude's chat website is claude.ai. Anthropic's company site, with model information, research and news, is anthropic.com, and the developer documentation is linked from there.

Sign in at claude.ai with an email or a Google account; the same account works in the desktop and mobile apps and in Claude Code. Developers create API keys in the Anthropic Console, which is separate from the chat subscription. Beware of look-alike domains and "Claude" apps from other publishers in app stores. The official mobile apps are published by Anthropic.

## What are Claude AI agents?

Claude agents are systems where Claude works towards a goal in a loop: it decides the next step, calls tools such as search, code execution or your own APIs, reads the results and continues until the task is done.

Claude Code is the best-known example: it reads files, runs commands and edits code on its own. Developers build their own agents with the Claude API's tool use, the Claude Agent SDK, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard from Anthropic for connecting models to data sources and tools. A useful agent has a narrow job, a small set of well-described tools, limits on what it may do without asking, and logs you can review. Start with one tool and one task, measure it, then widen the scope.

## Can I vibe code with Claude?

Yes. Vibe coding, describing what you want and letting the AI write the code while you steer by results, works well with Claude, especially in Claude Code or the artifacts panel on claude.ai.

It is a great way to prototype a hackathon idea or a personal tool in an afternoon. The risks show up when the code has to last: duplicated logic, missing error handling, insecure defaults and secrets committed to the repository. Keep a few rules: ask for tests alongside features, read every diff before accepting it, commit after each working step, keep API keys in environment files, and ask Claude to review its own code for security issues. Judges and interviewers can tell when you cannot explain your own project, so make sure you understand what was written.

# What do computer science students learn? Studying CS, jobs, internships and laptops
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/computer-science-student-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Computer science students learn how computers and software work and how to build them: programming, data structures, algorithms, computer architecture, operating systems, networks, databases, software engineering, discrete mathematics, and electives such as AI and security. I am a BCA student at VSICS and have mentored over 200 students since 2023, so this page covers what CS students learn and how to study and start, course length, why students drop out, IES eligibility, jobs, internships, laptops, and reasons to choose CS. What do computer science students learn? Computer science students learn programming and the theory behind it: data structures, algorithms, discrete maths, computer organisation, operating systems, networks, databases, compilers and software engineering, plus electives in AI, machine learning, security, graphics or web development. Early years focus on programming fundamentals, maths and logic; later years on systems and specialisations, with projects and often an internship. Indian programmes, B.Tech CSE, BCA and B.Sc CS, differ in depth: B.Tech is more engineering-heavy, BCA more application-focused. Across all of them, the skills that matter most for jobs are solid programming, problem solving, and the ability to build and ship working software. How should I study computer science? Study actively: write code for every concept, build small projects, solve problems regularly, and explain what you learn to others. Reading notes before exams is not enough for a subject that is learned by doing. Also asked as: how to study computer science A weekly rhythm that works: Attend or watch lectures, then implement the concept the same week. Solve a few data structures and algorithms problems several times a week. Build one project per semester connected to your interests. Use version control from day one and push work to GitHub. Join a club, community or study group. Teach juniors; explaining exposes gaps. Students I mentor who build alongside coursework consistently do better in interviews than those who only study for exams. How do I start learning computer science? Start with one programming language, usually Python or C, learn fundamentals through a structured course such as Harvard's free CS50, then move to data structures and algorithms while building small projects you care about. Also asked as: how to start learning computer science A beginner roadmap: Months 1 to 2: programming basics, problem solving, Git. Months 3 to 4: data structures and algorithms fundamentals. Months 5 to 6: a domain, such as web development or data, with two projects. Then: databases, operating systems and networks basics. Throughout: build in public, join a community and attend hackathons. Free resources from MIT OpenCourseWare and the "Teach Yourself Computer Science" guide cover the deeper theory when you are ready. How many years does it take to study computer science? In India, a B.Tech or B.E. in Computer Science takes four years, a BCA or B.Sc in Computer Science usually three years, and an MCA or M.Tech two years. Many new four-year undergraduate programmes follow recent education policy changes. Also asked as: how many years to study computer science Self-learners can cover core fundamentals in one to two years of consistent study, and become employable sooner in a focused area, such as web development, with strong projects. Learning never really ends in this field, because tools change every few years. What matters to employers is demonstrated skill, so use whichever path you choose to build a portfolio, not only to collect a degree. Why do computer science students drop out? Common reasons include difficulty with maths and programming early on, choosing CS under family or peer pressure without real interest, falling behind and losing confidence, financial pressures, mental health struggles, and feeling that coursework is disconnected from real jobs. Prevention helps: ask for help early from faculty, seniors or mentors; join study groups; focus on fundamentals rather than comparing yourself with peers who started coding earlier; and connect learning to projects you care about. If CS is truly not right, switching is not failure; many adjacent fields, such as design, product management and data analysis, value similar skills. Colleges with active mentoring and peer communities tend to keep more students engaged. Can a computer science student take the IES exam? Generally no. The UPSC Engineering Services Examination, often called IES, covers four disciplines: Civil, Mechanical, Electrical, and Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering. Computer Science is not one of them, so CS graduates usually are not eligible. Also asked as: can computer science student give ies exam Check the latest UPSC notification for exact eligibility, since rules can change. Alternatives for CS students interested in government roles include GATE-based recruitment to public sector undertakings, scientist and engineer recruitment at organisations such as ISRO and DRDO, the Civil Services Examination, banking and SSC technical posts, and state government IT positions. Each has its own syllabus, so prepare specifically. What jobs can computer science students get? CS graduates work as software developers, web and mobile developers, data analysts and scientists, machine learning and AI engineers, DevOps and cloud engineers, cybersecurity analysts, QA engineers, product managers, technical writers and researchers, among many others. Also asked as: what are jobs for computer science students Entry routes include campus placements, off-campus applications, internships converting to offers, startups, and freelancing. AI engineering is growing fast: building RAG systems, fine-tuning models and deploying AI features. Whatever role you target, employers look for problem solving, communication, and proof of building things. A portfolio of two or three real projects, deployed and documented, often matters more than grades alone for startups. How do computer science students find internships? Build two or three real projects, keep a clean GitHub and resume, then apply widely through platforms such as Internshala, LinkedIn and company career pages, reach out to alumni, contribute to open source, and use hackathons to meet companies. Also asked as: how to find internships for computer science students Tips: Apply early; many internships open months before they start. Tailor your resume to each role's skills. Message startups directly with a short note and a project link. Apply to programmes for students, such as those run by large tech companies. Participate in hackathons, where sponsors often recruit. Ask professors about research internships. Hackathons worked for my network: several students I know found internships through people they met at events. Is a MacBook good for computer science students? Yes, a MacBook is good for most CS work: it is fast, has long battery life, and macOS is Unix-based, which suits development. But it is not required, and some tasks are harder on it, such as certain Windows-only tools and NVIDIA GPU work. Also asked as: is macbook good for computer science students Consider your needs: for web, mobile and general programming, a MacBook works well, and it is required for iOS development. For machine learning with CUDA, a Windows or Linux laptop with an NVIDIA GPU, or cloud GPUs, is better. For tight budgets, a Windows laptop with at least 16 GB of RAM and an SSD, running WSL or Linux, does almost everything CS courses require. Check your college's software requirements before buying. Why choose computer science? Choose computer science if you enjoy solving problems, building things and learning continuously. It offers wide career options, the ability to create products that reach many people, flexible work, and skills that apply across every industry. It is also demanding: technology changes constantly, competition for entry-level jobs is strong, and coursework requires steady effort. Choose it because you are curious about how software and systems work, not only because of trends. If you are unsure, try a free course such as CS50 and build a small project; enjoying that process is a better signal than any ranking or salary survey.

# When Copilot becomes autopilot: roadmaps, best Copilot prompts, and Copilot courses
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-autopilot-prompts-courses/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

"When Copilot becomes autopilot" describes the move from AI assistants that help when you ask, to agents that take actions on their own when triggered, such as processing new invoices or summarising tickets every morning, within limits set by people. Microsoft's Copilot products now span both. This page explains that shift, where to follow the Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio roadmaps, the best prompts for Copilot in general, Excel, Outlook and meeting notes, and Microsoft's courses, certificates and a Copilot Studio tutorial. What does it mean when Copilot becomes autopilot? It means moving from a copilot, an assistant that suggests and drafts while you stay in control, to an autopilot-style agent that carries out tasks by itself when an event or schedule triggers it, such as handling routine requests without someone starting a chat. In Microsoft's ecosystem, Copilot Studio supports autonomous agents with triggers, and Microsoft 365 Copilot includes agents that perform multi-step work. Autonomy needs safeguards: narrow scope, limited permissions, human approval for consequential actions, logging and monitoring. Even in aviation, autopilot works under a pilot's supervision; good AI automation follows the same principle, with people reviewing outcomes and handling exceptions. Where is the Microsoft 365 Copilot roadmap? The Microsoft 365 roadmap website lists upcoming and rolling-out features; filter by the Microsoft 365 Copilot product to see planned, in-development and launched items with target dates. Release notes on Microsoft Learn describe what has already shipped. Admins use the roadmap to prepare training and change management before features reach users. Treat target dates as estimates, since rollouts happen in stages by region and release channel. For a quick view of recent changes, the "What's new" pages in Microsoft Learn's Copilot documentation are more reliable than news articles, which may describe previews or announcements that changed before release. Where is the Copilot Studio roadmap? Copilot Studio's upcoming features appear on the Microsoft 365 roadmap and in Power Platform release planning, while its documentation's "What's new" page lists recent releases. Microsoft also announces major changes at its developer and partner events. Also asked as: roadmap copilot m365 · roadmap copilot studio When building agents, check the roadmap before starting a custom solution, because a planned built-in feature might replace your workaround. Preview features may change or have limits, so avoid relying on them for critical production agents. Subscribe to official release notes or check them monthly if your organisation depends on Copilot Studio. What are the best Copilot prompts? The best Copilot prompts include four elements: the goal, the context, the source to use, and what you expect the output to look like. For example: "Summarise the decisions from the project sync meeting yesterday and the client's follow-up email, as five bullet points with owners and deadlines." General prompt patterns that work: "Draft [document] for [audience] using [file], in [tone], under [length]." "Compare [A] and [B] from [sources] in a table with [columns]." "What did [person] ask me for in the last [period]? List with links." "Turn [document] into a [number]-slide presentation outline." Microsoft's Copilot Prompt Gallery offers ready-made prompts to adapt and save. What are the best Copilot prompts for Excel? Good Excel prompts are specific about columns, calculations and outputs, and assume the data is formatted as a table. For example: "Add a column that calculates profit margin as (Revenue - Cost) / Revenue, formatted as a percentage." More examples: "Which three products had the largest month-on-month drop in sales?" "Highlight rows where the due date is past and status is not Paid." "Create a PivotTable of total sales by region and quarter." "Show a line chart of monthly signups for the last 12 months." "Explain this formula in plain words and suggest a simpler version." Check any formulas Copilot inserts on a few rows by hand before trusting the totals. What are the best Copilot prompts for Outlook? Outlook prompts work best when they state the recipient, purpose, tone and length. For example: "Reply to Priya accepting the Tuesday meeting, ask for the agenda in advance, keep it to three sentences, friendly but formal." More examples: "Summarise this thread and list the open questions directed at me." "Draft a follow-up to the vendor asking for the revised quote by Friday." "Rewrite my draft to be more concise and polite." "What are the action items from emails with the project team this week?" "Draft a meeting invite from this thread with a short agenda." Read every draft before sending; Copilot can add details that were never agreed. What are the best Copilot prompts for meeting notes? In Teams meetings with transcription on, ask Copilot for structured notes: decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions. For example: "Summarise this meeting as decisions, action items with owners and deadlines, and unresolved questions." More examples: "What did I miss in the last ten minutes?" "List the main arguments for and against the proposal discussed." "Draft a follow-up email to attendees with decisions and next steps." "Which questions were asked but not answered?" "Summarise what [person] said about the budget." Review notes before sharing, because summaries can merge points or drop important qualifications. Is there a Microsoft Copilot course? Yes. Microsoft Learn offers free training paths for Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio and GitHub Copilot, covering how to use Copilot in each app, prompt techniques, and building agents. Partner training and online learning platforms offer additional courses. Also asked as: copilot course microsoft A practical learning plan: complete the Microsoft Learn path for the Copilot you use, practise with the Prompt Gallery, then apply it to five real tasks from your work or studies. For Copilot Studio, follow a guided module and build a small agent. Microsoft also runs virtual training events; check Microsoft Learn's events pages for current sessions. Is there a Copilot course certificate? Microsoft Learn modules give badges and trophies for completion, which are not formal certifications. Formal credentials come from Microsoft certification exams and Microsoft Applied Skills, which include assessments related to Copilot and AI solutions. Check the Microsoft Learn credentials catalogue for current options related to Copilot, such as credentials for building agents or AI solutions. Third-party course certificates show completion but carry less weight with employers than Microsoft credentials or, better still, a demonstrable project such as a working Copilot Studio agent with documented results. Add verified credentials to LinkedIn with their links. Is there a Copilot Studio tutorial? Yes. Microsoft Learn has Copilot Studio tutorials and quickstarts. A good first project is a narrow agent, such as an FAQ assistant for a department, built from real documents and tested with real questions. Also asked as: tutorial copilot studio A first build: Open Copilot Studio and create an agent with a clear description and instructions. Add knowledge: a SharePoint site or uploaded policy documents. Write starter prompts users can click. Test with twenty real questions, including tricky ones, and refine instructions. Add one action, such as creating a ticket through a connector. Publish to Teams for a small pilot group and review conversations weekly. Keep scope narrow; reliable small agents earn trust for bigger ones.
