# What is vector search in Databricks? Indexes, GCP, Redis, SQLite, cost, and is it dead
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/databricks-vector-search/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Vector search in Databricks, called Mosaic AI Vector Search, is a managed service that indexes embeddings from your Delta tables and serves fast similarity search for RAG and recommendation applications, governed through Unity Catalog. It keeps indexes in sync with source data automatically. I build RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid retrieval, so this page covers Databricks Vector Search and its indexes, vector search on Google Cloud, Redis and SQLite, cost, whether vector search is dead, how Google uses it, and vector search engines. What is vector search in Databricks? Mosaic AI Vector Search is Databricks' built-in vector database. It creates vector indexes from Delta tables, serves similarity queries through endpoints, and integrates with Unity Catalog for access control and lineage, so retrieval follows the same governance as your data. It supports embeddings computed by Databricks-managed embedding models or your own, metadata filtering, and hybrid search combining keyword and vector similarity. Typical uses are RAG over enterprise documents stored in the lakehouse, product recommendations and semantic search. Its main advantage is integration: if your data and pipelines already live in Databricks, you avoid copying data to a separate vector database and managing sync yourself. How do I use vector search in Databricks? Create a vector search endpoint, then create an index from a Delta table with a primary key and either a text column for managed embeddings or an embedding column. Query it with the Python SDK, REST API or SQL. Also asked as: how to use vector search in databricks from databricks.vector_search.client import VectorSearchClient index = VectorSearchClient().get_index(endpoint_name=&quot;docs_ep&quot;, index_name=&quot;main.rag.docs_idx&quot;) hits = index.similarity_search(query_text=&quot;refund policy&quot;, columns=[&quot;id&quot;, &quot;text&quot;], num_results=5) Enable Change Data Feed on the source table for syncing. In RAG apps, pass retrieved text to a model serving endpoint and log retrievals. Check the documentation for current SDK names and options, which evolve. What is a vector search index in Databricks? A vector search index is the searchable structure built from your data's embeddings. Databricks offers Delta Sync indexes, which automatically stay in sync with a source Delta table, and Direct Vector Access indexes, where you write and update vectors yourself through the API. Also asked as: what is vector search index in databricks Delta Sync indexes can compute embeddings for you from a text column using a model endpoint, or use embeddings you computed in the table. Sync can be triggered or continuous. Direct Vector Access suits applications that produce vectors outside the lakehouse or need real-time writes. Both support filters on metadata columns. Choose Delta Sync when your source of truth is a Delta table, which is the common case. What is vector search in GCP? On Google Cloud, Vertex AI Vector Search, formerly Matching Engine, is the managed vector search service built on Google's ScaNN technology for low-latency search at large scale. Google Cloud also offers vector search in AlloyDB and Cloud SQL with pgvector, BigQuery and Firestore. Choose Vertex AI Vector Search for very large, high-throughput workloads; AlloyDB or Cloud SQL for applications that want vectors next to relational data; BigQuery for analytics-style similarity over warehouse data; and Firestore for app developers already using it. Vertex AI also offers RAG-focused services that manage chunking, embedding and retrieval for you. Can Redis do vector search? Yes. Redis supports vector similarity search through its query engine, with vector fields indexed using exact FLAT or approximate HNSW indexes, plus filtering on other fields and hybrid queries. Newer Redis versions also add a dedicated vector data structure. Redis keeps data in memory, so vector search is very fast, which suits real-time recommendations, semantic caching of LLM responses and session-level retrieval. The trade-off is memory cost for large collections. Many teams use Redis as a semantic cache in front of a model: if a new question's embedding is very close to a previous one, return the cached answer, saving cost and latency. Can SQLite do vector search? Yes, through extensions. sqlite-vec adds vector storage and similarity search to SQLite with no external dependencies, and runs anywhere SQLite runs, including browsers via WebAssembly and mobile devices. Some SQLite-based databases, such as libSQL, add native vector support. SQLite vector search suits local-first apps, desktop tools, mobile apps, prototypes and small to medium collections, where running a separate server would be overkill. Brute-force search over tens of thousands of vectors is fast enough for many uses. For millions of vectors with heavy concurrent traffic, a server database or dedicated vector store is more appropriate. Is vector search expensive? It can be cheap or expensive depending on scale. Costs come from computing embeddings, storing vectors, keeping indexes in memory and serving queries. Small projects can run on an existing PostgreSQL database at almost no extra cost; billions of vectors need serious infrastructure. Ways to control cost: Use an existing database with vector support before adding a new service. Choose smaller embedding dimensions where quality allows. Quantise vectors to cut memory, rescoring top results. Embed once and cache; re-embed only changed content. Filter by metadata to reduce search space. Measure cost per thousand queries and storage per million vectors for your setup before committing. Is vector search dead? No. Claims that it is dead usually come from long-context models that read whole documents and from coding agents that search with tools like grep instead of embeddings. Both are useful, but neither replaces retrieval over large knowledge bases. What is changing is that vector search is no longer used alone. Strong systems combine keyword search, vector search, metadata filters and reranking, and agents can choose among these tools. Long context helps after retrieval, letting models read more of the retrieved material. For millions of documents, fast similarity search remains essential, so expect vector search to be a standard component rather than a hype topic. Does Google use vector search? Yes. Google has described using neural matching and language models such as BERT in Search to understand the meaning of queries and pages beyond keywords, and it open-sourced ScaNN, its vector similarity search library, in 2020. Recommendations across its products rely on embeddings too. Google's public explanations say AI systems help connect concepts in queries to relevant pages, alongside many other ranking signals. Its cloud products, such as Vertex AI Vector Search, are built on the same research. For website owners, this means writing clearly about topics in natural language matters more than exact keyword repetition, because semantic matching recognises related wording. What is a vector search engine? A vector search engine is software that stores vectors and returns the most similar ones to a query vector, using approximate nearest-neighbour indexes. It powers semantic search, recommendations and RAG retrieval. Also asked as: what is vector search engine Options include libraries such as FAISS, ScaNN and hnswlib for in-process search; vector databases such as Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate and Pinecone; search engines with vector support such as Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Vespa; and database extensions such as pgvector. Choose by scale, filtering needs, hybrid search support, operations capacity and where your data already lives.

# Dev.to vs Hashnode vs Medium vs your own blog: where should a developer actually write in 2026?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/dev-to-vs-hashnode-vs-medium-for-developers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Where should a developer write in 2026: Dev.to, Hashnode or Medium?

**Your own domain first, for ownership and search equity; Dev.to second, for the fastest path to an engaged developer reader and a free posting API; Hashnode third, if you want a free custom-domain blog, though its API now sits behind a paid plan; Medium last, or not at all, because its paywall and algorithm work against an unknown technical writer. Publish on your own site, then syndicate to Dev.to with a canonical link back. That single habit captures most of the benefit of all four platforms.**


I publish across all of these plus my own site, and the pattern below is what actually moved readers and search rankings, not what each platform promises in its marketing [8][9].

> A platform can promote your post for a week. A domain you own compounds for years.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is Dev.to, and who is it for?

**A community-run publishing platform for developers, built on the open-source Forem software, with tags, reactions, comments and a genuinely active audience of working developers [1]. Its posting API is free, which makes it the natural platform to auto-publish to alongside your own site. Discovery happens through tags and the community feed rather than search, so a Dev.to post's first burst of readers comes from people who follow the tag, not from Google, though good posts do get indexed and found later [2].**


## What is Hashnode, and what changed with its API?

**A blogging platform built specifically for developers, with a free custom domain from day one, clean themes, and good default SEO, which made it a favourite for a personal tech blog without hosting to manage [3]. As of 2026 its programmatic posting API sits behind a paid plan, which matters if your workflow is automated publishing rather than writing by hand in its editor; manual posting through the dashboard remains free. If you write by hand and want a free-domain blog, it is still a solid choice; if you automate, check current pricing before building on it.**



## What is Medium, and should I bother with it?

**A general publishing platform with a metered paywall, a recommendation algorithm, and the Partner Program for earning from reads [4]. For an unknown technical writer, both work against you: the paywall costs some readers a click, and the algorithm favours engagement patterns that generic, punchy writing produces more than technical depth. Medium can still work if you already have an audience elsewhere, or if you want a specific piece to reach non-developer readers a technical platform would not. As a default home for developer writing, it is not the strongest choice in 2026.**


## Why does my own domain matter more than any platform?

**Because search rankings, backlinks and reader trust accumulate on the domain the content lives on, and that domain is the one thing a platform cannot take from you, change the rules on, or shut down. A post on your own site under your name builds your search presence for years; the same words on a platform mostly build the platform's. Google's canonical URL system exists precisely so the same content can appear in several places while search credit flows to one chosen original [5]. Choose your own site as that original.**



## What is syndication, and how do I do it properly?

**Publish the full post on your own site first. Then post the same content, or a shortened version with a link, on Dev.to and Hashnode, setting the canonical URL field to your original where the platform supports it, which tells search engines your site is the source [5]. Wait a day or two before syndicating so your own site gets indexed first. This way each platform brings you readers who click through, while your domain keeps the search credit.**



## Which should I pick if I can only maintain one?

**Your own site if you can spare an afternoon to set it up on a free host, because everything else follows from having a home. If you genuinely cannot maintain a personal site yet, Dev.to alone, for the free API and the community, is the single best substitute, and you can add your own domain later without losing the posts, since they stay live on Dev.to regardless.**




## What mistakes do developers make with technical writing platforms?

**Writing only on Medium and wondering why nobody in the developer community sees it. Cross-posting without a canonical link and accidentally competing with your own original for search rankings. Building an automated pipeline around an API that then moves behind a paywall, without a fallback. Spreading across five platforms and maintaining none well. Never writing on a domain you control, so years of writing build someone else's audience instead of yours.**



## Where should I start?

**If you do not have a personal site yet, start there this week; if you do, publish your next post on it first and syndicate to Dev.to the same day.** For a session on building a writing habit that compounds into a career, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Do you actually need a GPU for AI? A plain VRAM and hardware guide for students: what runs on a laptop, what needs to be rented, and what needs neither
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/do-you-need-a-gpu-for-ai-vram-and-hardware-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Do I actually need a GPU for AI work?

**Usually not, for most of what a student does. Calling a model through an API, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, needs no GPU at all; the provider's hardware does the generation, and your laptop only sends and receives text. The case that genuinely needs a GPU with real VRAM is running or fine-tuning an open-weight model locally, and even then, free cloud notebooks or an hourly rented GPU usually cover it without buying anything.**


Most of the production systems I run are API-first specifically to avoid this question entirely for the majority of the workload; the GPU question only comes up for the specific slice that touches an open model directly.

> Buy a GPU for the project that actually needs one, not for the fear that every AI project might.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What actually needs GPU memory, and what doesn't?

**Using a hosted model API: no GPU needed. Running a small open model locally for inference, chatting with a 7 to 8 billion parameter model through Ollama: modest VRAM, often fits on a good consumer GPU or even a strong CPU with patience. Fine-tuning a small to medium open model with LoRA or QLoRA: meaningful VRAM, but far less than full fine-tuning thanks to quantization [5]. Training a model from scratch: serious VRAM and usually multiple GPUs, essentially never a student's first project.**



## How much VRAM does a given model actually need?

**Roughly, for inference, a model needs about the number of parameters times the bytes per parameter: a 7 billion parameter model at 16-bit precision needs roughly 14 GB just to hold the weights, before accounting for the activation memory a request also uses. Quantizing to 8-bit roughly halves that, and to 4-bit roughly quarters it, which is why a model that needs 14 GB at full precision can often run in under 5 GB quantized [1][7]. Fine-tuning needs more on top of the base weights for gradients and optimiser state, which is exactly the memory pressure QLoRA was built to reduce [5].**



## What free options exist before I rent or buy anything?

**Google Colab's free tier gives a shared GPU with real, if variable, availability, enough for learning, small experiments, and light fine-tuning runs [2]. Kaggle offers free GPU and TPU hours on notebooks tied to your account, with a generous weekly quota [3]. Both are enough to complete most course exercises, small fine-tuning projects, and learning experiments without spending anything; the free tiers only become the bottleneck once a project needs sustained, guaranteed access or more memory than the free tier's GPU offers.**



## When should I rent a cloud GPU instead of using a free tier?

**When a task needs more VRAM or more sustained, guaranteed time than a free tier reliably offers, a bigger fine-tuning run, a longer training job, or repeated runs where waiting on shared free-tier availability costs more time than the rental costs money. Services that rent GPUs by the hour make this cheap for occasional use: a few hours of a mid-range GPU for a real fine-tuning experiment typically costs less than a two-week wait on an oversubscribed free tier [6].**



## When does buying a personal GPU actually make sense?

**When you run GPU-heavy work often enough that the cumulative cost of renting exceeds a GPU's price within a reasonable time, or when you specifically need a persistent local setup for reasons free and rented options do not cover, offline work, specific hardware experiments, or teaching others hands-on. For most students, this point arrives much later than the anxiety about needing a GPU does; do not buy hardware to solve a problem a free tier or an hour of rental already solves.**



## What mistakes do students make about GPU hardware?

**Assuming every AI project needs a GPU, when most API-based work needs none. Buying hardware before hitting an actual limit on free tiers. Ignoring quantization and assuming a model needs its full-precision memory footprint. Renting a much larger GPU than a quantized, LoRA-adapted fine-tuning run actually requires, paying for headroom nobody used. Never checking a model's actual memory footprint before assuming a task is impossible on the hardware already available.**


## GPU and hardware interview questions

**Explain what determines a model's memory footprint at inference time. Explain how quantization changes that footprint and its trade-offs. Describe when you would use an API instead of running a model locally. Explain the difference in memory needs between inference and fine-tuning. Describe how you would size a GPU rental for a specific fine-tuning job. The strongest answer includes a specific memory calculation you did for a real project.**

**Before assuming a project needs a GPU, check whether an API already covers it. # Does OCR use AI? OCR and neural networks, ChatGPT, and OCR in Word
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/does-ocr-use-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Yes, modern OCR uses AI. Today's optical character recognition relies on neural networks to find text in images and recognise it, and often on language models to fix likely errors; older OCR used hand-written rules and templates. OCR is part of computer vision, a branch of AI. This page explains OCR's relationship to AI and neural networks, why people sometimes do not count it as AI, how ChatGPT reads text in images, when to use OCR, and how to OCR images and scanned PDFs with Word and free tools.

## Does OCR use AI?

Yes. Modern OCR engines use machine learning: neural networks detect text regions and recognise characters and words, trained on large sets of text images. Many also use language models to choose the most likely words when characters are unclear.

Examples: Tesseract, the widely used open-source engine, uses an LSTM neural network for recognition; cloud OCR services from Google, Microsoft and Amazon use deep learning for layout and text; and newer document models and vision-language models read whole pages directly. This is why OCR now handles varied fonts, photos and some handwriting. AI also means errors can look plausible, so validation remains important for documents that matter.

## Is OCR part of AI?

Yes. OCR belongs to computer vision, the area of AI that interprets images, and to document AI, which extracts structured information from documents. Recognising text from pixels is a classic pattern-recognition problem that AI research worked on for decades.

OCR was one of the earliest practical successes of AI and machine learning, used in postal sorting and bank cheque processing long before today's chatbots. Modern document AI goes further than reading text: it understands layout, classifies document types and extracts fields such as dates and totals. DocuLens AI, for example, extracts fields from invoices and contracts with an LLM and validates them against a schema before scoring compliance.

## Does OCR use neural networks?

Modern OCR does. Typical systems use convolutional networks to extract visual features, recurrent or transformer layers to read sequences of characters, and a decoding method such as CTC to turn predictions into text. Detection networks find where text lines are.

Older OCR, before deep learning, used feature engineering and template matching, which worked for clean printed fonts but struggled with photos and handwriting. Neural networks learn from examples instead of hand-made rules, which is why accuracy improved sharply. The newest approach, vision-language models, uses a single large transformer that sees the page image and generates text or structured output.

## Why is OCR sometimes not seen as a good example of AI?

Because of the "AI effect": once a technology works reliably and becomes ordinary, people stop calling it intelligence. OCR is everywhere, in scanners, phones and banking, so it feels like a utility rather than AI, even though it is a machine learning application.

There is also a fair technical point: classic OCR performs a narrow perception task, recognising characters, without understanding what the text means. Many people reserve "AI" for systems that reason or generate. Modern document AI blurs that line, since vision-language models both read and understand documents. For exam answers, a balanced view is that OCR is a mature example of narrow AI, specifically pattern recognition, rather than general intelligence.

## Which OCR does ChatGPT use?

ChatGPT reads text in images with its vision-capable models, which process images directly and generate text about them, including transcriptions. OpenAI does not present a separate OCR engine for this, and it does not publish the internal details.

In practice, ChatGPT reads clear printed text well, handles many layouts and some handwriting, and can turn tables into Markdown. It may misread small, blurry or unusual text, and like any generative model it can occasionally produce plausible but wrong characters, especially numbers. For long documents or precise extraction, dedicated OCR or document AI services with page references are more reliable, and you should check important values against the original.

## When should I use OCR?

Use OCR whenever text exists only as an image and you need to search, copy, edit, translate, analyse or feed it to software: scanned documents, photos of notes, screenshots, image-only PDFs, receipts and forms.

Common uses:

- Making scanned archives and old PDFs searchable.
- Turning printed or handwritten notes into editable text.
- Extracting data from invoices, receipts and forms into spreadsheets.
- Preparing documents for RAG chatbots, which need text.
- Accessibility: making images of text readable by screen readers.

You do not need OCR for documents that already contain selectable text, such as most digitally created PDFs; extracting their text directly is faster and more accurate.

## How do I OCR in Word?

Word does not run OCR on pictures inside a document. To get text from an image, use OneNote's copy-text-from-picture feature, the Windows Snipping Tool's text actions, or Google Lens, then paste into Word. For scanned PDFs, open the PDF in Word, which converts it into an editable document.

For a single picture, OneNote is the quickest: insert the image into a page, right-click it and choose the option to copy text from the picture, then paste into Word. Word's PDF conversion works best on clear, simple layouts; complex tables and multi-column pages often need fixing afterwards. For many documents, a dedicated OCR tool and then pasting into Word is faster than repairing a messy conversion.

## How do I OCR an image into Word?

Extract the text first, then paste it into Word: use OneNote's copy text from picture, the Snipping Tool's text actions on Windows, Live Text on a Mac or iPhone, or Google Lens on Android or in the browser.

Steps with the Snipping Tool on Windows:

- Open the image and take a snip of the text area, or open the image in the Snipping Tool.
- Use the text actions button to detect text.
- Copy all text and paste it into Word.
- Fix formatting and check names and numbers.

For a whole page with structure, an AI assistant can transcribe it into headings and lists, which you then paste into Word. Keep the original image in case you need to check a word later.

## Can OCR convert a scanned PDF to an editable Word document?

Yes. Word can open a scanned PDF and convert it to an editable document, Adobe Acrobat exports scanned PDFs to Word with OCR, and Google Docs runs OCR when you open a PDF or image from Google Drive.

Quality depends on scan quality and layout. Plain text pages convert well; tables, columns, stamps and handwriting need checking. For best results, rescan at good resolution if possible, straighten pages and choose the correct language. If you only need searchable text rather than an editable layout, make a searchable PDF instead, for example with OCRmyPDF, and keep the original appearance.

## Can you convert a PDF to Word for free with OCR?

Yes. Free options include opening the PDF in Microsoft Word if you have it, uploading it to Google Drive and opening it with Google Docs, and free tools such as OCRmyPDF to make the PDF searchable before converting.

With Google Drive: upload the PDF, right-click, choose Open with Google Docs, and Drive runs OCR and creates an editable document, which you can download as a Word file. It works best for text-heavy pages and keeps limited formatting. Avoid uploading confidential documents to unknown free converter websites; prefer tools from Microsoft, Google, Adobe or offline open-source software for anything personal or sensitive.

# Does OpenCV have OCR? Document OCR with OpenCV, versions, docs, and is it AI
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/does-opencv-have-ocr/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

OpenCV does have OCR-related features: its deep neural network module can run text detection and recognition models, and the contrib text module wraps Tesseract. In practice, most developers use OpenCV for image preprocessing and pair it with a dedicated OCR engine such as Tesseract, PaddleOCR or a document AI model. I use OCR in the OCR and Speech Workspace and DocuLens AI, so this page covers OpenCV's OCR options, document workflows, why LLMs struggle with OCR, documentation, versions, and whether OpenCV is AI. Does OpenCV have OCR? Yes, partially. OpenCV's DNN module provides TextDetectionModel and TextRecognitionModel classes that run pretrained networks, such as EAST or DB for detection and CRNN for recognition. The opencv_contrib text module also includes scene text detection and a Tesseract wrapper. These work, but you must download and configure models yourself, and accuracy depends on the models you choose. Most teams find it simpler to use OpenCV for preprocessing and a full OCR library for recognition: pytesseract for clean scans, PaddleOCR or EasyOCR for photos, or a vision language model for complex layouts. OpenCV remains the best toolkit for the image work around OCR. A good rule: if your images are clean scans, skip OpenCV's recognition models and call Tesseract directly; if they are photos with perspective, glare and clutter, invest in OpenCV preprocessing first, because no recogniser can read text it cannot see clearly. How do I use OpenCV for document recognition with OCR? Use OpenCV to find and clean the document, then pass the result to an OCR engine. The typical pipeline: detect the page edges, apply a perspective transform to flatten it, convert to grayscale, denoise, threshold and deskew, then run OCR. Also asked as: how to use opencv for document recognition with ocr import cv2, pytesseract img = cv2.imread(&quot;receipt.jpg&quot;) gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY) gray = cv2.fastNlMeansDenoising(gray, h=10) bw = cv2.adaptiveThreshold(gray, 255, cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C, cv2.THRESH_BINARY, 31, 15) print(pytesseract.image_to_string(bw, config=&quot;--psm 6&quot;)) For forms, crop fixed regions after alignment and OCR each field separately with validation rules. Check intermediate images by saving them to disk while developing; most OCR problems are visible in the thresholded image before recognition even runs. Why do LLMs still have problems with OCR? Multimodal LLMs read documents impressively, but they can skip lines, misread small or dense text, garble tables and invent plausible text where an image is unclear. They often downscale images internally, losing detail, and give no character-level confidence scores. Also asked as: why llms still have problems with ocr Long documents add risk: models may summarise rather than transcribe, or merge pages. Numbers, IDs and handwriting are especially error-prone, which matters for invoices and records. Practical defences: split documents into pages, use dedicated OCR for exact transcription, validate fields against schemas and rules, and compare against a second method for critical values. DocuLens AI validates extracted fields against schemas for this reason, and flags documents whose values fail checks for human review rather than guessing. Where is the OpenCV documentation? The official documentation is at docs.opencv.org, with separate versions for each release, such as 4.x. It includes the API reference for C++ and Python bindings and tutorials covering core operations, image processing, video, machine learning and the DNN module. Also asked as: where is opencv documentation · why is opencv documentation so bad The OpenCV website also hosts courses and blog posts, and the GitHub repository contains samples in the samples folder. For Python users, the API reference shows C++ signatures with Python equivalents noted beneath. Make sure you are reading the documentation version that matches your installed OpenCV, since functions and parameters change between versions. Why is the OpenCV documentation considered hard to use? Common complaints are that the reference is generated from C++ code, so Python usage is secondary; examples are sparse for some functions; and documentation varies in depth across modules, especially contrib modules maintained by different contributors. Ways to cope: Use the tutorials section for guided examples before the reference. Read the samples folder in the GitHub repository. Use help(cv2.functionName) in Python for the binding's signature. Search issues and the OpenCV forum for specific problems. Cross-check with well-maintained tutorials from reputable sources. OpenCV is a large, volunteer-driven project, and contributions improving documentation are welcome. Which OpenCV versions are there? OpenCV 4.x is the current stable series, receiving regular releases, and OpenCV 5 has been in development with modernised APIs. Older 3.x and 2.x versions exist in legacy projects but are not recommended for new work. In Python, OpenCV is installed through pip packages: opencv-python for main modules, opencv-contrib-python for extra modules including text, and headless variants without GUI functions for servers. Install only one of these packages in an environment, because they conflict. Check the release notes when upgrading, since some functions move between modules. Which OpenCV version should I use? Use the latest OpenCV 4.x release for new projects unless a library you depend on requires a specific version. Choose opencv-python-headless for servers and Docker images, and opencv-contrib-python only if you need contrib modules. Pin the exact version in your requirements file so builds are reproducible. For Raspberry Pi and edge devices, use versions with prebuilt packages for your platform, or build from source with optimisations. If you follow an older tutorial, check whether functions it uses changed in 4.x; most code from 3.x needs only small changes. How do I check my OpenCV version? In Python, run import cv2; print(cv2.__version__). From the command line, use python -c "import cv2; print(cv2.__version__)". In C++, print the CV_VERSION macro, or use pkg-config --modversion opencv4 on Linux. Also asked as: how to check opencv version For more detail, print(cv2.getBuildInformation()) shows the build configuration, including whether CUDA, video backends and optimisations are enabled, which helps debug missing features. If the version is not what you expect, you may have multiple Python environments or conflicting pip packages installed; check with pip list | grep opencv. Is OpenCV AI? OpenCV is a computer vision library, not an AI model. It provides thousands of algorithms for image and video processing, many classical, such as filtering, edge detection and geometry, plus machine learning tools and a module to run deep learning models. Computer vision is a field of AI, so OpenCV is widely used in AI projects: preparing images for models, running detection or recognition networks, and post-processing outputs. Many OpenCV functions, though, are deterministic image operations with no learning involved. Think of OpenCV as the toolbox around vision AI rather than the AI itself. Learning it well pays off, because almost every vision project, from face recognition to document processing, needs reliable image handling before and after the model runs. Does OpenCV use AI? Parts of it do. OpenCV's DNN module runs pretrained deep learning models for detection, classification, segmentation, face detection and text recognition, and its ml module includes classic machine learning algorithms such as SVMs, decision trees and k-nearest neighbours. You can load models exported from PyTorch or TensorFlow, usually in ONNX format, and run them with OpenCV's inference engine on CPUs or supported accelerators. Its face detection uses neural network models in recent versions. Other functions, such as resizing, thresholding and contour finding, use no AI. Combining both kinds of tools is how practical vision pipelines are built.

# What are embedding models? OpenAI embeddings, dimensions, batches, Ollama and Hugging Face
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/embedding-models-openai-ollama/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Embedding models are neural networks that convert text, images or other data into vectors, lists of numbers, so that items with similar meaning end up close together. They power semantic search, RAG retrieval, recommendations, clustering and deduplication. Choosing and running the right one is a core part of building RAG systems like RAG.NextUpgrad. This page explains what embedding models are and how they work, why AI uses embeddings, OpenAI's embeddings, dimensions, cost and batching, and running open models with Ollama, Hugging Face and llama.cpp. What are embedding models? Embedding models are models whose output is a vector representation of their input rather than generated text. Given a sentence, they return a fixed-length vector capturing its meaning, which can be compared with other vectors by cosine similarity. Also asked as: what are embeddings models There are text embedding models for search and RAG, multimodal models such as CLIP that embed images and text into the same space, code embedding models, and specialised models for faces, audio and products. Options include hosted APIs from OpenAI, Google, Cohere and others, and open models such as BGE, E5, GTE, Nomic and Qwen3 Embedding, which you can run yourself. Leaderboards such as MTEB compare them across tasks. How do embedding models work? Most text embedding models are transformer encoders. They tokenise the text, process tokens through attention layers, then pool the token representations, for example by averaging or taking a special token, into one vector, often normalised to unit length. Also asked as: how do embeddings models work They learn through contrastive training: the model sees pairs that should match, such as a question and its answer or a title and its article, and pairs that should not, and adjusts so matching pairs score higher. Training on huge and varied pairs gives general-purpose embeddings; fine-tuning on domain pairs specialises them. Some models expect prefixes such as "query:" and "passage:" to distinguish questions from documents, so read each model card. Why do AI systems use embeddings? AI systems use embeddings because they turn messy inputs into numbers that capture meaning, letting algorithms compare, search and learn efficiently. Computers cannot compare the meaning of two sentences directly, but they can compare vectors in microseconds. Inside language models, every token becomes an embedding before processing. Outside them, embeddings enable retrieval for RAG, so models can use your documents; recommendation systems, which match users to items; and classification with little labelled data. Embeddings are also reusable: one embedding pass over your data supports search, clustering and analytics, which makes them one of the most practical tools in applied AI. How do OpenAI embeddings work? You send text to OpenAI's embeddings endpoint with a model name, such as text-embedding-3-small, and receive a vector for each input. Store the vectors, embed queries with the same model, and compare with cosine similarity. Also asked as: how openai embeddings work from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() resp = client.embeddings.create(model=&quot;text-embedding-3-small&quot;, input=[&quot;How do I reset my password?&quot;]) vector = resp.data[0].embedding OpenAI's vectors are normalised, so dot product equals cosine similarity. Inputs have a maximum token length, so chunk long documents first. Keep your API key in an environment variable, never in code. How many dimensions do OpenAI embeddings have? text-embedding-3-small returns 1,536 dimensions and text-embedding-3-large returns 3,072 by default. The older text-embedding-ada-002 also returns 1,536. The newer models accept a dimensions parameter to return shorter vectors. Also asked as: how many dimensions openai embeddings Shortening, for example to 512 or 256 dimensions, cuts storage and speeds search with modest quality loss, because these models were trained so that the leading dimensions carry the most information. Choose a size by testing retrieval recall on your own questions. Whatever size you pick, your vector index must be configured with the same dimension, and all stored vectors must come from the same model and size. Are OpenAI embeddings free? No. OpenAI charges for embeddings per token processed, though embedding costs are low compared with text generation, and the Batch API offers a discount for asynchronous jobs. New accounts may receive limited trial credits depending on current policies. Also asked as: is openai embeddings free If you need zero-cost embeddings, run open models locally with Ollama, Hugging Face Sentence Transformers or llama.cpp; they cost only your own compute. Many open models perform competitively on retrieval benchmarks. For production, compare total cost, including servers for self-hosting, against API costs and quality. Check OpenAI's pricing page for current rates before estimating. How do I batch embeddings with OpenAI's API? Send a list of texts in the input field of one request, up to the documented limits on inputs and tokens per request, and process the returned vectors in order. For very large jobs, use the Batch API, which runs asynchronously within a time window at lower cost. Also asked as: how can i use batch embeddings using openai&#x27;s api Tips: Group chunks into batches of a few hundred, staying under token limits. Retry failed batches with exponential backoff on rate-limit errors. Store each vector with its chunk ID so order mistakes cannot mix them up. For the Batch API, upload a JSONL file of requests, then download results when complete. Cache embeddings so unchanged chunks are never re-embedded. How do I use Ollama embeddings? Pull an embedding model, such as ollama pull nomic-embed-text, then call Ollama's embed endpoint or use its client libraries to get vectors locally, with no API key and no data leaving your machine. Also asked as: why do ais use embeddings · how to use ollama embeddings · how to use huggingface embeddings import ollama resp = ollama.embed(model=&quot;nomic-embed-text&quot;, input=[&quot;What is RAG?&quot;]) vector = resp[&quot;embeddings&quot;][0] Frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex have Ollama embedding integrations. Local embeddings suit private documents and offline apps; speed depends on your hardware, and a GPU helps for large collections. Use the same Ollama model for indexing and querying. How do I use Hugging Face embeddings? The easiest way is the Sentence Transformers library: install it, load a model from the Hugging Face Hub by name, and call encode. Models download once and run locally on CPU or GPU. from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer model = SentenceTransformer(&quot;BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5&quot;) vectors = model.encode([&quot;What is RAG?&quot;], normalize_embeddings=True) Choose models from the MTEB leaderboard filtered by your language and size limits; multilingual models exist for Hindi and other Indian languages. For serving at scale, Hugging Face's Text Embeddings Inference server provides an efficient API. Check each model's licence for commercial use. Can llama.cpp use Qwen3 embeddings? Yes. llama.cpp can run embedding models in GGUF format, including Qwen3 Embedding models, by starting its server with embeddings enabled and the pooling method the model expects, then calling the embeddings endpoint. Also asked as: can llamacpp use qwen3 embeddings Download a GGUF version of the Qwen3 Embedding model, run llama-server with the --embedding flag and the pooling option recommended on the model card, and send text to the OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint. Qwen3 Embedding models are multilingual and perform strongly on retrieval benchmarks. As with any model, verify the output dimension and test retrieval quality on your own data before switching production systems.

# What is engineering in college? Admission, difficulty and how to do well
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/engineering-in-college-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Engineering in college means a degree programme, usually a four-year BTech or BE in India, where you learn mathematics, science and the design of systems in a branch such as computer science, electronics, mechanical or civil engineering. The first year covers shared foundations, later years go deep into your branch with labs, electives, internships and a final project. This page explains how engineering colleges are organised, how admission works, when classes start, how hard it is, how to do well, what NSS is, and how to write your first resume.

## What is engineering in college?

Engineering in college is a professional degree, typically a four-year BTech or BE, that teaches you to apply maths and science to design, build and maintain systems, from software and circuits to machines and buildings.

The structure is similar across most colleges. The first year has common subjects such as mathematics, physics or chemistry, basic programming, engineering drawing and workshops. From the second year you focus on your branch: for computer science that means data structures, algorithms, databases, operating systems, networks and electives such as AI. Each semester mixes theory classes, lab sessions and internal assessments, ending with university exams. Summer internships and a final-year project complete the degree. Clubs, hackathons and technical festivals run alongside and often teach the most practical skills.

## Can you study engineering in college?

Yes. Engineering is studied at engineering colleges, institutes of technology and universities. In India you need class 12 with physics, chemistry and maths, and you usually enter through an entrance exam and counselling.

You can study engineering at IITs, NITs, IIITs, government and private engineering colleges, and private and deemed universities. Diploma holders can often join a BTech in the second year through lateral entry. If you did not take maths in class 12, a BTech is generally not open to you, but software careers still are through a BCA or BSc in computer science. I took the BCA route and still went on to ship production AI applications, so the door to tech is wider than the BTech alone.

## Is an engineering college a college or a university?

Usually a college. Most engineering colleges in India are affiliated to a university, which sets the syllabus, conducts exams and awards the degree. Some institutions, such as IITs, NITs and deemed universities, award their own degrees.

The difference affects you in practical ways. In an affiliated college, the university fixes the syllabus and exam schedule, so the college has less freedom to update courses. Autonomous colleges set their own syllabus and exams while the university still awards the degree. Institutes of national importance and universities design everything themselves. Check that a college is approved by AICTE for technical programmes and that its university is recognised by the UGC before you join.

## How do I get admission to an engineering college?

Take the entrance exams for the colleges you want, register for counselling, and choose colleges and branches in order of preference. Seats are allotted by rank, category and your choices.

The main routes in India:

- **JEE Main**: for NITs, IIITs and many other colleges, and the qualifier for JEE Advanced.
- **JEE Advanced**: for the IITs.
- **JoSAA counselling**: allots seats at IITs, NITs, IIITs and other centrally funded institutes.
- **State entrance exams and counselling**: for state government and private colleges.
- **Institute exams**: some private universities, such as BITS, run their own.

Keep documents ready: class 10 and 12 mark sheets, category certificates if applicable, and ID proof. Read the official brochure for each exam, because eligibility and dates change.

## When does engineering college start?

First-year engineering classes in India usually start between July and September, after entrance results and counselling rounds finish. Senior batches typically resume earlier in July or August.

The exact date depends on the counselling schedule. IITs and NITs start once JoSAA rounds end; state colleges follow their own counselling calendars, which can run later. Many colleges hold an induction programme in the first week or two, covering orientation, clubs, mentoring and basics such as programming. Use the gap between class 12 results and the start of college well: learn basic Python, set up a GitHub account and build one tiny project. You will start ahead of most of your batch.

## Is engineering in college hard?

Engineering is demanding: there is a lot of maths, many subjects each semester, labs, assignments and exams. It is manageable with steady work, and most difficulty comes from falling behind rather than from the material itself.

The first year is often the hardest adjustment because study habits from school do not transfer: classes move faster and you are expected to practise on your own. Subjects such as engineering mathematics, data structures and circuits need regular problem solving, not last-minute reading. Study in groups, solve previous years' papers, ask teachers and seniors early, and keep up with labs every week. Balance matters too: students who join one club and one project usually do better than those who only study or only do events.

## How do I excel in engineering college?

Keep your marks steady, but put your extra time into skills that compound: programming, projects, internships, hackathons and people. Those decide your options at graduation more than a small difference in grades.

A four-year plan that works:

- **Year 1**: fundamentals, one programming language, GitHub, a small project.
- **Year 2**: data structures and algorithms, a club or community, your first hackathon.
- **Year 3**: one serious project in the area you want to work in, and an internship.
- **Year 4**: placement preparation, a polished portfolio, or a startup if you have a real problem to solve.

This is the roadmap I share with first-year students: foundations and AI tools first, then hackathons and internships, then placements or a startup.

## Does the engineering college matter?

It matters for the first opportunities: top colleges attract more recruiters, stronger peers and better alumni networks. After your first job or two, skills and work history matter far more than the college name.

For software roles in particular, a student from a lesser-known college with deployed projects, an internship and hackathon results can compete with students from well-known colleges. What the college gives you is environment, so if yours is weaker, build your own: join online communities, contribute to open source, travel to hackathons and find mentors. Choose a college with good faculty, active clubs and real placement data for your branch, and then make the most of whatever you join.

## What is NSS in engineering college?

NSS is the National Service Scheme, a programme of the Government of India's Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports in which college students volunteer for community service. Most engineering colleges have an NSS unit.

NSS volunteers take part in activities such as blood donation camps, cleanliness drives, literacy programmes, health awareness and special camps in villages. It builds teamwork, leadership and communication, and certificates for completed service hours are recognised by many universities. For an engineering student it is also a source of real problems: many good hackathon projects start from something seen in community work, such as a farmer's information gap or a hospital queue. Joining is voluntary and usually happens at the start of the year.

## What should an engineering student's resume look like?

A one-page resume with your education, two or three projects with links and results, skills grouped by type, and any internships, hackathons or leadership roles. Projects carry the most weight for students.

A simple structure:

- **Header**: name, email, phone, GitHub, LinkedIn, portfolio link.
- **Education**: degree, college, years, CGPA if it helps.
- **Projects**: name, one line on the problem, the tech stack, what you built, a result such as users, accuracy or speed, and a live link.
- **Experience**: internships and freelance work with outcomes.
- **Skills**: languages, frameworks, tools, databases, cloud.
- **Achievements**: hackathon results, competitive programming ranks, certifications that matter.

Use action verbs and real numbers. Every line should be something you can explain in an interview.

# What is face recognition on iPhone? Face ID setup, twins, safety, and best models
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/face-recognition-iphone-face-id/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Face recognition on iPhone is Face ID: the TrueDepth camera projects and reads thousands of invisible infrared dots to build a depth map of your face, and a neural network on the device compares it with your enrolled face to unlock the phone, approve purchases and fill passwords. I built FaceVision, a browser-based face recognition app with liveness checks that stores only embeddings, never images, so this page covers Face ID setup and limits, failures, twins, safety and security, the best models for developers, and Facebook's face recognition. What is face recognition on iPhone? On iPhone, face recognition is Face ID, available on iPhone X and later models without a Home button. It uses the TrueDepth camera system, a dot projector, infrared camera and flood illuminator, to capture a detailed depth map and infrared image of your face. Also asked as: how many face recognition on iphone 13 · when face recognition fails A neural network converts these into a mathematical representation and compares it with the one stored at enrolment. Face ID checks for attention, that your eyes are open and looking at the phone, by default, and adapts over time to changes such as a beard or glasses. It works in the dark because it uses infrared. Apps can use Face ID for sign-in without ever receiving your face data. How many faces can Face ID store on iPhone 13? Face ID on iPhone 13 stores one main appearance and lets you add one alternate appearance, which can be a significantly different look of yourself or, in practice, another person. It cannot hold a list of multiple users like Touch ID's several fingerprints. iPhone 12 and later models, including iPhone 13, also support Face ID with a mask on recent iOS versions, recognising the area around the eyes. Set it up under Settings, then Face ID &amp; Passcode. If you share a phone with family, consider using the passcode instead of adding someone as an alternate appearance, since they would then access everything protected by Face ID. Where do I change face recognition settings on iPhone? Open Settings, then Face ID &amp; Passcode, and enter your passcode. There you can set up or reset Face ID, add an alternate appearance, enable Face ID with a mask, and choose what Face ID can unlock: iPhone, Apple Pay, App Store purchases, password autofill and other apps. Also asked as: where to change face recognition on iphone You can also turn "Require Attention for Face ID" on or off; keeping it on is more secure. "Reset Face ID" deletes your enrolled face so you can scan again, which often fixes recognition problems. Individual apps that use Face ID appear in the "Other Apps" list, where you can allow or deny each. Why does face recognition not work on my iPhone? Common causes include a blocked or dirty TrueDepth camera, holding the phone too close or at an odd angle, sunglasses that block infrared, a screen protector covering sensors, a major appearance change, or a software glitch. Hardware damage can also disable Face ID. Fixes to try: Clean the top of the screen and remove obstructing cases or protectors. Hold the phone 25 to 50 centimetres away, facing it directly. Restart the iPhone and update iOS. Add an alternate appearance or reset Face ID and enrol again. Check that Face ID is enabled for the feature you are using. If it says Face ID is unavailable after drops or water exposure, contact Apple Support. How does face recognition work with twins? Face ID compares fine details of face shape, but identical twins and siblings who look very alike can sometimes be falsely matched. Apple states that the probability of a false match is different for twins, look-alike siblings and children under 13, whose features are still developing. If you have an identical twin or similar-looking sibling, Apple recommends using a passcode for authentication. In general face recognition systems, twins remain one of the hardest cases, because the differences are subtle. That is why high-security systems combine face recognition with other factors, such as passcodes, devices or liveness checks, rather than relying on faces alone. Is face recognition safe? Face ID is designed with privacy in mind: your face data is encrypted and stored in the Secure Enclave on the device, is not backed up to iCloud and is not sent to Apple. Apps using Face ID only receive a yes or no result. Face recognition more broadly raises privacy concerns, especially when organisations collect face images without consent, store them centrally or use them for surveillance. Safer designs process faces on the device, store templates instead of images, encrypt data, obtain clear consent and allow deletion. FaceVision follows these principles: recognition runs in the browser, and the server stores only embeddings, never photos. Is face recognition secure? Face ID is secure for most people. Apple states the chance a random person could unlock your iPhone with Face ID is less than one in a million with a single enrolled appearance, compared with about one in 50,000 for Touch ID. Attention detection and infrared depth make photo or mask attacks hard. Risks remain: twins and children under 13 have higher false-match rates, and someone could hold your phone to your face while you sleep if attention detection is off. Other face recognition systems vary widely in security; ones using a single ordinary camera without liveness detection can be fooled by photos or videos. Always combine face recognition with liveness checks and fallback authentication. Which is the best face recognition model? For developers, models trained with angular margin losses, such as ArcFace and its successors in the InsightFace project, are among the most accurate open choices. NIST's ongoing face recognition evaluations compare commercial and research algorithms on large datasets. Choose based on your needs: accuracy on your demographic mix, speed on your hardware, licence terms and model size. For browser or mobile apps, smaller models exported to ONNX run on devices, as in FaceVision with ONNX Runtime Web. Always pair recognition with face detection, alignment and liveness detection, test for bias across groups, and obtain consent from everyone whose face you process. How does face recognition work on Facebook? Facebook shut down its automatic face recognition system for tagging photos in 2021, and Meta said it deleted the face templates of more than a billion people. Facebook no longer suggests tags by recognising faces in photos. Also asked as: how to face recognition on facebook Meta later introduced facial recognition in limited ways, such as detecting scam ads that misuse public figures' faces and helping users recover locked accounts with video selfies, in some regions and with user choice. Availability depends on local laws. Check your Facebook privacy and account settings for any face-related features offered where you live. When does face recognition fail? Face recognition fails more often with poor or uneven lighting, extreme angles, partial occlusion by masks or hands, low-resolution or blurry images, large appearance changes, twins and look-alikes, and demographic groups underrepresented in a model's training data. Spoofing attacks, using photos, videos or masks, defeat systems without liveness detection. Engineering fixes include better cameras or infrared sensors, liveness checks, quality checks that reject poor images, diverse training data, careful threshold tuning and fallback methods. In FaceVision, liveness and image quality checks run before recognition, so the system refuses unclear inputs rather than guessing.

# FastAPI for AI applications: async endpoints for LLM calls, dependency injection, streaming responses, and the patterns that hold up in production
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-for-ai-applications/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Why is FastAPI the default choice for serving AI applications?

**Because an AI application spends most of its request time waiting on slow network calls, a model API, an embedding call, a vector database query, and FastAPI's async support means the server can handle other requests during that wait instead of blocking a whole worker thread on it [1][6]. Combined with automatic request validation from type hints, a built-in docs UI, and dependency injection for clean wiring of providers and settings, it removes most of the boilerplate a Flask-based service would need to hand-build for the same job.**


Both production systems I run day to day, a RAG platform and a document extraction service, are FastAPI applications underneath, and the async layer is not a nice-to-have, it is the difference between a server that serves five concurrent users and one that serves fifty on the same hardware [11][12].

> A synchronous web server serving LLM calls is a waiter who stands at one table until the kitchen finishes a dish, ignoring everyone else in the restaurant. Async is the waiter who takes the next order while the first dish cooks.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does async actually help when the model call is still slow?

**The model call itself is not made faster by async; a five-second generation still takes five seconds. What async changes is what the server does during that five seconds: instead of one worker thread sitting idle waiting for the response, `await`ing an async HTTP call to the model API frees that worker to handle other incoming requests, and resumes this one when the model's response arrives [6]. One process can then hold many concurrent slow requests in flight, which is exactly the shape of load an LLM-backed API sees.**



## What is the single most common FastAPI mistake in AI apps?

**Calling a synchronous client inside an `async def` route. If your model provider's SDK, or your database driver, does not itself support async and you call it directly inside an async route without offloading it, that call blocks the event loop exactly the way a fully synchronous server would, silently cancelling the whole benefit of using FastAPI. The fix is to use the provider's async client if one exists, or run the blocking call in a thread pool with `run_in_threadpool` so it does not block the event loop while it waits.**



## How does dependency injection fit into an AI application?

**FastAPI's dependency injection system is where the clean project structure of settings, providers, and database sessions actually gets wired into each incoming request [2]. A `get_settings()` dependency provides typed configuration; a `get_llm_client()` dependency provides the model provider instance; a `get_db_session()` dependency provides a database session scoped to the request and closed automatically afterward. Routes declare what they need as parameters, and FastAPI resolves and injects them, which keeps route functions thin and makes swapping a provider or a database a change in one place, not a search-and-replace across the codebase.**




## How do I stream LLM responses token by token?

**Return a `StreamingResponse` whose body is an async generator that yields chunks as they arrive from the model provider's streaming API, rather than collecting the full response before returning anything [4]. Most model providers expose a streaming mode over server-sent events specifically for this [5]. The user sees the answer appear progressively, which cuts perceived latency dramatically even though total generation time is unchanged, because the wait for the first token is far shorter than the wait for the whole answer.**



## When do I need background tasks versus a real task queue?

**FastAPI's built-in `BackgroundTasks` is for quick, fire-and-forget work tied to a single request's lifecycle, sending a notification email after a response is returned, with no need to track its status or retry it [3]. A real task queue, Celery or an equivalent, is for anything that needs retries, scheduling, monitoring, or to survive the web server restarting, a long document-processing job, a nightly re-embedding run, a batch of API calls that must complete even if the request that triggered them is long gone [8]. Reaching for background tasks when you actually need a queue is how "fire and forget" jobs quietly disappear when the server restarts mid-job.**



## What does a clean FastAPI layer for an AI app look like?

**Routes stay thin: parse the request, resolve dependencies, call into the application's core logic, return a response, ideally streamed. All the actual work, retrieval, generation, validation, sits in the modules described in a proper project structure, not inline in the route function [10]. Settings come from dependency injection, never read directly from the environment inside a route. Errors from the model provider are caught and translated into clean HTTP error responses, not leaked as raw provider exceptions.**



## FastAPI interview questions for AI roles

**Explain why async matters specifically for LLM-backed APIs. Describe how dependency injection would wire a swappable model provider. Explain how you would stream a model's response to a frontend. Compare BackgroundTasks with a real task queue and say when each applies. Describe the most common way a FastAPI app silently loses its async benefits. The strongest answer includes a concurrency bug you found and fixed, not just the theory.**



## Where should I start?

**Take an existing script that calls a model API and wrap it in a FastAPI route with a streaming response and one dependency for the client. An evening turns a script into a real, concurrent-capable service.** For a hands-on session on serving AI applications with FastAPI, from a script to production, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Why is FastAPI so popular? Install, docs, ORM choices and production use
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-guide-orm-production/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


FastAPI is a modern Python web framework for building APIs, popular because it is fast to write and fast to run: you declare inputs with Python type hints, and FastAPI validates requests, converts data and generates interactive documentation automatically. It is the backend I used across my NextUpgrad applications, including RAG.NextUpgrad and FaceVision's embeddings service. This page covers its popularity and history, installation, the docs, how it achieves performance, ORM choices, production use, how it compares with Node.js, and FastAPI Cloud.

## Why is FastAPI so popular?

FastAPI is popular because it combines very quick development with strong correctness: type hints drive request validation, editor autocompletion and documentation, while async support gives good performance. Developers write less code and catch errors earlier.

Other reasons: automatic OpenAPI documentation with interactive Swagger UI, clear error messages for invalid requests, dependency injection for things like database sessions and authentication, and excellent documentation. It also fits the AI era well: most machine learning and LLM work happens in Python, so FastAPI is the natural way to wrap models, RAG pipelines and agents in a web API. For students, its tutorial is one of the best introductions to building APIs properly.

## When was FastAPI invented?

FastAPI was created by Sebastián Ramírez and first released in December 2018. It builds on Starlette for web handling and Pydantic for data validation.

It grew quickly over the following years as teams adopted it for machine learning services and microservices, and it became one of the most used Python web frameworks alongside Django and Flask. Its design reflected newer Python features, such as type hints and async, that older frameworks predated. The project is open source under the MIT licence and maintained on GitHub with a large community.

## How do I install FastAPI?

Create a virtual environment, install FastAPI with its standard extras, write a small app and run it with the FastAPI CLI.

```bash
pip install "fastapi[standard]"
```

```python
# main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}
```

```bash
fastapi dev main.py        # development server with auto-reload
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs` to see the interactive documentation. For production, use `fastapi run` or a server setup such as Uvicorn with multiple workers behind a reverse proxy. Pin versions in a `requirements.txt` file, keep the virtual environment out of Git, and read settings such as database URLs from environment variables, so the same code runs on your laptop and in deployment.

## What are FastAPI's docs?

FastAPI automatically generates an OpenAPI schema for your API and serves interactive documentation at `/docs`, using Swagger UI, and alternative documentation at `/redoc`. They update as you change your code.

The docs list every endpoint, its parameters, request bodies and response models, derived from your type hints and Pydantic models, and let you send test requests from the browser. Add descriptions, examples and tags in your code to make them clearer. For public APIs you can disable them or protect them in production. The underlying OpenAPI schema, at `/openapi.json`, can generate client libraries for front ends and other services.

## How does FastAPI achieve high performance?

FastAPI runs on ASGI, an asynchronous server interface, using Starlette and servers such as Uvicorn, so it can handle many concurrent requests efficiently when endpoints use `async` and non-blocking I/O. Pydantic's fast validation core adds to this.

Performance in practice depends on your code: blocking calls, such as a synchronous database driver or heavy CPU work inside an `async` endpoint, slow everything down. Use async database drivers or define those endpoints with plain `def`, which FastAPI runs in a thread pool. For CPU-heavy tasks, such as running a large model, use background workers or separate model servers. Most real bottlenecks are databases and external API calls, not the framework.

## Does FastAPI have an ORM?

No. FastAPI does not include an ORM; it leaves data access to you. Most projects use SQLModel or SQLAlchemy for SQL databases, or an ODM such as Beanie for MongoDB.

This keeps FastAPI focused and flexible: you choose the database layer that suits your project and can use raw SQL when needed. A common pattern is a dependency that provides a database session to each request and closes it afterwards, plus Alembic for schema migrations. Keep database models separate from API schemas when they differ, so you never accidentally expose fields like password hashes in responses.

## What is the best ORM for FastAPI?

SQLModel is the most natural choice for many projects because it is made by FastAPI's author and combines SQLAlchemy and Pydantic, so one class can serve as both the database table and the API schema. SQLAlchemy 2.0 is the most powerful and flexible option for complex applications.

Choose by need:

- **SQLModel**: simple CRUD apps and learning; less boilerplate.
- **SQLAlchemy 2.0**: complex queries, large codebases, full control; async support available.
- **Tortoise ORM**: an async-first, Django-like ORM.
- **Beanie**: MongoDB with Pydantic models.

Whatever you pick, use migrations with Alembic for SQL databases, connection pooling, and tests against a real database, not only mocks.

## Can FastAPI be used in production?

Yes. FastAPI is used in production by many companies and startups for APIs and machine learning services. Production readiness depends on how you deploy and operate it, not on the framework.

A production checklist:

- Run with `fastapi run` or Uvicorn workers behind a reverse proxy, or in containers.
- Use environment variables for configuration and secrets.
- Add structured logging, metrics and health checks.
- Validate inputs strictly and set request size and timeout limits.
- Handle authentication and rate limiting.
- Run database migrations and keep backups.
- Write tests with FastAPI's TestClient and run them in CI.

RAG.NextUpgrad and my other NextUpgrad apps shipped this way, with Docker, CI/CD, structured logging and metrics.

## FastAPI vs Node.js: which should I use?

Use FastAPI when your backend is close to Python's ecosystem, such as machine learning, data processing, RAG and AI agents. Use Node.js when your team works in JavaScript or TypeScript across front end and back end, or you rely on its large web ecosystem.

Both handle high concurrency well with async I/O. Node.js frameworks such as Express, Fastify and NestJS are mature and widely used; TypeScript gives strong typing comparable to FastAPI's type hints. FastAPI's automatic validation and docs are excellent out of the box. Many teams use both: a Next.js front end with its own server routes, and a FastAPI service for AI features, communicating over a clean API.

## Is FastAPI Cloud free?

FastAPI Cloud is a deployment platform from the team behind FastAPI, introduced to make deploying FastAPI apps simple. Its availability, plans and any free tier depend on its current offering, so check its official website.

FastAPI itself is free and open source, and you can deploy it on many platforms with free tiers for small projects, such as container hosts and serverless platforms that support Python. For student projects, a free tier on a platform such as Render, Railway or a cloud provider's free allowance is usually enough. Watch for cold starts on free tiers, keep secrets in environment variables, and add a health endpoint so the platform can check your app.
