# What is FastAPI in Python? Uses, examples, running it, Docker and templates
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-python-examples/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

FastAPI is a Python framework for building web APIs: you write functions with type hints, and FastAPI turns them into HTTP endpoints with automatic request validation, JSON responses and interactive documentation. It is widely used to serve machine learning models and LLM features, and it is the backend I used for RAG.NextUpgrad and my other NextUpgrad applications. This page explains what it is used for, shows examples, covers running it with and without Uvicorn and in notebooks, and gives a Dockerfile and production template guidance. What is FastAPI in Python? FastAPI is an open-source Python web framework for building APIs quickly and correctly. It uses standard Python type hints with Pydantic models to validate inputs and shape outputs, and runs on ASGI servers for asynchronous performance. You define endpoints as functions decorated with the HTTP method and path, such as @app.get("/items/{item_id}"). FastAPI reads the type hints to parse path, query and body parameters, rejects invalid requests with clear errors, and documents everything automatically at /docs. It also provides dependency injection, which handles shared resources such as database sessions and authentication cleanly. The result is less boilerplate and fewer bugs than hand-written validation. What is FastAPI used for in Python? FastAPI is used to build REST and JSON APIs, serve machine learning and LLM models, power retrieval-augmented generation backends, create microservices, handle webhooks, and build internal tools and admin backends. Common examples: An inference endpoint that runs a model and returns predictions. A RAG API that retrieves passages and streams a cited answer. A backend for a React or Next.js front end. Webhook receivers for payment or messaging services. Data and automation APIs that other teams call. Its async support suits I/O-heavy work, such as calling databases and external APIs; for heavy CPU work, pair it with background workers. Because it is plain Python, the code that loads a model or a vector index in a notebook moves into an endpoint with little change, which is why data scientists and ML engineers adopt it quickly. How do I use FastAPI in Python? Install it, create an app, define endpoints with type hints and Pydantic models, and run it with the FastAPI CLI. The interactive docs at /docs let you test endpoints immediately. Also asked as: how to use fastapi in python from fastapi import FastAPI from pydantic import BaseModel app = FastAPI() class Question(BaseModel): text: str top_k: int = 5 @app.post(&quot;/ask&quot;) def ask(q: Question): return {&quot;question&quot;: q.text, &quot;top_k&quot;: q.top_k, &quot;answer&quot;: &quot;stub&quot;} pip install &quot;fastapi[standard]&quot; fastapi dev main.py Send an invalid body, such as a string for top_k, and FastAPI returns a clear 422 error explaining what is wrong. What are some FastAPI examples in Python? Typical examples are a CRUD API with a database, a file upload endpoint, an authenticated endpoint with dependencies, a streaming response for LLM output, and a background task. Here is a streaming example. Also asked as: fastapi examples python from fastapi import FastAPI from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse import time app = FastAPI() def tokens(): for word in &quot;Retrieval augmented generation grounds answers in documents&quot;.split(): yield word + &quot; &quot; time.sleep(0.1) @app.get(&quot;/stream&quot;) def stream(): return StreamingResponse(tokens(), media_type=&quot;text/plain&quot;) Streaming like this is how chat interfaces show answers as they are generated. The FastAPI documentation has tutorials for each pattern, from path parameters to security. How do I run a FastAPI server? During development, run fastapi dev main.py, which starts a server with auto-reload on port 8000. In production, run fastapi run main.py or Uvicorn with several worker processes, usually behind a reverse proxy. Also asked as: how to run fastapi server Production basics: set the host to 0.0.0.0 inside containers so the server is reachable, choose the number of workers based on CPU cores, configure timeouts, and run behind a proxy or load balancer that handles HTTPS. Keep settings in environment variables. Add a health endpoint for monitoring and container orchestration. How do I run FastAPI with Uvicorn? Install Uvicorn, then point it at your app object with module:variable syntax, for example uvicorn main:app --reload for development or with workers for production. Also asked as: how to run fastapi with uvicorn uvicorn main:app --reload # development uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4 # production-style The FastAPI CLI uses Uvicorn under the hood, so fastapi run and uvicorn give similar results; the CLI just picks sensible defaults. Use --reload only in development, since it watches files and restarts. In containers, a single Uvicorn process per container with scaling handled by the platform is a common pattern. Can I run FastAPI without Uvicorn? Yes. FastAPI is an ASGI application, so any ASGI server can run it, such as Hypercorn or Granian. Uvicorn is simply the most common and the default used by the FastAPI CLI. Alternative servers may offer features such as HTTP/2 or different performance characteristics; benchmark with your workload before switching. For testing, you do not need a server at all: FastAPI's TestClient calls your app directly in Python, which is how unit tests usually work. Serverless platforms that support ASGI can also host FastAPI through adapters. Whichever server you choose, keep application code independent of it, so switching servers later is a one-line change in your start command or container configuration rather than a rewrite. Can I run FastAPI in a Jupyter notebook or Colab? Yes, with care. For testing logic, use TestClient in the notebook to call endpoints without a server. To run a real server, start Uvicorn in a background thread so it does not block the notebook's event loop. Also asked as: can i run fastapi in jupyter notebook from fastapi.testclient import TestClient client = TestClient(app) print(client.post(&quot;/ask&quot;, json={&quot;text&quot;: &quot;What is RAG?&quot;}).json()) For a live server in Colab, you would also need a tunnel to reach it from outside, which exposes your app publicly, so protect it and stop it afterwards. For anything beyond quick experiments, move the code into a .py file and run it with the FastAPI CLI locally or in a container. What is a good Dockerfile example for Python FastAPI? A simple, production-friendly Dockerfile uses a slim Python base image, installs dependencies first for caching, copies the app, and runs it with the FastAPI CLI on all interfaces. Also asked as: dockerfile example python fastapi FROM python:3.12-slim WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt COPY . . EXPOSE 8000 CMD [&quot;fastapi&quot;, &quot;run&quot;, &quot;main.py&quot;, &quot;--port&quot;, &quot;8000&quot;] Add a .dockerignore to keep virtual environments and secrets out of the image, pass configuration through environment variables, and run as a non-root user for better security. Build with docker build -t myapi . and run with docker run -p 8000:8000 myapi. What is a production-ready FastAPI template? The FastAPI team maintains a full-stack template with FastAPI, SQLModel, PostgreSQL, a React front end, Docker Compose, authentication, migrations and tests, which is a good reference for production structure. Also asked as: production-ready fastapi template (python What a production setup should include, whether from a template or your own: Structure: routers by feature, separate schemas and models, a settings module. Database: SQLModel or SQLAlchemy with Alembic migrations. Security: authentication, CORS configuration, input limits, secrets in environment variables. Observability: structured logging, metrics, health checks. Quality: tests with TestClient, linting and CI. Deployment: Dockerfile, Compose for local services, and a platform for production. Start from a template, but understand every piece; delete what you do not need.

# What are FastAPI and Uvicorn? Beginner tutorial, GitHub projects, and response models
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-uvicorn-tutorial/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

FastAPI is a modern Python framework for building APIs, using type hints to validate data and generate interactive documentation automatically. Uvicorn is an ASGI web server that runs FastAPI apps, receiving HTTP requests and handing them to your code. You write the app with FastAPI and serve it with Uvicorn. FastAPI is the back end of my AI products, including the FaceVision embedding service, so this page covers both tools, a beginner tutorial, GitHub examples, models, response models and PUT endpoints. What are FastAPI and Uvicorn? FastAPI is a Python framework for building web APIs with automatic validation, serialisation and OpenAPI documentation, built on Starlette and Pydantic. Uvicorn is a lightweight, fast ASGI server that runs asynchronous Python web apps such as FastAPI. Also asked as: what is fastapi and uvicorn Together they form a common stack for Python back ends: FastAPI handles routes, validation and business logic; Uvicorn handles network connections and the HTTP protocol. FastAPI is popular for AI and machine learning services because Python dominates that ecosystem and async support handles many concurrent requests, such as streaming model responses. Both are open source and widely used in production. Why does FastAPI need Uvicorn? FastAPI is an application framework, not a server. It defines how to respond to requests but does not listen on a network port. An ASGI server such as Uvicorn accepts connections, parses HTTP and calls your FastAPI app. ASGI, the Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface, is the standard connecting Python async servers and frameworks. Uvicorn is the most common choice, but alternatives such as Hypercorn and Granian also work. The fastapi dev and fastapi run commands use Uvicorn under the hood. In production, run Uvicorn with multiple workers, or behind a process manager, and put a reverse proxy in front for HTTPS. What is the difference between FastAPI and Uvicorn? FastAPI is the framework where you write endpoints, models and dependencies. Uvicorn is the server that runs the framework and handles HTTP connections. You need both: one defines behaviour, the other serves it. An analogy: FastAPI is the restaurant's menu and kitchen, deciding what to make; Uvicorn is the front desk taking orders and delivering food. You can swap the server without changing your app, or run other ASGI frameworks on Uvicorn. Errors in validation or business logic come from your FastAPI code; errors about ports, workers or connections usually come from the server layer. In development, fastapi dev restarts the server whenever you save a file; in production, fastapi run or a Uvicorn command with several workers serves traffic without reloading. What is a good FastAPI tutorial for beginners? The official FastAPI tutorial is the best starting point: clear, example-driven and current. Install FastAPI, write a first endpoint, run it, and explore the automatic docs at /docs. from fastapi import FastAPI app = FastAPI() @app.get(&quot;/hello/{name}&quot;) def hello(name: str): return {&quot;message&quot;: f&quot;Hello, {name}&quot;} Run pip install "fastapi[standard]", then fastapi dev main.py, and open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs. Next learn path and query parameters, request bodies with Pydantic, dependencies, database access, authentication and testing with TestClient. Build one small project as you go, such as a notes API with a database, so each chapter adds a real feature. Read error messages in the interactive docs, which show exactly which field failed validation and why. Where can I find a FastAPI tutorial on GitHub? The FastAPI repository on GitHub contains the documentation source with all tutorial examples, and the official full-stack FastAPI template shows a production-style project. Community collections list many more examples and libraries. Also asked as: fastapi tutorial github Useful repositories to study: The FastAPI repository's docs examples, organised by topic. The full-stack FastAPI template with PostgreSQL, authentication, tests and Docker. "Awesome FastAPI" community lists of tools and projects. Open-source apps built with FastAPI in your domain, such as ML serving. Read the code alongside the tutorial: see how routers, dependencies and settings are organised in larger projects, then apply that structure to your own app. What is a good example FastAPI project on GitHub? The official full-stack FastAPI template is the best-known example: a FastAPI back end with SQLModel and PostgreSQL, JWT authentication, tests, a React front end, Docker Compose and deployment configuration. Also asked as: example fastapi project github When building your own example project for a portfolio, include: routers split by feature, Pydantic schemas, a database layer with migrations, authentication, background tasks, tests, Docker, and a README with setup steps and API docs screenshots. An AI-flavoured project, such as a document question-answering API with streaming responses and citations, shows modern skills. Keep secrets in environment variables and provide an .env.example file. Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs tests on every push, which signals professional habits to anyone reviewing the repository. What is a FastAPI model example? In FastAPI, models are Pydantic classes that define data shapes. FastAPI uses them to validate request bodies, convert types and generate documentation automatically. from pydantic import BaseModel, Field class ItemIn(BaseModel): name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100) quantity: int = Field(ge=0) tags: list[str] = [] @app.post(&quot;/items&quot;) def create_item(item: ItemIn): return {&quot;received&quot;: item} If a client sends invalid data, such as a negative quantity, FastAPI returns a clear 422 error automatically. Separate input models from database models and output models so you never accidentally expose internal fields. What is a FastAPI response model example? A response model declares the shape of data an endpoint returns. FastAPI filters the output to that model, validates it and documents it, which prevents leaking fields such as password hashes. class UserOut(BaseModel): id: int email: str @app.get(&quot;/users/{user_id}&quot;, response_model=UserOut) def get_user(user_id: int): user = db_get_user(user_id) # may include hashed_password return user Even if user contains extra fields, only id and email are returned. You can also use return type annotations instead of response_model. Use response_model_exclude_none=True to drop empty fields where helpful. What is a FastAPI response example? FastAPI endpoints can return dictionaries, Pydantic models or lists, which become JSON automatically, or explicit response classes for other formats, status codes and headers, such as JSONResponse, HTMLResponse, FileResponse and StreamingResponse. from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse @app.get(&quot;/stream&quot;) def stream(): def gen(): for word in [&quot;Retrieval&quot;, &quot;augmented&quot;, &quot;generation&quot;]: yield word + &quot; &quot; return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type=&quot;text/plain&quot;) Streaming responses are how AI apps show answers as they are generated. Set status codes with status_code=201 on decorators, and add response examples in the OpenAPI docs to help API consumers. What is a FastAPI PUT example? A PUT endpoint replaces a resource with new data. Take the ID from the path and the full updated object from the request body, return 404 if it does not exist, and return the updated resource. from fastapi import HTTPException @app.put(&quot;/items/{item_id}&quot;, response_model=ItemIn) def update_item(item_id: int, item: ItemIn): if item_id not in items_db: raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail=&quot;Item not found&quot;) items_db[item_id] = item return item Use PATCH for partial updates, with a model whose fields are optional and item.model_dump(exclude_unset=True) to apply only provided fields. Add authentication so only permitted users can modify resources. Write a test for each case, a successful update, a missing item and invalid data, so changes to the endpoint never break silently.

# How to get your first tech job, and what FIRST Tech Challenge is
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/first-tech-job-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


"First tech" usually means one of three things: your first job in the tech industry, FIRST Tech Challenge, a school robotics competition, or First Tech Federal Credit Union, a US bank. This page is about the first two. Most of it covers how to get your first tech job, write the CV, why it feels so hard, how to survive the first months, how long to stay and how to recover if it goes wrong. The last two sections explain FIRST Tech Challenge for students interested in robotics.

## What is First Tech?

"First Tech" most often refers to someone's first job in tech, to FIRST Tech Challenge, a robotics competition for school students run by the non-profit FIRST, or to First Tech Federal Credit Union, a credit union in the United States.

If you came here about banking, First Tech Federal Credit Union's own website and support line are the right places for opening hours and account details. This page focuses on careers and robotics. For students and freshers in India, the career question is the one that matters most: how to get from a degree to a first role as a developer, data analyst, AI engineer or similar, and how to do well once you are there. FIRST Tech Challenge is relevant if you are in school and want hands-on engineering experience.

## How do I get my first tech job?

Build proof of skill, make it visible, and apply in a targeted way: two or three deployed projects, an internship or freelance work, an active GitHub and LinkedIn, and referrals to the companies you want.

A plan that works:

- **Pick a lane**: backend, frontend, data, mobile or AI. Depth beats a long skills list.
- **Build projects** that solve a real problem, deploy them, and write clear READMEs.
- **Get experience**: internships, freelance work for local businesses, open source or hackathons.
- **Network**: message engineers at target companies with a short note and your best project.
- **Apply consistently**: five to ten tailored applications a week, tracked in a sheet.
- **Practise interviews**: coding problems and explaining your projects aloud.

Expect it to take months, not weeks.

## How do I write a CV for my first tech job?

Keep it to one page, put projects near the top with links and results, list skills grouped by type, and tailor the wording to each job description. Recruiters skim, so every line must earn its place.

Structure for a fresher:

- **Header**: name, email, phone, GitHub, LinkedIn, portfolio.
- **Projects**: name, problem, stack, what you built, a measurable result, live link.
- **Experience**: internships and freelance work, with outcomes.
- **Skills**: languages, frameworks, databases, tools, cloud.
- **Education**: degree, college, years, CGPA if strong.
- **Achievements**: hackathons, competitive programming, relevant certifications.

Avoid skill bars, photos and objective statements. Use the same words as the job description where they are true, because many companies screen CVs automatically before a person reads them.

## Why is landing your first tech job harder than expected?

Because entry-level roles attract very large numbers of applicants, many companies prefer people with some experience, and AI tools have raised the bar for juniors. Generic CVs and certificate lists no longer stand out.

There is also a mismatch between what college teaches and what jobs need: deploying, debugging, working with Git, writing tests and explaining trade-offs. Many applicants apply through the same portals at the same time, so cold applications have low reply rates. What changes the odds is specificity: a project that matches the role, a referral, a hackathon result, or a short message that shows you understand the company's product. Rejections are normal and rarely personal; track them, adjust one thing at a time, and keep building.

## How can Gen Z land their first tech jobs?

Gen Z candidates have an advantage in using AI tools and building in public; use both. Ship projects with AI help that you fully understand, document them publicly, and use communities and hackathons to meet people who hire.

What works for this generation of graduates:

- Post short build logs on LinkedIn or X while you work on a project.
- Join developer communities and contribute: answer questions, run a session, help organise an event.
- Enter hackathons; they compress learning, teamwork and networking into a weekend.
- Learn to use AI coding tools well, and be ready to explain every line they wrote.
- Look beyond big brands: startups and small companies often hire on proof of skill.

I founded TechVerse Enclave, a community of 500+ developers, because communities are where students find mentors, teammates and openings.

## How do I survive my first tech job?

Focus on learning the codebase, asking good questions, delivering small things reliably, and communicating clearly. Nobody expects a fresher to know everything; they expect you to learn fast and be dependable.

Habits that help in the first months:

- Write down how to set up, build, test and deploy the project as you learn it.
- Ask questions after trying for a reasonable time, and show what you tried.
- Take small tickets first and finish them properly, with tests.
- Read code reviews carefully and apply feedback the next time.
- Give short, regular updates so your lead never has to chase you.
- Keep a "brag document" of what you shipped, for appraisals and your next move.

Protect your health; late nights every week are a warning sign, not a badge.

## How long should I stay at my first tech job?

Long enough to finish meaningful projects and learn deeply, which usually means around eighteen months to two years. Leave earlier if the job is harming your health, stopped your learning completely, or you have a clearly better opportunity.

Staying a reasonable time lets you see projects through, from building to running in production, which is where much of the learning is. It also gives you stories for your next interviews. Leaving very quickly is fine once; a pattern of short stints raises questions. Before switching, make sure you are moving towards something: a bigger scope, a better team or a field you care about, not only away from a bad week.

## How do you recover after getting fired from your first tech job?

Take a short pause, understand honestly what went wrong, fix the gap, and start applying again with a calm, factual explanation. Being let go early in a career is more common than people admit, and it is recoverable.

Steps that help:

- Ask your former manager or HR for specific feedback if you can.
- Separate causes you control, such as skills or communication, from ones you do not, such as layoffs or team changes.
- Spend a few weeks closing the main skill gap and ship a small project that shows it.
- Prepare a short, honest answer: what happened, what you learned, what you do differently now.
- Lean on mentors and peers for referrals.

Keep your finances and health steady during the search; panic decisions rarely help.

## What is FIRST Tech Challenge?

FIRST Tech Challenge is an international robotics competition for students roughly aged 12 to 18, run by the non-profit FIRST. Teams design, build and program robots to play a new game released at the start of each season.

Teams usually have up to fifteen students with adult mentors. They learn mechanical design, electronics, programming, project management and outreach, and they keep an engineering portfolio of their work. Awards recognise not only match results but also design, innovation, outreach and teamwork. For a school student interested in engineering or computer science, it is one of the best hands-on experiences available, and it gives material for college applications and later interviews. Check FIRST's website for teams and events near you.

## How does FIRST Tech Challenge work?

Each season FIRST announces a game. Teams then build a robot from a kit of reusable parts, program it in Java or a block-based tool, and compete in matches where alliances of teams score points in autonomous and driver-controlled periods.

A match starts with a short autonomous period in which the robot runs code with no human control, followed by a driver-controlled period. Teams form alliances, so collaboration matters as much as competition. Events progress from local qualifiers to regional or national championships and an international championship. Judging also looks at the team's engineering portfolio and interviews. The programming side is real software engineering: sensors, control loops, computer vision for detecting game elements, and testing under time pressure.

# Free AI tools every CS student should learn in 2026: coding assistants, models, notebooks, deployment and the ones I built, with no signup
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/free-ai-tools-for-students/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Which AI tools should a CS student learn first?

**Five categories, in this order: a coding assistant in your editor, so you build faster; a way to call a model, a free API tier or a local runner; a notebook with a free GPU, for experiments and fine-tuning; a database with a free tier, so projects have real persistence; and a platform to deploy on, so projects have a URL. Everything else is optional until a project demands it. Learn each by shipping something with it, not by watching a tutorial about it.**


I mentor 200-plus students through TechVerse Enclave and the same question arrives weekly: which tools? The list below is what I actually use and what students who finish projects actually use, with the free-tier limits that matter. Because signup friction stops more students than difficulty does, I also built fifteen tools that need no account at all, at tools.scult.in [15].

> A tool you have to sign up for is a tool you try tomorrow. A tool that opens in a tab is a tool you use now. That is the whole reason tools.scult.in exists.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Which coding assistant should students use?

**One you can afford and that lives in your editor. GitHub Copilot is free for verified students through the Student Developer Pack and works inside VS Code [5][6]. Cursor is an AI-first editor with a free tier [13]. Claude Code runs an agent in your terminal that can read, edit and run your project [14]. Pick one, learn its limits, and use it for boilerplate, tests, refactors and explanations of unfamiliar code. Turn it off when you are learning a fundamental for the first time, or you will not learn it.**



The rule I give mentees: assistants make you faster at what you understand and slower at learning what you do not. Write your first RAG pipeline by hand; use the assistant for the tenth.

## How do students get free access to LLMs?

**Three ways. Free API tiers: Google AI Studio gives Gemini API access with a free quota [10]; Groq offers fast inference on open models with a free tier [11]; OpenRouter routes to many models, some free [12]. Local models: Ollama runs open-weight models on your laptop with no account and no cost [4]. Hosted playgrounds: Hugging Face hosts thousands of models and free courses [3]. Start with a free API for speed, and Ollama for privacy and unlimited experimentation.**



Free tiers change often; the pricing pages are the truth and this table is a map [10][11][12].

## Where can students get free GPUs?

**Google Colab gives free GPU sessions with time and availability limits, enough for QLoRA on a small model [1]. Kaggle Notebooks give weekly GPU hours with a generous quota, and host datasets you can use directly [2]. Hugging Face Spaces can run demos with optional paid GPU [3]. For learning: fine-tune a 1 to 3B model on Colab, then move to Kaggle when you need longer runs. Save checkpoints to Drive or the Hub because sessions end.**


## Which databases and backends have free tiers good enough for projects?

**Supabase gives hosted Postgres with auth, storage and the pgvector extension on a free tier, which is a complete backend for a RAG project [7]. Firebase and MongoDB Atlas have free tiers too. For deploying a Python API, Railway and Render both offer free or trial tiers that sleep when idle [8][9]. GitHub Pages hosts static front ends for free, including this site. The pattern: one Postgres, one API host, one static host, all free until you have users.**




## What free tools did you build, and why no signup?

**Fifteen browser tools at tools.scult.in, a 1,211-prompt library where every prompt is stamped with the model and date it was tested against, a 50,000-plus agent-skills library, and a public MCP server so agents can call the same tools [15]. Thirteen of the fifteen tools never send a byte to a server; they run entirely in your browser, which is both faster and the simplest privacy story there is [17]. No signup because every signup screen is a place where a student decides to do it later.**



Every calculator shows its formula so you can check it rather than trust it, and the prompt library's stamps exist because a prompt that worked on one model version is a hypothesis on the next.

## How should students use AI tools without hurting their learning?

**Decide before each task whether the goal is output or understanding. For output, a deadline, a boilerplate, a refactor, use the assistant fully and review what it wrote. For understanding, a new algorithm, a first pipeline, a concept for an exam, write it yourself first, then ask the assistant to critique it. Never submit code you cannot explain line by line, because the interview will ask you to. The students who do best treat assistants like a senior colleague: consult often, copy never without reading.**



## Which AI tools help with research, writing and productivity?

**For reading papers: a chat model with the PDF, asking for the method and the limitations, then reading the paper anyway. For writing: an assistant for structure and clarity, never for facts you have not checked. For notes: any tool that exports plain text, so your notes outlive the tool. For search: AI answer engines for orientation, primary sources for anything you will cite. The habit that matters is checking the source, which no tool does for you.**


## What free AI tools are there for design and content?

**For diagrams and slides, most design tools now have free AI features; for images, be careful with licences and never present generated images as photographs of real events. For content, the same rule as writing: structure from the model, facts from sources. The colour palette generator and favicon generator at tools.scult.in cover the two design tasks every student project actually needs, with contrast checks built in [15].**



## Which tools will still matter in five years?

**None of the specific ones, probably, and all of the skills: prompting a model precisely, evaluating its output, deploying a service, reading documentation, reading a paper, and knowing when to switch the assistant off. Learn tools as instances of those skills, and the next tool is an afternoon, not a semester. My longer list with the reasoning is on the portfolio [16].**




## Where should I start today?

**Open tools.scult.in, use one tool, copy one stamped prompt into your assistant, and ship one page to GitHub Pages before you sleep.** For a hands-on session at your college that ends with every student having a deployed project built with free tools, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How should a fresher resume look? Example, headline, and no-internship tips
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fresher-resume-example/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

A fresher resume should be one clean, single-column page that proves you can do the job: a short headline and summary, two or three projects with links and results, grouped skills, education, and any internships, freelance work or achievements. Recruiters skim, so the strongest evidence goes first. This page walks through preparing it, the format, a computer science and BCA version with a full example, what to do with no internship, the headline, length, and whether to write "fresher". How should a fresher resume look? It should look simple and scannable: one page, one column, clear section headings, consistent fonts and spacing, and no photos, graphics or skill bars. Content should be specific, with links and numbers where possible. Also asked as: how should be a fresher resume A reader should understand in ten seconds what role you want, what you can do and where to see proof. That means a headline at the top, projects near the top for technical roles, and every bullet starting with an action verb and ending with a result. Use a standard template from Google Docs, Word or Overleaf, export as PDF, and check that text copies cleanly, because many companies screen resumes with software first. How do I prepare a resume as a fresher? Start from the job you want: collect three to five job descriptions for that role, list the skills they repeat, then gather your evidence for each skill from projects, courses, internships and activities, and write bullets that show it. Also asked as: how to prepare a resume for fresher Steps: Choose one target role, such as junior backend developer. List required skills from real job descriptions. Collect your evidence: projects, coursework, freelance work, hackathons. Write two or three bullets per item: action, tool, result. Fit everything on one page; cut what does not support the role. Tailor the summary and skills order for each application. Ask a senior or mentor to review it. Keep a longer master version and trim it per application. What is the right resume format for a fresher? Use a reverse-chronological, one-page format adapted for freshers: header, headline and summary, projects, skills, education, experience if any, and achievements. Put the most relevant section highest. Also asked as: what is the format of resume for a fresher For technical roles, projects come before education because they show ability; for roles where your degree is the main qualification, education can come first. Keep margins reasonable, fonts readable, and dates aligned. Avoid two-column templates, which often parse badly in applicant tracking systems. Name the file clearly, for example "FirstName-LastName-Resume.pdf". Use one date format throughout, such as "Jul 2025 to Dec 2025", aligned to the right so dates are easy to scan, and bold only headings and project names rather than random words. How do I make a resume as a computer science fresher? Lead with projects that match your target role, list technical skills grouped by type, include your GitHub and portfolio, and show problem-solving evidence such as competitive programming or hackathons. Also asked as: how to make resume for computer science student fresher What strong CS fresher resumes include: Projects: two or three, deployed, with stack, what you built and a result. Skills: languages, frameworks, databases, tools and cloud, only ones you can discuss. Links: GitHub with clean READMEs, a portfolio, LinkedIn. Education: degree, college, years, CGPA if it helps. Achievements: hackathon results, coding contest ratings, open source. For AI roles, one project with an LLM, retrieval or a fine-tuned model, documented with evaluation results, stands out. How do I build a resume with no internship experience? Replace internship experience with other evidence: personal and academic projects treated like work, freelance or volunteer work, hackathons, open-source contributions, teaching or tutoring, and leadership in clubs or communities. Also asked as: how do you build a resume as a fresher with no internship experience Make projects read like experience: "Built and deployed a document Q&amp;A web app with FastAPI and an LLM API; 40 classmates used it during exams; answers cite page numbers." Freelance work for a local business, even small, shows client delivery. Hackathons show teamwork under pressure. Founding or organising a community shows initiative; I founded TechVerse Enclave, which grew to 500+ developers, and that kind of role is worth a line. Then apply for internships with this resume; one internship changes the next resume. What is a resume headline for a fresher? A resume headline is one line under your name that states your target role and strongest skills, such as "Fresher Python Developer | FastAPI, PostgreSQL, LLM APIs | 3 Deployed Projects". It tells recruiters instantly what you offer. Also asked as: what is resume headline for fresher Good headlines are specific and true. Examples: "Junior Frontend Developer | React, Next.js, TypeScript | Hackathon Winner" "Data Analyst | SQL, Python, Power BI | Analysed 3 Real Datasets End to End" "GenAI Developer | Python, RAG, Vector Search | Built a Cited Document Assistant" Match the headline to the job you are applying for. Job portals such as Naukri also have a separate headline field; use the same idea there. What is an example of a fresher resume? Here is a complete example in plain text form for a computer science or BCA fresher targeting backend or GenAI roles. Also asked as: resume for fresher example YOUR NAME email@example.com | +91-XXXXXXXXXX | github.com/yourname | linkedin.com/in/yourname Fresher Backend Developer | Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, LLM APIs PROJECTS Campus Docs Assistant - FastAPI, pgvector, LLM API (live link) - Built a Q&amp;A app over 120 pages of college notices; answers cite page numbers. - Added keyword plus vector search; correct passage in top 5 for 45 of 50 test questions. Expense Splitter - Next.js, PostgreSQL (live link) - Group expense tracking with auth; used by 25 hostel residents for 2 months. SKILLS Languages: Python, JavaScript, SQL | Frameworks: FastAPI, Next.js Tools: Git, Docker, Linux | Cloud: Vercel, Render EDUCATION BCA, Your College, 2023-2026, CGPA 8.2 ACHIEVEMENTS Finalist, college hackathon (team of 4) | Organised 3 Python workshops for juniors Replace every line with your own real details. Where can I get a free BCA fresher resume template? Use a free single-column template from Google Docs, Microsoft Word or Overleaf, and adapt the example above. BCA freshers need the same structure as other tech freshers: projects, skills, education and achievements. Tips for BCA students: highlight projects and practical skills strongly, since recruiters may compare you with BTech candidates; mention your final-year project with a live link; and list any certifications that are directly relevant, such as a cloud fundamentals certification. Keep the design plain and the content specific. Avoid paid "premium" templates; content matters far more than design. How many pages should a fresher resume be? One page. A fresher rarely has enough relevant experience to fill two pages with strong content, and recruiters skim the first page in seconds. To fit one page, cut school-level details, generic skills, long objectives, course lists and hobbies that add nothing. Keep two or three bullets per project. If you have research publications or several substantial internships, a second page may be justified, but the first page must still carry your best evidence. A tight one-page resume also signals that you can prioritise, which employers value. Should I write "fresher" on my resume? You can mention it in a headline for roles that explicitly hire freshers, such as "Fresher Python Developer", but do not make it your selling point. Let projects, skills and results show what you can do. Also asked as: how to write fresher in resume Avoid phrases like "I am a fresher looking for an opportunity to learn", which say nothing about what you offer. Instead write a summary like "Final-year BCA student who has built and deployed three Python web apps, including a cited document assistant used by classmates." On job portals, choose "fresher" or "0 years experience" where the form asks, and let your profile content do the rest.

# From a BCA in India to GenAI engineer: how I got here, what actually mattered, and what I would tell my first-year self
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/from-bca-student-to-genai-engineer/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Can you become a GenAI engineer from a BCA at a college nobody has heard of?

**Yes. I did a Bachelor of Computer Applications at Dr. Virendra Swarup Institute of Computer Studies, 2023 to 2026, and by the first half of 2026 I had shipped five production AI systems as a GenAI engineer and was leading engineering for a 14-member team at SCULT INDIA. Not one interview that mattered asked about the college. Every one asked about what I had built and what broke. This page is the path, without the parts that make it sound inevitable.**


The full resume with dates is on the portfolio [1]. What follows is the version with the decisions in it.

> The certificate says BCA. The GitHub says five production AI apps, three first prizes, a 14-member team. Recruiters read the second document first when you give them a reason to.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What did the first year look like?

**Foundations, and a community that did not exist yet. In 2023 I started the BCA and started TechVerse Enclave, a developer community that began as a place for a few of us to learn web development together and became, over three years, a 500-plus member community where I have mentored more than 200 students. The first year was Python, JavaScript, Git, one deployed page, and the habit of teaching what I had learned the week before.**



That roadmap is the one I gave 100+ first-years at the VSICS induction in July 2025, because it is the one that worked, not the one that sounds impressive [8].

## How did the community change things?

**More than anything else. TechVerse Enclave started as a hackathon team and a group chat and became the place where I learned to teach, to organise, to run sessions and to be known for something. Mentoring 200 students meant answering the same questions until I understood them properly. The sessions I ran inside the community became the sessions colleges invited me to give. The people in it became teammates, clients and referrals. Every later opportunity traces back to it.**


The story of the first 500 members, with what worked and what did not, is written up separately [4]. The short version: the community did not grow because I promoted it; it grew because sessions happened every week whether five people or fifty showed up.

## What did hackathons teach that classes did not?

**Scope, demos and losing. Three first prizes: Changethon 2025 at the National Social Summit, IIT Roorkee, with KrishGyan, voice-first farming advice over WhatsApp; Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025, CSJMU, with BrandHive; and BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats, with Annapurna, surplus food coordination. A top-three at IIT Kanpur. And STROT, which we did not win, because we built more and explained less than the team that did. The loss is the one I quote most in talks.**



Everything I now teach about hackathon strategy comes from those four rooms [5].

## How did the first clients and SCULT INDIA happen?

**Through the community and through shipping small things well. SCULT INDIA is an AI-first software agency; from 2024 I led engineering for it, architecture, UI/UX, deployment and delivery for a 14-member cross-functional team, and designed SCULT Studio CRM, the internal platform that runs projects, clients and operations [9]. The client products came one at a time, a pest-control business site in Goa, a music label, a digital library, a media company, and each one taught delivery under a deadline, which no college project can.**


Leading fourteen people while still a student is its own story, mostly about saying no and writing things down [6].


## How did the GenAI role come, and what did it produce?

**From the portfolio. NextUpgrad Web Solutions hired me as a GenAI engineer for February to July 2026 on the strength of shipped systems, and in those six months I independently designed, built and shipped five production AI applications: RAG.NextUpgrad, a retrieval platform with hybrid search, reranking, streaming citations and a confidence gate; FineTune Studio, a QLoRA fine-tuning platform with live telemetry; DocuLens AI, schema-validated document extraction with deterministic compliance scoring; FaceVision, browser-only face recognition and liveness that stores embeddings, never images; and the OCR & Speech Workspace, page-batched OCR, live speech-to-text and document chat with page citations. All with Docker, CI/CD, structured logging and metrics [1][10].**


Six months, five systems, because the habits, shipping weekly, testing, writing READMEs, evaluating honestly, were already three years old. The role did not create the habits. The habits created the role.

## What actually mattered, in order?

**Shipping small things every week. A community to learn and teach inside. Hackathons for scope and demos. Real clients for delivery. Writing in public so people could find the work. Reading the papers that mattered with a notebook open. Saying yes to every session and judging invitation early. Applying before I felt ready. Not: the college's name, certificates, or waiting for a placement cell.**



## What would I tell my first-year self?

**Start the community in month one, not month six. Post the first project even though it is embarrassing; the embarrassment is the point. Go to the hackathon two hours away. Learn to write a README before learning a fourth framework. Talk to the strangers at events. Ask for the client work. Read the papers, they are shorter than the tutorials. And stop comparing your college to the ones with placement cells; compare your GitHub to theirs.**


The longer letter is on the portfolio [8]. Most of it is the list above, said more gently.

## Was it worth it, and what is next?

**Yes. The year of shipping, 2025 into 2026, produced the systems, the team and the sessions, and it produced this site: a hundred pages answering the questions students and engineers actually search, written from what I built [7]. Next is more of the same at a larger scale: GenAI roles and products, more campuses, more judging panels, and a community that outgrows me. If you are in a first-year seat in a college nobody has heard of, the path is open, and the first step is a project this week.**

# Where is the Gemini AI app? How to get it, use it, and is it safe
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gemini-ai-app-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The Gemini AI app is Google's assistant, available as an official app on Android from Google Play, on iPhone from the App Store, and in any browser at gemini.google.com. On many Android phones it has replaced Google Assistant as the default assistant. This page explains where to get it, whether there is a Windows app, how to use it, what it is good for, whether it is free, how the app differs from Gemini models, example prompts, and how to use it safely and spot fake versions.

## Where is the Gemini AI app?

On Android, get Gemini from Google Play; on iPhone, from the App Store; on a computer, open gemini.google.com in a browser. Check that the publisher is Google LLC before installing.

On many newer Android phones Gemini is already installed and opens when you hold the power button or say "Hey Google", depending on settings. On iPhone, the Gemini app is standalone, and you can also reach Gemini features through the Google app. On a laptop or desktop, the web version has the same core features as the mobile app, including file uploads and longer conversations, which makes it the best place for study and coding work.

## Does Gemini have an app?

Yes. Google publishes official Gemini apps for Android and iOS, and the full experience is available on the web. Gemini also appears inside Google products such as Gmail, Docs, Chrome and Android.

The apps let you chat by text or voice, use the camera to ask about what you see, upload photos and files, generate images and use Gemini Live for back-and-forth voice conversations. Your conversations sync across devices when you are signed in to the same Google account. If your college or employer uses Google Workspace, Gemini may also be available in your work account with different rules set by the administrator.

## Does Gemini have a Windows app?

Use Gemini on Windows through the browser at gemini.google.com. Chrome and Edge let you install the site as an app with its own window and taskbar icon, which works like a desktop app.

In Chrome, open Gemini, open the menu and choose the option to install the page as an app; in Edge, use the Apps menu to install the site. Google has experimented with desktop apps that bring Gemini and AI search to Windows, so check Google's official download pages for anything current. Avoid third-party "Gemini for Windows" downloads from unknown websites; they are a common way to spread malware or steal Google account sessions.

## How do I use the Gemini app?

Open the app, sign in with your Google account, and type or speak a request. Attach photos, files or screenshots with the plus button, and use Gemini Live for a voice conversation.

Tips that improve results:

- Give context: who you are, what you need and the format you want.
- Attach the material, such as lecture slides, a PDF or a photo of your notes.
- Use follow-ups to refine instead of starting over.
- Create a Gem, a custom assistant with saved instructions, for tasks you repeat.
- Turn on extensions such as Google Maps or YouTube when the answer needs them.

Try one real task a day for a week: a summary, a study plan, an explanation, a draft email and a coding question.

## What is the Gemini app used for?

People use the Gemini app to ask questions, learn and revise, write and edit, plan, summarise documents and videos, generate images, get coding help, and get answers about what the camera sees.

Useful examples for students and developers:

- Explaining a concept with examples and quizzing you on it.
- Summarising a long PDF or a YouTube lecture.
- Planning a study schedule or trip with Google Maps and Calendar context.
- Drafting emails and reports, then making them shorter or more formal.
- Debugging an error message and explaining code.
- Deep Research for a cited overview of a topic.

Its strongest advantage is integration with Google services you already use, such as Gmail, Drive, Docs, Maps and YouTube.

## Is the Gemini AI tool free?

Yes. The Gemini app is free to use with a Google account, with daily limits on the most capable model and some features. Paid Google AI plans raise the limits and add features such as more advanced models, Deep Research capacity and video generation.

The free tier is enough for most learning and everyday tasks. Google has also run student offers and telecom partnerships in India that include paid plans at no cost for a period; check Google's official pages for current eligibility. Developers can use Gemini models through Google AI Studio with free quotas for prototyping. Watch out for websites selling "Gemini Pro" access; buy only through Google or official partners.

## What is the difference between Gemini models and the Gemini app?

Gemini models are Google's family of AI models, in tiers such as Flash and Pro. The Gemini app is the consumer product built on those models, adding a chat interface, history, extensions, file handling and safety features.

Developers use the models directly through the Gemini API or Google AI Studio, choosing a model, writing a system instruction and building their own interface. App users get Google's choices of model, tools and settings. The same model may behave differently in each place because of different instructions, tools and limits. If you are building a project, prototype prompts in AI Studio, where you can see and control the settings, rather than in the app.

## What is a good example of a Gemini AI prompt?

A good prompt says who you are, what you want, the context and the format. For example: "I am a second-year BCA student. Explain how a hash table works with a simple example in Python, then give me three practice questions without answers."

More examples:

- "Summarise this PDF in ten bullet points for revision, then list five likely exam questions."
- "Here is my resume and a job description. List the skills I am missing and suggest one project for each."
- "Plan a seven-day study schedule for these four subjects; I can study three hours a day."
- "Look at this photo of my circuit and tell me what might be wrong."

If an answer is too general, add constraints such as word count, audience or examples.

## Is the Gemini AI app safe?

The official Gemini app is safe to install and use with normal care. Google applies security protections, but your conversations may be stored and, as Google states, some may be reviewed by trained reviewers to improve the service, so do not share confidential information.

Practical steps: review your Gemini activity settings to control how long conversations are saved and whether they are used to improve Google's services; delete conversations you no longer need; never enter passwords, OTPs, bank details or identity numbers; and check important answers, especially health, legal and financial ones, with official sources. On work accounts, your organisation's settings apply. Gemini can make mistakes, which the app itself notes.

## Is the Gemini app legit?

Yes, the Gemini app published by Google LLC on Google Play and the App Store is legitimate and official. Fake apps and websites using the Gemini name also exist, so check the publisher and the website address.

Signs of a fake: a developer name other than Google LLC, requests to pay for "Gemini Pro" outside Google's own billing, websites that are not on google.com domains asking you to sign in, and downloads for Windows from unknown sites. Fake AI apps are a common way to steal accounts or show aggressive ads. If you installed something suspicious, uninstall it, change your Google password, and review your account's security and connected apps in your Google Account settings.

# Which Gemini API is free? Models, limits, billing and how to call it
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gemini-api-free-tier/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The free Gemini API is the Gemini Developer API used with a key from Google AI Studio: several Gemini models are available on a free tier with rate limits, and you pay only if you enable billing for higher limits or certain models. This page explains what is free and what is paid, the model tiers, why developers choose the Gemini API, how to call it, the API URL, when limits reset, how to give it internet access, and why responses can be slow.

## Which Google Gemini API is free?

The Gemini Developer API, accessed with an API key from Google AI Studio, has a free tier. It covers several current models, typically the Flash and Flash-Lite tiers and sometimes Pro, within per-minute and per-day request limits.

To start, sign in to Google AI Studio with a Google account, create an API key, and call the API from your code or test prompts in the Studio interface. The free tier is generous enough for learning, college projects and prototypes. Two conditions matter: limits are low for production traffic, and Google's terms say free-tier prompts and responses may be used to improve its products, so avoid sending sensitive data on the free tier. Vertex AI on Google Cloud is the enterprise route and is billed from the start, often with new-account credits.

## Is the Gemini API paid?

It has both. The free tier costs nothing within its limits; the paid tier, enabled by linking a billing account, charges per token for input and output, with much higher rate limits and data that is not used to improve Google's products.

Paid usage is billed by tokens processed, with different rates for each model, for long prompts, and for extras such as grounding with search, context caching and media generation. You can set budgets and alerts in Google Cloud billing to avoid surprises. A practical path for students: build and test on the free tier, then enable billing only when you have real users or need higher limits. Check the pricing page for current rates, which change as models are released.

## Which Gemini API model is free?

Most current Flash and Flash-Lite models are available on the free tier, and some Pro models have been offered with tight free limits. Image, video and audio generation models and the newest previews may be paid only.

The rate-limits page in the documentation lists, for each model, the free-tier requests per minute, tokens per minute and requests per day, and AI Studio shows your project's current limits. Because Google rotates models, a model that is free today may be replaced or deprecated later, so avoid hard-coding assumptions; read the model name from configuration so you can switch quickly. For most projects, a Flash model is the best free choice: fast, capable and with the most room in its limits.

## What are the Gemini API models?

The Gemini API offers model tiers: Flash-Lite for the cheapest, fastest high-volume tasks, Flash for most applications, and Pro for complex reasoning and coding. Specialised models cover embeddings, image generation, speech generation and live audio conversations.

Each generation brings new versions of these tiers, with stable versions for production and preview versions for early access. Many models support thinking, where the model reasons before answering, with settings to control how much. Most accept text, images, audio, video and PDFs as input and support long context windows. The models page lists current names, context limits and capabilities; for embeddings, use the dedicated Gemini embedding model rather than a chat model.

## Why use the Gemini API?

Developers choose the Gemini API for a generous free tier, strong multimodal input including video and long audio, very long context windows, built-in grounding with Google Search, and competitive pricing on Flash models.

Good fits:

- Apps that analyse PDFs, images, audio or video in one call.
- High-volume tasks where Flash or Flash-Lite keeps costs low.
- Answers that need current web information through search grounding.
- Prototypes, since AI Studio lets you design and export prompts quickly.

Weigh it like any provider: test quality on your own task, check latency from your users' region, and design for switching. In RAG.NextUpgrad I used multi-provider fallback, so one provider's outage or slowdown does not take the product down.

## How do I call the Gemini API?

Install Google's official SDK, set your API key as an environment variable, and call `generate_content` with a model name and your prompt.

```bash
pip install google-genai
export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key"
```

```python
from google import genai

client = genai.Client()   # reads GEMINI_API_KEY
resp = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    contents="Explain retrieval-augmented generation in three sentences.",
)
print(resp.text)
```

The SDK also supports streaming, chat sessions, file uploads, structured JSON output with a schema, function calling and system instructions. SDKs exist for JavaScript, Go and Java too. Check the models page for the newest model names before you start a project.

## What is the Gemini API URL?

The Gemini Developer API base URL is `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com`. A typical request goes to `/v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent`, with your API key in the `x-goog-api-key` header.

A raw HTTP call looks like this:

```bash
curl "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/gemini-2.5-flash:generateContent" \
  -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"contents":[{"parts":[{"text":"Hello"}]}]}'
```

Use `streamGenerateContent` for streaming responses, and the `v1` path instead of `v1beta` when you only need stable features. Vertex AI uses a different, region-based endpoint on Google Cloud with service-account authentication instead of an API key. Never put your API key in front-end code or a mobile app, where anyone can extract it; call the API from your own backend and keep the key in an environment variable.

## When does the Gemini API limit reset?

Daily request quotas reset at midnight Pacific time. Per-minute limits on requests and tokens work as rolling windows, so they recover within a minute of easing off.

When you exceed a limit, the API returns a `429` error with a resource-exhausted status. Handle it with retries using exponential backoff and jitter, and queue work instead of sending bursts. To avoid hitting limits: cache repeated results, batch work where possible, use smaller models for simple tasks, and enable billing for higher tiers when you have real traffic. AI Studio shows your project's limits and usage, so check there before assuming you are blocked for other reasons.

## Can the Gemini API access the internet?

Not by default, but you can enable grounding with Google Search as a tool. The model then searches when needed, answers with current information, and returns citations and search suggestions in the response metadata.

Add the Google Search tool in your request configuration, and the model decides when to search. There is also a URL context tool that lets the model read specific web pages you provide. Grounding adds latency and may have separate pricing and limits, so enable it only for questions that need current information. Display the returned sources to users, both for trust and because Google's terms set requirements for showing search suggestions.

## Why is the Gemini API slow?

Responses slow down because of thinking time on reasoning-capable models, long prompts or files, large outputs, search grounding, peak load, or network distance. Each has a fix.

Ways to speed it up:

- Lower or disable the thinking budget for simple tasks, or use Flash-Lite.
- Stream responses so users see text immediately.
- Shorten prompts and send only relevant context; cache repeated long context.
- Limit the maximum output tokens to what you need.
- Use grounding only when current information is required.
- Measure latency per step to find the actual bottleneck.

If slowness is sudden and widespread, check Google's status pages and retry with backoff.

# What does Gemini Canvas do? Notebooks, models and how Gemini helps users
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gemini-canvas-notebooks-models/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Gemini Canvas is a workspace inside the Gemini app where you write and edit documents or code alongside Gemini, with the draft in its own panel and live previews for web code. Notebooks, in Google's ecosystem, usually means NotebookLM, which answers questions only from the sources you upload. This page explains how both work, which Gemini model to pick for general work and for coding, when Gemini launched worldwide and in India, and how Gemini helps draft emails in Gmail and slides in Google Slides.

## What does Gemini Canvas do?

Canvas gives you a dedicated editing space next to the chat. Gemini writes a document or code there, and you refine it together: highlight a section to change, adjust tone or length, or run and preview code such as a web page.

It is useful for longer pieces you will iterate on: an essay outline, a project report, a cover letter, a Python script or a small HTML app. For code, Canvas can show a live preview of web projects, so you can see a landing page or a simple game working and ask for changes. Canvas can also turn content into other formats, such as a web page or quiz, and export documents to Google Docs. It replaces the clumsy pattern of copying code from the chat into a file and back.

## How does Gemini Canvas work?

Select Canvas in the Gemini prompt bar, describe what you want, and Gemini opens the draft in a side panel. You then chat to revise it, or edit the draft directly, and Gemini updates the canvas rather than writing a new answer each time.

Useful moves inside Canvas:

- Highlight a paragraph and ask for it to be simpler, shorter or more formal.
- Ask for a specific change: "add error handling to the fetch call".
- Preview web code and describe what looks wrong.
- Export a document to Google Docs to keep editing there.

Keep the scope small, one document or one small app per canvas, and save versions you like before asking for big changes.

## What are Gemini notebooks?

In Google's AI tools, notebooks usually refer to NotebookLM: a research assistant where you create a notebook, add sources such as PDFs, Google Docs, websites or YouTube videos, and ask questions that are answered only from those sources, with citations.

Google has been connecting NotebookLM with the Gemini app, so you can work with notebook material inside Gemini as well. For students, NotebookLM is one of the best free study tools: add your lecture notes, textbook chapters and past papers, then ask for summaries, explanations, study guides or quizzes. Because answers come from your sources and link to the exact passages, they are easier to trust and check than general chatbot answers. It also creates audio overviews, a podcast-style discussion of your material.

## How do Gemini notebooks work?

You create a notebook in NotebookLM, upload or link sources, and ask questions. NotebookLM retrieves the relevant passages from your sources and has Gemini answer from them, citing each claim back to the source text.

This is retrieval-augmented generation scoped to your own material, the same principle behind the document chat I built in the OCR & Speech Workspace, where answers cite page numbers. Tips: keep one notebook per subject or project, add only sources you trust, and ask specific questions such as "compare the two definitions of normalisation in these notes". Click the citations to verify. Generated study guides and quizzes are good for revision, but check them against the sources before an exam.

## Which Gemini model is best?

For everyday tasks, Flash is best: fast and capable. For hard problems such as complex coding, maths and analysis, the Pro tier or a thinking mode is best. The newest generation of each tier is usually better than the previous one.

The Gemini app chooses a model automatically unless you pick one, and the options shown depend on your plan. Developers choose explicitly in the Gemini API: Flash-Lite for the cheapest high-volume tasks, Flash as the default for most products, and Pro for the hardest requests. A good production pattern is to start with Flash, measure where it fails, and route only those cases to Pro. Google's models page lists the current versions, which change several times a year.

## Which Gemini model is best for coding?

Use the most capable Pro model available to you, ideally with thinking enabled, for debugging, architecture and multi-file changes. Flash is fine for quick snippets, explanations and simple scripts.

For real projects, the model matters less than the tool. Google's coding tools, such as Gemini CLI, Gemini Code Assist in your editor and Antigravity, can read your whole project, run commands and tests, and propose edits, which makes their output far more reliable than code from a chat window. Whatever you use, give precise tasks, include error messages, keep a project context file with build and test commands, and review every change. Compare against other coding tools on one real task before settling.

## When was Gemini AI launched?

Google announced the Gemini model family in December 2023. Its chatbot Bard, launched in early 2023, was renamed Gemini in February 2024, when the Gemini app also arrived on Android and iPhone.

Since then Google has released several model generations with improvements in reasoning, coding, long context and multimodal understanding, added Gemini to Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Android and Chrome, and launched developer tools including AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini CLI and Antigravity. The technical report on the first generation describes models trained to handle text, images, audio and video together, a design choice that shapes how Gemini works with media today.

## When did Gemini launch in India?

Google's AI chatbot was available in India from 2023, under the Bard name, and the Gemini app launched in India in 2024 with support for English and several Indian languages.

Language support has expanded since, and Gemini works in Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam and Urdu, among others, which makes it useful for students and users more comfortable in their own language. Google has also run offers in India, including free plans for eligible students and a partnership with Jio. On Android phones in India, Gemini increasingly replaces Google Assistant as the default assistant. Check Google's Gemini help pages for the current list of languages and features.

## How does Gemini help users draft an email?

In Gmail, Gemini drafts an email from a short prompt with "Help me write", suggests replies in context, and can refine a draft to be more formal, shorter or more detailed. It can also summarise a long thread before you reply.

Write prompts that include the recipient, purpose and tone, for example "email my professor asking for a two-day extension for the project, polite and brief, mention I was unwell". Review the draft for facts: Gemini may add details or commitments you did not intend. For important emails, read it aloud once; if it does not sound like you, edit it. In Google Workspace accounts, administrators control which Gemini features are available.

## How does Gemini AI help users in slide creation?

In Google Slides, Gemini can generate slide content and layouts from a prompt, create images for slides, and help rewrite text. It speeds up the first draft, while you still shape the story and check every fact.

A good workflow: write a one-paragraph brief for the deck, its audience and key message; ask Gemini for an outline of eight to ten slides; generate slides one at a time and edit them; add your own data, screenshots and examples; and cut words, since slides work best with very little text. For college presentations, prepare speaker notes in your own words, because evaluators ask questions about what you present. Gemini-generated images should be labelled when they could be mistaken for real photos.
