# What is Gemini CLI, and why do Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Cursor have limits?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gemini-cli-and-ai-limits/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Gemini CLI is Google's open-source AI agent for the command line. You run it in a project folder, describe a task, and it uses Gemini models to read files, run commands and make edits, asking for approval as it goes. It competes with Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex CLI and GitHub Copilot CLI. The second half of this page explains why Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Cursor all limit how much you can use them, including file and image uploads, and how to work within those limits.

## Gemini CLI vs other coding CLIs: how do they compare?

Gemini CLI, Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex CLI and GitHub Copilot CLI are all terminal agents that read your codebase, edit files and run commands. They differ mainly in the models behind them, pricing and free tiers, and extras such as integrations.

Gemini CLI is open source and offers a free tier with a personal Google account, which makes it popular with students. Claude Code is widely used for complex multi-file work and has a large ecosystem of extensions. Codex CLI is open source and works with a ChatGPT plan or API key. Copilot CLI fits teams already on GitHub Copilot. All support the Model Context Protocol for extra tools. The honest way to choose is one real task in your own repository with each, judged on correctness and how much fixing the result needs.

## How does Gemini CLI work?

Gemini CLI runs a reason-and-act loop: it reads your request, decides which tool to use, such as reading a file, searching code, running a shell command or fetching a web page, observes the result, and repeats until the task is done.

Built-in tools cover the file system, shell commands, web fetch and Google Search grounding, and you can add more through MCP servers. A `GEMINI.md` file in your project gives it persistent context: build commands, conventions and rules. Before risky actions such as editing files or running commands, it asks for confirmation unless you change that setting. Because it sees your whole project and can run tests, its changes are more likely to work than code pasted from a chat window, but every diff still needs review.

## Is there a Gemini CLI tutorial?

Yes. The official repository's documentation covers installation and features, and a first session takes about ten minutes.

```bash
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
cd my-project
gemini
```

Sign in with your Google account when prompted, then try:

- "Explain this project's structure and how to run the tests."
- Create a `GEMINI.md` with the test command and coding rules.
- "Add input validation to the signup route and write a test for it."
- Review each proposed edit and command before approving.
- Run the tests yourself and commit.

Work in a Git repository so you can roll back anything you do not like.

## Is there a course for Gemini CLI?

Google's official documentation and codelabs are the best free starting points, and some online learning platforms offer short courses on Gemini CLI and AI coding agents. A course matters less than using the tool on a real project.

Look for courses that teach transferable skills: writing a good context file, breaking work into small tasks, connecting MCP servers, reviewing diffs and testing agent output. Those apply equally to Claude Code, Codex and Copilot. A practical self-made course: spend a week building a small FastAPI or Next.js app entirely through an agent, keeping notes on which prompts worked, where it went wrong and how you fixed it. That record is also good material for interviews and a blog post.

## Can Gemini CLI handle a complex RAG migration?

It can help a lot with a complex migration, such as moving a RAG system to a new vector store, embedding model or framework, if you break the work into stages, keep tests at every step and review each change.

A workable plan for any coding agent:

- Write the migration plan first and save it in the repository.
- Build an evaluation set of questions with known good answers before changing anything.
- Migrate one component at a time: ingestion, embeddings, index, retrieval, generation.
- After each stage, re-run the evaluation and compare retrieval recall and answer quality.
- Keep the old path working behind a flag until the new one matches it.

When I built RAG.NextUpgrad, the evaluation set was what made changes safe; without one, an agent can produce a migration that looks clean but quietly retrieves worse passages.

## Does Gemini have a limit?

Yes. The Gemini app has daily limits on prompts with the most capable models and on features such as Deep Research, image and video generation. Free accounts have lower limits than paid Google AI plans, and the API has separate rate limits.

When you reach a limit, Gemini usually switches to a faster model or tells you when the limit resets. Limits are counted per feature, so you might still use the fast model after exhausting the Pro allowance. Google lists the current limits in the Gemini Apps help centre, and they change as plans are updated. Developers using AI Studio or the Gemini API see rate limits per minute and per day for their project, which rise with paid usage tiers.

## Does Gemini have a limit for uploading images?

Yes. Gemini limits how many files and images you can upload per prompt and the maximum file size, and some limits differ between free and paid plans. The Gemini Apps help centre lists the current numbers.

If an upload fails, reduce the number of images per message, compress large photos, or combine screenshots into one image or PDF. For many pages of notes, a single PDF often works better than many photos. Image generation also has its own daily limit, separate from uploads. Developers using the Gemini API have different limits for inline images versus files uploaded through the Files API, which suits larger media. Check the documentation for the version you are using.

## Why does ChatGPT have a limit?

ChatGPT has limits because every reply uses expensive computing power, especially with the most capable and reasoning models. Limits share capacity fairly among users, keep the service responsive at busy times, and separate free and paid tiers.

Different features have separate limits: messages with advanced models, image generation, deep research, file uploads and agent tasks. When you hit one, ChatGPT may switch you to a lighter model until the limit resets. To get more from your allowance, write one clear, complete prompt instead of many small follow-ups, use the faster model for simple tasks, and start new chats instead of extending very long ones, which cost more to process. OpenAI's help centre lists the current limits per plan.

## Why does Claude AI have a limit?

Claude has usage limits because running large models costs significant computing resources, and longer conversations cost more, since Claude rereads the whole conversation with each reply. Limits keep the service available for everyone.

Claude's limits are measured over rolling time windows, and long chats with large attachments use your allowance faster than short ones. To stretch it: start a new chat for each task, use Projects to hold reference files instead of re-uploading them, keep prompts focused, and choose a lighter model for simple work. Paid plans raise limits substantially, and Claude Code usage counts against the same plan. Developers using the API pay per token and have rate limits that rise with usage tiers.

## Does Cursor AI have a limit?

Yes. Cursor's plans include a usage allowance for AI requests, with the most capable models costing more of it per request. Free plans have tighter limits, and paid plans include more, with options to pay for extra usage.

Cursor has changed how it meters usage more than once, so check its pricing page and the usage dashboard in your account for the current rules. Agent sessions with large context and premium models use the allowance fastest. To make it last, select a cheaper model for routine edits, point the agent at the right files rather than the whole repository, use a `.cursorignore` file to keep build outputs and data out of context, and keep sessions focused on one task.

# What is Gemini Live? Using Gemini on your phone, and Gemini tutorials
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gemini-live-and-phone-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Gemini Live is the real-time voice mode of Google's Gemini assistant: you talk naturally, interrupt whenever you like, and Gemini answers out loud; you can also share your camera or screen so it can see what you are looking at. On Android it is built into the phone's assistant; on iPhone it is in the Gemini app. This page explains how Live works, how to find and use Gemini on your phone, whether you can remove it, and short tutorials for Gemini in general, PDFs, Veo video generation and notebooks.

## What is Gemini Live?

Gemini Live is a conversational voice mode where you speak with Gemini in real time, as in a phone call. You can interrupt it, change topic, and ask follow-ups, and it keeps the conversation's context.

Live also lets you share your camera, so Gemini can talk about what it sees, such as a plant, a circuit board or a menu in another language, and your screen, so it can help with what you are looking at. It is useful for practising interviews or spoken English, brainstorming while walking, learning a topic by asking questions aloud, or getting help with something physical in front of you. Transcripts of Live conversations appear in your Gemini history.

## How does Gemini Live work?

Gemini Live streams your voice to Google's servers, where a Gemini model built for low-latency audio understands speech and generates a spoken reply, while listening for interruptions. Camera and screen sharing add a live video feed to the conversation.

Because it is designed for conversation, it uses natural turn-taking: it stops when you start speaking and picks up from where you interrupted. It needs an internet connection and uses mobile data, so expect higher data use on video. Voice options are in settings. Developers can build similar real-time voice and video experiences with the Gemini Live API. As with any assistant, check important facts it states aloud, since spoken answers are harder to verify at a glance.

## Where is Gemini on my phone?

On most recent Android phones, Gemini is the default assistant: hold the power button, swipe up from a bottom corner, or say "Hey Google". It is also an app called Gemini in your app drawer. On iPhone, open the Gemini app from the App Store.

If you do not see it on Android, update the Google app and Play Store apps, or install Gemini from Google Play. Some phones, such as certain Samsung models, also add a Gemini shortcut to the side button. On iPhone you can add Gemini to the Lock Screen or use a Shortcut to open it quickly. Make sure you install the official app published by Google LLC; fake "Gemini" apps exist.

## How do I use Gemini on an Android phone?

Open Gemini from the power button, a corner swipe or the app, then type, speak or tap the Live button for a voice conversation. Use the camera and screen options to ask about what you see.

Things worth trying:

- "Summarise this page" while a long article is on screen.
- Circle to Search on supported phones to ask about anything on screen.
- "Set a reminder to submit the assignment at 6 pm tomorrow."
- Photograph your notes and ask for a summary or quiz.
- Ask about a YouTube video while it plays, where supported.

Connected apps, such as Google Maps, Calendar, Keep and YouTube, let Gemini act on your behalf. Review which apps it can access in Gemini's settings.

## How does Gemini work on my phone?

Gemini on your phone sends your requests to Google's Gemini models in the cloud, uses on-device models for some quick features, and connects to apps such as Calendar, Messages, Maps and YouTube when you allow it.

Most answers come from cloud models, so an internet connection is needed. Some phones also run Gemini Nano, a small on-device model, for features such as summarising recordings or smart replies, which work faster and keep data on the device. When you ask Gemini to do something in another app, it uses that app's permissions. Your conversations are saved to your Google account according to your activity settings, which you can change or turn off in Gemini's privacy settings.

## Can I remove Gemini from my phone?

On most Android phones you can switch the default digital assistant away from Gemini in settings, and disable or uninstall the Gemini app. Whether you can fully remove it depends on your phone and Android version.

Look in Settings, then Apps, then Default apps, then Digital assistant app, to change the assistant. To stop Gemini opening from the power button, change the power button setting. If the Gemini app came preinstalled as a system app, you may only be able to disable it or uninstall its updates. Google has been replacing Google Assistant with Gemini on Android, so switching back may not be available on every device. On iPhone, simply delete the app.

## Is there a Gemini tutorial for beginners?

Yes. Google's Gemini help centre has guides for each feature, and the fastest way to learn is to try five everyday tasks in your first week.

A beginner's week:

- **Day 1**: ask Gemini to explain a topic you are studying and quiz you.
- **Day 2**: upload a PDF and ask for a one-page summary.
- **Day 3**: use Gemini Live to practise answering interview questions aloud.
- **Day 4**: create a Gem, a custom assistant with saved instructions, for a task you repeat.
- **Day 5**: connect Google Calendar and plan your week.

Write prompts with context: who you are, what you need and the format you want. Check facts in every answer.

## How do I use Gemini with a PDF?

Upload the PDF in the Gemini app with the plus button, then ask questions: a summary, explanations of difficult sections, key terms, or practice questions. Gemini can read long documents and point you to relevant parts.

Good prompts for study:

- "Summarise this chapter in ten bullet points for revision."
- "Explain section 3.2 as if I am new to the topic, with an example."
- "List all definitions in this PDF as a glossary."
- "Write five exam-style questions from this document, then check my answers."

For scanned PDFs, Gemini can read the images, but accuracy drops with poor scans. For courses with many documents, NotebookLM is often better, because it keeps sources together and cites the exact passages.

## How do I use Veo 3 in Gemini?

In the Gemini app, choose the video option, describe the scene you want, and Gemini generates a short clip with Google's Veo model, including sound. Access depends on your plan and country, and there are daily limits.

Write prompts like a director: subject, action, setting, camera movement, lighting, style and sound, for example "a slow dolly shot of a student coding at night in a small hostel room, warm desk lamp, rain on the window, soft keyboard sounds". Generate several versions and keep the best. Clips are short, so plan longer videos as several shots edited together. Generated videos carry a visible or invisible watermark; label them as AI-generated when you share them, and never create videos of real people without consent.

## How do I use Gemini notebooks?

Notebooks in Google's AI tools usually means NotebookLM: create a notebook, add sources such as PDFs, Docs, websites or YouTube videos, then ask questions answered only from those sources, with citations. Google has also been connecting notebooks to the Gemini app.

A study workflow: create one notebook per subject, add your syllabus, lecture notes and textbook chapters, and ask for a study guide, a list of likely exam questions, and explanations of the hardest topics. Click citations to check each answer against your material. Audio overviews turn your sources into a podcast-style discussion you can listen to while travelling. Keep sources accurate and current, because answers are only as good as what you upload.

# How to get Gemini Pro for free, and what Gemini Pro offers
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gemini-pro-free-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


You can use Gemini Pro for free in three ways: the free Gemini app gives limited access to Google's Pro model, Google AI Studio lets developers try Pro models with free quotas, and Google has run time-limited offers that include the paid Google AI Pro plan at no cost for eligible students and for some telecom customers in India, such as Jio users. This page explains those routes, what the Pro plan adds, how Gemini, Flash, Pro and thinking modes differ, daily limits, family sharing, and how Gemini relates to Antigravity.

## How can I get Gemini Pro for free?

Use the free Gemini app, which includes limited access to the Pro model, use Google AI Studio for free developer access, or claim an official offer that includes Google AI Pro at no cost if you are eligible.

The options in order of effort:

- **Free Gemini app**: sign in at gemini.google.com or the mobile app; free accounts get some Pro model use with lower limits.
- **Google AI Studio**: a developer playground where you can try current models, including Pro, with free usage quotas.
- **Official offers**: Google has run student offers and telecom partnerships that include the paid plan for a limited period.

Offers change often, so confirm eligibility on Google's own pages. Avoid "free Gemini Pro" links shared in groups; they are a common route for phishing and account theft.

## Is Gemini Pro free for students?

Google has offered its paid AI plan free for a limited period to students in several countries, including India, through verification with a college email or student ID. Whether an offer is open today depends on the country and date.

When an offer is live, you sign in with a personal Google account, verify student status through Google's verification partner, and the plan is applied for the stated period. It usually renews at the normal rate afterwards unless you cancel, so note the end date. Even without an offer, students can do a lot on the free tier: explaining concepts, debugging code, summarising lecture notes and planning projects. NotebookLM, also from Google, is free and very good for studying from your own notes and papers.

## How do I get Gemini Pro with Jio?

Reliance Jio and Google announced a partnership in 2025 that gives eligible Jio users access to Google AI Pro at no cost for a limited period. Eligible users claim it from the MyJio app with the Google account they want to use.

Open the MyJio app, look for the Google Gemini or Google AI Pro offer banner, check the eligibility conditions, which have depended on age group and plan, and follow the steps to link your Google account. The benefit then appears in the Gemini app and Google One. Rules, eligible plans and duration are set by Jio and Google and have changed since launch, so rely on the MyJio app and Google's announcement, not on screenshots shared online. Never enter OTPs or passwords on links that claim to unlock the offer.

## What does Gemini Pro offer?

The Google AI Pro plan gives higher access to Google's most capable Gemini models, longer context for big files, Deep Research, video and image generation with higher limits, Gemini inside Gmail and Docs, NotebookLM with higher limits, and extra cloud storage.

For students and developers the useful parts are:

- More use of the Pro model and thinking modes for hard maths and code.
- Deep Research, which browses many sources and writes a cited report.
- Uploading long PDFs and codebases thanks to a large context window.
- Gemini in Gmail, Docs and Sheets for drafting and analysis.
- Higher limits in Google's coding tools.

The exact feature list and limits change as Google updates the plan, so check the plan page on Google One. If you mostly ask quick questions, the free tier is enough.

## What is the difference between Gemini and Gemini Pro?

Gemini is Google's family of AI models and the name of its assistant app. Gemini Pro refers either to the Pro model, the most capable tier in a Gemini generation, or to the Google AI Pro subscription that gives more access to it.

The model family has tiers: Flash-Lite for the cheapest, fastest tasks, Flash for most everyday work, and Pro for complex reasoning and coding. Some generations also add a deeper thinking mode on top. The Gemini app picks a model for you unless you choose one. The subscription changes your limits and features, not the model itself: a free user and a paid user asking the Pro model the same question get the same quality of answer, but the free user runs out sooner.

## What is the difference between Gemini Flash and Pro?

Flash is the faster, cheaper model tuned for everyday tasks and high volume. Pro is the more capable model for complex reasoning, difficult code and long multi-step work, and it is slower and more expensive per request.

In practice:

- Use **Flash** for summaries, emails, quick explanations, extraction from documents and chat features in your app.
- Use **Pro** for debugging a tricky bug, designing a system, solving hard maths, or long analysis where a wrong step costs more than waiting.

For developers building with the Gemini API, Flash is usually the right default because latency and cost matter at scale. Start with Flash, measure where it fails, and route only those cases to Pro. That routing pattern is how most production AI apps keep costs under control.

## When should I use Gemini Pro vs thinking mode?

Pro is a model tier; thinking is a way of running a model, where it reasons step by step before answering. Use a thinking mode when the task needs several steps of logic, and a standard fast mode when it does not.

Thinking helps with maths and physics problems, competitive programming, debugging, planning a project and comparing options with many constraints. It adds waiting time and uses more of your limits, so it is wasted on simple questions, rewriting text or quick facts. If an answer from the fast mode seems shallow or contradicts itself, rerun the same prompt with thinking on. For developers, the Gemini API exposes thinking controls on models that support it, so you can set how much reasoning to spend per request.

## How many Gemini Pro queries do I get per day?

It depends on your plan: free accounts get a small daily allowance of Pro model prompts, and paid plans get much more. Google lists the current limits in the Gemini Apps help centre, and they change from time to time.

Limits are also counted per feature: Pro model prompts, Deep Research reports, image generation and video generation each have their own allowance. When you reach a limit, the app usually falls back to a faster model or asks you to wait. To stretch a free allowance, use Flash for routine tasks, write one clear, complete prompt instead of many short follow-ups, and save Pro and thinking for the problems that need them. Developers using the API have separate rate limits shown in Google AI Studio.

## Can I share Gemini Pro with family?

Partly. Google AI Pro is a Google One plan, and its cloud storage can be shared with up to five family members in a Google One family group. Whether the Gemini features are shared too depends on the plan and country.

Set up a family group from your Google account, invite members, then enable sharing in Google One settings. Each member keeps their own private files and chats; sharing never exposes your Gemini conversations or Drive files to others. Google has been extending AI benefits to family members in some regions, so check the Google One help pages for your country before assuming everyone in the group gets Pro features. Offer-based plans, such as student or telecom offers, may have their own sharing rules.

## Does Gemini Pro include Antigravity?

Antigravity is Google's agent-first coding environment and is offered separately from the Gemini app. Individuals have been able to use it without a paid plan within rate limits, and Google AI subscriptions have come with higher limits.

Antigravity runs coding agents that plan and carry out tasks across an editor, a terminal and a browser, using Gemini models and some models from other providers. Because it is new, its pricing, limits and the benefits attached to Google AI plans have changed several times, so check Google's Antigravity site and the plan page before deciding. For learning to code with AI, the free options, such as Antigravity's free limits, Gemini in the browser, or Gemini Code Assist's free tier for individuals, are usually enough.

# Why does Gemini add a watermark? SynthID, images, text, and who owns Gemini
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gemini-watermark-synthid/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Gemini adds watermarks so that images, video and audio it generates can be recognised as AI-made. Many images carry a small visible Gemini mark, and Google embeds an invisible digital watermark called SynthID in generated media, designed to survive cropping, compression and filters. This page explains why, how it applies to edited photos and to text, how to check for watermarks, why removing them is a bad idea, who made and owns Gemini, and the real risks of using it.

## Why does Gemini add a watermark?

To make AI-generated content identifiable. As generated images and videos become realistic, watermarks help people, platforms and fact-checkers tell synthetic media from real photos and footage, reducing misinformation and misuse.

Google uses two layers. A visible mark tells viewers at a glance that an image came from Gemini. SynthID, developed by Google DeepMind, embeds an imperceptible signal in the content that detection tools can read even after common edits. Google has also joined industry efforts on content provenance, such as the C2PA standard, which attaches information about how content was made. Watermarking is part of responsible deployment and increasingly expected by platforms and regulators.

## Why does Gemini add a watermark to images?

Generated and AI-edited images can be mistaken for real photos, so Gemini marks them. A visible watermark appears on many images created in the Gemini app, and SynthID is embedded invisibly in the pixels.

The invisible watermark matters more than the visible one: a logo can be cropped out, but SynthID is designed to remain detectable after resizing, compression, colour changes and screenshots, though no watermark is impossible to defeat. Whether a visible mark appears can depend on the product, plan and feature, and Google has changed this over time. For professional use, check the current terms for your plan, and in any case disclose that an image is AI-generated when it could mislead.

## Does Gemini put a watermark on photos you edit?

Yes. When Gemini edits a photo with AI, the result is treated as AI-generated or AI-modified media and receives SynthID, and often a visible mark, even though it started as your own photo.

That is intentional: an edited photo with a changed background, added objects or altered faces is exactly the kind of image that could mislead if presented as unedited. For harmless uses, such as a cleaner background for a project poster, the watermark simply records the edit. For official documents, such as ID or passport photos, do not use AI edits at all; use a real photo and approved tools. Never edit images of other people in ways they have not agreed to.

## Does Gemini add a watermark to text?

Google has developed SynthID for text, which subtly adjusts how the model chooses words to embed a statistical signal, and it has applied this in its Gemini products. Unlike images, text watermarks are fragile and do not prove authorship.

Text watermarking works by nudging token choices in a way that is invisible to readers but detectable statistically over enough text. Heavy editing, paraphrasing, translation or very short passages weaken the signal. Google published the method and open-sourced a version for developers. For students, the key point is that neither watermarks nor "AI detectors" are reliable judges of whether an essay was AI-written; follow your college's rules on AI use and be transparent about how you used it.

## Can you tell if text was written by Gemini?

Not reliably by reading it, and not reliably with public AI detectors, which produce many false positives, including on genuine human writing. SynthID text detection exists, but it needs access to the watermark scheme and enough unedited text.

Signs often cited, such as generic phrasing, certain words or very even structure, appear in human writing too, so they are weak evidence. If you are a teacher or reviewer, ask the writer to explain their work, show drafts or discuss the topic; understanding is the real test. If you are a student using AI, keep your notes and drafts, write in your own voice, and declare AI assistance where required. Accusations based only on detector scores are unfair and often wrong.

## How do I check for a Gemini watermark?

Look for the visible Gemini mark on the image, and use Google's SynthID verification tools, which Google has made available for checking whether content contains its watermark, including through the Gemini app for images.

Upload or share the image to the verification feature and it reports whether SynthID was detected. A negative result does not prove an image is real: it may come from another AI tool that uses no watermark, or the watermark may have been damaged. Provenance metadata under the C2PA standard can also show an image's history where supported. For news and claims that matter, combine tools with traditional checks: reverse image search, the original source and context.

## What is the best Gemini watermark remover?

Removing watermarks to hide that an image is AI-generated is deceptive, can break Google's terms of use, and may break platform rules or laws in some places, so this page does not recommend tools for it. The invisible SynthID watermark is also designed to survive most edits.

If the visible mark gets in the way of a legitimate use, better options are: check whether your plan or a different Google tool offers outputs suited to professional use; generate the image with enough margin and compose it in a design tool without hiding its origin; or use stock photos or your own photography where a real image is needed. Labelling content as AI-generated is increasingly expected and builds trust with your audience.

## Who made Gemini?

Gemini was made by Google DeepMind, Google's AI research lab, formed in 2023 by merging Google Brain and DeepMind. Google announced the first Gemini models in December 2023.

The models were developed by large teams across Google DeepMind and Google Research, building on Google's earlier work, including the Transformer architecture published by Google researchers in 2017. The Gemini app, previously called Bard, is built by Google's product teams on these models. Gemini models are also available to developers through Google AI Studio, the Gemini API and Vertex AI on Google Cloud.

## Who owns Gemini?

Google owns Gemini. Google is a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc., so Alphabet is the ultimate parent company. Gemini products follow Google's terms of service and privacy policy.

That ownership matters for data: conversations in the Gemini app are stored in your Google account according to your activity settings and may be reviewed to improve services, as Google discloses; work and school accounts follow their organisation's Google Workspace settings. Developers using the Gemini API agree to Google's API terms, which differ between free and paid tiers. Read those terms before sending sensitive information.

## Is Gemini dangerous?

Gemini is not dangerous in itself, but like any powerful AI tool it has real risks: confident wrong answers, privacy exposure if you share sensitive data, realistic fake images in the wrong hands, and over-reliance that weakens your own skills.

Use it safely:

- Verify facts, especially health, legal and financial information, with official sources.
- Keep passwords, OTPs, identity numbers and other people's private information out of chats.
- Review activity settings and delete conversations you do not need kept.
- Label AI-generated images and never create misleading images of real people.
- Use it to learn faster, not to skip learning.

Google applies safety filters and watermarking, but responsible use is still up to you.

# GenAI and LLM interview questions with answers: RAG, fine-tuning, prompting, agents, evaluation and system design, from both sides of the table
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/genai-interview-questions/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What do GenAI engineer interviews actually ask?

**Six things, in some order: LLM fundamentals, tokens, context, attention, hallucination; RAG, how you build and evaluate retrieval; fine-tuning, when and how with LoRA; prompting and agents, including safety; evaluation and cost, how you know it works and what it costs; and one system design where you assemble the pieces. Plus a walkthrough of a project you built, which is where most decisions get made. Definitions get you past the first minute. Trade-offs and stories get you the offer.**


I have sat on both sides: interviewing candidates for SCULT INDIA and being interviewed for GenAI roles. The pattern is consistent enough that this page is the preparation I now give mentees, with the answers I would want to hear. Longer notes are on the portfolio [11][12].

> The question is never really "what is RAG". The question is "have you built one, and do you know what broke". Answer the second question every time.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## LLM fundamentals: what will they ask?

**Expect: what is a token and why does it matter for cost; what is the context window and one failure mode of long contexts; explain attention in one minute; what is hallucination and how do you manage it; open-weight versus API models for a given product; what is the difference between a base model and an instruct model. Answer each with the concept in one sentence, then a consequence for a product you built.**



## RAG interview questions

**Expect: explain RAG end to end; why is chunking important and how do you choose a size; why add keyword search to embeddings; what does a reranker do; how do you evaluate retrieval separately from generation; how do you stop the model answering when the documents do not contain the answer; how would you handle multi-tenant documents. Every question maps to a stage of the pipeline; know the pipeline and you know the questions.**



The paper to cite is Lewis et al. [1]; the metric framework most interviewers know is RAGAS [7]. The answer that separates candidates is to the evaluation question: "I measure retrieval recall on twenty labelled questions before I look at a single generated answer, because a system can be faithful to the wrong passage."

## Fine-tuning interview questions

**Expect: when would you fine-tune instead of using RAG; explain LoRA and QLoRA; how do you prepare a dataset; how do you read a loss curve; what is catastrophic forgetting; how do you evaluate a fine-tuned model honestly; can you fine-tune GPT. The trap question is "how would you teach the model our product facts", and the right answer is "I would not, I would retrieve them, and fine-tune only for the voice and format".**



## Prompt engineering and agent interview questions

**Expect: system prompt versus user prompt and why the split matters for security; what is prompt injection and how do you limit its damage; when does chain-of-thought help and when does it waste tokens; how do you test a prompt; what is an agent and where does the model's judgement actually belong; how would you stop an agent taking a harmful action; when is a workflow better than an agent. Safety questions are where candidates who have only prototyped get exposed.**


The references interviewers respect: chain-of-thought [5], ReAct for agents [6], OWASP for security [9], and Anthropic's guide for the workflow-versus-agent distinction [10]. The answer to "how do you stop a harmful action" is not a clever prompt; it is least-privilege tools and a human confirmation for anything irreversible.


## Evaluation and cost questions

**Expect: how do you know your system works; what metrics do you track; how do you test a prompt change before deploying; how much does this feature cost per month; how would you cut that cost in half; what do you log. The interviewer is testing whether you treat an LLM system like software. Answer with a fixed evaluation set, metrics per stage, a CI check, tokens logged per request, and a cost model: input plus output tokens times price times requests.**



## System design questions for GenAI roles

**Expect one design in 30 to 45 minutes: a support chatbot over company documents, a document extraction service, a coding assistant, a voice assistant for a regional language. Structure it: clarify users and constraints, draw the request path, name each component and its failure mode, say what you would measure, estimate cost, and state what you would cut for version one. Interviewers grade the trade-offs you name unprompted, not the boxes you draw.**



## Behavioural and project questions

**Expect: tell me about a project; what broke and what did you do; a time you disagreed with a technical decision; how you handle a requirement you think is wrong; why this role. For the project question, use one project and go deep: the problem, the decision you made, the failure you hit, the fix, the measured result. My RAG platform's confidence gate exists because of a failure; that story has done more for me in interviews than any definition.**


My separate note on the "tell me about a project" question, with the structure and a worked example, is on the portfolio [13].

## Coding rounds for GenAI roles

**Expect Python: parse and validate a JSON output against a schema; implement reciprocal rank fusion over two ranked lists; write a retry with backoff around an API call; chunk a text by paragraphs with a size cap; compute cosine similarity; write a small evaluation loop. Rarely leetcode-style puzzles. Write clear, typed, tested code, talk while you write, and handle the edge case out loud. The interviewer is watching how you work, not whether you finish.**


```python
def reciprocal_rank_fusion(*ranked_lists: list[str], k: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    """Fuse ranked lists of ids; 1/(k+rank) per list, summed. A common coding-round question."""
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranked in ranked_lists:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranked, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)
```

## How should freshers prepare for a GenAI interview?

**Build one RAG project and one fine-tune before the interview, so every answer has a story. Read four papers: transformer, RAG, LoRA, QLoRA. Write the evaluation set for your project, because the evaluation question is where freshers lose. Rehearse the project walkthrough with a timer, failure by failure. Prepare three questions to ask about how the team evaluates and ships. Then be honest about what you have not done; the sentence "I have not done that, here is how I would start" gets hired.**



## Questions to ask the interviewer

**How do you evaluate model changes before they ship? What does your logging show for a bad answer? How often do requirements change and how do you handle it? Who owns prompt versions? What was the last production incident and what changed after? These tell you whether the team treats LLM systems as engineering, and they tell the interviewer you do.**



## Want a mock interview or a session for your batch?

**I run GenAI interview preparation sessions for final-year batches and tech clubs, with a live system design and a project walkthrough clinic.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Top GenAI and LLM interview questions, plus how to answer coding rounds
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/genai-llm-interview-questions/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The top GenAI interview questions test three things: whether you understand how large language models work (tokens, embeddings, attention), whether you can design a real system with them (retrieval-augmented generation, fine-tuning, evaluation, cost), and whether you can explain a project you built in depth. Coding rounds still test data structures and algorithms in Python or Java. This page lists the questions that come up most and how to answer them, the types of interview rounds, the coding problems to practise, and how to perform in a live coding round.

## What are the top GenAI interview questions?

Expect questions on how LLMs work, how RAG and fine-tuning differ, how to evaluate outputs, how to reduce hallucinations, and how to control cost and latency. Then expect a deep dive into your own project.

Questions that come up again and again:

- What is a transformer, and what does attention do?
- What are embeddings, and how is semantic search built on them?
- RAG or fine-tuning: when would you use each?
- How do you chunk documents, and how do you choose chunk size?
- How do you evaluate a RAG system? Separate retrieval recall from answer faithfulness.
- How do you reduce hallucinations? Grounding, citations, refusal on weak evidence.
- What is LoRA, and why does it make fine-tuning cheaper?
- How do you handle prompt injection in an app with tools?

Answer each with a concept, a trade-off and an example from something you built.

## What do GenAI interviews actually test?

They test whether you can ship, not just define terms. Interviewers check fundamentals, judgement about trade-offs, and evidence that you have built and debugged a real GenAI feature.

A typical GenAI role interview has a screening call, a coding round, a machine learning or GenAI concepts round, a system design round such as "design a document question-answering system for a company", and a project deep dive. The deep dive decides many offers. Prepare a two-minute walkthrough: the problem, the architecture, one hard bug, and how you measured quality. When I describe RAG.NextUpgrad, the parts that make the conversation are the specific choices: hybrid dense plus BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion, re-ranking, and a confidence gate that refuses to answer on weak evidence. Specifics show you built it.

## What are the most asked LLM interview questions?

The most asked LLM questions cover architecture, training, inference and safety. A focused list beats memorising fifty answers you cannot explain.

Prepare short, clear answers to these:

- What is tokenisation, and why do token counts matter for cost?
- Self-attention and multi-head attention, in plain words.
- Encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder models: examples of each.
- Pretraining versus instruction tuning versus RLHF.
- What does temperature do? What is top-p sampling?
- What is a context window, and what happens when you exceed it?
- KV cache: why it speeds up generation.
- Quantisation: what 4-bit loading trades away.
- LoRA and QLoRA: what is trained and what is frozen.
- Why do models hallucinate, and how do you measure it?

For each, have one sentence of definition and one practical consequence.

## What do LLM interview questions test?

They test whether you understand why models behave as they do, so you can make engineering decisions: which model to use, how to prompt it, when to retrieve, when to fine-tune, and how to keep cost and latency under control.

Interviewers rarely want maths for its own sake. A question about temperature is really asking whether you know to use low temperature for extraction and higher for brainstorming. A question about context windows is asking whether you know that stuffing more text can make answers worse, and that retrieval of the right passages beats long prompts. A question about fine-tuning is asking whether you know it changes behaviour and format, while RAG supplies facts. Link every answer to a decision you would make in a product.

## What types of questions are asked in an interview?

Most tech interviews mix four types: technical concept questions, coding problems, design questions, and behavioural questions about how you work with people and handle problems.

What each type looks for:

- **Concept questions** check fundamentals in your area, such as Python, databases, networks or LLMs.
- **Coding problems** check problem solving and clean code under time pressure.
- **Design questions** check how you structure a system and reason about trade-offs.
- **Behavioural questions**, such as "tell me about a conflict in your team", check ownership and communication.

For behavioural answers use the STAR structure: situation, task, action, result. Prepare five stories from projects, hackathons or college work that you can adapt to most questions.

## What are the top Python coding interview questions?

Common Python coding questions are classic problems on arrays, strings and hash maps, plus Python-specific checks on lists, dictionaries, generators and complexity.

Practise these until you can solve them cleanly:

- Two Sum with a dictionary in one pass.
- Valid parentheses with a stack.
- Longest substring without repeating characters with a sliding window.
- Group anagrams with a dictionary of sorted keys.
- Merge intervals after sorting.
- Top K frequent elements with `collections.Counter` or a heap.
- Binary search on a sorted array, and its variants.
- Level-order traversal of a binary tree with `collections.deque`.

Also expect Python questions: list versus tuple, how dictionaries work, mutable default arguments, generators and `yield`, and the time complexity of common operations.

## What are the top coding interview questions in Java?

Java coding rounds use the same core problems as any language, with extra questions on collections, object-oriented design and Java specifics such as `HashMap` internals and immutability.

The problem list overlaps with Python: Two Sum, reverse a linked list, detect a cycle, merge two sorted lists, valid parentheses, binary tree traversals, lowest common ancestor, number of islands with BFS or DFS, and simple dynamic programming such as climbing stairs and coin change. Java-specific topics to revise:

- `HashMap` versus `TreeMap` versus `LinkedHashMap`, and how hashing and collisions work.
- `String` immutability, `StringBuilder`, and `equals` versus `==`.
- Interfaces versus abstract classes.
- Checked versus unchecked exceptions.
- Basic concurrency: threads, `synchronized` and `ExecutorService`.

Write clean method signatures and name variables well; it shows.

## How do I answer coding interview questions?

Talk through a clear process: clarify the problem, give a simple solution, improve it, write clean code, then test it with edge cases. Interviewers grade your reasoning as much as the final answer.

A structure that works in every round:

- Restate the problem and ask about input size, edge cases and constraints.
- Describe a brute-force solution and its complexity in one sentence.
- Find the bottleneck and improve it, usually with a hash map, two pointers, sorting or a heap.
- Write the code while explaining each part.
- Walk through a small example and edge cases: empty input, one element, duplicates.
- State the final time and space complexity.

If you get stuck, say what you are trying. Silence is the worst signal in a coding round.

## How should I code during an interview?

Write readable code first and clever code never. Use clear names, small helper functions and simple control flow, and test as you go rather than at the end.

Practical habits:

- Choose the language you are fastest in, usually Python, unless the role requires another.
- Write the function signature and a few test calls before the body.
- Prefer standard library tools such as `collections` and `heapq` in Python.
- Avoid premature optimisation; get a correct solution, then improve it.
- Handle edge cases explicitly instead of hoping they work.

In online assessments, read all the problems first and start with the one you can finish. Partial but correct solutions often score better than ambitious unfinished ones.

## Where can I practise coding interview questions?

LeetCode is the standard practice platform, and NeetCode organises the most useful LeetCode problems by pattern with video explanations. HackerRank and Codeforces are also widely used for assessments and contests.

Practise by pattern, not at random: arrays and hashing, two pointers, sliding window, stack, binary search, linked lists, trees, graphs, heaps, backtracking and dynamic programming. Solve a few problems per pattern until you can recognise it in a new problem. Track problems you could not solve and redo them a week later. Add timed mock interviews with a friend, a mentor or an AI interviewer that asks you to explain aloud. For GenAI roles, also build and deploy one small RAG project, because a working project answers many interview questions at once.

# How to use GGUF in ComfyUI: install ComfyUI-GGUF, where files go, LTX-2 and Qwen
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gguf-comfyui-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

To use GGUF models in ComfyUI, install the ComfyUI-GGUF custom node, put the GGUF model file in ComfyUI's unet or diffusion_models folder, restart, and replace the normal model loader in your workflow with the "Unet Loader (GGUF)" node. GGUF files are quantised, so large image and video models fit on GPUs with less memory. Quantisation is central to my FineTune Studio work with QLoRA, so this page covers what GGUF is, installing and placing files, a tutorial, examples, and LTX-2 and Qwen setups. How do I use GGUF in ComfyUI? Install ComfyUI-GGUF, place your .gguf diffusion model in ComfyUI/models/unet, restart ComfyUI, then load it with the "Unet Loader (GGUF)" node instead of the standard checkpoint or diffusion model loader. Also asked as: how to gguf comfyui Everything else in the workflow stays the same: text encoders, VAE, sampler and output nodes. If the model needs a text encoder that is also in GGUF format, load it with the GGUF CLIP loader nodes. Start from a known working workflow for the model, such as the examples in the model's repository, and swap only the loader, so you change one thing at a time when debugging. Can I use GGUF in ComfyUI? Yes, through the ComfyUI-GGUF custom node by city96, which adds loaders for GGUF-quantised diffusion models and text encoders. Native ComfyUI support has expanded over time, but the custom node remains the standard route for most GGUF models. GGUF lets you run large models, such as modern image and video transformers, on consumer GPUs that cannot hold full-precision weights. The trade-off is some quality loss at lower bit widths and sometimes slower speed than optimised formats. Check that the GGUF file matches a model architecture the node supports; the repository lists supported models and updates as new ones appear. What are GGUF models in ComfyUI? GGUF models are model weights saved in the GGUF file format, which came from the llama.cpp project and stores tensors, often quantised to 8, 6, 5, 4 or fewer bits, together with metadata. In ComfyUI, they are usually quantised versions of diffusion and video models or text encoders. Also asked as: what are gguf models comfyui · where to put gguf models comfyui File names show quantisation levels, such as Q8_0, Q5_K_M or Q4_K_S. Higher numbers keep more quality and use more memory; lower numbers save memory with more quality loss. Q8 is close to full precision, Q5 and Q4 are popular balances, and lower levels suit very limited GPUs. Compare outputs on your own prompts to choose. Where do I install the GGUF node in ComfyUI? Install ComfyUI-GGUF into the ComfyUI/custom_nodes folder, either through ComfyUI-Manager by searching for "GGUF", or with Git, then install its Python requirement and restart ComfyUI. Also asked as: where to install gguf comfyui With Git: cd ComfyUI/custom_nodes git clone https://github.com/city96/ComfyUI-GGUF pip install --upgrade gguf For the Windows portable build, use the embedded Python, for example python_embeded\python.exe -s -m pip install -r ComfyUI\custom_nodes\ComfyUI-GGUF\requirements.txt from the portable folder. After restarting, search the node menu for "GGUF" to confirm the loaders appear. If they do not, check the ComfyUI console for import errors, which usually point to a missing gguf package installed into a different Python environment from the one ComfyUI uses. Keep the node updated, since support for new model architectures arrives in updates. Where do I put GGUF files in ComfyUI? Put GGUF diffusion or video model files in ComfyUI/models/unet or, in newer ComfyUI versions, ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models. The "Unet Loader (GGUF)" node lists files from these folders. Also asked as: where to put gguf files comfyui If a file does not appear in the loader's dropdown, check that it is in the right folder, has the .gguf extension, and that you restarted ComfyUI or refreshed the node list. Do not put GGUF diffusion models in the checkpoints folder, which is for full checkpoint files containing model, text encoder and VAE together. Keep a consistent naming scheme with the quantisation level in the filename. Where do I put GGUF text encoder models in ComfyUI? Put GGUF text encoder files, such as quantised T5 or other language encoders used by image and video models, in ComfyUI/models/clip or ComfyUI/models/text_encoders, and load them with the GGUF CLIP loader nodes. Models such as Flux use two text encoders, so use the dual CLIP loader variant with one GGUF and one standard encoder if needed. VAE files stay in models/vae and load with the normal VAE loader. Quantising text encoders saves significant memory, because some encoders are larger than you might expect, with modest effect on prompt understanding at Q8 or Q5. Is there a ComfyUI-GGUF tutorial? Yes. The ComfyUI-GGUF repository's README explains installation, supported models and loader nodes, and many community video tutorials walk through specific models. A simple tutorial flow follows. Steps: Install ComfyUI and confirm a standard workflow runs. Install ComfyUI-GGUF and its Python dependency. Download a GGUF quantisation of your model from its Hugging Face page. Place the model, text encoder and VAE in their folders. Open an example workflow for the model and swap in GGUF loaders. Generate, then compare Q8 and Q4 outputs and speed. Monitor GPU memory to choose the highest quality that fits. What are some ComfyUI-GGUF examples? Common examples include running Flux image models in Q4 or Q5 on GPUs with limited memory, video models such as Wan or LTX variants with GGUF transformers, and combining GGUF models with LoRAs for styles or characters. Model repositories on Hugging Face that publish GGUF files often include example workflows as images or JSON that you can drag into ComfyUI. Check that example workflows match your installed node versions; outdated workflows may reference renamed nodes. When sharing your own workflows, note the quantisation level and node versions so others can reproduce results. How do I install and configure LTX-2 GGUF models in ComfyUI? Update ComfyUI and ComfyUI-GGUF to recent versions, download an LTX-2 GGUF quantisation along with the required VAE and text encoder listed on the model card, place each in its folder, and load an official or model-card workflow, replacing the model loader with the GGUF loader. Also asked as: how to install and configure ltx-2 gguf models in comfyui: complete 2026 guide Video models are memory-hungry, so start with short clips, low resolution and fewer frames, then scale up. Use the sampler settings recommended on the model card, since video models are sensitive to steps and schedulers. If you run out of memory, try a lower quantisation, enable ComfyUI's memory-saving options, or offload the text encoder to the CPU. New model releases often need the latest ComfyUI version, so update before troubleshooting. How do I use Qwen-Image-Layered GGUF in ComfyUI? Update ComfyUI and ComfyUI-GGUF, download the GGUF quantisation and the matching text encoder and VAE from the model's page, place them in the correct folders, and start from the workflow provided by the model authors or quantisation publisher, swapping in GGUF loaders. Also asked as: how to use qwen-image-layered gguf in comfyui: complete installation and usage guide Layered image models output separate layers, such as foreground and background, so check the workflow's output nodes to save each layer, often as PNGs with transparency. Read the model card for supported resolutions and prompts. As with any new architecture, if loading fails, confirm your ComfyUI and node versions support the model, since support usually arrives in updates shortly after release.

# Does your GitHub profile matter? How to make, design and update a great one
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/github-profile-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Yes, your GitHub profile matters if you want a job, internship or freelance work in software: it is public evidence of what you can build. Recruiters, hackathon judges and clients look at pinned projects, READMEs and how you write code. A strong profile does not need hundreds of repositories; it needs a clear introduction and a few well-presented projects. This page covers whether it matters, how to make and design one, README generators and widgets, profile pictures, views, privacy, updating and finding your profile.

## Does a GitHub profile matter?

Yes, especially for students and freshers with little work experience. A GitHub profile lets employers see real code, how you structure projects, how you document them and how consistently you build, which a resume cannot show.

What matters is quality, not activity streaks. A profile with three well-documented, deployed projects that match the roles you want is far stronger than hundreds of tutorial clones or a green contribution graph full of trivial commits. Recruiters often spend a minute or two: they read your bio, open a pinned project, read its README and maybe skim the code. Make that minute count. For non-developer roles, GitHub matters less, but a portfolio of some kind still helps.

## How do I make a GitHub profile?

Sign up at github.com with an email you check, choose a professional username, then fill in your profile: name, photo, bio, location, links, a profile README, and pinned repositories.

Steps:

- Choose a username close to your name, since it appears in your profile URL.
- Add a clear photo and a one-line bio stating your focus, such as "GenAI and backend developer".
- Link your portfolio, LinkedIn and email.
- Create a repository named exactly like your username to add a profile README.
- Pin your best three to six repositories.
- Enable two-factor authentication.

Students can also apply for the GitHub Student Developer Pack, which includes free tools and services.

## How do I design a great GitHub profile?

Keep it clean and focused: a short profile README that says who you are, what you build and what you are looking for, followed by pinned projects with clear names, descriptions and live links. Design comes second to clarity.

A profile README structure:

- One or two lines about you and your focus.
- Three to five highlights: projects shipped, hackathon results, roles.
- Your main stack as plain text or a few icons.
- Links: portfolio, LinkedIn, email.
- Optional: one small stats card, if it adds information.

Each pinned repository needs a README with what it does, a screenshot or demo GIF, how to run it, the tech stack and a live link. Avoid walls of badges, animations and widgets that slow the page and distract from your work.

## What is the best GitHub profile README generator?

Generators that offer form-based builders for profile READMEs can give you a quick starting layout with sections, icons and stats cards. Use one for structure, then rewrite the content in your own words and remove anything unnecessary.

Popular tools in the community let you pick sections, add tech-stack icons, social links and stats widgets, and copy the generated Markdown into your profile repository. The risk is a generic profile that looks like thousands of others. Recruiters notice specifics: "built a RAG app used by my department, with citations" is more memorable than a grid of 40 technology logos. Keep the generated layout, write a real introduction, and link to real work.

## What is the best GitHub profile generator for stats and widgets?

Community stats cards and widgets can show language breakdowns, contribution streaks and repository stats inside your profile README by embedding images from third-party services. Use at most one or two.

Before adding widgets, ask what each tells a reader. A top-languages card can show your focus; a streak counter mostly signals activity, not skill. Third-party image services can be slow or stop working, leaving broken images on your profile, so check them occasionally. If you enjoy automation, you can generate your own stats images with a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow, which is itself a small project worth showing.

## What should my GitHub profile picture be?

Use a clear, friendly photo of your face with a plain background, the same or similar to your LinkedIn photo, so recruiters recognise you across platforms. A professional illustration or avatar is acceptable but less personal.

Tips: good lighting, face filling most of the frame, no group photos, no heavy filters, and a square crop that looks good small, because GitHub shows it at small sizes in many places. Consistency across GitHub, LinkedIn and your portfolio builds a recognisable personal brand. Avoid default identicons, which make a profile look abandoned.

## Can GitHub see who viewed my profile?

No. GitHub does not show you who visited your profile. Third-party profile view counters, added as images in your README, can show a total number of views, but not who viewed it.

Repository owners can see traffic data for their repositories, such as views, unique visitors and referring sites over recent weeks, in the repository's Insights tab, but not individual identities. So you can learn whether a project gets attention and where it comes from, for example from LinkedIn posts, but not which recruiter looked. Focus on making the profile worth viewing rather than tracking views.

## Can I hide my GitHub profile?

Your profile page is public by default and cannot be fully hidden like a private social account, but you can control what appears: make repositories private, hide private contribution details, remove pinned items and limit personal information. Check GitHub's profile settings for current privacy options.

Practical privacy steps: make repositories private when they contain personal or client work, keep your email private in settings, and remove location or other details you do not want public. Never commit secrets such as API keys or passwords; if you do, rotate them immediately, because public history keeps them even after deletion. If you want a completely separate identity for experiments, use a separate account, following GitHub's terms.

## How do I update my GitHub profile?

Click "Edit profile" on your profile page to change name, bio, links and photo; edit the README in your username repository to update the introduction; and use "Customise your pins" to change pinned repositories.

A simple routine: after each meaningful project or achievement, update the pinned repositories, refresh the README highlights and make sure the project's own README and live link work. Every few months, archive or unpin old tutorial repositories and check that links and badges still load. An up-to-date profile signals that you are actively building.

## Where do I find my GitHub profile?

Your GitHub profile is at github.com/your-username. When signed in, click your profile picture at the top right and choose "Your profile". The URL in the address bar is the link to share on your resume and LinkedIn.

Add the link to your resume header, LinkedIn contact info, portfolio and email signature. For a specific project, link directly to its repository, or better, to its live demo with the repository linked from there. If you have changed your username, update old links everywhere, because the old URL may stop redirecting if someone else claims that name.

# What is Google AI certification? Essentials, cloud certs, cost of time, value
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/google-ai-certification-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


"Google AI certification" covers several credentials. Google AI Essentials, offered through Grow with Google and Coursera, is a short beginner certificate on using generative AI tools at work. Google Cloud's professional certifications, such as Professional Machine Learning Engineer, test whether you can build, deploy and run ML systems on Google Cloud, and newer certifications cover generative AI for leaders. This page explains each, how long they take, free routes, their real value for jobs, and how they compare with AWS and Microsoft certifications.

## What is Google AI certification?

Google AI certification refers to credentials from Google that show AI knowledge or skills. The main ones are Google AI Essentials, a beginner certificate, and Google Cloud certifications for machine learning engineers and for leaders of generative AI projects.

They serve different audiences. AI Essentials suits anyone, from students to office workers, who wants to use tools such as Gemini responsibly and productively. Google Cloud certifications suit engineers and technical decision-makers working on Google Cloud, and include a proctored exam. Before choosing, decide your goal: using AI in your current work, or building AI systems as an engineer.

## What is the Google AI Essentials certificate?

Google AI Essentials is a short, self-paced course with a certificate that teaches how to use generative AI tools at work: writing effective prompts, using AI for tasks such as drafting and analysis, and using AI responsibly, including bias and privacy.

It needs no technical background or coding. It is useful for students in any field and for professionals who want a structured introduction. It does not teach you to build AI applications, train models or write code with AI APIs, so it is not a substitute for technical learning if you want an AI engineering role. Think of it as AI literacy: a sensible first step, after which engineers should move to hands-on building.

## What is the Google AI professional certification?

For technical professionals, Google's main AI credential is the Google Cloud Professional Machine Learning Engineer certification, which tests designing, building, deploying and monitoring ML solutions on Google Cloud. Google Cloud also offers a Generative AI Leader certification aimed at business and technical leaders.

The ML Engineer exam covers framing ML problems, data preparation, model development with Vertex AI, MLOps pipelines, serving and monitoring, and responsible AI. It expects real experience with Google Cloud services. Google also offers professional certificates through Coursera in areas such as data analytics and AI-related skills. Check Google Cloud's certification page for the current list, exam guides and recommended experience before booking.

## Which Google AI course should I take for a certificate?

If you are new to AI, start with Google AI Essentials. If you want to build on Google Cloud, use Google Cloud Skills Boost learning paths that prepare for the Professional Machine Learning Engineer exam. If you lead AI projects, look at the Generative AI Leader path.

For students aiming at AI engineering, a strong sequence is: a beginner course for vocabulary, then free technical learning such as Google's Machine Learning Crash Course, then a hands-on project using the Gemini API or Vertex AI, and only then a cloud certification if your target employers use Google Cloud. Certificates make the most sense as a checkpoint on skills you are already building, not as the starting point.

## How long does Google AI certification take?

Google AI Essentials takes roughly a day or two of focused study, or a few weeks part-time. Google Cloud professional certifications typically take two to six months of preparation, depending on your experience.

Professional certification preparation includes learning paths, hands-on labs and practice questions, and Google recommends prior industry experience with its cloud. The exam itself is a timed proctored test, taken online or at a test centre. Certifications expire after a set period and need renewal, which keeps them current but means ongoing effort. Plan study around a project: preparing while building something on Google Cloud makes both the exam and interviews easier.

## Can I get Google AI certification for free?

Sometimes. The learning material for many Google courses is free or low cost, Coursera offers financial aid for its certificates, Google Cloud Skills Boost has free labs and periodic free credit programmes, and Google has run scholarships for students in India.

The exams for professional cloud certifications usually have a fee, and vouchers are sometimes offered through events, training programmes or student initiatives. Free learning paths, the Machine Learning Crash Course and Google's AI documentation give you the knowledge without the certificate. Be careful with third-party sites offering "free Google certification"; get certificates only from Google, Coursera or Google Cloud directly.

## Is Google AI certification worth it?

AI Essentials is worth it for AI literacy and a quick CV line, especially for non-technical roles. Google Cloud's ML Engineer certification is worth it for engineers targeting roles on Google Cloud. For most technical hiring, projects and experience count more than any certificate.

Value depends on the job market you target. Some employers, especially IT services firms and cloud partners, value certifications because they help them meet partner requirements. Product companies and startups care more about what you have built. The best combination is a certification that matches your target stack plus a deployed project using that stack, so the certificate is backed by evidence.

## Can you get a job with a Google AI certification?

A certification alone rarely gets you a job, but it can help you pass resume screening and show initiative, especially combined with projects. For engineering roles, interviews will test whether you can actually build and explain systems.

What gets jobs: deployed projects, internships, problem-solving skills and the ability to explain trade-offs. Use the certification to structure your learning and to signal familiarity with a cloud platform. Then build something with it, for example a document Q&A system on Vertex AI or the Gemini API, with a README, a demo video and evaluation results. That combination is far stronger than the certificate alone, and it gives you real stories for interviews.

## AWS vs Google AI certification: which is better?

Neither is better in general; choose the cloud your target employers use. AWS has the largest overall cloud market share, so AWS certifications appear in more job listings, while Google Cloud is strong in data and AI and its certifications suit companies on its platform.

AWS offers certifications such as AI Practitioner and Machine Learning Engineer Associate, plus specialty and professional levels; Google offers Professional Machine Learning Engineer and Generative AI Leader. Check job descriptions in the roles and cities you want and count which cloud appears more. Concepts such as data pipelines, model deployment, monitoring and cost control transfer between clouds, so learning one deeply makes the second much easier.

## Microsoft vs Google AI certification: which should I choose?

Choose Microsoft if you target companies built on Azure and Microsoft 365, which includes many enterprises and IT services firms in India. Choose Google if your targets use Google Cloud or you are already building with Gemini and Vertex AI.

Microsoft's AI credentials include Azure AI Fundamentals for beginners and role-based certifications for Azure AI engineers, with free learning on Microsoft Learn. Students can also use Azure for Students credits to practise. Google's equivalents are AI Essentials for beginners and the cloud certifications for engineers. If unsure, start with the free fundamentals courses from both, build one small project on each platform, and let job listings decide which certification to pay for.
