# How to build a developer portfolio website: what to include, what to cut, free hosting, and the three-second test recruiters actually apply
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-build-a-developer-portfolio-website/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What should a developer portfolio website include?

**A home page that states what you build in one sentence and links everywhere else. Three to five project write-ups, each with the problem, the decision you made, a demo or screenshot, and what you would do differently. An about section that is two paragraphs, not a biography. A contact method that is one click away. Talks or writing if you have them. Nothing else. The whole site should answer what do you build, is it real, and how do I reach you, inside ten seconds of landing.**


My own site exists for exactly this, and it is the page every organiser and recruiter opens before a call [9]. My longer notes on the README format that feeds project pages, and on which projects to include, are on the portfolio [7][8].

> A portfolio site is not a museum of everything you have touched. It is three doors, each opening onto something real.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How do I write a project page that gets read?

**Problem in one sentence: who had it and what it cost them. The decision you are proud of, in three sentences, including the trade-off. A demo video or three screenshots, never a wall of code. What you would do differently now, which shows growth more than any feature list. A link to the repository and, if it exists, a live demo. Skip the tech stack badge wall at the top; put it at the bottom if at all. A reader should understand the project without opening the code.**



## Which projects should I put on my portfolio?

**Three to five, chosen for range and depth, not for count. One that solved a real problem for a real person. One that shows a technical decision you can defend for twenty minutes. One that is live and usable right now. Cut anything that is a tutorial clone, a copy of a template, or unfinished. A portfolio with three strong projects reads as more capable than one with twelve thin ones, because reviewers judge by the best page they see, not the total.**


## What should I leave off my portfolio?

**Certificates, unless a project sits behind them. A skills matrix with progress bars, which nobody trusts. Every course you have completed. Tutorial clones with no changes of your own. A blog if you are not going to keep writing, better a single pinned post than an abandoned feed. Stock photography. A dense biography above the fold. The test is simple: does this page help someone decide to talk to you in the next thirty seconds; if not, cut it.**




## Where should I host a portfolio for free?

**GitHub Pages for a fully static site, free forever on a public repository, with a custom domain supported [2]. Netlify and Vercel's free tiers for a site with a build step, also generous and free for personal use [3]. Cloudflare Pages as another free, fast option [4]. A `.dev`, `.me` or `.in` domain costs a small yearly fee if you want one; the hosting itself should never cost anything for a personal portfolio. Avoid managed website builders with monthly fees; a static site is simpler, faster and free.**



## How fast and accessible should it be?

**Fast enough that it loads before the recruiter's attention moves on: a static site with optimised images and no heavy frameworks for a simple portfolio easily hits good Core Web Vitals scores [1]. Accessible enough that a screen reader can navigate it: real headings, alt text on images, sufficient colour contrast, keyboard-navigable links [5]. Neither takes more than an afternoon to get right, and both are things a recruiter or organiser will notice without naming, as a site that either feels solid or feels broken.**


## How do I keep it updated without it becoming a chore?

**Update it the moment something changes: a project ships, a talk happens, a link breaks. Do not schedule quarterly overhauls, which is how portfolios go a year stale. Keep the write-up template from this page in a notes file so a new project page takes twenty minutes, not a weekend. Delete a project the moment you would not want it asked about; an outdated portfolio actively works against you, so removing is as valid an edit as adding.**



## What mistakes do developer portfolios make?

**A home page with no clear statement of what you build. A skills wall that reads like a résumé keyword dump. Ten projects, all thin. Broken links to deleted repositories or dead demos. No way to contact you without hunting. A design so custom it is confusing to navigate. Copy-pasted README text with no framing for a human reader. Every one of these is fixed by the ten-second test: would a stranger know what to do next.**



## Developer portfolio interview questions

**"Walk me through a project on your site" is the most common opener once a recruiter has read it, so every project page should survive twenty minutes of follow-up questions. Prepare the decision, the trade-off, the failure and the fix for each of your three to five projects before the interview, not during it. The portfolio's job is to earn this question; your job is to answer it well.**



## Where should I start?

**Pick your best three projects, write the problem-decision-demo-lesson page for the first one tonight, and deploy on GitHub Pages or Netlify this week.** For a session on building a technical portfolio that gets you interviews, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to build an AI app and deploy it for free: architecture, stack, hosting, costs and the checklist that survives real users
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-build-an-ai-app/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I build an AI app?

**Build a normal web application and put the model call behind one function. The front end collects input and shows output, the API validates the input, calls the model with a prompt and any retrieved context, validates the output, stores what happened, and returns it. Add authentication, a database, logging and a deploy pipeline, and you have an AI app. The model is one dependency, and everything around it is what makes the product work when a stranger uses it.**


I shipped five production AI applications between February and July 2026, a RAG platform, a fine-tuning platform, a document extraction service, a browser face recognition system and an OCR and speech workspace, each with Docker, CI/CD, structured logging and metrics [12]. The stack below is the one they share, and the checklist at the end is what each of them taught me the hard way.

> The model call is thirty lines. The other three thousand lines are why the app is still up next month.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is the architecture of an LLM app?

**Five layers. A client: a web page, a mobile app, a WhatsApp bot. An API layer that authenticates, validates and rate-limits. A model layer: the prompt, the provider client, retries and fallbacks, and optionally retrieval, tools or a fine-tuned model. A data layer: a relational database for users and logs, a vector index for documents, object storage for files. And an operations layer: deploy pipeline, logs, metrics, alerts. Most AI apps are small enough that the API and model layers live in one service.**



The longer write-up of the FastAPI and Next.js version of this, with the folder layout, is on the portfolio [13].

## Which tech stack should I use for an AI app?

**Python for the back end, because every model library, SDK and example is in Python, with FastAPI for the API [1]. Postgres for data, with pgvector when you need embeddings [3]; Supabase gives you Postgres, auth and storage on a free tier [4]. Any front end you already know, plain HTML, React or Next.js. Docker to package it [2]. GitHub Actions to test and deploy [8]. One platform host. Add nothing else until a real need appears.**



On frameworks such as LangChain: excellent for a first prototype and for loaders; for production, I write the model wrapper myself, because a bug under three abstraction layers costs a day and a bug in my own fifty lines costs ten minutes.

## How do I deploy an AI app for free?

**Package the app in Docker and deploy to a platform with a free or trial tier: Railway, Render or Fly.io for a container, Hugging Face Spaces for a demo with a GPU option, Supabase for the database, and a static host such as GitHub Pages, Netlify or Cloudflare Pages for the front end. Free tiers sleep or cap hours, so design the app to start fast and hold no state in memory. The model API itself is not free beyond trial credits, so budget tokens from day one.**



Free tiers change; the platform documentation is the source of truth and this table is a map, not a guarantee [4][5][6][7]. RAG.NextUpgrad, with hybrid retrieval, reranking and streaming, runs in about 220 MB of memory on a free tier, which is the proof that a real AI app does not need a large server [12]. My deployment write-up walks through it step by step [14].


## How much does it cost to run an AI app?

**Hosting can be zero at first. The model API is the real bill: input tokens plus output tokens, times the price per million, times requests. Estimate it before launch: measure the tokens of a typical request, multiply by expected daily requests, multiply by the provider's rate. Then set a hard monthly cap at the provider, a per-user daily limit in your code, and an alert at half the cap. An app with no cap is one viral post away from a bill you did not plan.**



## How do I make an AI app reliable?

**Wrap every model call with a timeout, a bounded retry with backoff, and a fallback to a second provider or a smaller model with the same prompt. Validate outputs against a schema and fail closed when they do not parse. Stream responses so users see progress. Make the app stateless so it can restart. Test the prompt against a fixed set of inputs in CI. Log every request with its tokens, latency and outcome. My apps fall back across providers automatically, and that single feature has kept them up through several API outages.**


```python
async def generate(prompt: str, schema: type[BaseModel]) -> BaseModel:
    for provider in PROVIDERS:                      # identical prompt, ordered by preference
        for attempt in range(2):
            try:
                raw = await asyncio.wait_for(provider.complete(prompt, max_tokens=800), timeout=30)
                return schema.model_validate_json(raw)   # fail closed if it does not parse
            except (TimeoutError, ProviderError, ValidationError) as e:
                log.warning("provider=%s attempt=%d err=%s", provider.name, attempt, e)
                await asyncio.sleep(0.5 * (attempt + 1))
    raise ServiceUnavailable("all providers failed")
```

## How do I secure an AI app?

**Treat every input, and every document or tool result the model reads, as untrusted. Keep instructions in the system prompt and data in delimited user content. Give tools the least permission they need and require a human confirmation for irreversible actions. Never put secrets in prompts. Rate-limit per user. Validate outputs before acting on them. Log prompts and outputs with user consent and a retention policy. OWASP's list of LLM application risks is the checklist to review before launch [9].**


The most common student mistake is the API key in the front-end code, where anyone can read it and run up your bill. The key lives on the server, always, and the server enforces the limits.

## Should I build an AI agent or a simple app?

**A simple app, until a decision appears that you cannot write as code. Most "AI agents" that succeed in production are workflows: code decides the steps, a model does the language work at each step. Reach for a real agent loop only when the task is open-ended and the model must choose actions at run time, and then add limits, permissions and confirmations before anything else [11].**



## How do I get users for an AI app?

**Build it for a group you belong to, your class, your club, a family business, and put it in front of them the day it works. Ask what they tried to do that failed, and fix that. Post a demo video where those people are. Ten real users teach more than a thousand sign-ups from a launch post, and they are how a student project becomes a line on a resume that a recruiter believes.**



## What mistakes kill AI apps after demo day?

**No cap on API spend. The key in the front end. No logs, so the first complaint is undebuggable. State held in memory on a host that sleeps. Prompts edited in production with no test set. One provider and no fallback. No per-user limits, so one script drains the budget. A model output acted on without validation. Each is on the checklist above; each I have either done or watched a mentee do.**



## What are common AI app interview questions?

**Design an LLM feature end to end and name where it can fail. Estimate its monthly cost. Explain how you would handle a provider outage. Explain where prompt injection can enter and what limits its damage. Describe how you would test a prompt change. Say what you would log. Each answer is a section above, and the best evidence is a live app you can open during the interview.**



## Where should I start?

**Take a problem someone near you has, build the smallest version with FastAPI, one model call with a timeout and a fallback, Postgres on Supabase, Docker, and deploy it on a free tier this weekend. Log everything. Show it to three people. Then read the checklist again.** All five of my production apps are open source and follow this shape [12]. If your college wants a workshop that ends with every student having a deployed AI app, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to build a Copilot agent, how it works, and what it can do
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-build-copilot-agent/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To build a Copilot agent, open Microsoft 365 Copilot and use Agent Builder for a simple agent made of instructions and knowledge, or use Copilot Studio when the agent needs actions, API calls, triggers or multi-step workflows. An agent combines instructions, knowledge sources and actions, and a language model decides how to use them for each request. This page shows how to create one and how it works, then answers what agents can do: read PDFs and SharePoint lists, call APIs, send email, run on a schedule, call other agents and be shared, plus which agent to use for coding.

## How do I create a Copilot agent?

In Microsoft 365 Copilot, choose to create an agent, describe what it should do in plain language, add knowledge such as SharePoint sites or files, test it in the preview pane, and share it. For actions and workflows, build it in Copilot Studio instead.

A first agent in under an hour:

- **Purpose**: one narrow job, such as answering questions about your department's policies.
- **Instructions**: who it serves, what it should and should not answer, tone, and when to hand over to a person.
- **Knowledge**: the SharePoint site or documents that hold the answers.
- **Starter prompts**: three example questions users can click.
- **Test**: ask twenty real questions, including tricky ones, and fix instructions where answers go wrong.

Start narrow; a focused agent that answers well beats a broad one that guesses.

## How does a Copilot agent work?

When a user sends a message, the agent's orchestrator reads its instructions, decides whether to search its knowledge sources, call an action or reply directly, runs those steps, and has the language model compose an answer, citing sources where it used them.

Knowledge searches retrieve relevant passages, respecting each user's permissions, which is retrieval-augmented generation. Actions are tools with descriptions, such as "create a ticket" or "look up an order", and the model picks them based on those descriptions, so clear names and descriptions matter. In Copilot Studio you can also define topics, fixed conversation paths for cases that must follow exact steps. Every conversation can be reviewed in analytics and transcripts, which is how you improve the agent after launch.

## Which Copilot agent is best for coding?

For coding, use GitHub Copilot: agent mode in VS Code and other editors for interactive multi-file changes, and the Copilot coding agent on GitHub for issues you hand off and review as pull requests. Microsoft 365 agents are built for work content, not codebases.

GitHub Copilot's agents can read the repository, run commands and tests, and iterate on failures. Give them well-scoped tasks with acceptance criteria, keep a `.github/copilot-instructions.md` file with build and style rules, and review every change through normal code review. For comparison, other strong coding agents include Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex and Google's Gemini CLI; try one real task in each if your team is choosing.

## Can a Copilot agent read a PDF?

Yes. Agents can use PDFs as knowledge, either uploaded directly in Agent Builder or Copilot Studio, or stored in a SharePoint site or OneDrive folder the agent searches. They answer from the text and cite the document.

Results are best with text-based PDFs; scanned PDFs need text recognition first, so run OCR on them before adding them. Large manuals answer better when split into sensible sections with clear headings. Keep one current version of each document, because outdated copies lead to conflicting answers. In my OCR & Speech Workspace, page-batched OCR and page citations made answers on scanned documents checkable, which is the same principle: clean text in, citations out.

## Can a Copilot agent read a SharePoint list?

Yes. Copilot Studio agents can use SharePoint lists as knowledge for questions, and can read and update list items through the SharePoint connector as actions. Results respect the user's permissions on the list.

Use the list as knowledge when users ask questions such as "which laptops are available in the IT pool?". Use connector actions when the agent must do something precise, such as filter items, create a new request or update a status, because actions return exact records rather than a summarised search. Clear column names and consistent values help the model a lot. For large lists, filter in the action rather than asking the model to scan everything.

## Can a Copilot agent call an API?

Yes. In Copilot Studio, agents call APIs through prebuilt connectors, custom connectors, Power Automate flows, or REST API actions defined with an OpenAPI description. In Microsoft 365 Copilot, developers add API plugins to declarative agents.

Steps for a custom API: describe the endpoints in an OpenAPI file with clear operation names and descriptions, set up authentication such as OAuth or an API key stored securely, add it as an action, and write instructions on when to use it. Test with realistic requests and check the inputs the model sends, since vague parameter descriptions lead to wrong calls. Validate responses and handle errors, so the agent says "I could not reach the system" instead of inventing an answer.

## Can a Copilot agent send an email?

Yes, through an action such as the Office 365 Outlook connector or a Power Automate flow in Copilot Studio. Agents can also draft emails for the user to review and send, which is safer for most cases.

For anything external or important, have the agent draft and ask for confirmation before sending, and log what was sent. Decide whose mailbox sends the email: the signed-in user's or a shared service account, which changes permissions and how replies are handled. Limit who can trigger email actions and what recipients are allowed, to avoid misuse or accidental mass emails. Test with your own address before connecting real users.

## Can a Copilot agent be scheduled?

Yes. Copilot Studio supports autonomous agents with triggers, including recurring schedules and events such as a new file, email or record, so an agent can run without a user starting a chat.

Examples: every Monday at 9 a.m., summarise last week's support tickets and post the summary to a Teams channel; when a new invoice lands in a folder, extract the fields and create an approval request. Scheduled agents run under a configured identity, so check what data and actions that identity can reach. Add monitoring: review run history, set alerts for failures, and keep a human approval step before irreversible actions. Power Automate scheduled flows are an alternative when the logic is fixed and needs no AI judgement.

## Can a Copilot agent call another agent?

Yes. Copilot Studio supports multi-agent setups, where a main agent hands specific tasks to other agents, such as an IT agent passing a request to a separate HR or procurement agent, each with its own knowledge and actions.

Multi-agent designs work well when domains are clearly separate and owned by different teams. They add complexity: more places for errors, harder debugging and more permissions to manage. Start with one agent and split only when instructions become too long or knowledge sources conflict. Give each agent a clear description of what it handles, because the orchestrator chooses agents by those descriptions, just as it chooses actions. Test hand-offs with tricky requests that sit between two domains.

## Can a Copilot agent be shared?

Yes. You can share agents with specific people, security groups or the whole organisation, depending on your role and your organisation's policies. Copilot Studio agents can also be published to channels such as Teams, websites and Microsoft 365 Copilot.

Before sharing, check that everyone who will use the agent may see its knowledge sources; agents respect user permissions for SharePoint content, but uploaded files and some connectors may expose data more widely. Admins can control who may create and share agents and review agents across the organisation. Give the agent an owner who reviews conversations and updates its knowledge, because an unmaintained agent quietly goes out of date.

# How to evaluate a RAG system: recall, faithfulness, RAGAS, building a test set and the metrics that actually predict user complaints
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-evaluate-a-rag-system/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I evaluate a RAG system?

**In two separate stages. Retrieval: build a set of real questions each labelled with the passage that answers it, run the retriever, and measure how often the right passage appears in the top k results. Generation: for each question, judge whether the answer is faithful to the retrieved passages, whether it actually answers the question, and whether it cites correctly. Then track both sets of numbers on every change, in CI, so a chunking tweak or a model upgrade cannot silently make the system worse.**


RAG.NextUpgrad, the production platform I built in 2026, carries 196 automated tests, and the ones that catch real regressions are the retrieval recall tests over a labelled question set [10]. Everything on this page is what those tests taught me, with the papers underneath. My shorter notes on the metrics are on the portfolio [11][12].

> If the right passage is not in the top thirty, stop. No prompt, no model, no reranker can answer from a document it never saw. Measure that first, and measure it alone.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building RAG.NextUpgrad</cite>

## Why evaluate retrieval and generation separately?

**Because they fail differently and are fixed differently. A wrong answer can come from retrieval returning the wrong chunk, which is a chunking or search problem, or from the model ignoring a correct chunk, which is a prompt or model problem. A single end-to-end score hides which one happened. Measure retrieval with the labelled passages, measure generation given the passages actually retrieved, and the failure points name themselves.**



Barnett et al.'s seven failure points map almost one to one onto the categories that fall out of this loop [7].

## How do I build an evaluation set for RAG?

**Start with twenty real questions: from logs if you have users, from the people who own the documents if you do not, or from yourself reading the documents and writing what a user would ask. For each, mark the chunk or passage that answers it, and write the answer you would accept. Include hard cases: questions with no answer in the corpus, questions whose answer spans two sections, and questions using different words from the document. Grow the set from every production complaint. Twenty is enough to start; two hundred is enough to trust.**



Synthetic questions generated from chunks are useful to widen coverage cheaply, and ARES shows how to use them with a small human-labelled set for calibration [5], but they tend to use the document's own phrasing, which overstates recall. Keep the real ones as the reference.

## What are the retrieval metrics?

**Recall at k: the share of questions for which a correct passage appears in the top k results; the metric that matters most, at the k you actually send to the reranker. Precision at k: the share of the top k that are relevant, which matters for prompt cost. Mean reciprocal rank: how high the first correct passage ranks, on average. Hit rate is recall at k under another name. Report recall at your retrieval k and at your generation k, because they answer different questions.**



The definitions are classical information retrieval, covered in the Manning textbook's evaluation chapter [8]; BEIR is the benchmark most embedding models are compared on [6], and it is not your corpus, so measure your own.

## What are the generation metrics?

**Faithfulness: the fraction of claims in the answer that are supported by the retrieved passages, which is the metric for hallucination. Answer relevance: whether the answer addresses the question asked. Context relevance or precision: whether the passages sent were needed. Citation correctness: whether each citation points to a passage that supports the sentence. Refusal accuracy: whether the system said "not in the documents" exactly when it should. RAGAS defines the first three and scores them with an LLM judge [1][2].**



## Can I trust LLM-as-a-judge metrics?

**Partly. Judge models correlate with human ratings well enough to be useful for tracking changes, and they are cheap enough to run on every commit; Zheng et al. measured the agreement and its biases, including position and verbosity effects [3]. They are not a substitute for a human-labelled sample, because a judge can be faithful to the wrong passage or fooled by confident wording. Calibrate: label fifty answers by hand, compare with the judge, and only then trust the judge on the other thousand.**



## How do I evaluate hybrid search and reranking?

**Ablate. Run recall at k for dense retrieval alone, BM25 alone, and the fused list, on the same question set. Then run recall over the top five after reranking versus the top five before. Each stage should raise recall at its output k, and if a stage does not, remove it. In RAG.NextUpgrad the fused list beat either retriever alone on the labelled set, and the reranker's job was visible as recall at five rising while recall at thirty stayed flat [10].**


## How do I evaluate chunking and embedding model choices?

**The same way: fix the question set, vary one component, compare recall at k. Index the corpus at three chunk sizes and compare. Embed with two models and compare. Prepend headings and compare. Every configuration decision in a RAG system is an experiment against the labelled set, and the set is what makes the decision defensible rather than a guess copied from a tutorial. Models that look worse on a public leaderboard sometimes win on your documents.**


## How do I run RAG evaluation in CI?

**Store the question set and labels in the repository. Write a test that indexes a fixed fixture corpus, runs retrieval for every question, and asserts recall at k above a threshold you set from the current baseline. Write a second test that generates answers for a subset and asserts faithfulness and refusal accuracy above thresholds, using a cheap judge model, and fails the build on regression. Cache embeddings so the test runs in minutes. Review the failures as part of code review, not after deployment.**


```python
def test_retrieval_recall_at_10(index, eval_set):
    hits = 0
    for q in eval_set:
        top = index.search(q.question, k=10)
        hits += any(p.id in q.relevant_ids for p in top)
    recall = hits / len(eval_set)
    assert recall >= 0.85, f"recall@10 dropped to {recall:.2f}"   # baseline set from the last release
```

That test, and its siblings for BM25, fusion and reranking, is a large part of why RAG.NextUpgrad has 196 tests and why chunking changes ship with confidence [10].

## What numbers should I aim for?

**Recall at the reranker's input k, say thirty, above ninety percent on your labelled set, or retrieval is the problem. Recall at the generation k, say five, above eighty-five. Faithfulness above ninety-five percent on questions with an answer, and refusal accuracy near one hundred on questions without one. These are targets from production experience, not universal thresholds; the right numbers depend on how costly a wrong answer is for your users.**



## What do users actually complain about, and which metric predicts it?

**Confident wrong answers, which faithfulness predicts. "It said it does not know" when the answer was there, which recall predicts. Slow answers, which no quality metric predicts, so track latency alongside. Answers that ignore the newest document, which is index freshness, so track it. The metrics above cover the first two; the last two are operations, and they belong on the same dashboard.**



## RAG evaluation interview questions

**Why evaluate retrieval separately from generation? Define recall at k and faithfulness. How would you build an evaluation set with no users yet? How do you know your reranker helps? What are the risks of LLM-as-a-judge? How would you put evaluation in CI? What number would you look at first when a user reports a wrong answer? Every answer is above, and a repository with a labelled set and a recall test is the strongest evidence you can bring.**



## Where should I start?

**Write twenty real questions against a document set you know, mark the passage that answers each, and compute recall at ten for your current retriever. Read the misses. That afternoon will tell you more about your system than any framework's dashboard.** For a hands-on session on building and evaluating retrieval systems at your college or team, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to fine-tune an LLM: LoRA, QLoRA, datasets and evaluation, from building a fine-tuning platform
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-fine-tune-an-llm/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is fine-tuning an LLM?

**Fine-tuning is continuing to train a pre-trained language model on your own examples so that its weights shift toward your task: your tone, your output format, your domain's vocabulary, or a narrow skill the base model does badly. You start from a model that already understands language and nudge it, which is why a few thousand good examples can change behaviour that no prompt could.**


The base model learned from trillions of tokens of general text. Fine-tuning shows it a comparatively tiny, curated set of input and output pairs and adjusts the weights to make those outputs more likely. The result is a model that behaves differently by default, without a long prompt reminding it every time.

I built FineTune Studio in 2026 to turn this into a product workflow: upload a dataset, pick a base model, set LoRA or QLoRA hyper-parameters, launch a run, and watch the loss stream to the browser in real time [15]. Most of what follows is what that platform taught me about which decisions matter.

> Fine-tuning is not how you teach a model facts. It is how you teach a model habits. If you remember one line from this page, make it that one.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building FineTune Studio</cite>

## How does fine-tuning an LLM work?

**Training runs the model on each example, compares its predicted next tokens with the target answer, computes a loss, and adjusts weights by gradient descent to lower that loss. Full fine-tuning updates every weight, which needs enormous memory. Parameter-efficient methods freeze the base model and train a small set of added weights instead, which is what almost everyone outside a large lab does today.**



Lialin et al. survey the parameter-efficient family, adapters, prompt tuning, LoRA and their relatives, and the trade-offs between them [3]. In practice the field has converged: LoRA when memory allows, QLoRA when it does not.

## When should I fine-tune instead of using RAG or prompting?

**Fine-tune when the problem is behaviour: consistent style, strict structured output, a domain's phrasing, a classification or extraction skill, or when you need a small model to do one thing well and cheaply. Use RAG when the problem is knowledge that changes or must be cited. Use prompting first in every case, because a prompt is free to change and a fine-tune is not.**



The order I insist on with clients: prompt, then retrieval, then few-shot examples in the prompt, then fine-tuning. Each step is more expensive and less reversible than the last. Teams that fine-tune first usually end up fine-tuning again a month later when the requirements move.

### Does fine-tuning add knowledge to a model?

**Only weakly and unreliably. Fine-tuning on facts can make a model repeat those facts, but it cannot cite them, it forgets them as the world changes, and it tends to blend them with what it already believed. If the answer must be correct and traceable, retrieve it.** LIMA showed that a thousand carefully chosen examples were enough to teach strong instruction-following, and that the knowledge came almost entirely from pre-training [6]. That is the clearest evidence for "fine-tune for behaviour, retrieve for facts".


## What is LoRA?

**LoRA, low-rank adaptation, freezes the original model weights and trains two small matrices per targeted layer whose product approximates the weight update. Instead of updating billions of parameters you train a few million, the adapter, which is a few megabytes on disk and can be swapped or merged. Hu et al. introduced it in 2021 and showed quality comparable to full fine-tuning at a fraction of the memory [1].**


The word LoRA also names a long-range radio protocol, which is why half the search results for "what is LoRA" are about antennas. In machine learning it is always low-rank adaptation.

Two settings define an adapter:

- **Rank (r).** The inner dimension of the two matrices. Higher rank means more capacity and more memory. Typical values run from 8 to 64; I start at 16.
- **Alpha.** A scaling factor applied to the adapter's output. A common rule is alpha equal to rank or twice the rank; what matters is the ratio, since it changes the effective learning rate of the adapter.

### What are the target modules?

**Target modules are the layers inside the transformer that get an adapter. Attention projections (query, key, value, output) are the classic choice; adding the feed-forward projections usually improves results at some memory cost.** The QLoRA paper found applying adapters to all linear layers mattered more than rank for matching full fine-tuning [2].


## What is QLoRA, and what is the difference between LoRA and QLoRA?

**QLoRA is LoRA on top of a base model quantised to 4 bits. The frozen weights are stored in a compact NormalFloat4 format and de-quantised on the fly during the forward pass, while the small adapters train in higher precision. Dettmers et al. showed a 65B model fine-tuning on a single 48 GB GPU with quality matching 16-bit full fine-tuning [2]. The difference from LoRA is memory: same adapters, much smaller base.**



The memory figures are orders of magnitude, not promises; they move with sequence length, batch size and gradient checkpointing. The reason QLoRA matters to students is simple: it is the technique that puts a 7B model on a free Colab T4 or a 16 GB laptop GPU. FineTune Studio's whole premise is that fine-tuning is a browser workflow, not a cluster job, and QLoRA is why that premise holds [15].

### What is quantisation, and what are GGUF, AWQ and GPTQ?

**Quantisation stores weights in fewer bits, 8 or 4 instead of 16, which shrinks memory and speeds inference at a small accuracy cost. GGUF is the file format used by llama.cpp for running quantised models on CPUs and consumer GPUs [13]; AWQ and GPTQ are post-training quantisation methods aimed at GPU inference. QLoRA's NormalFloat4 is a quantisation for training. Quantise after fine-tuning and merging, not before, unless you are doing QLoRA.**


## How do I prepare a dataset for fine-tuning?

**Write the behaviour you want as a spec, then collect or write examples that follow it exactly, in the chat format the base model expects: a system message, a user turn and the ideal assistant answer. Deduplicate, validate every row, hold out ten to twenty percent for evaluation, and read a random sample by eye before training. Consistency beats size; a thousand examples that all follow the spec outperform fifty thousand that mostly do.**



Alpaca popularised the instruction, input, output format with 52,000 generated examples [8]; ShareGPT-style multi-turn conversations followed. Both are just JSON shapes. What the model actually sees is the rendered chat template, so use the tokenizer's template function rather than hand-writing the special tokens [11]. Mismatched templates are the most common reason a fine-tuned chat model produces garbage.

### How much data do I need to fine-tune an LLM?

**For style, tone and format, a few hundred high-quality examples produce a visible change. For a classification or extraction skill, a few thousand. For a new domain's language, tens of thousands. Below a hundred, prompting with examples usually does as well.** LIMA's thousand examples are the reference point for how little alignment data can be if it is clean [6].


### Can I use synthetic data for fine-tuning?

**Yes, and most teams do, by having a stronger model generate examples from a spec or from seed documents. It works when you filter hard: validate every synthetic example against the spec, deduplicate, and mix in real examples so the model does not learn the generator's tics.** Alpaca itself was trained on synthetic data generated from 175 human-written seeds [8].


## Which base model should I fine-tune?

**Pick the smallest open-weight model that already does the task acceptably with a prompt, in a size that fits your GPU with QLoRA, with a licence you can ship under. Start from the instruct variant when your task is conversational and from the base variant when you are teaching a completion format from scratch. Small models, 1 to 4 billion parameters, fine-tune faster, serve cheaper and are often enough.**


In my own write-up of a run on FineTune Studio, a 1.7-billion-parameter model fine-tuned with QLoRA in about 3.2 GB of VRAM [16]. That is laptop territory. The trade-off you accept is ceiling: a small model learns a narrow behaviour well and generalises less. For a support-ticket classifier that is exactly right. For an open-ended assistant it is not.

### Can I fine-tune GPT or other closed models?

**Yes, through the vendor's API. OpenAI offers fine-tuning of selected models with an upload-and-train workflow, priced per training and inference token [14]. You get no weights, no adapter file and no local inference; you get a model identifier. It is the right choice when you already depend on that vendor and do not want to run inference yourself, and the wrong one when you need control, portability or offline use.**


## How do I fine-tune an LLM on a free GPU or locally?

**Use QLoRA with a 1 to 7 billion parameter model, a sequence length trimmed to your data, gradient checkpointing, a small batch with gradient accumulation, and a library that handles the memory tricks: Hugging Face PEFT with TRL's SFTTrainer, or Unsloth for faster and leaner runs. A free Colab T4 with 16 GB handles a 7B QLoRA run at short sequence lengths; a 12 to 16 GB laptop GPU handles 1 to 4B comfortably.**



The minimal PEFT and TRL recipe, trimmed to the lines that matter:

```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, BitsAndBytesConfig
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig

bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
                         bnb_4bit_compute_dtype="bfloat16")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE, quantization_config=bnb, device_map="auto")
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE)

lora = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
                  target_modules="all-linear")
cfg = SFTConfig(output_dir="out", num_train_epochs=2, learning_rate=2e-4,
                per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=8,
                gradient_checkpointing=True, max_length=1024, eval_strategy="steps",
                eval_steps=50, logging_steps=10)
trainer = SFTTrainer(model=model, args=cfg, train_dataset=train, eval_dataset=val,
                     processing_class=tok, peft_config=lora)
trainer.train()
```

Argument names shift between library versions, so check the current TRL and PEFT documentation rather than copying blindly [9][10]. Unsloth wraps the same idea with custom kernels that cut memory and time further [12].


## Which hyper-parameters matter for fine-tuning?

**Four: learning rate, number of epochs, LoRA rank with its alpha, and effective batch size. Learning rate too high and the loss spikes or the model forgets; too low and nothing changes. More than two or three epochs on a small dataset usually means memorising it. Rank 8 to 32 covers most tasks. Everything else, dropout, warm-up, scheduler, stays at library defaults until an experiment says otherwise.**


A defensible starting grid, which is what FineTune Studio pre-fills: learning rate 2e-4 for adapters, 2 epochs, rank 16 with alpha 32, effective batch size 16 through accumulation, warm-up of a few percent of steps. Change one variable per run, keep the eval set fixed, and write down what you changed. Fine-tuning without a lab notebook is guessing with a GPU bill.

## How do I read the loss curve?

**Watch two lines: training loss should fall steadily; validation loss should fall with it and then flatten. The moment validation loss turns upward while training loss keeps falling, the model is memorising the training set and you should stop at the earlier checkpoint. A training loss that never falls means the learning rate is too low, the data is inconsistent, or the template is wrong. A loss that collapses to near zero in the first steps means leaked labels or duplicated data.**



Live telemetry is the feature I built FineTune Studio around: loss, learning rate and throughput stream to the browser over WebSockets so a run can be judged in the first few hundred steps rather than discovered as a waste hours later [15].

## How do I evaluate a fine-tuned model honestly?

**Hold out prompts the model never trained on and compare the base model and the fine-tuned model on the same prompts side by side, scored against your spec by a rubric, by exact match where outputs are structured, and by a human for a sample. Report the comparison, not the fine-tuned model alone; a fine-tune that is not better than the base with a good prompt should not ship. Also test a few general prompts to catch forgetting.**


Perplexity on held-out text is cheap and tells you the model has learned the distribution; it does not tell you the outputs are useful. For structured outputs, parse them and measure exact-field accuracy. For free text, a rubric scored by a stronger model plus a human sample is the workable compromise. FineTune Studio shows base and fine-tuned answers to the same prompt next to each other for exactly this reason: the effect of a run should be visible before anything is deployed [15].

### What is catastrophic forgetting?

**Catastrophic forgetting is when fine-tuning on a narrow task degrades the model's general abilities, because the weights that encoded them were overwritten. Luo et al. measured it across model sizes and found it increases with more aggressive training [7]. LoRA reduces it by touching fewer weights; lower learning rates, fewer epochs, and mixing a slice of general instruction data into your dataset reduce it further.**


## What are instruction tuning, RLHF and DPO?

**Instruction tuning is supervised fine-tuning on instruction and response pairs so a base model learns to follow requests. RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, then trains a reward model on human preference rankings and optimises the LLM against it, the recipe behind InstructGPT [4]. DPO, direct preference optimisation, reaches a similar result without a separate reward model or reinforcement learning loop by training directly on preferred versus rejected answer pairs [5]. For most teams, supervised fine-tuning first, DPO if you have preference data.**



TRL ships trainers for all three, and DPO on top of a supervised fine-tune is the practical path for a student project that wants to demonstrate preference tuning [10].

## How do I deploy a fine-tuned model?

**Merge the adapter into the base weights if you want a single artefact, or keep the adapter separate and load it at runtime if you will serve several adapters on one base. Quantise the merged model to GGUF for CPU and consumer-GPU serving with llama.cpp, or to AWQ or GPTQ for GPU servers, then serve with vLLM, llama.cpp, or a Hugging Face endpoint. Keep the exact prompt template from training in the serving code.**



Serving multiple LoRA adapters on one base model is how a single GPU can host several fine-tuned behaviours, one per client or per task, which is often the difference between a fine-tuning idea that pays and one that does not.

## What mistakes do beginners make when fine-tuning?

**Fine-tuning before trying a better prompt. Training on facts and expecting recall. Using the wrong chat template. Training for ten epochs on a thousand examples. Skipping the validation split. Never comparing with the base model. Quantising before training instead of after. Shipping without the training-time prompt. Each one I have either made or watched a mentee make, and each is cheap to avoid.**



## Is fine-tuning worth it? What does it cost?

**Compute is the cheap part: a QLoRA run on a small model costs a few GPU hours, which is free on Colab or a few dollars rented. The real costs are the dataset, weeks of a person's time to write and clean examples, and the maintenance, since every requirement change means another run and another evaluation. It is worth it when the behaviour is stable, the volume is high enough that a small fine-tuned model saves inference cost, or no prompt on any model gets the format right.**


The honest test I apply before quoting a client: write the twenty examples first. If writing twenty consistent examples is hard, the spec is not ready and the fine-tune will encode the confusion. If it is easy, the fine-tune will probably work, and those twenty become the first rows of the dataset.


## Where should a student start with fine-tuning?

**Read the LoRA and QLoRA papers for the idea, then fine-tune a 1 to 2B instruct model on a few hundred examples you wrote yourself, on a free GPU, and compare it with the base model on prompts you held out. Ship the adapter to Hugging Face with a model card that reports the comparison. That single project demonstrates dataset design, training, evaluation and honesty, and it fits in a weekend.**


I run sessions on exactly this for college tech clubs, and it is one of the five talks I offer. If your club or hackathon wants one, my email is pranjulrathour41@gmail.com and the details are at pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to get an AI internship as a student in India: where to apply, the portfolio that gets replies, cold emails that work, and what to do when your college has no placements
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-get-an-ai-internship/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I get an AI internship as a student?

**Build three live projects that look like the work, put them on a GitHub profile a recruiter can read in two minutes, and apply where AI work is visible: startups, agencies and small product companies, through their websites, founders' inboxes and the events they sponsor. Large companies mostly hire interns through campus programmes with degree and college filters; do not spend your energy fighting that filter in year two. My own first work came through a community I built and hackathons I entered, not through a placement cell, and that route is open to every student reading this.**


The longer versions of the outreach and the year-two decision are on the portfolio [8][9]. This is the operational page.

> Nobody replied to my resume. People replied to a link where they could click on something I had built and it worked.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Which companies actually hire AI interns?

**Three kinds, in the order you should approach them. Startups and small product companies shipping AI features: they need hands, hire on portfolios, and a founder reads the inbox. Agencies and studios building AI for clients, such as the one I lead engineering for: varied projects, real deadlines, fast learning. Research labs and large companies: structured programmes, degree filters, campus channels, worth applying to but not worth waiting on. Remote-first companies abroad hire Indian students on portfolios and time-zone overlap.**



## Where should I look for AI internships?

**Internshala and Unstop for volume in India, filtered hard for roles that mention specific work, RAG, LLM, computer vision, not "AI intern" alone [1][4]. Wellfound for startups, including remote [2]. LinkedIn Jobs with alerts for your city plus the stack [3]. Google Summer of Code for paid open-source work with mentors [5]. Devfolio and other hackathon platforms, because sponsors recruit from the teams they watch [6]. And the inboxes of founders whose products you have used, which is where the best internships I know of came from.**


## What projects get internship replies?

**Three, each live at a URL with a README and a two-minute demo video. A RAG assistant over a real document set with measured retrieval recall. A small fine-tuned model with a base-versus-tuned comparison. One useful web app that a real person uses, even if that person is your club. Together they prove retrieval, training, evaluation and shipping. Match one of them to each company you write to; the reply rate on a matched project is many times that of a generic resume.**



The projects that get interviews, with reasons, are written up separately [10], and the GitHub profile that makes them findable is its own note [12].

## How do I write a cold email for an internship?

**Five sentences. Who you are and what you are studying, one line. One specific thing about their product or a recent post of theirs, which proves you looked. One link to a project of yours that resembles their work, with a one-line result. One specific ask: a four-to-eight-week internship on a named area, paid or unpaid stated plainly, remote or on-site. A thank-you. Under 120 words, from a real email address, with a subject line that names the company and the ask. Follow up once after a week.**


```
Subject: GenAI internship, RAG work, VSICS student

Hi Neha,

I'm Aarav, second-year BCA at VSICS. I used your document-search
product last month and noticed it returns whole pages rather than passages.

I built a RAG assistant over my college's syllabus with hybrid retrieval and
measured recall@10 of 0.9 on 40 real questions: <link to live demo and repo>.

Would you consider a six-week remote internship on retrieval quality this
summer? Paid or unpaid, I'd like to know which upfront.

Thank you for reading.
Aarav Singh · <portfolio> · +91 9xxxx xxxxx
```

Every line does a job. My longer notes on cold outreach, including what got replies and what did not, are on the portfolio [8].


## What if my college has no placement cell or AI companies do not visit?

**Then you are in my situation, and the route is the same one I took. Build the three projects. Start or join a community and teach in it, because communities are where referrals come from. Enter hackathons, in person when you can, because sponsors and judges hire. Contribute to an open-source project a target company uses. Post one build a week where engineers read. Apply remotely with the portfolio. The placement cell is one channel; these are five, and they work from any campus.**



## Should I take an unpaid internship, freelance instead, or start something?

**Take an unpaid internship only if the work is real, the mentor is real and it is short; otherwise freelance for small clients, which pays and teaches delivery, or build a product for a community you belong to. In year two I chose client work through the agency route and it taught more than any internship offer I had, but it is not the right answer for everyone. The decision framework is written up separately [9].**



## How do I get a remote AI internship?

**Portfolio first, writing second. Remote teams cannot see your college and do not care; they see your GitHub, your README and how clearly you write in email. Target companies that already hire remotely, contribute to their open-source tools, apply with a matching project, and be explicit about your time-zone overlap, which for Europe is India's structural advantage. Practise asynchronous communication by writing good READMEs and posts, because that is the interview.**


My notes on getting hired for remote AI work from India cover the companies and the communication habits in detail [11].

## How do I convert an internship into a job?

**Ship something visible in the first two weeks. Write a short weekly note of what you did and what you learned, and send it to your mentor. Take the unglamorous tasks and finish them completely. Ask questions in public channels so the team sees you learning. A month before the end, ask directly: what would it take to continue, and in what role? Most conversions happen because the intern asked, not because the company remembered.**




## What mistakes do students make applying for AI internships?

**Sending a resume with no links. Listing courses instead of projects. Applying only to large companies through portals. Generic emails to fifty founders. Projects that are tutorial clones with the name changed. A GitHub with one commit per project. Giving up after ten applications, when the pipeline needs a hundred. Waiting for the placement cell. Every one of these has a fix on this page.**



## Want help with your first application?

**I run career sessions for tech clubs that end with each student having a project pitch and a cold email drafted, and I review portfolios in mentoring sessions through TechVerse Enclave.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to give a guest lecture in college: preparing a technical talk, handling Q&A, and becoming a speaker colleges invite back
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-give-a-guest-lecture-in-college/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I get invited to give a guest lecture at a college?

**Do something specific, describe it in public, and make it easy to book you. Colleges and tech clubs invite people whose credential fits in one sentence, "shipped five production AI apps", "won Changethon at IIT Roorkee", and who have a page or a post that shows what a session with them looks like. Start with your own college and clubs you belong to, offer a concrete topic and two dates, say it is free for students, and post about the first session the same week. The second invitation comes from the first post.**


My first sessions were at VSICS, my own college, to first-years and to the coding club: a career roadmap, a session on AI in the software lifecycle, a debate [1][2][3]. Each one produced a post with photos, each post produced the next invitation, and the pattern has not changed since. A page listing the talks I offer, with formats and logistics, is what organisers now book from [8].

> Nobody invites you to talk about AI. They invite you to talk about the thing you built, because you are the only person who can.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What should a guest lecture cover?

**One outcome. Decide what students should be able to do on Monday because of your session, then build backwards. For first-years: a roadmap and permission to start. For second- and third-years: one skill demonstrated live and a project to try. For final-years: what the industry actually hires for and how to show it. A talk that covers a whole topic teaches nothing; a talk that changes one action teaches something.**



The three-year roadmap I gave 100+ first-years at the VSICS induction was one outcome: know what year one, two and three are for, and start year one this week [1].

## How do I structure a 60- or 90-minute technical talk?

**Open with a two-minute story that has a failure in it. Show the map: three or four ideas, on one slide, that the session will cover. Do one live demo of something real, ten minutes at most. Give the roadmap: what to do next, in order. Then stop early and take questions for the rest of the slot. Students remember the story, the demo and one line from the roadmap. Slides are cue cards with one idea each; nobody reads paragraphs on a screen.**



My full outline for a 90-minute GenAI session, with the demo and the roadmap slides, is written up on the portfolio [6].

## How do I prepare a guest lecture?

**Ask the organiser five questions: who is in the room and how many, what year, what they already know, what the room has, and what they want students to leave with. Write the one outcome. Build the demo first and rehearse it on the machine you will use. Then write slides, no more than one per two minutes. Rehearse once with a timer, once without slides, and cut a third. Arrive early and test the projector with your laptop.**



The longer version of how I prepare is on the portfolio [4]; the short version is that the demo is built before a single slide exists.

## How do I handle a quiet room or a difficult question?

**A quiet room is a setup problem. Ask a question with no wrong answer, "who here has used ChatGPT for an assignment?", raise your own hand, and wait a full five seconds. Take the first answer seriously and build on it. For a question you cannot answer, say so, say what you would check and how, and offer to follow up by email. For a hostile question, restate it calmly, answer the part that is fair, and move on. Students forgive not knowing; they do not forgive bluffing.**


I wrote a separate piece on handling Q&A after technical talks, because it is where most speakers either win or lose the room [5]. The single most useful habit: repeat every question aloud before answering, so the back row hears it and you get three seconds to think.


## Should I use slides, a demo or a whiteboard?

**All three, in that priority reversed: demo first, whiteboard for the one idea that needs drawing, slides as cue cards. A live demo of a real system is the part students talk about afterwards and the part that proves you have built things. A whiteboard sketch of an architecture lands harder than a diagram slide because they watch it appear. Slides carry structure, links and the roadmap. Never read from them.**



## Are guest lecturers paid? Should I charge?

**Some are, many are not, and universities often have fixed honoraria under their rules. I speak at student communities for free, on-site with travel covered or remote at no cost, because those rooms are where the people I want in the industry sit, and because I was helped the same way. Early on, speak for free and for the post. Later, charge companies and conferences, and keep colleges free if you can. Say your terms in your first reply so nobody is embarrassed.**


## How do I become a hackathon judge or mentor as well?

**The same way, one step further: attend hackathons, then mentor at one, then ask the organiser to sit on the panel. Organisers want judges who have built and shipped, who can brief a rubric and who show up on time. Once you have judged once, the invitations come with the speaking ones. Publish your rubric, because organisers copy it and remember where it came from.**


My path from participant to judge, and what organisers told me they look for, is written up separately [7].

## What mistakes do first-time speakers make?

**Covering everything. Reading slides. Forty minutes of context before anything concrete. A demo that has never run on the presenting laptop. No questions asked of the room until the end. Running over time into the next session. Bluffing an answer. Leaving without sharing slides or a way to reach you. Each is fixable before the session with the checklist above; none is fixable during it.**



## How do I turn one talk into a lasting relationship with a college?

**Send the slides and links within a day. Reply to every student email for a month. Post the photos and tag the college and the club. Then propose the next thing: a hands-on workshop, a judging slot at their hackathon, monthly office hours for the club. Three of my longest mentoring relationships with student clubs started as a single session followed by one email I bothered to send.**



## Where can I start speaking?

**At your own college's club, next month, on the thing you built last semester. Offer two dates, one topic and a demo. If you would like to see how I structure sessions, the talk menu and the 90-minute outline are public [6][8].** If your college wants a session, or wants a speaker to show your students how to become speakers, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to improve your public speaking for tech talks: structure, nerves, filler words, and the practice that actually moves the needle
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-improve-public-speaking-for-tech-talks/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I actually get better at public speaking for tech talks?

**By practising the specific talk out loud, repeatedly, more than by practising "public speaking" as a general skill. Generic advice, power poses, deep breathing, helps a little with nerves in the moment, but the bigger lever for a technical talk is structure: a clear problem, a logical build, a strong close, rehearsed enough times that you are not simultaneously thinking about content and delivery. Most improvement comes from removing the specific things you are afraid of, forgetting what comes next, losing the room, running over time, one rehearsal at a time.**


I have given technical talks to rooms from twenty to several hundred students, and the improvement that actually showed up in feedback came almost entirely from rehearsal discipline, not from any general public-speaking technique.

> Confidence on stage is not a personality trait. It is the residue of having rehearsed the specific talk enough times that nothing in it can surprise you.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Why does structure matter more than delivery style for a technical talk?

**Because an audience that cannot follow the logical thread of a talk will not be won over by good delivery, and an audience that can follow a clear structure will forgive an imperfect delivery. A technical talk needs a stated problem, a build toward the solution with one idea per section, and a close that restates what changed for the listener. Delivery, pace, tone, eye contact, matters, but it amplifies a structure that already works; it cannot rescue a talk that has no clear thread [3][4].**



## How do I handle nerves before and during a talk?

**Nerves rarely disappear with experience; they get quieter because thorough preparation removes the specific fears driving them. Rehearse the opening thirty seconds until it is close to memorised, since a strong start calms the rest of the talk. Arrive early enough to test the room's tech, slides, mic, clicker, so equipment surprises do not add to the nerves. Accept a slightly faster heartbeat as normal rather than fighting it, and use the first minute's adrenaline for energy rather than trying to suppress it entirely.**




## How do I cut filler words like "um" and "so"?

**Replace the filler with a deliberate silent pause instead of trying to suppress it through willpower alone; a pause reads as confidence, while "um" reads as searching. Filler words cluster at points where you have not fully decided what comes next, so the real fix is often tightening your structure and rehearsal, not a speech habit in isolation. Recording yourself and counting fillers in a five-minute segment makes the habit visible, which is usually enough to start correcting it, since most people underestimate how often they do it until they hear it back.**



## What is the single most effective practice habit?

**Rehearsing the actual talk out loud, standing, at full volume, as many times as the stakes justify, rather than silently reading slides or rehearsing only in your head. Silent rehearsal does not train the muscle memory of speaking, the timing, or where you actually stumble; those only show up when you say the words aloud. Recording one full out-loud rehearsal and watching it back, however uncomfortable, surfaces more fixable problems in ten minutes than a week of silent preparation.**



## How do I read a room and adjust in real time?

**Watch for the visible signals: heads down on phones, note-taking, confused frowns, nodding along, and adjust pace or depth accordingly, slowing down and adding an example when you see confusion, moving faster when you see impatience. This is trainable by deliberately watching the room instead of only your slides or notes during rehearsal-adjacent early talks, and by asking a trusted person in the audience to flag specific moments afterward where the room's energy visibly shifted.**


## What mistakes do people make trying to improve their public speaking?

**Practising general public-speaking exercises instead of the actual talk they need to give. Reading slides silently and calling it rehearsal. Trying to eliminate nerves entirely instead of channelling them. Adding more content when a talk runs long instead of cutting it, which makes nerves worse under time pressure. Never recording themselves, so the gap between how a talk feels and how it actually sounds stays invisible.**



## Public speaking interview and evaluation questions

**"Tell me about a time you presented to a group" is asked in almost every interview, technical or not, and the strongest answers describe a specific talk, its structure, and what you changed after getting feedback, not a general claim of being "good at public speaking". Toastmasters-style structured feedback, or simply asking a trusted listener for one specific thing to improve, builds this evidence faster than unstructured practice alone [1].**



## Where should I start?

**Record yourself giving your next talk's opening two minutes, out loud, standing, and watch it back once. That single exercise usually surfaces more than a week of reading advice.** For a workshop on technical public speaking for students and early-career engineers, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to invite a guest speaker to your college: the email, the one-pager, fees, logistics and what makes a speaker say yes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-invite-a-guest-speaker-to-your-college/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I invite a guest speaker to my college?

**Send one clear email with six things: who you are and which club or department you represent, who will be in the room and how many, two or three proposed dates with a time window, the format and duration you want, the topic you hope they will cover and the outcome you want for students, and what you can offer, travel, a certificate, a recording, a meal. Then follow up once after five days. Speakers say yes to invitations that make the decision easy.**


I receive these invitations regularly, and the ones I accept fastest share a shape. This is the template, written from the receiving end, with what actually decides a yes [1].

> "Can you come and speak about AI?" is the most common invitation I get and the hardest to say yes to, because "AI" is not a talk. "Can you run a 90-minute session on building a RAG system for 60 third-years on 12 or 19 October?" is a talk.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What should the invitation email say?

**Subject: "Guest session on [topic] for [college], [month]". Body: one line on who you are, one on the audience, the two dates, the format, the topic and outcome, the offer, and a link to your club's page or last event. Under 200 words. Attach nothing; link instead. Sign with a name, a role and a phone number.**


```
Subject: Guest session on GenAI engineering for VSICS, October

Hi Pranjul,

I'm Aditi, secretary of the coding club at VSICS. We run monthly
sessions for 60 to 80 second- and third-year BCA and B.Tech students.

Would you run a 90-minute session on building a RAG system, ending with
students having a working demo? Proposed dates: Sat 12 Oct or Sat 19 Oct,
11:00 to 12:30, in our seminar hall (projector, Wi-Fi, 80 seats).

We can cover travel within the city, provide a certificate and lunch, and
will post photos and a recap tagging you the same week.

Last month's session: <link>. Happy to adjust the topic to your menu.

Aditi Sharma, Coding Club, VSICS, +91 98xxx xxxxx
```

Every sentence answers a question the speaker would otherwise have to ask. That is the whole trick.

## How do I find a guest speaker for a college event?

**Start with alumni working in the field, then practitioners in your city, then people who already post about speaking at colleges on LinkedIn. Search LinkedIn for your city plus the topic and "workshop" or "session", check who has spoken at nearby colleges' events, ask community organisers at Google Developer Groups on Campus or Microsoft Learn Student Ambassadors chapters, and look at who judges local hackathons. People who already give their time to students are the ones who will give it to you.**



Community programmes such as Google Developer Groups on Campus and Microsoft Learn Student Ambassadors exist partly to connect chapters with speakers, and their organisers know who is active in your region [6][7]. Major League Hacking's community does the same for hackathon-adjacent speakers [8].

## Are guest speakers paid? What does a guest lecturer cost?

**It varies. Many working engineers, including me, speak at student communities for free, on-site with travel covered or remote at no cost, because that is how we were helped. Professional speakers and senior executives often charge a fee. Universities sometimes have a fixed honorarium for guest lecturers under their academic rules. Ask directly in the first email: "We can offer travel and a certificate; if you have a fee, please tell us." Nobody is offended by that sentence.**


My own rule: free for student communities and colleges, on-site anywhere in India with travel covered, remote anywhere at no cost [3]. The reason is not generosity; it is that the students in those rooms are exactly the people I want in the community and, later, in the industry.

## What topics should I ask a speaker to cover?

**Ask for a topic that ends with students able to do something, not knowing something. "Build a RAG system in 90 minutes", "How hackathon judges score, from a judge", "From BCA to GenAI engineer: the roadmap", "Ship your first AI app for free". Pick from the speaker's own menu if they publish one, and say which of your students it is for: first-years need a roadmap; final-years need a project and interview preparation.**



The five talks I offer, with the audience each is built for, are listed on the portfolio [2]. Most practitioners who speak regularly have a similar page; asking for one of their listed talks gets a faster yes than asking them to invent one.

## What does a speaker need from the organisers?

**A one-pager a week before the event: the exact venue and how to reach it, the audience size and year, start and end times, the schedule around their slot, the tech setup, projector input, Wi-Fi, microphone, whiteboard, two contact numbers, and what you will need from them, a bio, a photo, a title. On the day: someone to meet them, water, a working projector tested with their laptop, and a hard stop you protect.**



The single most common failure I see is the projector: a laptop that will not connect, an adapter nobody has, ten minutes of the session gone. Test with the speaker's actual laptop, or ask them to send slides to run from yours.


## How do I introduce a guest speaker?

**In under a minute: their name, what they do now, one specific thing they have built or achieved that this audience will respect, why they are here today, and their name again. Do not read their whole LinkedIn. Do not list every award. One concrete credential lands harder than ten adjectives.**


For example: "Pranjul Rathour is a GenAI engineer who shipped five production AI systems this year and won first prize at Changethon at IIT Roorkee. He did his BCA at this college. He's here to show you how a RAG system is actually built. Please welcome Pranjul." Forty seconds, done.

## What is the difference between a guest lecture, a seminar, a workshop and a webinar?

**A guest lecture is one expert speaking to a class, usually 45 to 90 minutes with questions. A seminar is a session built around discussion, often with several speakers or student presentations. A workshop is hands-on: students build or practise something with the speaker's guidance, and it needs laptops, more time and a smaller room. A webinar is any of these delivered online. Ask for the format that matches your goal: a lecture to inspire, a workshop to equip.**



## How do I get a speaker for a remote or online session?

**The same email, minus travel, plus the platform you will use and whether you will record. Remote sessions are the easiest yes a speaker can give, so use them for speakers outside your city, for shorter formats and for follow-ups after an in-person session. Test the platform with the speaker for five minutes the day before, assign a moderator to read questions, and send the recording link within a week.**


I speak remotely for any student community anywhere at no cost, which is true of many practitioners; the constraint is never the speaker's willingness, it is whether the invitation is concrete [3].

## How do I turn one session into a lasting relationship?

**Post the photos and a recap the same week, tagging the speaker and the college. Send a two-line thank-you with one thing students did as a result. Then ask for the next specific thing: judging your hackathon, a follow-up workshop, an office-hours call for the club, feedback on three student projects. Speakers remember organisers who follow through, and the second yes is always faster than the first.**


Three of my longest mentoring relationships with student clubs started as one session; what they had in common was an organiser who wrote back a week later with photos and a question.


## What mistakes do organisers make?

**Vague topics. One date offered with no alternative. Asking two days before the event. No mention of the audience. Attachments instead of links. Forgetting to say whether the session is online or on-site. Not testing the projector. Ending late and eating into the speaker's next commitment. Never posting afterwards. Each is fixed by the checklist above, and each one I have experienced as a speaker.**



## Can I invite you?

**Yes. Send the six things above to pranjulrathour41@gmail.com, or use the invite page, which lists the five talks, the formats and the logistics I need [4].** Free for student communities, on-site across India with travel covered, remote anywhere. The abstract and bio come back the same day.
