# How to win a hackathon: what judges score, how to pick an idea, and the demo that works live, from three first prizes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-win-a-hackathon/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is a hackathon?

**A hackathon is a timed competition, usually 24 to 48 hours, sometimes a few weeks online, where small teams build a working prototype that solves a stated problem and then pitch it to judges. The output is a demo, not a plan. The prize is usually cash, credits or an incubation offer, but the lasting value is the project, the repository and the people you built it with.**


The word blends "hack", in the sense of building something quickly, with "marathon". In India the format ranges from a two-day event in a college seminar hall to Smart India Hackathon, the government-run national competition with a months-long process [1]. AI hackathons are the same format with problem statements that expect a model, an agent or a data pipeline in the solution.

I have been on both sides of the table: three first prizes as a builder, at IIT Roorkee, CSJMU and MeetKats, a loss I learned more from than any win, and time as a judge and mentor at college events. This page is the version of the talk I give students, with the parts that made the difference between winning and not.

> Every hackathon I won, we solved a smaller problem than the teams we beat. Every hackathon I lost, we tried to solve a bigger one.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does a hackathon work?

**Registration opens weeks ahead. Teams form, usually two to five people. On the day, organisers reveal or confirm the problem statements, the timer starts, and teams build. Mentors circulate. At the end, each team submits code and a short deck and gets a few minutes to demo and answer questions. Judges score against a rubric, and prizes follow.**



The single most important line in that timeline is "skeleton with the demo path stubbed end to end" in the first six hours. A team that can click through a fake version of the final demo at hour 6 will have a real one at hour 30. A team that builds features in isolation integrates at hour 33 and demos a crash.

## How do I find and join a hackathon in India?

**Devfolio and Unstop list most Indian college and company hackathons, Major League Hacking lists student events worldwide, Devpost covers global online ones, and Smart India Hackathon runs through colleges via its official portal. Follow the tech clubs of IITs, NITs and nearby colleges on Instagram and LinkedIn, because campus hackathons are announced there first. Register early; good events fill.**



Sources for these listings are the platforms themselves [2][3][4][5]. My recommendation for a first-year: one campus hackathon within a two-hour train ride, in person, before any online one. You learn more from watching thirty teams demo in one room than from a month of tutorials.

### Can a beginner participate in a hackathon?

**Yes, and you should, before you feel ready. Most college hackathons have a beginner track or no prerequisites at all. Join a team where one person can already build a basic web or Python app, take the role that matches what you can do, design, research, presentation, testing, and build the skill of finishing under a deadline. Nobody is judged on their first hackathon; they are judged on their demo.**


## How do I pick a hackathon idea that can win?

**Pick a problem a specific person has, that you can demonstrate end to end in three minutes, where the hardest part is something your team can actually build in the time you have. Start from the problem statement's audience, list five problems that person has, choose the one with the clearest before-and-after, and cut everything that is not on the path from the user's pain to your demo.**


Ideas that won for us, and why:

- **KrishGyan, Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee.** Farming advice in the farmer's own voice and language over WhatsApp: pest control, crop health and weather, spoken back, no reading or typing needed. It won because the demo was a voice note in and a voice note out, which any judge could follow, and because the audience was real and underserved [6].
- **BrandHive, Product Genesis at CSJMU.** A platform for small businesses and emerging influencers to grow organically without a marketing budget. It won because we showed the whole loop, not a slide of features [7].
- **Annapurna, BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats.** Coordinating surplus food between donors, NGOs and volunteers, with four roles and a verified-impact layer. It won on clarity of roles and a demo that walked one meal from a hotel kitchen to a shelter [8].

And the one that did not: STROT, where we built more and explained less, and a simpler team took the prize [9]. That loss is why every timeline I give now starts with cutting scope.


### What are good AI hackathon project ideas?

**The winning AI ideas apply a model to one narrow workflow with real inputs: voice-first advice for people who do not type, document extraction for a specific paper form, a RAG assistant over one institution's documents, a vision check for one quality problem, an agent that completes one repetitive task end to end. "ChatGPT for X" loses to "this one task, done, with this evidence".**


A frame that produces ideas fast: pick an audience, farmers, first-year students, small shops, clinics, college offices; pick a friction, a form, a queue, a language barrier, a lost document; ask what the AI removes. KrishGyan came out of exactly that frame: farmers, the reading barrier, voice.

## What do hackathon judges actually look for?

**Judges score four things, whatever the rubric calls them: feasibility, does it work and could it exist; innovation, is there a real insight, not just a new coat of paint; practicality, would the stated user actually use it; and problem solving, did you understand the problem before you built. Presentation and teamwork are usually smaller weights. A working demo of a modest idea beats a slide deck of a grand one every time.**



These four criteria, feasibility, innovation, practicality and problem solving, are the ones I put on the screen when I brief a room as a judge, and the ones I wrote about after sitting on panels [10]. The weights change; the questions do not.


### What questions do judges ask in Q&A?

**Who is this for and have you spoken to them? What happens when this fails? How is this different from the existing solution? What would you build next with a month? Which part did you write yourselves versus take from a library? Judges use Q&A to find out whether you understand your own project, so short honest answers beat confident vague ones.**


## How do I pitch a hackathon project?

**In three minutes: thirty seconds on who has the problem and what it costs them, ninety seconds of live demo on the happy path, thirty seconds on how it works with one architecture slide, and thirty seconds on what you would do next and what you are asking for. Say the user's name, not the technology's, in the first sentence. Rehearse it three times with a timer.**



For Smart India Hackathon the format is more formal and the template is prescribed, but the same order inside it wins: problem, demo, how, next. Teams that open with a slide of technologies lose the room in the first fifteen seconds.

### How do I give a demo that works live?

**Freeze your code at least two hours before demos. Rehearse the exact click path three times on the machine you will present from, on the venue Wi-Fi if you can. Seed the data so the demo never depends on a live network call you do not control. Record a backup video of the full path and have it open in a tab. Assign one person to drive and one to talk.**


The demo that failed for us at STROT failed on a live API call over venue Wi-Fi. Every demo since has run on seeded data with a recorded fallback, and none has failed.

## How should a hackathon team be formed?

**Three people with three roles: one who builds the core, one who owns the interface and the data, one who owns the problem, the deck and the pitch and also tests everything. Decide roles before the event, not at hour one. A friend who cannot code but can research users and present is worth more than a fourth developer.**


Every first prize we won was a team of three with those roles. Teams of five spend their first three hours negotiating and their last three merging conflicts.


## What is Smart India Hackathon and how do I crack it?

**Smart India Hackathon is a national competition run by the Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell in which student teams solve problem statements posted by government ministries and industry. Teams register through their college, are shortlisted internally, then compete at the national level. To do well: pick a problem statement whose owner you can reach, build a working prototype early, and make the presentation about the ministry's outcome, not your stack.**


The official portal carries the current year's problem statements, timeline and eligibility, and it changes each cycle, so read it rather than any summary, including this one [1]. What stays constant: the internal college round eliminates most teams, so treat the internal presentation as the real competition, and the national judges are domain experts from the problem's ministry, so the domain matters more than the demo polish.

## Do hackathons help your career or resume?

**Yes, when you turn them into evidence: a public repository with a readable README, a two-minute demo video, and a short write-up of the problem, the decision you made and the result. A line saying "participated in 6 hackathons" does nothing. A line saying "1st prize, Changethon 2025, IIT Roorkee, built a voice-first farming assistant over WhatsApp" with a link does the work of a semester of grades.**


On LinkedIn, add the hackathon under Honours & awards with the issuer and date, and post the demo video the same week; hackathon posts travel further than any other student content, in my experience running a 500-member community. On the resume, one line per win, with the problem and the result, and the repository link.

## What mistakes make teams lose?

**Building for 34 hours and presenting for 2. Choosing a problem to impress rather than to solve. No roles, so everyone builds the same screen. A live demo that depends on Wi-Fi. A deck that opens with the tech stack. Not talking to a single real user. Sleeping zero hours and demoing incoherently. Every one of these is cheaper to avoid than to recover from.**



## What should I do after the hackathon?

**Within a week: clean the repository, write the README, publish the demo video, and post the story. Within a month: decide whether the project deserves users, and if so, ship the smallest real version. Annapurna went from a hackathon prize to a tool people used because we kept the roles that worked and threw away the parts built for the judges.**



## Can I invite a judge or mentor to my college hackathon?

**Yes. Organisers can reach me for judging, mentoring or a session on hackathon strategy before your event, on-site across India or remote. What I need from you is the date, the format, the problem statements if fixed, and the rubric you plan to use, or I will bring the four-criteria one above.**


The details and the invite form are at pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite, and my email is pranjulrathour41@gmail.com. Free for student communities.

# How to write a tech resume as a fresher in India: the one-page format, what to put instead of a skills wall, and a free resume website that beats a PDF
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-write-a-tech-resume-for-freshers-in-india/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How should a fresher write a tech resume?

**One page. A header with your name, one line describing what you build, and links to email, GitHub and a portfolio, no photo, no objective paragraph. A projects section with three entries, each with the problem, the decision, and a measurable outcome, ahead of education. A short skills line, not a wall. Education below projects, since for a fresher the projects are the evidence and the degree is context. Nothing that needs a second page has earned its place yet.**


I have reviewed enough fresher resumes at hackathons and campus sessions to see the same mistakes repeat: a skills wall with forty items, an objective paragraph nobody reads, and projects buried under a "certifications" section three times its length. This page is the fix, plus the free resume-website option that often works better than the PDF itself [6].

> A resume is not a list of everything you know. It is three pieces of evidence that you can do the job, arranged so a tired recruiter finds them in ten seconds.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What should be at the top of the resume?

**Your name, a phone number, an email you actually check, and three links: GitHub, a portfolio or LinkedIn, and one more if relevant. Under that, one line: what you build and one proof, the same sentence your LinkedIn headline should carry [3]. Not "Computer Science student seeking opportunities". Not a paragraph. One sentence a recruiter can read while scrolling past forty other resumes.**



## What goes in the projects section, and how should it read?

**Three projects, each three lines: the problem in one sentence, the decision or hard part in one sentence, and the outcome in one sentence, ideally with a number. "Built a RAG system over 40 pages of college documents; added a confidence gate after early demos returned wrong answers confidently; recall at 5 improved from 61 percent to 89 percent, measured on a 30-question set." That is one project entry. It proves you can scope, iterate, and measure, in three lines.**



My guide to which projects to choose for this section, and the ones that actually get interviews, is written up separately [7].

## Should I have a skills section, and what should it look like?

**A short line or two, grouped by category, not a wall with progress bars: "Languages: Python, JavaScript. Tools: FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Git, Docker." No percentages, no five-star ratings for how well you know a language, which nobody trusts and which ATS systems ignore anyway. List what you can actually discuss for ten minutes in an interview, and nothing you would freeze on if asked a follow-up question.**




## How do I get past an ATS without gaming it?

**Use plain, standard section headings, Experience, Projects, Education, Skills, so parsing software reads them correctly. Avoid tables, columns, text boxes and graphics that confuse a parser, however good they look to a human eye. Mirror the language of the job posting honestly where it matches what you actually did, a posting that says "REST APIs" should be met with "REST APIs" in your resume if that is what you built, not a synonym. None of this is gaming a system; it is writing clearly enough that both a machine and a human parse the same document correctly.**


## What should education look like for a fresher?

**Degree, institution, graduation year, and a CGPA only if it genuinely helps, one line, below the projects section. Coursework only if a specific course is directly relevant and not implied by the degree itself. No list of every subject studied. A recruiter reading a fresher's resume already expects a degree; the projects section is what differentiates one BCA or B.Tech graduate from another.**


## Should I use a resume website instead of a PDF?

**Both, for different moments. Send a clean one-page PDF when a form or an email asks for a resume, since that is the expected format. Link a simple resume or portfolio website in the header for everyone who wants more, because it can hold live demo links, a longer project write-up, and updates without you re-sending a file [6]. A resume website is not a replacement for the PDF; it is the deeper layer the PDF's links point to.**



## What mistakes do freshers make on tech resumes?

**A two-page resume with a full page of certificates and half a project. An objective paragraph that says nothing a recruiter could not guess. A skills wall claiming expert-level everything. Projects described by technology stack instead of outcome, "Built using React, Node.js, MongoDB" with no sentence on what it did or what was hard. Broken links to private repositories. A resume never updated after the first draft, still listing a project from first year as the newest thing built.**



## Tech resume interview questions

**Not asked directly, but tested by every "walk me through a project" question: can you defend every line on the resume for ten minutes without notes. If a bullet point cannot survive a follow-up question, it should not be on the resume. The strongest resumes are the ones the candidate wrote entirely from memory of what they actually did.**



## Where should I start?

**Cut your current resume to one page tonight: header, three projects in three lines each, a short skills line, education last. Then link a portfolio site from the header.** For a resume and portfolio workshop that turns a semester of projects into an interview-ready one-pager, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How does a vector database work? Examples, choosing one, and do you need it for RAG
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-vector-databases-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A vector database stores embeddings, numeric vectors that represent meaning, together with the original data and metadata, and answers queries by finding the vectors closest to a query vector. Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes make this fast even over millions of items. That is the retrieval step behind semantic search and RAG. This page explains how it works and what vector search is, gives examples, helps you choose, answers whether RAG needs one and how to build one, covers Supabase, NoSQL and dimensions, and whether vector databases are dead.

## How does a vector database work?

You insert items with an embedding vector, an ID and metadata. The database adds each vector to an index. At query time, you send a query vector, and the database uses the index to return the nearest stored vectors, optionally filtered by metadata.

Exact search compares the query with every vector, which is slow at scale, so vector databases use approximate indexes. HNSW builds a layered graph where each vector links to near neighbours, and search walks the graph towards the query. Inverted-file indexes cluster vectors and search only the nearest clusters. Product quantisation compresses vectors to save memory. Databases add what libraries lack: persistence, updates and deletes, filtering, access control, replication and scaling.

## What is vector search in a database?

Vector search finds items whose embeddings are most similar to a query embedding, measured by cosine similarity, dot product or Euclidean distance. It retrieves by meaning rather than exact words.

For example, searching "laptop overheating" can find a help article titled "fan noise and high temperature on notebooks" even with no shared keywords. Many databases now support vector search alongside their normal queries: PostgreSQL with pgvector, OpenSearch and Elasticsearch, MongoDB Atlas and others. Combining vector search with keyword search, called hybrid search, usually gives the best results, because keywords catch exact terms such as product codes that embeddings blur.

## What are some examples of vector databases?

Examples include pgvector for PostgreSQL, Pinecone as a managed service, Qdrant, Weaviate and Milvus as open-source dedicated vector databases, Chroma for lightweight local use, and vector search features in OpenSearch, Elasticsearch and MongoDB Atlas.

Related tools that are not full databases: FAISS, a library for fast similarity search in memory, and hnswlib, an index library. Cloud providers also offer vector capabilities in their managed databases and storage services. The landscape changes quickly, but the core ideas, embeddings, approximate indexes, filtering and hybrid search, stay the same across products.

## Which vector database should I choose?

Choose the simplest option that meets your needs: pgvector if you already use PostgreSQL, Chroma or FAISS for prototypes, Qdrant, Weaviate or Milvus for a dedicated open-source service, and Pinecone if you want fully managed scaling.

Questions to decide:

- How many vectors now and in a year: thousands, millions or billions?
- Do you need metadata filters, multi-tenancy or access control?
- Do you need keyword plus vector search?
- Who will operate it: your team or a vendor?
- Where must data live for privacy or compliance?

For most student and startup projects, pgvector on a hosted PostgreSQL is enough. Measure retrieval recall on your own questions before switching for performance reasons.

## Does RAG need a vector database?

RAG needs retrieval, not necessarily a dedicated vector database. For small document sets, an in-memory index such as FAISS, or pgvector in your existing database, is enough; some systems even use keyword search alone.

What RAG really needs is good retrieval: clean chunks, a suitable embedding model, hybrid keyword plus vector search, reranking and evaluation. RAG.NextUpgrad runs hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion and re-ranking in about 220 MB on a free tier, which shows that heavy infrastructure is not required. Move to a dedicated vector database when scale, filtering, concurrency or operations demand it.

## How do I create a vector database for RAG?

Chunk your documents, embed each chunk with one embedding model, store chunks with their vectors and metadata in a vector store, then retrieve with the same model at query time. With PostgreSQL and pgvector, it is a table with a vector column and an index.

```sql
create extension if not exists vector;
create table chunks (id bigserial primary key, doc text, page int, content text, embedding vector(768));
create index on chunks using hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
-- query: nearest 5 chunks to a query embedding
select doc, page, content from chunks order by embedding <=> $1 limit 5;
```

Match the vector dimension to your model, add a full-text index for keyword search, and store page numbers for citations.

## Does Supabase have a vector database?

Yes. Supabase supports vector storage and search through pgvector, a PostgreSQL extension, so you can store embeddings next to your other data and query them with SQL or through Supabase's client libraries.

Enable the extension, create a table with a vector column, add an index, and write a database function for similarity search that your app calls. Supabase's AI documentation includes guides for semantic search and RAG. Because it is PostgreSQL, you also get row-level security for access control, joins with user data and transactions, which dedicated vector databases may not offer. For student projects, Supabase's free tier is a convenient way to build a full RAG backend.

## Is a vector database NoSQL?

Usually it is described as a NoSQL-style system, because dedicated vector databases do not use relational tables and SQL as their main model. But vector search also exists inside SQL databases, such as PostgreSQL with pgvector.

Dedicated vector databases expose APIs for collections of points or objects with vectors and metadata, closer to document stores. SQL databases with vector extensions let you mix vector similarity with joins, filters and transactions. The classification matters less than the features you need: query language, filtering, consistency, scale and operations. Many teams prefer keeping vectors in the same database as their application data to avoid syncing two systems.

## Is a vector database 3D?

No. Vectors in a vector database usually have hundreds or thousands of dimensions, such as 384, 768 or 1536, not three. Each dimension is a learned feature of meaning, not a spatial direction.

Three-dimensional pictures of embeddings in tutorials are simplifications made with dimension-reduction methods such as PCA, t-SNE or UMAP, which squash high-dimensional vectors into two or three dimensions for visualisation. They help intuition, showing that similar items cluster, but distances in the picture are distorted. Search always happens in the full high-dimensional space.

## Is the vector database dead?

No, but it is changing. Vector search is becoming a standard feature of general-purpose databases and storage services, long context windows reduce the need for retrieval in some cases, and agentic search with keywords works for some tasks. Dedicated vector databases still matter at large scale and for specialised needs.

The durable part is retrieval itself: most AI applications still need to find the right information quickly, cite it and control access. Whether that runs in a dedicated vector database, PostgreSQL with pgvector, a search engine or a library depends on scale and team. Focus on retrieval quality and evaluation, and keep your design portable, so the storage choice can change as the market does.

# How does vector search work? History, Postgres speed, and other meanings of vector
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-vector-search-works/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Vector search finds items by similarity of meaning or content: an embedding model turns each document, image or query into a vector of numbers, and the search returns the stored vectors closest to the query vector. It powers semantic search, recommendations and the retrieval step in RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad. This page explains how it works and what it is used for, its history, checking vector size, making Postgres vector and trigram search fast, how Postgres became a strong vector database, and the other meanings of "vector" in graphics and physics. How does vector search work? Each item is converted into an embedding vector by a model and stored in an index. A query is embedded with the same model, and the index returns the vectors with the highest similarity, usually cosine similarity or dot product, along with their items. Also asked as: how do vector searches work Comparing a query with every stored vector is exact but slow at scale, so systems use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes. HNSW builds a graph linking each vector to near neighbours and walks it towards the query; inverted-file indexes cluster vectors and search only nearby clusters; quantisation compresses vectors to save memory. These trade a little accuracy for large speed gains. In production, vector search is usually combined with keyword search, filters and reranking. What is vector searching used for? Vector searching is used wherever you need to find things that are similar in meaning or content, not just matching words: semantic search, question answering over documents, recommendations, duplicate detection, image and audio search, and memory for AI agents. Examples: a support portal that finds help articles for a question phrased differently from the article; an e-commerce site that recommends similar products; a photo app that finds pictures by description; and a RAG chatbot that retrieves passages from a college handbook before answering. Its weakness is exact identifiers, such as order numbers, which keyword search handles better, so hybrid search is common. How long have vector databases been around? Similarity search over vectors has been studied for decades in information retrieval and computer science, but dedicated vector databases as a product category became prominent around 2019 to 2022, driven by deep learning embeddings and then by large language models. Key milestones include research on approximate nearest-neighbour methods, libraries such as FAISS released in 2017, graph indexes such as HNSW published in 2016, and then databases and services built around them, along with vector extensions for existing databases such as pgvector for PostgreSQL. After ChatGPT's launch in late 2022, RAG made vector search a mainstream need, and many general databases added vector features. When were vector databases introduced? Purpose-built vector databases emerged in the late 2010s, with open-source and managed products appearing around 2019 to 2021 and growing rapidly after 2022. Before that, teams used libraries and search engines with custom code for vector similarity. Also asked as: when was vector database introduced The timeline matters less than the trend: vector search is becoming a standard feature rather than a separate category. Today you can choose dedicated vector databases, vector extensions in relational databases, search engines with vector support, or libraries for in-memory use. Pick based on scale, filtering needs and the database your team already runs. How do I check a vector's size? For embeddings, the size is the vector's dimension: the number of values it contains, such as 384, 768 or 1536. In Python, check len(vector) or array.shape; the model card lists its embedding dimension, which must match your index configuration. Also asked as: how to check vector size emb = model.encode(&quot;hello&quot;) # sentence-transformers example print(len(emb)) # e.g. 384 Mismatched dimensions are a common error when switching embedding models: the index was created for one size and new vectors have another. In pgvector, the column type vector(768) fixes the dimension. In programming languages, "vector size" can also mean the number of elements in a dynamic array, such as std::vector::size() in C++. How do I get sub-second trigram or vector search in Postgres on long strings? Use the right index for each kind of search, search on shorter fields where possible, and limit candidates before expensive ranking: a GIN trigram index with pg_trgm for fuzzy text, an HNSW index with pgvector for semantic search, and filters applied with indexed columns. Also asked as: how to achieve sub 1s trigram/vector search in postgres when searching long strings Tips that help: Index trigrams on the field users actually search, not entire long documents. For long text, split into chunks with their own rows and embeddings. Use LIMIT and rely on index-ordered queries for vectors. Tune HNSW search parameters for the recall and speed you need. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm indexes are used. Combining trigram or full-text results with vector results through rank fusion gives hybrid search inside one database. How did PostgreSQL become a better vector database? PostgreSQL became a strong vector database through the pgvector extension, which added a vector data type, distance operators and approximate indexes, notably HNSW, plus later improvements such as more efficient storage options and better query performance. Also asked as: how we made postgresql a better vector database Advantages of using Postgres for vectors: vectors live alongside your relational data, so you get joins, transactions, backups and row-level security in one system; full-text search enables hybrid retrieval; and the operational tooling is mature. Limits appear at very large scale or extreme query loads, where specialised vector databases may perform better. For most applications, starting with Postgres and pgvector is a sensible default. Is vector better than raster? In graphics, vector images, made of shapes and paths, scale to any size without losing sharpness and are ideal for logos, icons and illustrations. Raster images, made of pixels, are better for photographs and detailed textures. Neither is better overall. Use vector formats such as SVG for logos, diagrams and UI icons, especially on websites, where they stay crisp on every screen and are often small files. Use raster formats such as JPEG, PNG or WebP for photos. Many projects use both: an SVG logo and WebP photos. This "vector" is unrelated to vector search, although both use the mathematical idea of vectors. What is a free vector in physics? In physics, a free vector is a vector defined only by its magnitude and direction, not by a specific point of application, so it can be moved parallel to itself without changing its meaning. Displacement and velocity of a rigid body's translation are common examples. Also asked as: what is free vector in physics It contrasts with a bound or fixed vector, tied to a specific point, such as a force acting at a particular point on a body, where the point of application affects rotation, and a sliding vector, which can move along its line of action. The same vector concept, a list of components with magnitude and direction, underlies embeddings in AI, where each dimension is a learned feature. What is the vector method? The vector method usually refers to solving problems in mathematics and physics using vectors: representing quantities with magnitude and direction, and using operations such as addition, dot products and cross products to find results like angles, areas and forces. In geometry, vector methods prove properties of shapes and find distances and angles without coordinates for every point. In physics, they resolve forces and motions into components. In machine learning, vector methods represent data as vectors and use similarity measures, which is the basis of vector search: cosine similarity is simply the dot product of two normalised vectors, measuring how closely they point in the same direction.

# Hybrid search and reranking in RAG: BM25 plus embeddings, reciprocal rank fusion, cross-encoders, and why this pair fixes most bad answers
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hybrid-search-and-reranking-in-rag/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is hybrid search in RAG?

**Hybrid search runs two retrievers on every query, a keyword retriever such as BM25 and a dense embedding retriever, and merges their ranked results into one list. Keyword search catches exact terms, product codes, names, error numbers and rare words that embeddings blur together. Embedding search catches paraphrases and meaning that share no words with the document. Fusing them gives higher recall than either alone, and the fusion itself can be a dozen lines of code with no tuning.**


Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion and a cross-encoder reranker is the core of RAG.NextUpgrad's query path, and it is the part of the platform that moved retrieval recall most on the labelled question set [13]. My shorter notes on each half are on the portfolio [11][12]. This page is the pair together, with the papers and the code.

> Users ask for "error E-4021" as often as they ask "why did my upload fail". Only one of those is a semantic query. Ship both retrievers or you will fail half your users.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building RAG.NextUpgrad</cite>

## Why does vector search alone miss results?

**Because embeddings compress meaning and lose exact strings. A product code, a person's name, an error number, an acronym or a version string carries little meaning to the model, so its vector lands near other codes and names rather than near the exact match. Numbers and negation blur too. Dense retrieval was shown to beat keywords for open-domain questions on average [3], and the average hides exactly the queries that matter most in support, legal and technical corpora.**


## What is BM25, and why is it still used?

**BM25 is a ranking function from classical information retrieval that scores a document for a query by how often the query's terms appear in it, weighted by how rare each term is across the collection and normalised for document length [1]. It needs no training, runs in microseconds over an inverted index, and finds exact terms perfectly. It cannot see that "reset my password" and "credential recovery" are the same request, which is exactly what embeddings are for. Together they cover each other's blind spots.**



Learned sparse models such as SPLADE bring some semantic expansion to the keyword side [6], and late-interaction models such as ColBERT keep per-token vectors to recover exact-term precision on the dense side [5]. Both are worth knowing; BM25 plus a dense model plus fusion remains the practical default.

## What is reciprocal rank fusion?

**Reciprocal rank fusion merges several ranked lists into one by giving each document a score equal to the sum, over every list it appears in, of one divided by a constant plus its rank in that list. Documents ranked high in either list rise; documents ranked high in both rise most. The constant, usually 60, dampens the influence of top ranks. It needs no score normalisation, because it uses ranks not scores, and Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher showed it beating more complex fusion methods [2].**


```python
def reciprocal_rank_fusion(*ranked_lists: list[str], k: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranked in ranked_lists:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranked, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)

fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion(dense_top_40, bm25_top_40)[:30]   # then rerank these
```

That function is in RAG.NextUpgrad almost exactly as written, because the paper's simplicity is the point: no learned weights, no score scales to reconcile, nothing to retune when you swap an embedding model [13].

## What is reranking, and why not just retrieve more?

**A reranker is a model that reads the question and a candidate passage together and outputs a relevance score. Retrievers compare a query vector with passage vectors that were computed separately, for speed; a cross-encoder looks at the pair jointly, which is far more accurate but too slow to run over the whole corpus. So you retrieve wide with the fast methods, thirty to fifty candidates, and rerank narrow, to the best three to eight. Retrieving more without reranking sends noise to the model, and models use long contexts unevenly [8].**


Passage reranking with BERT-style cross-encoders was introduced by Nogueira and Cho and remains the recipe [4]; Sentence Transformers publishes pretrained rerankers you can run on a CPU for small candidate sets [10].


## How do I choose k at each stage?

**Measure recall at each boundary on a labelled question set. Retrieve enough from each retriever that recall at the fusion output is above ninety percent; forty each is a common starting point. Fuse and keep enough that the reranker sees every plausible passage, twenty to fifty. Rerank down to what the model needs, three to eight, and check recall at that k is still above eighty-five. If recall drops sharply at the rerank step, the reranker is wrong for your domain; if it drops at fusion, one retriever is starving the other.**




## How much does hybrid search and reranking improve results?

**On the labelled sets I have worked with, fusion raised recall at thirty over either retriever alone, and the reranker raised recall at five without touching recall at thirty, which is exactly what each is supposed to do. Public benchmarks such as BEIR show dense models varying widely across domains and BM25 remaining a hard baseline on several [7], which is the research version of the same lesson. Your gain depends on your queries: corpora heavy in codes, names and numbers gain most from BM25; corpora of prose gain most from the reranker.**



## How do I implement hybrid search?

**Keep a keyword index alongside the vector index: Postgres full-text search or a BM25 library over the same chunks [9]; Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Qdrant, Weaviate and others also offer sparse or hybrid support. At query time, run both, fuse with the function above, rerank with a cross-encoder from Sentence Transformers or a hosted reranking API [10], and send the top few to the model. The whole path is a few hundred lines; the design decisions are the k values and the reranker choice.**



## When is hybrid search not worth it?

**Rarely, but there are cases. A tiny corpus where everything fits in the prompt does not need retrieval at all. A corpus of pure prose with no codes or names, where the reranker alone recovers what dense misses. A latency budget so tight that even microseconds matter, which is unusual. In every other case I have seen, the cost of a second retriever is small and the recall gain on exact-term queries is large. Default to hybrid and let your measurements argue you out of it.**



## Hybrid search and reranking interview questions

**Explain why embeddings miss exact terms and BM25 misses paraphrase. Explain reciprocal rank fusion and why it needs no normalisation. Explain the difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder and why you cannot rerank the whole corpus. Describe how you would choose k at each stage and measure it. Say when you would use learned sparse or late interaction models. A retrieval system you built and ablated is the best evidence.**




## Where should I start?

**Add BM25 next to your vector search over the same chunks, fuse with the twelve-line function, and measure recall at thirty on twenty real questions before and after. Then add a cross-encoder and measure recall at five. Both changes take an afternoon and usually deliver the largest quality jump the system will ever see.** For a hands-on retrieval session at your college or team, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to impress hackathon judges: what they look for, and how to do well
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/impress-hackathon-judges/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Hackathon judges look for a real problem, a working solution, sound technical choices, credible impact and a clear pitch, roughly in that order of weight at most events. I have sat on both sides of the table: winning first prizes at Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee, Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025 and BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats, and judging and mentoring at others. This page shares what judges actually score, how to impress them and do well, what you do at a hackathon, whether it is hard, hackathon tests, Unstop and other sites, and where the word and idea came from. What do hackathon judges actually look for? Most rubrics score five things: problem relevance, the working solution, technical execution, impact or feasibility, and presentation. Judges reward teams that solve a specific problem well over teams that attempt everything. Also asked as: what hackathon judges actually look for: a rubric from both sides of the table A typical rubric, seen from both sides: Problem: is it real, specific and important to an identifiable user? Solution: does the demo work live, end to end? Technical depth: are choices sensible, and can the team explain them? Impact and feasibility: could this be used, scaled or deployed? Presentation: is the story clear within the time limit? As a judge, I trust teams that show what does not work yet and how they would fix it; honesty reads as understanding. How do I impress hackathon judges? Lead with the user and the problem, show a live demo of one complete flow, explain why you chose your approach, quantify impact where possible, and answer questions directly and honestly. Also asked as: how to impress hackathon judges Specific moves that work: Open with one person's problem, not your tech stack. Demo the core feature within the first minute or two. Mention one hard technical decision and why you made it. Show evidence: a user quote, a test result, a small dataset you validated on. Admit limitations and give a next-step plan. Keep slides minimal; the demo is the star. KrishGyan stood out at Changethon 2025 because the demo showed a farmer asking in their own voice and language and getting a useful answer. How do I do well in a hackathon? Pick a narrow problem, plan scope in the first hour, divide roles, integrate early, freeze features well before the end, and rehearse the demo and pitch several times. Also asked as: how to do well in a hackathon A time plan for a 24-hour event: Hour 0 to 1: choose the problem, define one user and one core flow. Hours 1 to 4: skeleton app deployed, front end and back end connected. Hours 4 to 16: build the core feature; cut anything non-essential. Hours 16 to 20: polish, fix bugs, prepare slides. Final hours: rehearse, record a backup demo, rest a little. Talk to mentors early; one good suggestion can save hours. What do we have to do in a hackathon? In a hackathon, you form or join a team, choose or receive a problem, build a working prototype within the time limit, and present it to judges, usually with a short demo and slides. Organisers provide themes, rules, mentors and judging criteria. Also asked as: what we have to do in hackathon The typical flow: registration and team formation, an opening session explaining rules and themes, building time with mentor check-ins, a submission deadline for code and slides, and final presentations. Some events add idea rounds before shortlisting. You are expected to write most of your project during the event, though rules on starter templates and AI tools vary, so read them. Is a hackathon hard? Hackathons are demanding because of tight time limits, teamwork pressure and things breaking at the last minute, but they are designed to be accessible. Beginners regularly take part and learn a lot, especially at events with beginner tracks and mentors. Also asked as: is hackathon hard What makes them manageable: choosing a small problem, using tools you know, splitting work clearly, asking mentors for help, and aiming to finish something rather than to win your first time. Skills improve quickly with each event. The hardest part for many people is the first one; after that, you know what to expect. What is a hackathon test? A hackathon test usually refers to an online assessment used to shortlist participants, such as a coding test, quiz or idea submission round, before the main build event. Hiring hackathons by companies often use coding tests to screen candidates. Also asked as: what is hackathon test Formats include timed coding problems, multiple-choice questions on fundamentals, and written idea proposals with a presentation. Prepare with practice problems on data structures and algorithms, review basics of the event's technology theme, and for idea rounds, write a clear problem statement, proposed solution and implementation plan. Read instructions carefully; many submissions fail on format rather than ideas. What is an Unstop hackathon? Unstop is an Indian platform, formerly known as Dare2Compete, where companies and colleges host hackathons, coding contests, case competitions, quizzes and hiring challenges. An "Unstop hackathon" is a hackathon listed and run through it. Also asked as: what is unstop hackathon Students use it to discover competitions, register teams, submit entries and follow results. Many college tech fest events and company hiring hackathons appear there. As with any platform, read each event's rules, timeline, eligibility and prize terms, and prefer events from organisers you can verify. It is one of the easiest ways for Indian students to find many competitions in one place. What is the best hackathon website? There is no single best one; use a few. Devfolio and Unstop list many Indian hackathons; Major League Hacking and Devpost list student and global events; Kaggle hosts data competitions; and college tech fest sites list campus events. Tips for choosing events: Prefer events with clear judging criteria and mentors. Mix online events for volume with offline ones for networking. Check past winners' projects to understand the bar. Follow organisers on social media to catch registrations early. Over time, you will learn which events suit your interests, whether AI, social impact, fintech or hardware. Why is it called a hackathon? "Hackathon" combines "hack", in the programmer's sense of building something clever and quick, and "marathon", an intense, sustained effort. It describes an event where people build intensively for a fixed period. The word has nothing to do with breaking into systems; "hacker" originally meant an enthusiastic, skilful programmer. Over time, hackathons spread beyond software to hardware, design, policy, health and social impact, but the core idea remains: small teams, short time, real prototypes. Variants include ideathons, focused on ideas, and datathons, focused on data analysis. Who invented the hackathon? No single person invented it. The term appeared in 1999, used independently around events by the OpenBSD project and by Sun Microsystems around its JavaOne conference, where developers built software intensively over a short period. Also asked as: who invented hackathon Collaborative coding sprints existed before, but the name and format spread through the 2000s via tech companies, open-source communities and universities. Today hackathons run worldwide, from corporate innovation events to national programmes such as Smart India Hackathon. The format endures because it compresses learning, teamwork and creation into a memorable experience.

# Should I install Ollama? Install on Windows, Mac, Linux, WSL and Docker
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/install-ollama-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Install Ollama if you want to run open-weight language models such as Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral or DeepSeek on your own machine, for privacy, offline use, learning or building prototypes without per-token costs. It installs in a few minutes on Windows, macOS and Linux, and runs in Docker. This page helps you decide, then covers installing on Windows including a D drive, where models are stored, macOS, Ubuntu, WSL, Docker and pulling models inside a container, and running DeepSeek models.

## Should I install Ollama?

Yes, if you want to learn how language models work hands-on, keep data private, work offline, or prototype apps without paying per token. No, if you only want the best answers for hard tasks, where hosted models such as Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini are much stronger.

Your hardware decides the experience. With 8 GB of RAM you can run small models of a few billion parameters at usable speed. With 16 to 32 GB of RAM or a GPU with 8 GB or more of video memory, mid-size models become practical. Larger models need serious GPUs. Ollama itself is free and open source, and uninstalling it is simple, so trying it costs nothing but disk space: models range from a couple of gigabytes to tens of gigabytes each.

## How do I install Ollama on Windows?

Download the Windows installer from ollama.com, run it, and Ollama starts in the background with an icon in the system tray. Then open a terminal and run a model.

```powershell
ollama --version
ollama run llama3.2
```

The first `run` downloads the model, then opens an interactive chat; type `/bye` to exit. Ollama also serves an API on `http://localhost:11434`, which tools such as LangChain and Open WebUI use. If you have an NVIDIA or AMD GPU, keep its drivers updated so Ollama can use it; check with `ollama ps` while a model runs to see whether it is on the GPU or CPU.

## Can I install Ollama on the D drive?

Yes. The models are what take space, and you can store them on any drive by setting the `OLLAMA_MODELS` environment variable, for example to `D:\ollama\models`, then restarting Ollama. The installer also accepts a custom install directory.

Steps for the models folder:

- Quit Ollama from the system tray.
- Open "Edit environment variables for your account" in Windows settings.
- Add a variable `OLLAMA_MODELS` with the value `D:\ollama\models`.
- Start Ollama again and pull a model; it downloads to the new folder.

To install the program itself elsewhere, the Windows installer supports a directory option documented in Ollama's Windows guide. Moving existing models is as simple as moving the folder to the new path before restarting.

## Where does Ollama install models?

By default, models are stored in a `.ollama/models` folder in your home directory: `C:\Users\<you>\.ollama\models` on Windows and `~/.ollama/models` on macOS. On Linux, when installed as a service, they are under the `ollama` user's home, typically `/usr/share/ollama/.ollama/models`.

Set `OLLAMA_MODELS` to change the location on any system. Models are stored as layered blobs with manifests, so the folder will not show friendly filenames; use `ollama list` to see installed models and `ollama rm <name>` to delete one and free space. Several models can share layers, so deleting one may free less space than its listed size. If disk space is tight, keep only the models you actually use.

## How do I install Ollama on a Mac?

Download the macOS app from ollama.com, move it to Applications and open it. It adds the `ollama` command to your terminal, and you can run a model straight away with `ollama run llama3.2`.

Apple Silicon Macs, with M-series chips, run local models well because the GPU shares fast unified memory with the CPU, so a Mac with 16 GB or more can run mid-size models comfortably. Intel Macs work but are slower. You can also install through Homebrew if you prefer managing tools that way. Keep the app running in the menu bar so the local API at port 11434 stays available for other apps.

## How do I install Ollama on Ubuntu?

Run the official install script, which installs Ollama and sets it up as a systemd service that starts automatically.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
ollama run llama3.2
```

Check the service with `systemctl status ollama` and view logs with `journalctl -u ollama`. For NVIDIA GPUs, install the proprietary drivers first; the script detects them. To change settings such as the models folder or listening address, edit the service with `sudo systemctl edit ollama` and add environment variables like `OLLAMA_MODELS` or `OLLAMA_HOST`, then restart the service. As with any script piped to a shell, you can download and read it first.

## Can I install Ollama on WSL?

Yes. Inside WSL 2 on Windows, install Ollama with the Linux install script, and with up-to-date NVIDIA drivers on Windows, Ollama in WSL can use the GPU. Alternatively, install the Windows version and call it from WSL over the local network.

Choose based on your workflow. If your projects live in WSL, running Ollama there keeps everything in one environment. If you also use Windows tools, the Windows app is simpler and you can reach it from WSL at the Windows host's address. Avoid running both at once on the same port. WSL needs enough memory allocated; if models fail to load, raise the memory limit in your WSL configuration.

## Should I install Ollama in Docker?

Docker is a good choice for servers, reproducible setups and running Ollama alongside other services such as a web UI or a database. On a personal laptop, the native installer is simpler and usually uses the GPU with less setup.

Run the official image with a volume so models persist:

```bash
docker run -d --name ollama -p 11434:11434 -v ollama:/root/.ollama ollama/ollama
```

For NVIDIA GPUs, install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and add `--gpus=all`. With Docker Compose, you can define Ollama, Open WebUI and your app together. Do not expose port 11434 to the internet without authentication in front of it; the Ollama API has no built-in login.

## How do I pull Ollama models in a Docker container?

Run the `ollama pull` command inside the running container with `docker exec`, and the model is saved in the mounted volume, so it survives restarts.

```bash
docker exec -it ollama ollama pull llama3.2
docker exec -it ollama ollama list
docker exec -it ollama ollama run llama3.2 "Explain BM25 in one line"
```

For automated setups, pull models in a start-up script or call the API's pull endpoint from your app on first run. Keep the volume, named `ollama` above, when updating the image, so you do not re-download models. If another container needs Ollama, connect them on the same Docker network and use `http://ollama:11434` as the address.

## Can I install DeepSeek on Ollama?

Yes. DeepSeek's open-weight models, including distilled versions of its reasoning model, are available in Ollama's library. Run one with `ollama run deepseek-r1`, adding a size tag to choose a smaller or larger variant.

Pick a size that fits your memory: small distilled versions run on ordinary laptops, while the largest DeepSeek models need multiple high-end GPUs and are not practical locally. Reasoning models print their thinking before the final answer, so expect longer responses. Running locally means your prompts stay on your machine, which addresses privacy concerns some people have about using hosted services. Test on your own tasks; smaller distilled models are much weaker than the full model.

# How to install OpenCV with pip, conda, VS Code, PyCharm and Jupyter
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/install-opencv-python/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To install OpenCV for Python, run `pip install opencv-python` in the environment you use, then `import cv2` in your code. Use `opencv-contrib-python` if you need extra modules, and a `-headless` variant on servers without a display. Most installation problems come from installing into a different Python environment from the one your editor or notebook runs. This page covers pip and conda, VS Code, PyCharm and Jupyter, macOS and Linux, and two functions everyone uses early: resize and findContours.

## How do I install OpenCV?

For Python, create a virtual environment, activate it, and run `pip install opencv-python`. Check it with `python -c "import cv2; print(cv2.__version__)"`.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install opencv-python
python -c "import cv2; print(cv2.__version__)"
```

For C++ projects, install OpenCV through your system's package manager or build it from source with CMake, following the official installation guides. For most students, the Python package is enough for image processing, video and classic computer vision, and pairs well with NumPy, and with PyTorch or ONNX Runtime for deep learning models.

## Can you pip install OpenCV?

Yes. The official Python packages on PyPI are `opencv-python` for the main modules, `opencv-contrib-python` for main plus extra modules, and `opencv-python-headless` and `opencv-contrib-python-headless` for servers without GUI functions.

Rules that avoid strange errors:

- Install only one of these packages in an environment; they conflict.
- Use headless versions in Docker and on servers, where `cv2.imshow` is not needed.
- Upgrade pip first if installation tries to build from source: `python -m pip install --upgrade pip`.
- Use `python -m pip` so pip matches the Python you run.

If `import cv2` fails after installing, the package is almost certainly in another environment.

## How do I install OpenCV in VS Code?

Open your project folder, create a virtual environment, select it as the interpreter with "Python: Select Interpreter" in the command palette, then run `pip install opencv-python` in VS Code's terminal, which uses that environment.

If VS Code shows "Import cv2 could not be resolved", the editor is using a different interpreter from the one where you installed OpenCV. Check the interpreter shown in the status bar, select the `.venv` one, and reload the window. Also confirm the integrated terminal has the environment activated before installing. Install the Python extension from Microsoft for IntelliSense and debugging support.

## How do I install OpenCV in PyCharm?

Open Settings, then Project, then Python Interpreter, make sure your project's virtual environment is selected, click the plus button, search for `opencv-python` and install it. Or run `pip install opencv-python` in PyCharm's terminal, which uses the project interpreter.

If the import still fails, check that the run configuration uses the same interpreter as the project. PyCharm can create a separate environment per project, so a package installed in one project will not appear in another. For autocompletion of `cv2`, recent OpenCV packages include type hints; if completion is poor, restart PyCharm so it re-indexes the environment.

## How do I install OpenCV in a Jupyter Notebook?

Install OpenCV into the same environment as the notebook's kernel. The safest way is to run `%pip install opencv-python` in a notebook cell, which installs into the active kernel, then restart the kernel.

If you use several environments, register each as a Jupyter kernel with `python -m ipykernel install --user --name myenv` and select the right kernel in the notebook. Note that `cv2.imshow` opens a separate window and does not display inline; in notebooks, convert the image from BGR to RGB with `cv2.cvtColor` and show it with Matplotlib's `plt.imshow`. In Google Colab, OpenCV is usually preinstalled, and Colab provides a patched display helper for images.

## How do I install OpenCV through conda?

Use the conda-forge channel: `conda install -c conda-forge opencv`, inside a conda environment you created for the project. Then `import cv2` as usual.

```bash
conda create -n cv python=3.11
conda activate cv
conda install -c conda-forge opencv
```

Avoid mixing conda's OpenCV with a pip-installed OpenCV in the same environment, because they can conflict. If you mostly use pip packages, a plain virtual environment with `opencv-python` is simpler. Conda is useful when you also need other compiled libraries that conda manages well, such as specific scientific packages.

## Does OpenCV work on Mac?

Yes. OpenCV works on macOS, including Apple Silicon Macs, through pip with `pip install opencv-python` or through conda-forge or Homebrew. Prebuilt wheels support both Apple Silicon and Intel Macs.

Tips for Mac users: use a Python from python.org, Homebrew or a virtual environment rather than the system Python; grant camera permission to your terminal or editor in System Settings when using `cv2.VideoCapture(0)`; and remember that `cv2.imshow` windows need `cv2.waitKey` to refresh. For deep learning inference on Apple Silicon, combine OpenCV for image processing with frameworks that use the Mac's GPU.

## Does OpenCV work on Linux?

Yes. OpenCV works very well on Linux, which is the most common platform for computer vision servers and research. Install it with pip in a virtual environment, or through your distribution's package manager.

On servers and in Docker, use `opencv-python-headless` to avoid GUI dependencies; otherwise you may see errors about missing libGL libraries, which you can fix by installing the system library or switching to the headless package. For GPU-accelerated OpenCV functions with CUDA, you need to build from source with CUDA enabled; the pip packages do not include CUDA support. Many projects instead run deep learning on the GPU with PyTorch or ONNX Runtime and use OpenCV for pre- and post-processing.

## How does OpenCV resize work?

`cv2.resize` scales an image to a new width and height, computing new pixel values with an interpolation method. Note that the size argument is `(width, height)`, while NumPy image shapes are `(height, width, channels)`.

```python
import cv2
img = cv2.imread("photo.jpg")
small = cv2.resize(img, (640, 360), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)       # shrinking
big = cv2.resize(img, None, fx=2, fy=2, interpolation=cv2.INTER_CUBIC)  # enlarging by factor
```

Use `INTER_AREA` for shrinking, which avoids moire patterns, and `INTER_LINEAR` or `INTER_CUBIC` for enlarging. To keep the aspect ratio, compute one dimension from the other. For OCR, upscaling small text images often improves recognition.

## How does OpenCV findContours work?

`cv2.findContours` traces the boundaries of white shapes in a binary image and returns them as lists of points, plus a hierarchy describing which contours are inside others. You then measure, filter or draw them.

```python
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
_, binary = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)
contours, hierarchy = cv2.findContours(binary, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
big = [c for c in contours if cv2.contourArea(c) > 500]
cv2.drawContours(img, big, -1, (0, 255, 0), 2)
```

Use `RETR_EXTERNAL` for outer shapes only, `RETR_TREE` for nested ones. Objects should be white on black; invert the threshold if needed. Contours are useful for counting objects, measuring sizes and cropping documents.

# Is AI a good career in India? Roles, what hiring actually looks like, what fresher paths exist, and how to get in without an IIT tag
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/is-ai-a-good-career-in-india/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Is AI a good career in India?

**Yes, if you build things, and the qualifier matters more than the yes. Companies across India are adding AI features to products and hiring engineers who can ship them; the roles pay at or above general software roles at the same level, and the work is genuinely interesting. But entry-level AI hiring demands proof of shipped work earlier than most fields, and a stack of certificates without a deployed project does not get interviews. I got into GenAI work from a BCA programme without a placement cell by building and posting weekly, and that path is open to anyone willing to do the same [9].**


This page is my honest answer to the question students ask me most at campus sessions, with the industry references that back it [1][2][3] and the paths I have watched work and fail. My roadmap for GenAI engineering in India is written up separately [4].

> The question is never whether AI is a good career. It is whether you will be one of the people with something to show when the interview comes.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What AI roles actually exist in India?

**GenAI or AI engineer: builds features on top of models, RAG systems, agents, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment; the most-hired role for freshers with projects. Machine learning engineer: trains and serves models, more infrastructure and data pipelines. Data scientist: analysis, experimentation, classical models, business communication. AI product engineer: full-stack developer who integrates AI well. Applied researcher or research engineer: papers and new methods, mostly requires a master's or PhD. Then MLOps, data engineering and annotation or evaluation roles around them. Most openings for freshers are in the first and fourth.**



## How does AI hiring actually work for freshers?

**Campus placements at top colleges bring companies to you; everywhere else, hiring happens through referrals, cold outreach, hackathons, communities and remote applications, and it evaluates what you have built. The interview usually has a coding round, a project deep-dive where you defend your decisions, and a system-design or take-home task such as building a small RAG or extraction pipeline. The project deep-dive is where most candidates fail and where a real shipped project makes you pass [6][7].**



## Do I need an IIT, NIT or IIIT degree?

**For campus placements at those colleges, the tag is the door. For everything else, it is a mild signal that a portfolio overrides. Remote companies, startups and most mid-size product firms evaluate the GitHub, the deployed demo and the interview, and referrals from communities and hackathons open the same doors a tag does [5][10]. I have watched BCA and tier-three B.Tech students get GenAI roles with strong projects and IIT students get rejected with none. The tag saves time; it does not substitute for work.**


## Do I need a master's or PhD for an AI career?

**Not for engineering roles, which are most of the roles. GenAI engineers, ML engineers, AI product engineers and MLOps engineers are hired on demonstrated ability to build. A master's helps for research roles and for some ML engineer roles at large labs, and a PhD is effectively required for research scientist positions. If you want to build products, build products; if you want to publish papers, the degree path is the right one. Choose by what you want to do daily, not by what sounds impressive.**



## What skills do AI jobs in India test for?

**Python, thoroughly. Working with model APIs and structured outputs. Retrieval-augmented generation: chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, reranking, evaluation. Fine-tuning basics with LoRA and when not to fine-tune. Evaluation: how you know it works. Deployment: an API, a container, a free-tier host, logging. Data handling and SQL. Git and a readable repository. Communication: explaining a technical decision to a non-technical person. Not tested for freshers in most roles: deriving backpropagation by hand, training models from scratch, or reciting paper titles.**



## What are the real risks of an AI career?

**Entry-level roles are competitive and demand shipped proof early, so students who only study fall behind students who build. Tools change fast, so the specific framework you learn will be replaced; the skills that persist are evaluation, data handling and systems thinking. Hype produces bad job descriptions and some companies that do not know what they need. Some roles labelled AI are data entry or annotation. And AI tools make junior generalist coding cheaper, which raises the bar for what a junior must bring. None of these is a reason to avoid the field; each is a reason to build rather than collect certificates.**



## What does a first AI job pay in India?

**Enough to be worth it, with wide variance by city, company type and role, and I will not invent numbers here. Startups and remote roles often pay above local service companies for the same skills; product companies pay above both for strong candidates. Compensation rises quickly in the first three years for engineers who ship. The practical advice: research current ranges on public sites for the specific role and city, and negotiate your first offer, because most freshers do not and leave money on the table [8].**


## Which path should I take: placement, remote, startup or freelance?

**Campus placement if your college has good AI hiring; it is the easiest door. Remote roles at foreign startups if you can show shipped work and communicate well; they pay well and evaluate portfolios [5]. Indian startups if you want to learn fast and take ownership early. Freelance and building for local businesses if you want cash flow and real users while you look, which is what I did. Many people combine them: a freelance project becomes a portfolio piece becomes a remote offer.**




## What should my first eighteen months look like?

**Months one to three: Python, one model API, one small deployed app. Months four to six: a RAG system over real documents, measured and deployed; start posting weekly. Months seven to nine: a vision or fine-tuning project with an evaluation; first hackathon. Months ten to twelve: an internship, freelance project or open-source contribution; second hackathon; polish the portfolio. Months thirteen to eighteen: apply widely, interview, iterate on feedback, and keep shipping. My full roadmap with the specific resources is on the portfolio [4].**



## Is AI a good career for non-CS students?

**Yes for engineering roles if you learn to program properly, which takes months of daily practice, not weeks. Domain knowledge is an advantage: a pharmacy student building a prescription reader, a commerce student building an invoice extractor, a biology student building a lab-report assistant each has a project no CS student can match. The route is the same: Python, one API, one deployed project, weekly posts, communities. My sessions for non-CS audiences exist because this route works [7].**



## Where should I start?

**Tonight: install Python, make one API call to a model, and put the script on GitHub with a README. This week: post what you built. Next month: a RAG system over documents you actually have. The career follows from the habit.** For a career session at your college on getting into AI from anywhere in India, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
