# What is an n8n workflow? How n8n works, AI workflows, templates and tutorial
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/n8n-workflow-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


An n8n workflow is an automation built from connected nodes: a trigger node starts it, for example a new form submission, a schedule or a webhook, and the following nodes fetch, transform, decide and send data across apps and APIs. n8n is a workflow automation tool that you can self-host or use as a cloud service, with code steps in JavaScript or Python when visual nodes are not enough. This page explains how workflows run, AI and agentic workflows, sub-workflows, publishing, examples, templates and a first tutorial.

## What is an n8n workflow?

An n8n workflow is a visual automation made of nodes connected on a canvas. Each node does one job, such as receiving a webhook, reading a Google Sheet, calling an API, filtering items or sending a Slack message, and data flows from node to node.

Workflows can be simple, such as "when a form is submitted, add a row to a sheet and email a confirmation", or complex, with branches, loops, error handling and AI steps. Data moves between nodes as items in JSON format, and you can reference any earlier node's output in later fields with expressions. Every run is recorded as an execution, so you can inspect what happened at each step, which makes debugging much easier than with scripts scattered across servers.

## How does an n8n workflow work?

A trigger node starts an execution, which passes items through each connected node in order. Nodes call services with stored credentials, transform data with expressions or code, branch with IF and Switch nodes, and the execution log records inputs and outputs at every step.

Key concepts:

- **Triggers**: webhooks, schedules, app events, manual runs, chat messages.
- **Items**: n8n processes a list of JSON items; most nodes run once per item.
- **Expressions**: insert values from earlier nodes into fields.
- **Credentials**: stored securely and reused across workflows.
- **Error workflows**: a separate workflow that runs when another fails.

In test mode you run workflows manually and inspect data; once published, the production trigger runs automatically.

## What is the n8n workflow automation tool?

n8n is a workflow automation platform for connecting apps, APIs and AI models without writing a whole application. It offers hundreds of integrations, a visual editor, code nodes, self-hosting and a cloud version.

It is popular with developers because it is source-available under n8n's Sustainable Use License, can be self-hosted with Docker for data control, and lets you drop into JavaScript or Python when needed. That licence allows free self-hosting for your own use but restricts reselling n8n as a service, so it is fair-code rather than open source in the strict sense. Compared with Zapier, n8n gives more control and lower cost at scale; compared with code-only orchestrators, it is much faster to build and easier to hand to non-developers.

## What is an n8n AI workflow?

An n8n AI workflow uses language model nodes as steps: classifying messages, extracting fields from documents, summarising content, generating replies or answering questions from a vector store, with the rest of the workflow handling data and actions.

A typical example: a Gmail trigger receives a support email, an LLM node classifies it and extracts the order number as JSON, an IF node checks the confidence, and the workflow either looks up the order and drafts a reply for approval or routes it to a person. n8n supports major model providers and local models through Ollama, plus vector stores for retrieval. Treat AI steps carefully: require structured output, validate it, and keep deterministic rules for decisions with money or legal effect, the approach I used in DocuLens AI.

## What is an n8n agentic workflow?

An agentic workflow in n8n uses the AI Agent node: you give it a model, instructions, memory and a set of tools, such as other nodes, HTTP requests or sub-workflows, and it decides which tools to call to complete a request.

That differs from a fixed workflow where you define every step. For example, a chat agent for a college office could have tools to search the notice board, look up a student's application status and create a ticket, choosing among them based on the question. Keep agents narrow, describe each tool clearly, limit what tools can change, add human approval for sensitive actions, and log every run. When the steps are predictable, a regular workflow is more reliable and cheaper than an agent.

## What is a sub-workflow in n8n?

A sub-workflow is a workflow called by another workflow through the Execute Workflow node. It receives input from the parent, runs its own steps and returns output, letting you reuse logic and keep workflows small and readable.

Use sub-workflows for repeated tasks, such as "normalise a customer record", "send a formatted Slack alert" or "look up a user by email", that many workflows need. They are also how you give an AI Agent node complex tools: wrap the logic in a sub-workflow and expose it as a tool. Define clear inputs and outputs, test the sub-workflow on its own, and version it carefully, since changes affect every parent that calls it.

## What does publishing a workflow mean in n8n?

Publishing, called activating in some versions, makes a workflow live: its production trigger starts listening, so webhooks, schedules and app events run it automatically without you pressing a button.

Before publishing, test with real sample data, check that credentials work in production, and add an error workflow that alerts you on failure. Note that webhook triggers have separate test and production URLs; external services must call the production URL once the workflow is live. After changes, re-test and republish. Monitor executions for the first days, because real data is messier than test data. If you self-host, make sure your instance is reachable and backed up.

## What are some n8n workflow examples?

Common examples include saving form submissions to a sheet and notifying a team, syncing contacts between a CRM and email tool, posting new blog articles to social channels, sending daily reports, triaging support emails with AI, and backing up data on a schedule.

Examples for students and small teams:

- Hackathon registrations: form to sheet, validation, confirmation email, team channel alert.
- Daily digest: fetch RSS feeds, summarise with an LLM, send to Telegram.
- Lead capture: website form to CRM, with a follow-up email two days later.
- Document intake: PDF arrives by email, extract fields, add to a database for review.
- Uptime alert: check a website every five minutes and message you if it is down.

## Where can I find n8n workflow templates?

n8n's website has a large library of community workflow templates that you can import with one click, covering AI agents, marketing, sales, IT operations and more. You can also import workflows shared as JSON files.

Treat templates as starting points: read every node before running one, replace credentials with your own, check what data it sends where, and add error handling. Community templates vary in quality and may call paid services or expose data if you do not adjust them. Once a template works for you, rename nodes clearly and add notes on the canvas so you, or a teammate, can understand it months later.

## Is there an n8n workflow tutorial for beginners?

Yes. n8n's documentation includes beginner courses and step-by-step tutorials. A first workflow takes about thirty minutes.

A beginner tutorial:

- Run n8n locally with Docker or start a cloud trial.
- Add a Schedule trigger set to every morning.
- Add an HTTP Request node to fetch weather or news from a public API.
- Add a Set or Code node to format a short message.
- Add a Telegram, Slack or email node to send it to yourself.
- Test, check each node's output, then publish.

Next, add an LLM node to summarise the content, and an error workflow to alert you when something fails.

# Where is OCR in Adobe? OCR text, Adobe Scan, Tesseract on PDFs and handwriting
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/ocr-in-adobe-and-tesseract/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

OCR text is the text that optical character recognition extracts from an image of a page, making a scan searchable, copyable and editable. In Adobe Acrobat, OCR is in the Scan &amp; OCR tool, where Recognize Text turns a scanned PDF into a searchable one; the free Acrobat Reader cannot run OCR. This page also explains Adobe Scan, using any OCR scanner, running Tesseract on PDFs and finding its parameters, the best options for handwriting, and how to build invoice OCR in a Chrome extension, drawing on the page-batched OCR in my OCR &amp; Speech Workspace. What is OCR text? OCR text is the machine-readable text produced by optical character recognition from an image of text. In a searchable PDF, it is usually an invisible text layer placed under the page image, so the page looks the same but you can search, select and copy. You can tell whether a PDF has OCR text by trying to select a sentence or search for a word: if nothing selects, the PDF is image-only. OCR text quality varies with scan quality; errors often appear in numbers, names and tables. Software that indexes documents, such as search engines and RAG chatbots, needs this text, so OCR is usually the first step in processing scanned archives. Where is OCR in Adobe Acrobat? In Adobe Acrobat, open the PDF, go to All tools and choose Scan &amp; OCR, then select Recognize text, In this file. Acrobat runs OCR and adds a searchable text layer. Menu names vary slightly between versions. You can also set the OCR language and choose whether to keep the original image or convert pages to editable text. For editing, the Edit PDF tool runs OCR automatically on scanned pages so you can change text directly. These features require a paid Acrobat plan; Adobe's online tools also offer some conversions. If you only need occasional OCR, free alternatives exist, covered below. How do I OCR a PDF in Adobe Acrobat? Open the scanned PDF in Acrobat, choose Scan &amp; OCR, then Recognize text and In this file, pick the language and pages, and run it. Save the file, and it becomes a searchable PDF. Also asked as: how to ocr a pdf in adobe acrobat Tips for better results: Set the correct document language, including other languages if mixed. Use Enhance scanned file first if the scan is skewed or faint. Check a few pages by searching for known words. For editable output, export to Word after OCR and review formatting. For many files, use Acrobat's batch actions. If text is still poor, the scan resolution may be too low; rescanning at a higher resolution helps more than any setting. Can you OCR in Adobe Reader? No. The free Adobe Acrobat Reader can view, comment on and sign PDFs, but it cannot run OCR. OCR needs Acrobat Standard or Pro, or Adobe's paid online services. Free alternatives: open the PDF from Google Drive with Google Docs, which runs OCR; use Microsoft Word to open and convert a scanned PDF; use OCRmyPDF, a free open-source command-line tool that adds a text layer; or use the Adobe Scan mobile app for documents you are scanning yourself. For sensitive documents, prefer offline tools over uploading to unknown websites. What does OCR mean in Adobe Scan? In Adobe Scan, Adobe's mobile scanning app, OCR means the app automatically recognises text in the documents you photograph, so the PDFs it creates are searchable and you can copy text from them. Adobe Scan detects page edges, corrects perspective, enhances contrast and runs OCR on each page. Results sync to Adobe's cloud, where you can open them in Acrobat. Good capture habits improve OCR: flat pages, even light without shadows, the phone parallel to the page, and one page per shot. Check the app's settings for OCR language. As with any cloud service, avoid scanning highly sensitive documents unless your organisation approves it. How do I use an OCR text scanner? Open the scanner app, capture the page in good light, let it crop and straighten the image, confirm OCR is on and the language is correct, then save as a searchable PDF or copy the recognised text. Also asked as: how to use ocr text scanner Steps that work in most apps, such as Adobe Scan, Google Lens, Microsoft OneNote or your phone's notes app: Place the page on a contrasting, flat surface. Hold the phone directly above, parallel to the page. Capture each page separately; review crops. Choose PDF for documents, text for quick copying. Search or select text to confirm OCR worked. For handwriting, accuracy drops, so check carefully. For multi-page documents, scan into one PDF and name it clearly. Does Tesseract OCR convert a PDF to text? Not directly. Tesseract reads images, so you first convert PDF pages to images, then run Tesseract on each. Alternatively, OCRmyPDF uses Tesseract to add a text layer to the whole PDF in one command. Two approaches: ocrmypdf --language eng scanned.pdf searchable.pdf # searchable PDF in one step from pdf2image import convert_from_path import pytesseract pages = convert_from_path(&quot;scanned.pdf&quot;, dpi=300) text = &quot;\n&quot;.join(pytesseract.image_to_string(p, lang=&quot;eng&quot;) for p in pages) If the PDF already contains text, as most digitally created PDFs do, extract it directly with a PDF library instead, which is faster and exact. How do I find the parameters supported in Tesseract's config file? Run tesseract --print-parameters to list every parameter with its default value and a short description. Then set values in a config file or pass them on the command line with -c name=value. Also asked as: how to find parameters supported in tesseract ocr config file Useful options to know: --psm sets page segmentation mode, for example 6 for a single block of text or 7 for a single line; --oem selects the OCR engine mode; -c tessedit_char_whitelist=0123456789 restricts recognised characters, useful for digits; and preserve_interword_spaces=1 keeps spacing. Config files placed in Tesseract's configs folder can be referenced by name. Change one setting at a time and measure accuracy on a small sample. What is the best OCR model for handwritten text? Modern vision-language models and specialised handwriting recognition services handle handwriting best. Traditional engines such as Tesseract are designed for print and perform poorly on handwriting. Options include large multimodal models from major AI providers, cloud document services with handwriting support, and open models such as TrOCR for line-level recognition. Results depend heavily on writing neatness, language and scan quality. Always review handwritten OCR, ask models to mark uncertain words, and keep the original image for checking. For notes taken with a stylus, built-in conversion in notes apps is often more accurate than OCR of photos, because it uses pen strokes. How do I OCR invoices in a Chrome extension? First try the PDF's own text layer, using a PDF library such as PDF.js in the browser; only if a page has no text, send its image to an OCR service on your server. Then parse fields such as invoice number, date and total with rules or a model, and validate them. Also asked as: how to ocr invoices in a chrome extension: pdf text layer, server ocr, and field parsing A robust design: Text layer first: extract text and positions with PDF.js; most digital invoices have it. Server OCR fallback: send scanned pages to a backend running Tesseract or a document AI service. Field parsing: regular expressions for dates and amounts, or an LLM with a strict JSON schema. Validation: totals equal the sum of line items, dates are valid, required fields present. Privacy: tell users what leaves the browser, and process locally where possible. That is the pattern behind DocuLens AI: extraction with schema validation before anything is trusted.

# OCR tutorial: how to OCR an image, the best OCR models, Mistral and DeepSeek OCR
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/ocr-tutorial-best-models/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Yes, you can OCR almost any image that contains text: phone photos of notes, screenshots, scanned pages and image-only PDFs. OCR, optical character recognition, finds the text and turns it into something you can copy, search or process. This page is a practical tutorial: OCR in a few lines of code, how OCR models work, which models are best including on Hugging Face, whether multimodal LLMs beat OCR, step-by-step use of Mistral OCR, DeepSeek-OCR and NAPS2, and classifying document images without OCR. I built page-batched OCR with Mistral into my OCR & Speech Workspace, so the advice comes from real use.

## Can I OCR an image?

Yes. On a phone, Google Lens or Apple's Live Text copy text from any photo. On a computer, OneNote, the Windows Snipping Tool's text actions, Google Lens in the browser, or free tools such as Tesseract extract text from images.

Accuracy depends on the image more than the tool. For best results, use a sharp image with good contrast, straighten tilted pages, crop away backgrounds, and choose the correct language. Screenshots of digital text are the easiest case; handwritten notes, curved book pages and low-light photos are the hardest. For anything important, such as invoices or certificates, check names, dates and numbers after OCR.

## What is a simple OCR tutorial?

Install Tesseract, then use Python with pytesseract and Pillow to read an image. This works offline and for free.

```python
# pip install pytesseract pillow   (and install the Tesseract engine for your OS)
from PIL import Image, ImageOps
import pytesseract

img = Image.open("receipt.jpg")
img = ImageOps.grayscale(img)                         # simple clean-up
text = pytesseract.image_to_string(img, lang="eng")
print(text)
```

For better results, resize small images up, increase contrast, and try different page segmentation modes with the `config="--psm 6"` option for uniform blocks of text. To get word positions, use `image_to_data`. For scanned PDFs, OCRmyPDF adds a searchable text layer in one command.

## How does an OCR model work?

An OCR pipeline first detects where text is in the image, then recognises the characters in each region with a neural network, then puts the pieces in reading order. Modern end-to-end models can read a whole page directly.

Classic deep-learning OCR uses a detection model to find text lines or words, and a recognition model, often a convolutional network with a sequence model and CTC decoding, or a transformer, to read each line. Layout analysis finds columns, tables and reading order. Vision-language models replace the pipeline with one model that sees the page image and generates text, Markdown or JSON, using context from the whole page. That context helps with messy layouts but adds the risk of plausible-looking mistakes.

## Which OCR model is the best?

It depends on the document type. For clean printed text, Tesseract and cloud OCR services are accurate and cheap. For complex layouts, tables, forms and handwriting, AI document models from providers such as Mistral, Google and Microsoft, and strong vision-language models, perform best.

Pick by need:

- **Free, offline, printed text**: Tesseract or PaddleOCR.
- **Forms and invoices**: Azure AI Document Intelligence or Google Document AI.
- **Whole pages to Markdown with tables**: Mistral OCR or a vision-language model.
- **Self-hosted AI OCR**: open models such as DeepSeek-OCR on your own GPU.
- **Handwriting**: vision-language models, with human review.

Benchmark on twenty of your own documents; public benchmarks rarely match your exact layouts and languages.

## What is the best OCR model on Hugging Face?

Hugging Face hosts many OCR and document models: traditional engines such as PaddleOCR, transformer recognisers such as TrOCR, OCR-free document models such as Donut, and newer open document-reading models such as DeepSeek-OCR, plus general vision-language models that read documents well.

Choose based on your task: TrOCR for recognising single lines of printed or handwritten text, Donut for extracting structured fields without a separate OCR step, and modern document vision-language models for full-page conversion to Markdown. Check each model card for licence, supported languages, hardware needs and benchmark results, and try the model's demo space on your own images before integrating it. Newer models appear often, so sort by recent activity and downloads.

## Is a multimodal LLM better than an OCR model?

For complex documents, often yes: multimodal LLMs understand layout, tables and context, and can output structured data directly. For simple printed text at scale, dedicated OCR is cheaper, faster and less likely to invent words.

The key risk with LLM-based OCR is hallucination on unclear regions: a smudged number may come back as a plausible but wrong value, whereas traditional OCR tends to produce visible garbage. Mitigations include asking the model to mark uncertain text, cross-checking key fields with a traditional OCR pass, validating with rules, such as totals adding up, and keeping page references. A hybrid often works best: OCR for text, an LLM for structure and extraction, then validation, the pattern behind DocuLens AI's schema-validated extraction.

## How do I use Mistral OCR?

Mistral OCR is an API that converts PDFs and images into Markdown, page by page, preserving headings, lists and tables, and returning images it finds. You call it with your Mistral API key and a document URL or uploaded file.

```python
# pip install mistralai
from mistralai import Mistral
client = Mistral(api_key="YOUR_KEY")   # read from an environment variable in practice
resp = client.ocr.process(
    model="mistral-ocr-latest",
    document={"type": "document_url", "document_url": "https://example.com/notes.pdf"},
)
for page in resp.pages:
    print(page.index, page.markdown[:200])
```

Process long PDFs in page batches and store each page's Markdown with its page number, so later answers can cite pages. Check the Mistral documentation for current model names and limits.

## How do I use DeepSeek-OCR?

DeepSeek-OCR is an open document OCR model from DeepSeek, available on Hugging Face, that converts document images into text or Markdown. You run it yourself with Python and a GPU, using the Transformers library or a serving engine such as vLLM.

Steps: check the model card for hardware requirements and the exact loading code, install the listed versions of PyTorch and Transformers, load the model and processor with `trust_remote_code` as the card instructs, then pass page images with the recommended prompt for Markdown output. Because it runs locally, documents stay on your infrastructure, which helps with privacy. Test it against a hosted OCR service on your own pages, checking tables and numbers carefully, before choosing.

## How do I use NAPS2 for OCR?

NAPS2, short for Not Another PDF Scanner, is a free, open-source scanning app for Windows, macOS and Linux. Scan or import images, enable OCR with your language, and save a searchable PDF.

Steps:

- Install NAPS2 from its official website.
- Scan from your scanner, or import images and PDFs.
- Open the OCR settings, enable OCR and download the language you need, for example English or Hindi.
- Reorder, rotate or deskew pages if needed.
- Save as PDF; the OCR text layer makes it searchable and copyable.

NAPS2 uses Tesseract for OCR, so the same image-quality tips apply: flat pages, good resolution and correct language.

## Can you classify document images without OCR?

Yes. You can train an image classifier, such as a fine-tuned vision transformer or a convolutional network, to recognise document types such as invoices, ID cards or certificates from their visual layout, without reading the text. OCR-free document models such as Donut can also classify and extract.

Visual classification works well when document types look different, for example a passport page versus a receipt. When types look similar and differ mainly in wording, combining text from OCR with layout features, or using a vision-language model, is more accurate. A practical pipeline classifies first with a fast image model, then runs the right extraction for each type, which saves cost and improves accuracy.

# What is the Ollama base URL? Commands, ollama ps, updates and setup
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/ollama-base-url-and-commands/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The Ollama base URL is `http://localhost:11434` on the machine where Ollama runs; its native API lives under `/api`, such as `/api/chat`, and its OpenAI-compatible API under `/v1`. You change it with the `OLLAMA_HOST` setting or by calling a different host. This page explains how to find the base URL in different setups, the cloud URL, what a base URL is, the essential Ollama commands including `ollama ps`, how to update, what `ollama.exe` is, a good setup for development, and when Ollama launched.

## What is the Ollama base URL?

By default, Ollama listens on `http://localhost:11434`. Tools that use Ollama's native API need that base URL; tools that speak the OpenAI API format use `http://localhost:11434/v1`.

Examples of where you enter it:

- **LangChain**: `ChatOllama(base_url="http://localhost:11434", model="llama3.2")`.
- **OpenAI SDK**: `OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama")`.
- **Web UIs and editor extensions**: an "Ollama URL" or "API base" setting.

Test it by opening `http://localhost:11434` in a browser; it replies "Ollama is running" when the server is up. If it does not, start the Ollama app or run `ollama serve`.

## Where do I find the Ollama base URL?

It is `http://localhost:11434` unless someone changed it. If Ollama runs elsewhere, the base URL is that machine's address and port: a server's IP, a Docker service name, or a custom host set with `OLLAMA_HOST`.

Common setups:

- **Same machine**: `http://localhost:11434`.
- **Docker Compose**: `http://ollama:11434`, using the service name from another container.
- **From a Docker container to Ollama on the host**: `http://host.docker.internal:11434` on Docker Desktop.
- **Another computer on your network**: `http://<server-ip>:11434`, after setting `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0` on the server.

Opening Ollama to the network exposes an API with no login, so restrict access with a firewall, VPN or authenticated reverse proxy.

## What is the Ollama cloud base URL?

For Ollama's hosted cloud models, the API is served from ollama.com, and requests need an API key from your Ollama account. Alternatively, sign in your local Ollama and keep using `localhost:11434`, which forwards cloud-model requests for you.

Direct calls look like requests to `https://ollama.com/api/chat` with an `Authorization: Bearer <key>` header and a cloud model name. Using the local app as a gateway is simpler for development, because your code does not change between local and cloud models except for the model name. Keep the key in an environment variable. Check Ollama's documentation for the current cloud endpoints, as the service is still evolving.

## What is a base URL in an API?

A base URL is the common starting part of every request to an API: the scheme, host, port and sometimes a version path. Each endpoint adds its own path to it.

For example, with a base URL of `http://localhost:11434`, the chat endpoint is `http://localhost:11434/api/chat` and the model list is `http://localhost:11434/api/tags`. For OpenAI-style clients the base URL includes `/v1`, and the client adds `/chat/completions`. Keeping the base URL in configuration, such as an environment variable, lets the same code talk to a local server in development and a hosted service in production. Many integration bugs come from a missing or extra `/v1` or a trailing slash, so check that first.

## What are the main Ollama commands?

The commands you will use most are `ollama run`, `pull`, `list`, `ps`, `stop`, `rm`, `show`, `create` and `serve`.

```bash
ollama run llama3.2        # chat with a model (downloads it first if needed)
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b     # download or update a model
ollama list                # installed models and sizes
ollama ps                  # models loaded in memory, CPU or GPU
ollama stop llama3.2       # unload a model to free memory
ollama rm llama3.2         # delete a model from disk
ollama show llama3.2       # details, parameters, template
ollama create mymodel -f Modelfile   # build a custom model
ollama serve               # start the server manually
```

Inside a chat, `/bye` exits and `/set` changes options. `ollama help` lists everything for your version.

## What does ollama ps do?

`ollama ps` lists the models currently loaded in memory, with their size, how much runs on GPU versus CPU, and when each will be unloaded. It is the quickest way to diagnose slow responses.

If the processor column shows 100% GPU, the model fits in video memory and runs fast. A split such as 40% CPU and 60% GPU means part of the model did not fit, which slows responses sharply; try a smaller model or quantisation, or reduce the context size. Models stay loaded for a few minutes after the last request so follow-ups are quick, then unload automatically. Use `ollama stop <model>` to unload one immediately, for example before running another memory-hungry program.

## How do I update Ollama?

On Windows and macOS, the app checks for updates and offers to restart into the new version; you can also download and run the latest installer. On Linux, re-run the official install script. In Docker, pull the new image and recreate the container.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh      # Linux
docker pull ollama/ollama                          # Docker, then recreate the container
```

Updating Ollama does not update your models. To refresh a model to its latest version, run `ollama pull <model>` again; only changed layers download. Check the version with `ollama --version`. After major updates, read the release notes, because defaults such as context length or engine behaviour can change.

## What is ollama.exe?

`ollama.exe` is the Ollama program on Windows: the command-line tool and server that run local language models. It is legitimate when installed from ollama.com and located in your user's Ollama install folder.

When the Ollama app runs, `ollama.exe` serves the local API on port 11434 and loads models into memory, so it can use significant RAM or GPU memory while a model is active. That is expected. To stop it, quit Ollama from the system tray. If you find `ollama.exe` on a computer where you never installed Ollama, or in an unusual folder, treat it as suspicious and scan the system, since malware can use familiar names.

## What is the best Ollama setup?

For development, run Ollama natively with GPU support, keep two or three models you actually use, store models on a drive with space, raise the context size when you need it, and connect a chat UI and your code to the same local server.

A practical setup:

- **Models**: a general 7B or 8B instruct model, a coding model, and an embedding model for RAG.
- **Storage**: set `OLLAMA_MODELS` to a large drive.
- **Interface**: Ollama's app or a web UI for chat; LangChain or plain HTTP for code.
- **Docker**: for servers, run the official image with a persistent volume and GPU access.
- **Security**: keep the API on localhost unless protected by authentication.

Check `ollama ps` regularly to confirm models run on the GPU.

## When did Ollama launch?

Ollama launched in 2023, first for macOS, then expanded to Linux and later Windows. It grew quickly as open-weight models such as Llama made local language models practical on ordinary hardware.

Since launch, it has added a large model library, an OpenAI-compatible API, support for vision and embedding models, tool calling, a desktop app interface and optional cloud models. It is open source under the MIT licence, built on the GGML ecosystem that also powers llama.cpp. Its simple `ollama run` experience is a large part of why running models locally became common among students and developers.

# Is Ollama Cloud free? How Ollama cloud models work, privacy and limits
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/ollama-cloud-free/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Ollama Cloud lets you run large open models, ones too big for a laptop, on Ollama's own servers while using the same `ollama` commands and API you use for local models. It has a free tier with usage limits and paid plans with higher limits. This page explains whether and how it is free, how it works, what happens to your data, whether cloud models are quantised, the API and keys, which models to try, how it differs from deploying Ollama on your own cloud server, and how to build on it.

## Is Ollama Cloud free?

Ollama Cloud has a free tier that lets you try cloud models with usage limits, plus paid plans with higher limits and priority. Local Ollama remains completely free.

The free tier is meant for experimenting: chatting with a very large model, testing whether it handles your task better than a local one, or prototyping. Heavy or production use needs a paid plan or another provider. Limits are measured over time windows and depend on the model, and Ollama adjusts them as the service grows, so check Ollama's pricing page for current details. If cost is your main concern, local models on your own hardware are free per token, and Gemini's free API tier is another option for prototypes.

## Does Ollama have free cloud models?

Yes. Cloud models are marked with a cloud tag in Ollama's library, and you can run them on the free tier within its limits. They are typically large open-weight models, such as big coding and reasoning models, that would need data-centre GPUs to run locally.

Run one like a local model, with its cloud tag, after signing in:

```bash
ollama signin
ollama run <model>:<size>-cloud
```

The exact names change as new models are added, so browse the cloud section of the library. Nothing large downloads to your disk; prompts go to Ollama's servers and responses stream back. When you hit the free limit, wait for the window to reset or switch to a local model.

## How does Ollama Cloud work?

Your local Ollama app acts as a client: when you run a cloud-tagged model, it sends the request to Ollama's hosted servers instead of loading a model on your machine, then streams the response back through the same CLI and API.

That means existing tools that talk to `localhost:11434`, such as LangChain, coding extensions and web UIs, can use cloud models without code changes beyond the model name. You can also call the cloud API directly at ollama.com with an API key, which is useful on servers where you do not run the Ollama app. Mixing is easy: a small local model for quick, private tasks and a large cloud model for hard ones, both through one interface.

## Are Ollama cloud models private?

Ollama states that it does not retain your prompts and responses from cloud models, but your data does leave your machine and is processed on its servers. Read Ollama's current privacy policy and terms before sending anything sensitive.

The privacy trade-off is the same as with any hosted AI service: local models keep everything on your device; cloud models require trusting the provider's handling, security and location of processing. For college projects and public data, cloud models are generally fine. For client data, health information, personal identity documents or company code under strict policies, prefer local models or a provider your organisation has approved with a data processing agreement. In any case, keep secrets and passwords out of prompts.

## Are Ollama cloud models quantised?

Cloud models generally run at the precision their publishers released them in, or close to it, rather than the heavy 4-bit quantisation typical for local use. Each model's page in the library lists its details.

Precision matters because quantisation trades some accuracy for smaller memory and faster speed. On a laptop, 4-bit versions of 7B or 8B models are the practical choice. In the data centre, there is enough GPU memory to run large models at higher precision, which is part of why cloud models answer better on hard tasks. Some modern models are released natively in low-precision formats, so "full precision" varies by model. If accuracy on your task matters, compare the same model locally and in the cloud on your own test prompts.

## Is the Ollama Cloud API free?

The cloud API shares the same free tier and limits as cloud models in the app: you can call it free within those limits using an API key from your ollama.com account, and paid plans raise them. The local API is always free and needs no key.

Create a key in your account settings and send it as a bearer token when calling the hosted API, or sign in your local Ollama app so local API calls to cloud models are authenticated automatically. Keep the key in an environment variable, not in code or front-end apps. For production traffic, compare limits, latency and terms with other providers and consider a fallback, because a free tier is not designed for guaranteed uptime.

## What is the best Ollama cloud model?

The best one depends on your task: large coding models for agentic coding, large reasoning models for analysis and maths, and general instruction models for chat and writing. Test two or three on your own prompts.

How to compare:

- Write five prompts that represent your real work, such as a bug fix, a summary and a design question.
- Run each prompt on two cloud models and one local model.
- Judge correctness, clarity and how much editing each answer needs.
- Note speed and how quickly each uses your limits.

The cloud lineup changes as new open models are released, so revisit the comparison every few months. A large cloud model is often worth it only for hard tasks; routine work runs fine locally.

## Can an Ollama model be deployed on the cloud?

Yes, in two ways. You can use Ollama Cloud, where Ollama hosts the models, or self-host Ollama on your own cloud server, such as a GPU virtual machine, with Docker or the Linux installer, keeping full control of data and configuration.

Self-hosting steps: rent a GPU instance, install drivers, run the official Docker image with a persistent volume and GPU access, pull your models, and put an authenticated reverse proxy in front of port 11434, since Ollama's API has no login. For many concurrent users, a serving engine such as vLLM handles batching more efficiently than Ollama. Self-hosting costs money for the GPU even when idle, so compare it with per-request pricing from hosted options.

## How do I build my own AI platform with Ollama cloud models?

Put a thin backend in front of Ollama that handles users, authentication, logging and model routing, and call local or cloud models through the same Ollama API. Keep the model choice in configuration so you can switch providers.

A workable architecture:

- **Backend**: FastAPI or Node.js with user accounts and per-user limits.
- **Model layer**: an interface that can call local Ollama, Ollama Cloud or another provider.
- **Retrieval**: a vector store for your documents, with citations in answers.
- **Fallback**: if one model is slow or failing, try another, as RAG.NextUpgrad does with multiple providers.
- **Observability**: log prompts, latency, errors and costs.

Start with one use case, such as a document Q&A assistant for a college department, before generalising.

## How do beginners start with Ollama cloud models?

Install Ollama, create a free account on ollama.com, run `ollama signin`, then run one cloud model and compare it with a local model on the same prompt. That shows quickly whether the cloud is worth using for your tasks.

A first-hour plan:

- `ollama run llama3.2` locally and ask three questions you care about.
- Sign in and run a large cloud model with the same questions.
- Try both from Python through the local API, changing only the model name.
- Note quality, speed and how much of the free limit you used.

From there, use local models for private and routine work, and the cloud model for the hard cases. Read the privacy terms before sending anything sensitive.

# Does Ollama have limits? Rate limits, UI options, server setup and speed fixes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/ollama-limits-ui-server/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Ollama running on your own computer has no usage limits, rate limits or quotas: you can send as many requests as your hardware can handle. Limits apply only to Ollama's optional cloud models, and to the licences of the models you run. This page covers limits and concurrency settings, restrictions, user interfaces, running the server and logging requests, why Ollama or model downloads can be slow, and whether Ollama does video generation.

## Does Ollama have limits?

Locally, no: Ollama does not limit how many requests you make or how many tokens you generate. The practical limits are your RAM or GPU memory, which decide which models fit, and your CPU or GPU speed, which decides how fast they run.

Other limits to know: each model has a maximum context length, and Ollama uses a default context window that you can raise with `num_ctx`; only so many models fit in memory at once; and very long generations take time. Ollama's cloud models, which run on its servers, have usage limits by plan. If you need more throughput than one machine provides, run several instances behind a load balancer or use a serving engine such as vLLM.

## Does Ollama have rate limits?

Not locally. Instead of rate limits, Ollama has concurrency settings: `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` controls how many requests a loaded model processes at once, and `OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE` controls how many requests can wait before new ones are rejected.

When requests exceed what the model can process, they queue, so latency rises rather than requests failing, until the queue is full. `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS` limits how many models stay in memory together. Raising parallelism increases memory use, because each parallel request needs its own context memory. If you expose Ollama to a team, add your own rate limiting in a proxy or backend so one user cannot monopolise the machine.

## Does Ollama have restrictions?

Ollama itself is open source under the MIT licence with few restrictions on use. The restrictions that matter come from the models you run, each with its own licence, and from Ollama's terms if you use its cloud services.

Model licences vary: some are permissive, such as Apache 2.0, while others have custom terms with conditions on commercial use, attribution or acceptable use. Read the licence on each model's page before using it in a product. Models also carry built-in safety behaviour from their training. If you run Ollama on a shared server, add your own access control, because the local API has no authentication by default.

## Does Ollama have a UI?

Yes. Ollama's desktop app for Windows and macOS includes a chat interface, and the command line offers an interactive chat with `ollama run`. For a richer web interface, tools such as Open WebUI connect to Ollama's local API.

The built-in app is enough for chatting with local models and trying files. Web UIs add features such as conversation history, multiple users, document upload for RAG, model management and prompt libraries. Editor extensions bring Ollama models into VS Code for coding help. All of these talk to the same server at `http://localhost:11434`, so you can use several at once.

## What is the best UI for Ollama?

Open WebUI is the most popular full-featured web interface for Ollama, with chat history, document chat, user accounts and model management. Ollama's own app is the simplest choice for personal use.

How to choose:

- **Personal, simple**: Ollama's desktop app.
- **Feature-rich, multi-user, self-hosted**: Open WebUI, usually run with Docker.
- **Coding**: an editor extension that supports Ollama.
- **Mac-native experience**: several community Mac apps connect to Ollama.

Run web UIs on your own machine or private network, set strong passwords if multiple people use them, and keep them updated, since they handle your conversations and documents.

## How do I run an Ollama server?

On desktop installs, the Ollama app runs the server automatically. On Linux, the install script sets up a systemd service. To run it manually, use `ollama serve`. The server listens on `http://localhost:11434` by default.

```bash
OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434 ollama serve        # listen on all interfaces
```

On Linux services, set environment variables with `sudo systemctl edit ollama` and restart the service. To use it from other devices, set `OLLAMA_HOST`, open the port only on your private network, and add an authenticated reverse proxy if anyone outside can reach it. In Docker, publish port 11434 and mount a volume for models.

## How do I log input requests and output responses in the Ollama server?

Set `OLLAMA_DEBUG=1` before starting the server to get detailed logs, then read the server log. For full prompt and response logging, put a small proxy or your own backend in front of Ollama and log requests and responses there.

Log locations: on Linux services, use `journalctl -u ollama`; on macOS and Windows, the app's menu can open the logs folder. Debug logs show model loading, GPU use and request handling, which helps diagnose slowness and errors, but they are not designed as a clean audit trail of prompts. A thin FastAPI or Node proxy that forwards requests to Ollama and writes prompt, response, latency and token counts to a database gives you a proper record, and is also where you add authentication.

## Why is Ollama slow?

Ollama is usually slow because the model does not fully fit in GPU memory and part of it runs on the CPU, the context window is set very large, or the model is simply too big for the hardware.

Fixes:

- Run `ollama ps`; if it shows CPU use, choose a smaller model or lower quantisation.
- Reduce `num_ctx` if you raised it; large contexts use lots of memory.
- Update GPU drivers and Ollama itself.
- Close other GPU-heavy apps.
- Keep the model loaded between requests; the first request after loading is slower.

On laptops without a capable GPU, 3B to 4B models give the best experience. Speed is measured in tokens per second; compare before and after each change.

## Why is ollama pull so slow?

Model downloads are large, several gigabytes, so speed depends on your internet connection, network congestion, Wi-Fi quality, and sometimes proxies or VPNs that throttle large downloads.

Tips: use a wired connection or a stronger Wi-Fi signal; pause other downloads; try at off-peak times; disable a VPN if it slows traffic; and if a download stalls, cancel and run `ollama pull` again, which resumes from the layers already downloaded. Choose smaller model sizes or quantisations if bandwidth is limited. On shared or campus networks, firewalls may block or slow large transfers; try another network to confirm.

## Does Ollama have video generation?

No. Ollama focuses on running language models, vision-language models that understand images, and embedding models. It does not generate videos.

For video generation, use dedicated tools: hosted services such as Google's Veo in Gemini, OpenAI's Sora or Adobe Firefly, or open video models run through frameworks such as ComfyUI on a strong GPU. Ollama can still help in a video workflow, for example writing scripts and shot lists, generating prompts for a video model, or describing frames with a vision model.

# How many GB is Ollama? Model sizes, best models under 5 GB, and Windows setup
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/ollama-size-and-windows/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Ollama itself is a small download compared with the models it runs; the space goes to models, which range from about 1 GB for tiny ones to 4 to 5 GB for popular 7B and 8B models at 4-bit, and tens of gigabytes for large ones. This page explains how to estimate a local model's size, which models fit under 5 GB, what parameters and tokens mean in Ollama, how many models it supports, where it installs on Windows, whether to use Windows or WSL, and how to get started.

## How many GB is Ollama?

The Ollama application is small relative to models, though its Windows installer includes GPU libraries that add some size. Plan your disk space around the models: a typical setup with three or four models uses 10 to 25 GB.

Check sizes with `ollama list`, which shows each installed model and its size on disk, and free space with `ollama rm <model>`. The download page shows the current installer size. If your system drive is small, store models elsewhere with the `OLLAMA_MODELS` environment variable. Remember that running a model also needs RAM or video memory roughly equal to its file size plus extra for the context, so disk space is not the only limit.

## How many GB is a local LLM?

Roughly the number of parameters multiplied by the bytes stored per parameter. At 16-bit precision that is 2 bytes per parameter; at the 4-bit quantisation common in Ollama it is about 0.5 to 0.6 bytes, so a 7B or 8B model is around 4 to 5 GB.

Approximate sizes at 4-bit:

- **1B to 3B models**: about 1 to 2 GB.
- **7B to 8B models**: about 4 to 5 GB.
- **12B to 14B models**: about 8 to 9 GB.
- **30B to 34B models**: about 18 to 20 GB.
- **70B models**: about 40 GB.

Higher-precision versions, such as 8-bit, are about twice as large and slightly more accurate. Quantisation is the same idea QLoRA uses to fine-tune large models on one GPU: store weights in 4 bits to save memory.

## What is the best Ollama model under 5 GB?

For general use, a 7B or 8B instruction model at 4-bit, from families such as Llama, Qwen or Mistral, gives the best quality under 5 GB. For low-memory laptops, 3B to 4B models such as small Llama, Gemma or Phi variants are faster and still useful.

Choose by task:

- **Chat and writing**: a recent 7B or 8B instruct model.
- **Coding**: a coding-tuned 7B model, such as a Qwen coder variant.
- **Speed on 8 GB RAM**: a 3B or 4B model.
- **Embeddings for RAG**: a dedicated embedding model, which is much smaller.

New models arrive often and smaller ones keep improving, so check the Ollama library and compare two candidates on your own prompts. Quality differences show quickly on real tasks.

## How many parameters do Ollama models have?

Ollama runs models of many sizes, from under one billion parameters to hundreds of billions. The parameter count is usually in the model tag, such as `llama3.2:3b` or `qwen2.5:7b`, and `ollama show <model>` displays details.

Parameters are the learned weights of the network. More parameters generally mean more knowledge and better reasoning, but also more memory and slower responses. What you can run depends on your RAM or GPU memory: roughly, a 4-bit model needs a little more memory than its file size. On a laptop with 16 GB RAM, models up to about 8B to 14B are practical; beyond that you need a strong GPU or a server.

## How many models does Ollama support?

Ollama's library offers hundreds of models and many more variants, covering major open families such as Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi and DeepSeek, plus embedding and vision models. You can also import other compatible models in GGUF format.

To import a model from Hugging Face or your own fine-tune, create a Modelfile pointing to the GGUF file and run `ollama create`. Many GGUF repositories on Hugging Face can also be run directly by reference. Each model has tags for sizes and quantisation levels, so one family may have dozens of versions. Stick to well-known publishers and popular variants unless you have a reason to experiment, because quality varies widely among community uploads.

## How many tokens can Ollama handle?

It depends on the model's maximum context length and Ollama's `num_ctx` setting. Ollama uses a modest default context window, often a few thousand tokens, even when the model supports far more, to keep memory use reasonable.

Raise it per request through the API options, in a Modelfile with `PARAMETER num_ctx 16384`, or with environment settings in recent versions. A larger context lets you pass longer documents or conversations, but uses more memory and slows responses. If answers ignore the start of a long document, the context window is likely too small and the text is being cut off. For long documents, retrieval of relevant chunks usually works better than one huge context, especially with small models.

## Where is Ollama installed on Windows?

By default, Ollama installs into your user profile's local app data folder, and models are stored in `C:\Users\<you>\.ollama\models`. The `ollama` command is added to your path, and the app runs from the system tray.

To store models on another drive, set the `OLLAMA_MODELS` environment variable and restart Ollama. Logs, useful when something fails, are in the Ollama folder under your local app data; the tray icon's menu can open them. Ollama's local API listens on `http://localhost:11434`. If another app already uses that port, or you want to reach Ollama from other devices, set `OLLAMA_HOST`, and add protection before exposing it beyond your machine.

## Should I run Ollama on Windows or WSL?

Run it natively on Windows unless your development work already lives in WSL. The Windows app is simpler, starts automatically and uses supported GPUs directly; WSL makes sense when your Python projects, Docker setup and tools are all inside Linux.

Either way, you can reach Ollama from the other side: WSL can call the Windows app over the local network, and Windows tools can reach Ollama in WSL through forwarded localhost ports. Avoid running two copies on the same port. WSL needs enough memory assigned in its settings, or larger models fail to load. If GPU acceleration does not work in WSL, update the Windows GPU driver first; the WSL GPU support depends on it.

## Is there an Ollama tutorial for Windows?

Yes. Install from ollama.com, open PowerShell, run a model, then connect it to a chat interface or your code. A first session takes about fifteen minutes.

```powershell
ollama run llama3.2          # downloads, then opens a chat
ollama list                  # installed models
ollama ps                    # running models and CPU or GPU use
```

Then try the API from Python:

```python
import requests
r = requests.post("http://localhost:11434/api/generate",
                  json={"model": "llama3.2", "prompt": "Explain BM25 briefly.", "stream": False})
print(r.json()["response"])
```

For a graphical chat, use Ollama's own app interface or install a web UI that connects to the local API.

## How do I use Ollama on Windows day to day?

Keep Ollama running in the tray, pull the few models you actually use, and work from either the chat interface, the terminal or your code through the local API. Clean up models you no longer need.

Useful habits:

- `ollama pull <model>` to update a model to its latest version.
- `ollama stop <model>` to free memory after use.
- `ollama rm <model>` to reclaim disk space.
- Use a coding editor extension that supports Ollama for local code help.
- Point LangChain or your own scripts at `http://localhost:11434`.

If responses are slow, check `ollama ps` to see whether the model runs on the GPU; if it shows CPU, the model may be too large for your video memory, so try a smaller size or quantisation.

# Ollama vs Claude, using Ollama with Claude Code, and LangChain with Ollama
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/ollama-vs-claude-langchain/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Ollama and Claude are different kinds of things. Ollama is a free tool that downloads and runs open-weight language models on your own computer; Claude is Anthropic's family of proprietary models, used through Anthropic's apps and API. So "Ollama vs Claude" really means local open models versus a hosted frontier model: privacy and zero per-token cost against much higher capability. This page compares them, explains whether you can use Ollama with Claude Code, which local models suit coding, and how to use Ollama with LangChain, including fine-tuned models and chunking JSON for RAG.

## Ollama vs Claude: which should I use?

Use Claude when you need the strongest reasoning, coding and long-document work. Use Ollama when data must stay on your machine, you want to experiment offline, or you need zero per-token cost for simple, high-volume tasks.

A sensible split for students and developers: Claude for hard problems, real coding sessions and writing; Ollama for learning how models work, private documents, prototyping RAG pipelines without an API bill, and simple tasks such as classification or extraction with a small model. Many projects use both: a local model for cheap first passes and a hosted model for the difficult cases. Hardware decides what Ollama can do: an 8 GB laptop runs small models comfortably, while larger models need a strong GPU or lots of memory.

## How does Ollama compare to Claude?

On capability, Claude's frontier models are well ahead of models small enough to run on a typical laptop, especially for multi-step reasoning, large codebases and long documents. Large open models on powerful hardware narrow the gap but need serious GPUs.

Other differences:

- **Privacy**: Ollama keeps everything local; Claude sends data to Anthropic under its privacy terms.
- **Cost**: Ollama is free per token but needs hardware; Claude costs per use or plan.
- **Speed**: depends on your hardware for Ollama; Claude is fast and consistent.
- **Context length**: Claude handles very long inputs; local models are usually configured with much smaller windows.
- **Maintenance**: with Ollama you choose, update and test models yourself.

For a college project, prototyping locally and switching to a hosted model for the demo is a practical path.

## Does Ollama have Claude?

No. Claude models are proprietary and not released as open weights, so they cannot be downloaded or run in Ollama. Ollama runs open-weight models such as Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi and DeepSeek.

You may see community models in Ollama's library with "Claude" in the name; these are not Anthropic's models, and some are fine-tunes trained on outputs from other models. Treat them like any community model: test them yourself and check the licence. If you need Claude, use claude.ai, Claude Code or the Claude API. If you need a local model with strong coding, choose an open coding model from a reputable publisher.

## Can you use Ollama with Claude Code?

Claude Code is built for Anthropic's models, but it can be pointed at another server that implements Anthropic's API, and Ollama has added ways to serve local models to tools like Claude Code. Expect much weaker results with small local models.

Check the current Ollama and Claude Code documentation for the supported setup, since both change quickly. Agentic coding is demanding: the model must follow long instructions, call tools in the right format, keep track of many files and recover from errors. Small local models often break the tool-calling format or lose track of the task. If you try it, use the largest coding model your hardware can run, a small repository, and narrow tasks. For serious work, Claude Code with Claude models, or a local-first agent designed for open models, is the more reliable choice.

## Which Ollama model is best for Claude Code?

For local agentic coding, use the strongest open coding model your hardware can run, such as recent Qwen coder models or other open models tuned for code and tool use. Larger variants work much better than small ones.

How to choose:

- Prefer models trained for coding and tool calling, from established publishers.
- Pick the largest size that fits your GPU memory with room for a long context window.
- Increase the context length setting; agents need long context to hold files and instructions.
- Test with one real task, such as adding a function with tests, before relying on it.

Open models improve fast, so check Ollama's library and recent independent coding benchmarks for current options. Expect to review more carefully than with frontier hosted models.

## Can LangChain work with Ollama?

Yes. LangChain supports Ollama through the `langchain-ollama` package, which provides `ChatOllama` for chat models, `OllamaLLM` for plain completion and `OllamaEmbeddings` for embeddings. Ollama must be running locally with the model pulled.

Install and pull a model:

```bash
pip install langchain-ollama
ollama pull llama3.1
ollama pull nomic-embed-text
```

The older classes in `langchain_community` still appear in many tutorials but are deprecated in favour of `langchain-ollama`, so use the new package in new code. Because the interface matches other LangChain chat models, you can develop locally with Ollama and later swap in a hosted model, such as Claude, by changing one line.

## What are some LangChain Ollama examples?

Here is a minimal chat call and an embedding call with LangChain and Ollama:

```python
from langchain_ollama import ChatOllama, OllamaEmbeddings

llm = ChatOllama(model="llama3.1", temperature=0)
print(llm.invoke("Explain BM25 in one sentence.").content)

emb = OllamaEmbeddings(model="nomic-embed-text")
vec = emb.embed_query("hybrid search combines keywords and vectors")
print(len(vec))
```

From there, common patterns are a prompt template piped into the model for structured tasks, a retriever over a vector store for RAG, and tool calling with models that support it. For RAG, keep the embedding model the same for indexing and querying, and evaluate retrieval on real questions before tuning prompts.

## How do I use a fine-tuned model with LangChain's Ollama class?

Package your fine-tuned model for Ollama first: convert or merge it into a GGUF file, write a Modelfile that points to it, run `ollama create`, then use that model name in LangChain.

```
FROM ./my-finetuned-model.gguf
PARAMETER temperature 0.2
SYSTEM "You are a helpful assistant for college admissions questions."
```

```bash
ollama create admissions-bot -f Modelfile
```

Then `ChatOllama(model="admissions-bot")` in the `langchain-ollama` package, which replaces the deprecated `langchain_community.llms.Ollama` class. If you trained a LoRA adapter, either merge it into the base model before converting, or use the Modelfile's `ADAPTER` instruction with a compatible base. Make sure the chat template matches the one used in training, or answers degrade.

## How do I efficiently chunk and embed JSON with Ollama and ChromaDB?

Chunk JSON by its natural units, one record or object per chunk, rather than by character count. Turn each record into readable text with its keys, and store filterable fields as metadata in ChromaDB.

A practical recipe:

- Flatten each record into lines such as `name: ...`, `category: ...`, `description: ...`, so the embedding sees keys and values.
- Split only very long records, and repeat the record's ID and title in each piece.
- Put fields like `category`, `date` or `id` in metadata for filtering.
- Embed in batches with one consistent model, for example `nomic-embed-text` through Ollama.
- Store the original JSON or its ID so answers can cite the exact record.

Test retrieval with real questions; if exact identifiers matter, add keyword search alongside embeddings, as hybrid retrieval does in RAG.NextUpgrad.

## Is there a LangChain Ollama course?

Yes. LangChain's documentation has tutorials that work with Ollama, and many free videos and courses build local RAG apps with LangChain and Ollama. The fastest learning comes from building one project end to end.

A good self-paced project: a local assistant for your college notes. Load PDFs, chunk them, embed with Ollama, store in ChromaDB, retrieve the top passages, and answer with a local chat model that cites page numbers. Then add an evaluation set of twenty questions and measure how often the right passage is retrieved. Finally, swap the local model for a hosted one and compare. That single project teaches loaders, chunking, embeddings, vector stores, retrieval, prompting and evaluation.

Hugging Face and Ollama do different jobs in the open-model world. What are Ollama and Hugging Face? Ollama is an open-source application for running language models on your own computer with a simple CLI and local API. Hugging Face is where you discover a model, read its model card and licence, download weights, fine-tune it, or deploy it through hosted inference. # Ollama vs llama.cpp vs LM Studio: differences, speed and the Ollama API
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/ollama-vs-llama-cpp/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Ollama and llama.cpp both run language models locally, but at different levels. llama.cpp is the open-source C/C++ inference engine that made fast local LLMs on ordinary hardware possible; Ollama is a user-friendly tool built on the same GGML ecosystem, adding one-command model downloads, a background server and a simple API. LM Studio is a desktop app with a graphical interface for the same job. This page explains how they relate, why speeds differ, how the Ollama API works, whether it is free or needs a key, its OpenAI compatibility, and how to reuse Ollama's downloaded models in llama.cpp.

## Ollama vs llama.cpp: which should I use?

Use Ollama if you want local models working in minutes, with easy model management and an API for your apps. Use llama.cpp if you want maximum control over performance settings, the newest features first, or to embed inference directly in your own software.

Ollama handles downloading, storing and updating models, runs as a service, and keeps models loaded between requests, which suits developers building apps and students experimenting. llama.cpp gives you command-line tools and a server with many flags for quantisation, batch size, GPU layer offloading, sampling and more, and supports a very wide range of hardware. Many people start with Ollama and move to llama.cpp when they need to squeeze out performance or use a model Ollama does not yet package.

## What is the difference between Ollama and llama.cpp?

llama.cpp is an inference engine and toolkit: it loads GGUF model files and runs them efficiently on CPUs and GPUs. Ollama is an application around local inference: a model registry, a CLI, a background server, a REST API and packaging through Modelfiles.

Practical differences:

- **Setup**: Ollama installs with one installer; llama.cpp is built from source or downloaded as release binaries.
- **Models**: Ollama pulls by name from its library; llama.cpp uses GGUF files you download.
- **Configuration**: Ollama has sensible defaults; llama.cpp exposes every knob.
- **Updates**: llama.cpp gets new model support first; Ollama follows after packaging.

Both are open source, and both run models privately on your own machine.

## Does Ollama use llama.cpp?

Ollama was built on llama.cpp and the GGML library, and it still relies on GGML for much of its inference. It has also developed its own engine for some newer models, especially multimodal ones, so the relationship is close but not identical.

That shared foundation is why Ollama uses the same GGUF model format and similar quantisation types as llama.cpp. It also explains why support for a brand-new model architecture often appears in llama.cpp first and reaches Ollama after the Ollama team integrates and packages it. If a model you want is not yet in Ollama's library, check whether llama.cpp supports it and whether a GGUF version exists on Hugging Face that you can import into Ollama with a Modelfile.

## Why is Ollama slower than llama.cpp?

When Ollama seems slower, the cause is usually different settings: context length, how many layers run on the GPU, batch sizes, parallel request settings or an older engine version. Tuned the same way on the same model file, the gap is usually small.

Things to check:

- **GPU offload**: run `ollama ps`; if part of the model is on CPU, speed drops sharply.
- **Context size**: a large `num_ctx` uses more memory and can push layers to CPU.
- **Quantisation**: compare the same quantisation level in both tools.
- **Versions**: llama.cpp releases frequently; Ollama may lag.
- **Concurrency**: parallel requests share the same hardware.

Benchmark with the same prompt, model file and settings before drawing conclusions. For a single user on a laptop, either is fast enough when the model fits in GPU memory.

## Ollama vs llama.cpp vs LM Studio: how do they compare?

All three run local models. Ollama is CLI and API first, ideal for developers. llama.cpp is the engine for maximum control. LM Studio is a polished desktop app with a chat interface and model browser, popular with people who prefer a graphical tool.

LM Studio lets you search and download GGUF models from Hugging Face, chat with them, adjust settings with sliders, and run a local server with an OpenAI-compatible API. It is free for personal use; check its terms for work use. LM Studio is not open source, while Ollama and llama.cpp are. A sensible setup: LM Studio to explore models visually, Ollama for app development, and llama.cpp when you need fine-grained tuning or to deploy on unusual hardware.

## What is the difference between Ollama and Llama?

Llama is a family of open-weight language models made by Meta. Ollama is a tool for running language models locally, including Llama and many others such as Qwen, Gemma, Mistral and DeepSeek. The names are similar, but one is a model and the other is software that runs models.

So "Ollama Llama" usually means running a Llama model inside Ollama, for example `ollama run llama3.2`. Llama models come with Meta's licence, which allows wide use with some conditions, while Ollama is under the MIT licence. You can run Llama models in llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM or on cloud providers too. Choosing a model and choosing a runtime are separate decisions.

## Is the Ollama API free?

Yes. The local Ollama API is free: once Ollama runs on your machine, any app can call it at `http://localhost:11434` without limits or charges. Your only costs are your hardware and electricity.

The API covers generating text, chat, embeddings, model management and more. Because it runs locally, there are no rate limits other than your hardware's speed. Ollama also offers optional cloud features that run larger models on its servers, which have their own plans and limits. If you expose your local API to a network, put authentication in front of it, since the local API has no login of its own and anyone who can reach it can use your machine's resources.

## Where do I find an Ollama API key?

You do not need one for the local API: requests to `localhost:11434` work without any key. Keys only apply to Ollama's optional cloud features, and you create them in your account settings on ollama.com.

Some tools built for OpenAI-style APIs insist on an API key field even when talking to Ollama locally; in that case, any placeholder string works, because the local server ignores it. If you run Ollama on a server for a team, add your own authentication layer, such as a reverse proxy with API keys or a VPN, rather than leaving the port open. Never paste real keys for other services, such as OpenAI or Anthropic, into tools that do not need them.

## Does Ollama support the OpenAI API?

Yes. Ollama provides an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so many apps and libraries written for OpenAI's API can use local models by changing the base URL to `http://localhost:11434/v1` and the model name.

```python
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama")  # key is ignored locally
r = client.chat.completions.create(model="llama3.2",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in Hindi."}])
print(r.choices[0].message.content)
```

Compatibility covers the common endpoints, such as chat completions and embeddings, but not every OpenAI feature. Test the features your app relies on, such as tool calling or JSON mode, with the specific local model you choose.

## How do I use models downloaded with Ollama in llama.cpp?

Ollama stores models as GGUF blobs in its models folder, so you can point llama.cpp at the blob file directly. Find the right blob through the model's manifest, or use `ollama show --modelfile <model>`, which shows the `FROM` path.

The steps: run `ollama show --modelfile llama3.2`, copy the blob path from the `FROM` line, then run llama.cpp with that file, for example `llama-server -m <path-to-blob> -c 8192 -ngl 99`. Some newer models packaged by Ollama for its own engine may not load in llama.cpp, and file layouts can change between versions. If that happens, download the GGUF version of the model from Hugging Face instead, which avoids depending on Ollama's internal storage.
