# What does open source mean? Open LLMs, and is OpenAI, Claude or Ollama open
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/open-source-llms-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Open source means software whose source code is published under a licence that lets anyone use, study, modify and share it. In AI, many "open" language models are more precisely open-weight: you can download and run the trained model, but the training data and full training code are not published. This page explains the meaning, which LLMs are open and which are best, why and how to run them, and answers whether OpenAI, Claude, Ollama, Pinecone and LangChain are open source.

## What does open source mean?

Open source means the source code is freely available under a licence that grants everyone the rights to use it for any purpose, study how it works, change it and share copies or improvements. The Open Source Initiative maintains the formal definition.

Common open-source licences include permissive ones such as MIT and Apache 2.0, which allow almost any use including commercial, and copyleft ones such as GPL and AGPL, which require sharing changes under the same licence in certain cases. "Source-available" licences publish code but restrict some uses, such as offering the software as a competing service; those are not open source by the strict definition. Always read the licence before building a product on a project.

## What are open-source LLM models?

Open-source or open-weight LLMs are language models whose trained weights are published for download, so you can run, inspect and fine-tune them yourself. Well-known families include Meta's Llama, Alibaba's Qwen, Mistral's open models, Google's Gemma, DeepSeek's models, Microsoft's Phi and OpenAI's open-weight releases.

Licences vary: some use permissive licences such as Apache 2.0, while others have custom terms that restrict certain uses or very large companies. Few release full training data, so most are open-weight rather than open source in the strict sense. They are available on Hugging Face and through tools like Ollama, and many come in several sizes and variants, such as instruct, coding and vision models.

## What are the best open-source models?

The best open models change every few months. Strong general families include the latest Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral and Gemma releases, plus OpenAI's open-weight models; specialised coding and embedding models lead in their niches. The best choice depends on your hardware and task.

How to choose:

- **Laptop with 8 to 16 GB RAM**: 3B to 8B models at 4-bit quantisation.
- **Single strong GPU**: 14B to 32B models, or mixture-of-experts models with small active size.
- **Coding**: coder-tuned variants.
- **RAG**: a good open embedding model plus a mid-size instruct model.
- **Languages**: test Indian-language performance yourself if you need it.

Check recent independent evaluations and test on your own prompts before settling.

## Why use an open-source LLM?

Use open models for privacy, since data never leaves your infrastructure; for cost control at high volume; for customisation through fine-tuning; for offline or on-device use; and for independence from a single vendor's pricing and policy changes.

Trade-offs to weigh: frontier hosted models are still stronger on the hardest reasoning and coding tasks; you are responsible for hosting, updates, security and evaluation; and GPUs cost money even when idle. A common pattern is to use an open model for routine, high-volume or sensitive tasks and a hosted model for hard ones. FineTune Studio exists because adapting open models with QLoRA is one of the main reasons teams choose them.

## How do I run an open-source LLM?

The easiest way is Ollama: install it, then run `ollama run llama3.2` or another model, and use the local API from your code. For more control, use llama.cpp or LM Studio; for serving many users on a GPU server, use vLLM.

```bash
ollama run qwen2.5:7b
```

```python
import requests
r = requests.post("http://localhost:11434/api/chat", json={
    "model": "qwen2.5:7b", "stream": False,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain RAG in two sentences."}]})
print(r.json()["message"]["content"])
```

Match model size to your memory, check `ollama ps` to confirm GPU use, and keep the local API private unless protected by authentication.

## Is OpenAI open source?

OpenAI's flagship models, such as the GPT models behind ChatGPT, are proprietary and available only through its apps and API. OpenAI has released some open models and tools, including open-weight language models and the Whisper speech recognition model, and open-source libraries such as the Codex CLI.

Despite the name, OpenAI moved away from releasing its main models openly years ago, citing safety and competition. Its open-weight releases are a separate line from its frontier models. So you can run some OpenAI models locally, but not the ones powering ChatGPT. For truly local alternatives to GPT-class assistants, use the strongest open models your hardware allows.

## Is Claude an open-source LLM?

No. Claude, made by Anthropic, is a proprietary model family available through claude.ai, Claude Code, the Claude API and cloud platforms such as Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI. Its weights are not published.

Anthropic does publish research, safety work and open standards, such as the Model Context Protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and data, which is open source. If you need a model you can run entirely on your own hardware, choose an open-weight model; if you need Claude's capabilities, use it through its official channels and review the data terms for your use case.

## Is Ollama open source?

Yes. Ollama is open source under the MIT licence, with its code on GitHub. It is free to use for running open models locally, and it offers optional cloud features with their own plans.

Ollama builds on the open GGML ecosystem that also powers llama.cpp. The models you run through Ollama have their own licences, separate from Ollama's, so check each model's licence for commercial use. Because it is open source, you can inspect what it does, run it fully offline, and contribute fixes. It is one of the simplest ways to start with open LLMs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

## Is Pinecone open source?

No. Pinecone is a proprietary, fully managed vector database service. You use it through its cloud API and client libraries; the database itself is not open source.

If you need an open-source vector database, popular choices include Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and Chroma, and pgvector, an open-source extension for PostgreSQL. Open options let you self-host for data control and avoid vendor lock-in, at the cost of running the infrastructure yourself. For many projects, especially student and early-stage ones, pgvector or Chroma is simpler and free, and you can move to a managed service later if scale requires it.

## Is LangChain open source?

Yes. LangChain is open source under the MIT licence, with Python and JavaScript libraries on GitHub. LangGraph, its framework for stateful agents, is also open source. The company offers paid hosted products, such as observability and deployment tools, alongside the open libraries.

LlamaIndex, another popular framework for RAG and agents, is also open source under the MIT licence. Open frameworks let you inspect how retrieval and agent loops work, which helps debugging. They change quickly, so pin versions, read migration notes when upgrading, and keep your own code's core logic simple enough that you could replace the framework if needed.

# Open source software and open source AI: what counts, and which models are open
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/open-source-software-and-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Open source software is software whose source code is published under a licence that lets anyone use, study, change and share it; Linux, Python, PostgreSQL, Git and VS Code's core are famous examples. In AI the term is contested: most models called open source are really open-weight, meaning you can download the trained weights, while the training data and full code stay private. This page lists essential open source software, explains open source AI, names the open models and agents, answers whether Google AI, n8n, Next.js and Supabase are open source, and shows how to contribute.

## What is the best open source software?

The most valuable open source software for students and developers includes Linux, Git, Python, VS Code's open-source core, PostgreSQL, Docker's engine, Firefox, LibreOffice, VLC, GIMP and Blender, plus AI tools such as PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers and Ollama.

By need:

- **Development**: Git, Python, Node.js, VS Code's core, PostgreSQL, Redis.
- **AI and data**: PyTorch, scikit-learn, Jupyter, Hugging Face libraries, Ollama, llama.cpp.
- **Web**: Next.js, React, Supabase, FastAPI.
- **Everyday use**: Firefox, LibreOffice, VLC, Thunderbird, Bitwarden.
- **Creative**: GIMP, Inkscape, Blender, OBS Studio, Audacity.

Much of the modern internet and nearly every AI product runs on open source. Learning to read and contribute to these projects is one of the best ways to grow as an engineer.

## What is an open source AI model?

An open source AI model is one whose weights, and ideally code and training details, are published under a licence that lets anyone use, study, modify and share it. In practice, most models called open source are open-weight models with varying licence terms.

With an open-weight model you can download it, run it on your own hardware, fine-tune it with methods like QLoRA, and inspect its behaviour, which is not possible with closed models served only through APIs. Licences differ: some are fully permissive, such as Apache 2.0 or MIT, while others restrict commercial use above certain scales or certain uses. Always read the licence on the model card before building a product on a model.

## What does open source mean in AI?

The Open Source Initiative's Open Source AI Definition says an AI system is open source when it grants the freedoms to use, study, modify and share it, which requires access to the model weights, the full code for training and running it, and enough information about the training data to reproduce a substantially equivalent system.

By that standard, few popular models qualify fully, because companies rarely release complete training data details. That is why careful writers say open-weight for models whose weights are downloadable but whose data and training pipelines are not. Fully open models from research groups do exist and publish data, code and checkpoints. For most engineering decisions, the practical questions are: can I download the weights, does the licence allow my use, and can I fine-tune and deploy it?

## Which AI models are open source?

Widely used open-weight model families include Meta's Llama, Alibaba's Qwen, Mistral's open models, Google's Gemma, DeepSeek's models, Microsoft's Phi and OpenAI's open-weight releases. Licences range from permissive to custom terms with restrictions.

Popular choices by use:

- **General chat and reasoning**: Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek models.
- **Small and on-device**: Gemma, Phi, small Llama and Qwen variants.
- **Coding**: coder variants of Qwen and others.
- **Embeddings for RAG**: open embedding models on Hugging Face.
- **Speech**: OpenAI's Whisper for transcription.

You can run them with Ollama, llama.cpp or vLLM, or through hosted providers. GPT, Claude and Gemini models are proprietary and only available through their companies' apps and APIs.

## Is Google AI open source?

Partly. Google's Gemini models are proprietary, available through Google's apps and APIs. Google also releases Gemma, a family of open-weight models, and open-sources major tools such as TensorFlow and JAX.

Gemma models come in several sizes, including small ones that run on laptops and phones, and variants for specific uses. They are released under Google's Gemma terms, which allow broad use, including commercial use, with some conditions, so read the licence. Google researchers also published the original Transformer architecture, which underpins almost all modern language models. For students, Gemma is a good open model for experiments and fine-tuning practice, while Gemini is accessible through AI Studio's free tier.

## Which AI agents are open source?

Open-source AI agents include coding agents such as OpenHands, Aider, Cline and the command-line agents Codex CLI and Gemini CLI, general agents such as Goose, and frameworks for building agents such as LangGraph, CrewAI and AutoGen.

Open-source agents let you inspect exactly what the agent does, run it with local models, and adapt it to your workflow. Many work with several model providers, so you can switch between hosted models and local ones through Ollama. Quality depends heavily on the model behind them: an open agent with a weak local model performs far worse than the same agent with a frontier model. Read the permissions model of any agent before letting it run commands on your machine.

## Is n8n open source?

Not by the strict definition. n8n's source code is public and you can self-host it, but it uses the Sustainable Use License, a fair-code licence that restricts some commercial uses, such as offering n8n itself as a paid service. The Open Source Initiative does not recognise that as open source.

n8n chose this model to keep the code visible and free for internal use while protecting its business from competitors reselling it. For most users, including students, individuals and companies automating their own workflows, self-hosting n8n is allowed. If you plan to build a product that embeds or resells n8n, read the licence carefully or contact n8n about commercial terms. Fully open-source alternatives exist for some automation needs.

## Is Next.js open source?

Yes. Next.js, the React framework maintained by Vercel, is open source under the MIT licence, and its code is on GitHub. You can use it for any project, commercial or not, and deploy it anywhere, not only on Vercel.

Vercel funds most of its development and offers hosting optimised for it, but self-hosting with Node.js or Docker is fully supported. The MIT licence only requires keeping the copyright notice. Next.js is a good project to learn from: its issues, discussions and examples show how a large open-source framework is run, and documentation fixes are a realistic first contribution.

## Is Supabase open source?

Yes. Supabase, a backend platform built on PostgreSQL, is open source, with most of its code under the Apache 2.0 licence on GitHub. You can use the hosted service or self-host the stack with Docker.

Supabase combines open-source components: PostgreSQL for the database, PostgREST for an automatic REST API, a Realtime server, authentication, storage and edge functions, plus pgvector support for AI applications such as RAG. Self-hosting gives you control over data location and costs, but you take on maintenance, backups and security. For student projects, the hosted free tier is usually the quickest start; check its current limits.

## How do I contribute to open source AI projects?

Pick a project you already use, read its contributing guide, start with documentation fixes, tests or issues labelled "good first issue", and open small, well-explained pull requests. Consistency matters more than size.

A practical path:

- Use the project in a real task and note where you got stuck.
- Improve the docs or examples that confused you.
- Reproduce a reported bug and add a failing test.
- Fix small bugs, following the project's style and running its tests.
- Join the community channels and help answer questions.

Hugging Face libraries, LangChain, Ollama, vLLM and many model evaluation tools welcome contributions. Contributions on GitHub are public evidence of skill, and maintainers notice reliable contributors.

# What are OpenAI API keys? Getting one, data storage, models and expiry
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/openai-api-keys-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


An OpenAI API key is a secret token that lets your own code call OpenAI's models through its API, with every request billed to your OpenAI account. You create keys on the OpenAI platform, keep them in environment variables, and use them with OpenAI's SDKs or plain HTTP. This page covers what keys are and look like, where to get one, expiry, what happens to your data, how the API works, which models it offers, whether the API is itself an LLM, who owns it, and, for comparison, how Gemini API keys work.

## What are OpenAI API keys?

OpenAI API keys are secret credentials that identify your project when your code sends requests to OpenAI's API. Anyone with your key can make requests charged to your account, so keys must be kept private like passwords.

Keys belong to projects within an organisation, so you can separate keys for different apps, set spending limits and permissions per project, and revoke a key without affecting others. Never put a key in front-end JavaScript, a mobile app, a public GitHub repository or a screenshot. Call the API from your backend and keep the key in an environment variable or a secrets manager. If a key leaks, revoke it immediately in the dashboard and create a new one.

## What does an OpenAI API key look like?

An OpenAI API key is a long random string beginning with `sk-`; newer project keys begin with `sk-proj-`. The full key is shown only once, when you create it, so copy it straight into a password manager or your `.env` file.

The dashboard later shows only a masked version, so if you lose it, create a new key. In code, read it from the environment rather than pasting it in:

```python
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()   # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment
```

Tools such as GitHub's secret scanning detect committed keys, and providers may disable keys found in public places, which is another reason to keep them out of code.

## Where do I get an OpenAI API key?

Sign up on the OpenAI platform, add billing details or credits for your organisation, then open the API keys page and create a key for your project. A ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription does not include API usage; the API is billed separately.

Steps:

- Create or sign in to your account on the OpenAI platform.
- Set up billing and, ideally, a monthly spending limit.
- Create a project for your app.
- Generate an API key in that project and copy it once.
- Store it as `OPENAI_API_KEY` in your environment.

Buy credits only from OpenAI's own platform. Websites selling "cheap OpenAI keys" are reselling stolen or shared keys, which breaks OpenAI's terms and can expose your data.

## Do OpenAI API keys expire?

OpenAI API keys do not expire automatically; they work until you revoke them. However, a key can stop working if it is deleted, if the project or organisation is suspended, if billing fails, or if OpenAI disables a key detected as leaked.

Good practice is to rotate keys periodically and whenever someone with access leaves a project. Use separate keys for development and production, and for each service, so revoking one does not break everything. If your app suddenly gets authentication errors, check the key in the dashboard, your billing status and whether the key belongs to the right project. Monitor usage so unexpected spikes, a sign of a leaked key, are noticed quickly.

## Does the OpenAI API store data?

OpenAI states that data sent through the API is not used to train its models by default. API inputs and outputs are retained for a limited period, typically up to 30 days, for abuse and misuse monitoring, unless you qualify for zero data retention.

Some features store data by design: files you upload, assistants, conversation state and stored responses persist until you delete them or as configured. Enterprise customers can get stronger commitments, including zero data retention for eligible endpoints and data residency options. Before sending personal or sensitive data, read OpenAI's current enterprise privacy page and your organisation's policies, minimise what you send, and avoid including identity numbers or passwords in prompts.

## How does the OpenAI API work?

Your code sends an HTTPS request with your API key, a model name and input such as messages or a prompt; OpenAI runs the model and returns the output, along with token usage that determines cost.

The main pieces:

- **Text generation**: send input and instructions, get a response; stream it for responsive UIs.
- **Tools**: let the model call your functions, search the web or run code.
- **Structured outputs**: require JSON that matches a schema.
- **Embeddings**: turn text into vectors for search and RAG.
- **Images and audio**: generate images, transcribe speech, synthesise voice.

Requests are stateless unless you use features that store conversation state. Handle rate-limit and server errors with retries and backoff, which the official SDKs do automatically.

## What models does the OpenAI API offer?

The OpenAI API offers families of models for different jobs: GPT models for text, reasoning and coding, smaller fast models for high-volume tasks, embedding models for search, image generation models, speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, and realtime models for voice.

Model names and versions change frequently, so check the models page for current options, context lengths and pricing. A practical approach: start with a mid-sized general model, measure quality on your task, then try a smaller model for cost or a reasoning model for hard cases. Pin a specific model version in production so behaviour does not change unexpectedly, and test before upgrading.

## Is the OpenAI API an LLM?

No. The API is the interface, a web service, through which you access OpenAI's models, many of which are large language models. The LLM is the model running behind it; the API is how your software talks to it.

The distinction matters when designing systems. You can swap the model behind the same API call, use multiple providers through similar interfaces, or run an open-weight LLM locally behind an OpenAI-compatible API, as tools like Ollama and vLLM offer. Your application logic, such as retrieval, validation and tools, sits outside the model. In RAG.NextUpgrad, multi-provider fallback works precisely because the app talks to models through interchangeable interfaces.

## Who owns the OpenAI API?

OpenAI owns and operates the OpenAI API. OpenAI is the company that develops the GPT models and ChatGPT. Microsoft is a major partner and investor and offers OpenAI models through its own Azure OpenAI Service, which is a separate product with Microsoft's terms.

If your organisation uses Azure, the Azure version may be preferred for billing, compliance and regional hosting; the API shape is similar but authentication, endpoints and model availability differ. For individual developers and students, the OpenAI platform is the direct route. In both cases, the usage policies of the provider apply to your application.

## How many Gemini API keys can I have?

You can create multiple Gemini API keys, typically within Google Cloud projects through Google AI Studio. Rate limits and quotas generally apply per project, not per key, so extra keys in one project do not give you more free usage.

Use multiple keys to separate environments or apps and to rotate keys safely, not to get around limits; doing that through many accounts or projects can break the terms of service. Restrict keys where possible, such as limiting which APIs a key can call, store them in environment variables, and delete unused keys. If you need higher limits, enable billing on the project, which moves it to higher usage tiers.

# What is the OpenAI SDK? APIs, compatible APIs, Python examples and PDFs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/openai-sdk-and-api-examples/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

The OpenAI SDK is OpenAI's official client library, mainly for Python and JavaScript or TypeScript, that wraps its APIs so you can generate text, use tools, create embeddings, process files, generate images and transcribe audio with a few lines of code. Because many providers and local servers copy OpenAI's API format, the same SDK often works with them too. This page covers the SDK and APIs, OpenAI-compatible APIs, Python and GitHub examples, processing PDFs, Sora, the SDK versus LangChain, using the OpenAI SDK with Anthropic, and transcription options from OpenAI, Groq and Mistral. What is the OpenAI SDK? The OpenAI SDK is the official library for calling OpenAI's APIs from code, handling authentication, requests, retries, streaming, typed responses and errors. The main SDKs are for Python and JavaScript or TypeScript, with official libraries for other languages as well. Also asked as: what is openai sdk Install it with pip install openai or npm install openai, set the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable, and create a client. The SDK mirrors the API: methods for responses or chat completions, embeddings, files, images, audio, fine-tuning and batches. It retries transient errors automatically and supports async usage. Use the SDK rather than raw HTTP for real projects; it prevents many small mistakes. What are the OpenAI APIs? OpenAI's APIs give programmatic access to its models: text generation with tools and structured outputs, embeddings for search, image generation and editing, speech-to-text and text-to-speech, realtime voice, file handling, batch processing and fine-tuning. Also asked as: what are openai apis The core is text generation: you send input and instructions, and receive output, optionally with tool calls your code executes. Embeddings turn text into vectors for semantic search and RAG. Audio APIs transcribe and speak. The Batch API processes large jobs asynchronously at lower cost. All are billed per use, separately from ChatGPT subscriptions, and governed by OpenAI's data policies, under which API data is not used for training by default. What are OpenAI-compatible APIs? OpenAI-compatible APIs are services that accept the same request and response format as OpenAI's API, especially chat completions and embeddings, so you can use the OpenAI SDK with them by changing the base URL, API key and model name. Also asked as: what are openai compatible apis Examples include local servers such as Ollama, vLLM and LM Studio, and many hosted providers of open models. This makes switching providers easy: from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url=&quot;http://localhost:11434/v1&quot;, api_key=&quot;ollama&quot;) # local Ollama r = client.chat.completions.create(model=&quot;llama3.2&quot;, messages=[{&quot;role&quot;: &quot;user&quot;, &quot;content&quot;: &quot;Hi&quot;}]) Compatibility usually covers common features, not every OpenAI capability, so test tool calling and structured outputs with each provider. What are some OpenAI examples in Python? The basic pattern is: create a client, call a generation method with a model and input, and read the output. Here is a minimal text generation and an embedding call. Also asked as: openai examples python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() # reads OPENAI_API_KEY resp = client.responses.create(model=&quot;MODEL_NAME&quot;, input=&quot;Explain BM25 in two sentences.&quot;) print(resp.output_text) emb = client.embeddings.create(model=&quot;EMBEDDING_MODEL&quot;, input=&quot;hybrid search&quot;) print(len(emb.data[0].embedding)) Replace the model names with current ones from the models page. From here, add streaming for chat interfaces, tools for actions, and structured outputs with a JSON schema for data extraction. Where can I find OpenAI examples on GitHub? The OpenAI Cookbook on GitHub has hundreds of notebooks and guides covering embeddings and search, RAG, function calling, agents, evaluation, fine-tuning, audio and more. The official SDK repositories also include example code. Also asked as: openai examples github Use the Cookbook to learn patterns, then adapt them to your project. Some notebooks use older model names or APIs, so check the date and the current documentation before copying. Many open-source projects on GitHub show complete applications built with the SDK, which are useful for seeing how pieces fit together in production, such as configuration, error handling and testing. How can I process a PDF using OpenAI's APIs? You can upload PDFs as file inputs to OpenAI's models, which read both text and page images, then ask questions or extract data. In ChatGPT and custom GPTs, you attach PDFs as files or knowledge. For large collections, extract text and build a RAG pipeline. Also asked as: how can i process a pdf using openai&#x27;s apis (gpts Approaches by need: One document, questions or summary: send the PDF as a file input with your instructions. Structured extraction: request JSON matching a schema and validate the output. Many documents: extract text, chunk with page numbers, embed, and retrieve relevant passages for each question. Scanned PDFs: run OCR first or rely on the model's vision for small volumes. DocuLens AI follows the extraction pattern: model output validated against a schema before anything is trusted. Are there OpenAI examples for Sora? Yes. OpenAI provides documentation and examples for Sora, its video generation model, both in the Sora app and, where available, through the API for developers. Examples show prompt structure and how to request and retrieve generated videos. Also asked as: openai examples sora Good Sora prompts describe the scene like a director: subject, action, setting, camera movement, lighting, style and duration. Generating video takes longer than text, so applications typically submit a job and check for completion. Availability, limits and pricing vary by plan and region, so check OpenAI's current documentation. Label AI-generated videos when publishing, and avoid generating real people without consent. What is the difference between the OpenAI SDK and LangChain? The OpenAI SDK is a thin, official client for OpenAI's APIs. LangChain is a framework for building LLM applications, with abstractions for prompts, chains, retrieval, tools, agents and memory across many providers, including OpenAI. Also asked as: difference between openai sdk and langchain Use the SDK when you want direct control, fewer dependencies and the newest features as soon as they are released. Use LangChain, or LangGraph for agents, when you want ready-made integrations for many vector stores, loaders and providers, or a structured way to build multi-step agents. Many production teams use the provider SDK directly with a small amount of their own code, because it is easier to debug; others use frameworks to move faster. Why use the OpenAI SDK with the Anthropic API? Anthropic provides an OpenAI SDK compatibility layer so developers can test Claude models with existing OpenAI-style code by changing the base URL, API key and model name. It is useful for quick comparisons and migrations. Also asked as: why use openai sdk with anthropic api For full access to Claude's features, such as extended thinking controls, prompt caching options and other Claude-specific capabilities, Anthropic recommends its own SDK. A practical path: evaluate Claude through the compatibility layer, then move to the Anthropic SDK if you adopt it. Design your code with a thin provider interface so switching or falling back between providers, as RAG.NextUpgrad does, is straightforward. OpenAI vs Groq vs Mistral for transcription: which should I use? All three offer speech-to-text APIs: OpenAI provides its transcription models, Groq hosts Whisper models on very fast inference hardware, and Mistral offers its own speech-understanding models. Choose by accuracy on your audio, speed, features, data terms and cost. Also asked as: transcription apis – openai vs. groq vs. mistral How to decide: Transcribe 20 of your real recordings with each and compute word error rate against corrected transcripts. Measure latency for your file sizes or streaming needs. Check language support, especially Indian languages and mixed speech. Compare features: timestamps, speaker labels, translation. Read data retention terms. For privacy or zero per-minute cost, self-host open Whisper models instead; my OCR &amp; Speech Workspace taught me that once speech becomes text, every other step gets easier.

# Personal branding for developers and CS students: building in public, LinkedIn and GitHub that get you hired, and speaking your way into a reputation
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/personal-branding-for-developers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is personal branding for a developer, really?

**A public, searchable record of what you have built, explained clearly enough that a stranger can judge it, published on a schedule. That is the whole thing. It is not a logo, a colour palette or a tagline. Recruiters, founders and event organisers search for people who can do a specific thing; a brand is what makes you findable for that thing and credible when found. Mine is "GenAI engineer from India who ships production AI systems and speaks at colleges", and every post, repository and talk feeds that one sentence.**


I built a developer community to 500-plus members, won three hackathons, spoke at colleges and landed GenAI work without a placement cell, and the thread through all of it was posting what I built every week for years [4][5]. This page is that habit, made explicit, with the profile and channel decisions that mattered.

> Nobody discovers you. They search for something specific and find the person who has been publicly doing it for a year. Be that person for one thing.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What should a developer post about?

**What you built this week, what broke, what you learned, and what you would do differently. A build log with a screenshot beats an announcement. A failure explained beats a success declared. Specific beats general: "I cut RAG latency from 4 seconds to 1.2 by reranking to five passages" is a post; "AI is transforming everything" is noise. Post about the work, the decision and the result, in that order, and tag the tools and people involved when it is true.**



## Which platforms matter for a developer in India?

**LinkedIn, because recruiters, founders, faculty and event organisers in India live there and search there; it is where every speaking and hiring conversation I have had began [1][10]. GitHub, because it is where anyone serious verifies the claims [2]. A personal site, because it is the one place you control where everything resolves [3]. Then one writing home, Dev.to or a blog, for longer pieces [11]. X, Instagram and others are optional amplifiers. Two platforms done consistently beat six done occasionally.**



## How should a CS student set up LinkedIn?

**Headline: what you do and one proof, not your college and year. Banner: a photo from a session, a demo or a hackathon, not a stock image. About: five lines, first person, what you build, one result, what you are open to, how to reach you. Featured: three projects with demo links. Experience: projects and communities count; write them as outcomes. Post weekly. Comment substantively on ten posts a week in your field, because comments are how people without followers get seen.**


My longer guides to LinkedIn for students and to what recruiters actually search for are on the portfolio [6][10]. The single highest-leverage change most students can make in ten minutes: replace "Student at X College" in the headline with what you build.

## How should a developer set up GitHub?

**A profile README with your one sentence, your city, and three links. Five pinned repositories, each with a README that has the problem in one sentence, a screenshot or demo link, how to run it, and what you would do next. Steady commits over weeks rather than one upload per project. Archive tutorial clones. Recruiters spend under two minutes; those minutes should land on finished things with clear explanations.**


The GitHub note, with the README template I use, is written up separately [7].


## How do I write technical posts without a following?

**Start with what you just learned, because a beginner explaining a concept to last-month's self is the most useful writer for the many people at that stage. Structure: the problem, what you tried, what worked, what you would tell someone starting. Include one screenshot or code block. Publish on Dev.to or your blog and post a three-line summary with the link on LinkedIn. Nobody reads the first ten; the eleventh gets found by search, and search does not care about followers.**


My notes on writing a first technical post, and why this site exists as a search-first project rather than a follower-first one, are on the portfolio [8].

## How do I turn projects into talks and a speaker brand?

**Every shipped project is a talk waiting for a room. Offer your college club a session on what you built, with a live demo, then post the photos. Two or three sessions become a page listing the talks you offer, and that page is what organisers book from. Judging a hackathon after mentoring at one adds a second credential. Within a year, invitations arrive with the posts, because organisers search LinkedIn for people who have visibly done sessions before.**



The speaker-brand version of this, with what changed after my first campus sessions, is written up separately [9].

## How do I stay consistent without it eating my week?

**Reuse and schedule. One project produces a post, a demo video, a carousel, a talk and a blog piece; write once, cut five ways. Batch: one afternoon a month to draft four posts, scheduled weekly. Keep a running notes file of things that broke and lessons learned, so posts are extracts, not blank pages. Automate what can be automated, publishing and cross-posting, and keep the writing human. My own posting runs on a pipeline I built for exactly this, so the habit survives busy months.**



## What mistakes do students make with personal branding?

**Posting certificates instead of projects. Announcing instead of showing. Chasing virality with hot takes. Six platforms, none consistent. A LinkedIn headline that says only the college. Copying influencer formats that do not fit a student. Posting nothing for months and then a flood. Faking expertise, which experts spot instantly and never forget. The fix for all of them is the same weekly build log, in your own words.**

**Not asked directly, but present in every interview: "tell me about a project" is easier when you have written about it ten times; "how do you learn" is answered by your posts; "why should we hire you" is answered by a profile the interviewer already read. The brand is the pre-read. Make it accurate.**

# What is Pinecone DB? Uses, ownership, and Pinecone vs Chroma, FAISS, Milvus, Weaviate
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/pinecone-db-and-alternatives/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Pinecone is a fully managed vector database: you send it embeddings with metadata, and it handles indexing, scaling and fast similarity search through an API, without servers to run. It is a common choice for RAG and semantic search when teams want minimal operations. This page explains what it is and when to use it, who owns it, its free plan, whether it uses FAISS, and how it compares with Chroma, FAISS, Milvus and Weaviate, including Weaviate's hybrid search and local installation. What is Pinecone DB? Pinecone is a cloud-native, serverless vector database for storing embeddings and querying them by similarity, with metadata filtering, namespaces for separating data, and support for hybrid search with sparse and dense vectors. Also asked as: pinecone vs chroma db You create an index with a dimension and distance metric, upsert vectors with IDs and metadata, and query with a vector to get the nearest matches. Pinecone also offers integrated features such as hosted embedding and reranking models in some configurations. Because it is managed, scaling, replication and maintenance are handled for you, which is its main appeal compared with self-hosted options. When should I use Pinecone? Use Pinecone when you want production vector search without operating a database, need to scale to large collections or many tenants, and are comfortable with a proprietary managed service and its pricing. Also asked as: when to use pinecone Good fits: startups shipping RAG features quickly, teams without database operations capacity, and multi-tenant SaaS products using namespaces. Consider alternatives when you already run PostgreSQL and your data is modest, so pgvector is simpler; when data must stay on your own infrastructure; or when you want open-source control with Qdrant, Weaviate or Milvus. Measure retrieval quality on your own data either way; it depends more on chunking, hybrid search and reranking than on the database. Who owns Pinecone? Pinecone is developed and owned by Pinecone Systems, a privately held company founded in 2019 by Edo Liberty, who previously led research on large-scale machine learning at Amazon. The company is venture-backed. For users, ownership matters for support, longevity and data terms. Pinecone runs on major cloud providers in several regions, and its documentation describes security and compliance options. As with any managed service, keep your source documents and a way to rebuild your index, so you are not locked in if requirements change. Abstract your vector store behind a small interface in your code, with functions such as upsert, query and delete, so switching to pgvector, Qdrant or another service later means rewriting one module rather than your whole application. Does Pinecone have a free plan? Yes. Pinecone offers a free starter plan with usage limits, suitable for learning, prototypes and small projects, and paid plans for production scale. The details of free limits have changed over time, as the company has revised its plans. Also asked as: how we planned and re-planned the free plan on pinecone Check the current pricing page before building, and set up usage alerts. For student projects, the free plan is usually enough for a few thousand chunks and light traffic. Alternatives with free options include pgvector on a free hosted Postgres tier, Chroma locally, or self-hosted open-source databases. Avoid designs that depend on a free tier for production users. Does Pinecone use FAISS? Pinecone does not present itself as a FAISS-based service; it uses its own proprietary indexing and storage designed for serverless scale. FAISS is an open-source library from Meta that you can use directly to build vector search in your own application. The practical difference: with FAISS you manage indexes, persistence, updates and scaling yourself; with Pinecone those are handled by the service, but you cannot inspect or customise its internals. Both perform approximate nearest-neighbour search. Choose FAISS for control, offline use and cost-free local search; choose Pinecone for managed scale and operations. Whichever you use, measure recall on your own questions, because approximate search settings trade a little accuracy for speed, and the right balance depends on your data and latency target. Pinecone vs Chroma: which should I use? Choose Chroma for local development, prototypes and small to medium apps where simplicity and open source matter. Choose Pinecone for managed, scalable production search without running infrastructure. Comparison: Hosting: Chroma runs in-process, as a server, or via its cloud; Pinecone is managed only. Licence: Chroma is open source; Pinecone is proprietary. Scale: Pinecone is built for large, multi-tenant workloads; Chroma suits smaller ones well. Cost: Chroma is free to self-host; Pinecone has a free tier and paid plans. A common path is prototyping in Chroma and moving to a managed service later if scale requires it, keeping retrieval code behind a small interface. FAISS vs Milvus: what is the difference? FAISS is a library for fast vector similarity search inside one process; Milvus is a distributed, open-source vector database built for production, with persistence, scaling, filtering and management features. Milvus can use FAISS-style index types internally. Use FAISS for research, offline batch jobs, notebooks and applications where you manage the index yourself. Use Milvus when you need a database service: concurrent users, updates and deletes, metadata filtering, horizontal scaling and operational tooling. Milvus is a Linux Foundation AI and Data project, with a managed cloud offered by the company Zilliz. Weaviate vs FAISS: which should I choose? Weaviate is an open-source vector database with an API, schema, filtering, hybrid search and modules for embeddings; FAISS is a library for in-memory vector search. Choose Weaviate for a full database service, FAISS for lightweight embedded search under your control. Weaviate stores objects with properties and vectors, supports BM25 keyword search alongside vector search, and can generate embeddings through integrated modules. FAISS has no built-in persistence, metadata filtering or keyword search; you add those yourself. For a RAG application with filtering and hybrid needs, Weaviate saves engineering time; for a quick prototype or a research benchmark, FAISS is simpler. Does Weaviate support hybrid search? Yes. Weaviate supports hybrid search that combines BM25 keyword search with vector search in one query, with an alpha parameter to weight the two and fusion methods to merge results. An alpha near 1 favours vector similarity, near 0 favours keyword matching; tune it on your own queries. Hybrid search helps with technical content containing names, codes and acronyms, which embeddings alone may miss. Combine it with filters on properties and, if needed, a reranker for the top results. Check the documentation for the current query syntax in your client library. How do I install Weaviate locally? The usual way is Docker: use Weaviate's configuration tool or documented Docker Compose file to run Weaviate locally, then connect with the client library. Weaviate also offers an embedded option for some clients, which starts a local instance from code. Also asked as: how to install weaviate locally Steps with Docker: Install Docker Desktop or Docker Engine. Generate or copy a Docker Compose file from Weaviate's documentation. Run docker compose up -d and wait for the service to start. Connect from Python with the Weaviate client to localhost on the configured port. Mount a volume so data persists across restarts. Keep the instance on your private network; enable authentication before exposing it anywhere.

# Pinecone vs Postgres and OpenSearch, and fixing common Pinecone problems
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/pinecone-vector-database-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Pinecone is a managed vector database for storing embeddings and finding similar ones quickly, widely used for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension and OpenSearch are the most common alternatives. The right choice depends on your existing stack, scale and whether you need strong keyword search. This page compares them, explains vector databases versus vector stores and why RAG needs them, and fixes the Pinecone problems people hit most: setup errors, repeated results, weighting, listing vectors and parent-document retrieval.

## Postgres vs Pinecone: which should I use?

Use PostgreSQL with pgvector if you already run Postgres and your collection is small to medium, so vectors, text and metadata live in one database with SQL filters and joins. Use Pinecone if you want a fully managed service that scales vector search without operating a database.

Trade-offs:

- **pgvector**: one system, transactions, familiar SQL, free and open source; you tune indexes and scale it yourself.
- **Pinecone**: serverless scaling, fast setup, metadata filtering and namespaces; another service to pay for and keep in sync with your main database.

For student projects and most startups, pgvector on a hosted Postgres such as Supabase is simpler. Move to a dedicated vector service when scale, latency or operational load justifies it, and measure first.

## Pinecone vs OpenSearch: which is better?

OpenSearch is a search engine with strong keyword search, aggregations and vector search in one place; Pinecone is a specialised managed vector database. Choose OpenSearch if keyword relevance, log or document search and filtering are central; choose Pinecone for simple, managed vector retrieval.

RAG quality often depends on keyword search as much as vectors, because exact terms such as product codes, names and error messages are missed by embeddings. OpenSearch gives you BM25 and vectors together, so hybrid search is natural, at the cost of running and tuning a cluster or paying for a managed one. Pinecone supports hybrid search with sparse and dense vectors too. Decide by your team's skills and existing infrastructure, then test retrieval recall on your own questions.

## What is the best open-source vector database for RAG?

There is no single best. pgvector is the simplest if you use PostgreSQL; Qdrant, Weaviate and Milvus are popular dedicated open-source vector databases; Chroma is easy for prototypes; FAISS is a fast library rather than a database.

How to choose:

- **Already on Postgres**: pgvector.
- **Prototype or notebook**: Chroma or FAISS.
- **Dedicated service with filtering and scale**: Qdrant, Weaviate or Milvus.
- **Need keyword plus vector search**: OpenSearch or Weaviate's hybrid search.

Retrieval quality depends more on chunking, embeddings, hybrid search and reranking than on the database. RAG.NextUpgrad runs hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion and re-ranking in about 220 MB on a free tier, so start simple and optimise what measurement shows matters.

## What is the difference between a vector database and a vector store?

A vector database is a full database system for vectors: storage, indexing, filtering, updates, access control and scaling. A vector store is a looser term, often used in frameworks like LangChain, for any component that stores embeddings and returns similar ones, from an in-memory list to a full database.

So every vector database can serve as a vector store, but not every vector store is a database. FAISS in memory, a Chroma collection on disk, pgvector and Pinecone can all be "vector stores" in LangChain. The distinction matters in production: persistence, concurrent updates, backups, filtering and monitoring are database features you will need once real users depend on the system.

## Why are vector databases critical for RAG systems?

RAG needs to find the passages most relevant to a question among thousands or millions of chunks, quickly. Vector databases index embeddings so similarity search is fast at scale, and add metadata filters, updates and persistence that real systems need.

Without an index, you would compare the question with every chunk on every query, which becomes slow as data grows. Vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, such as HNSW, to return results in milliseconds. Filters, for example by department, date or user permissions, keep answers relevant and secure. Still, vectors are not enough on their own: combining them with keyword search and a reranker usually gives the biggest quality gains.

## How do I fix a Pinecone setup error?

Most Pinecone setup errors come from using old client code, a missing or wrong API key, or an index dimension that does not match your embedding model. Update the client, use the current initialisation style and check dimensions.

The current Python client looks like this:

```python
from pinecone import Pinecone
pc = Pinecone(api_key="YOUR_KEY")          # better: read from an environment variable
index = pc.Index("my-index")
index.upsert(vectors=[{"id": "doc1#0", "values": vec, "metadata": {"source": "doc1"}}])
```

Old tutorials use `pinecone.init(...)` and an environment parameter, which newer clients reject. Make sure the index dimension equals your embedding size, for example 1536 or 768, and that the metric matches your embeddings. Read the full error message; it usually names the cause.

## Why does Pinecone keep returning the same result for different documents?

Usually because of your data, not Pinecone: duplicate chunks, IDs reused so new upserts overwrite old vectors, boilerplate text such as headers dominating every chunk, or a bug where the same embedding is computed for every input.

Check in this order:

- Confirm IDs are unique per chunk; reusing an ID overwrites the earlier vector.
- Print a few stored vectors and confirm they differ.
- Strip repeated headers, footers and navigation text before embedding.
- Confirm you query the right namespace and index.
- Check that the query embedding uses the same model as the stored ones.
- Deduplicate near-identical chunks.

After fixing, re-index and test with questions whose correct chunk you know.

## How do I add weights to rank results in Pinecone?

Use hybrid search with both sparse and dense vectors and weight them: scale the dense vector by alpha and the sparse vector by one minus alpha before querying, so alpha controls how much semantic versus keyword matching counts.

Sparse vectors come from keyword methods such as BM25 or learned sparse models; dense vectors come from your embedding model. An alpha near 1 favours meaning, near 0 favours exact terms. Tune alpha on a test set of real questions. For other signals, such as recency or document authority, retrieve a larger candidate set and re-score it in your code or with a reranker. A cross-encoder reranker on the top results often improves ranking more than weighting alone.

## How do I fetch all vectors in a Pinecone namespace?

List the vector IDs in the namespace, page by page, then fetch the vectors by ID in batches. Pinecone's client provides a list operation for serverless indexes that returns IDs, optionally filtered by an ID prefix.

```python
for ids in index.list(namespace="docs"):
    batch = index.fetch(ids=ids, namespace="docs")
```

Designing IDs with prefixes, such as `doc42#chunk3`, makes it easy to list or delete all chunks of one document. If you need a full export regularly, keep your source of truth elsewhere, such as your documents and a database table of chunks, and treat the vector index as a rebuildable cache. That also makes switching vector databases much easier later.

## How do I implement a parent document retriever with Pinecone?

Index small child chunks for precise matching, store each child's parent ID in metadata, and keep the larger parent sections in a separate store. At query time, retrieve the best children, then return their parents to the model.

Steps:

- Split each document into parents, such as sections, and children, such as paragraphs.
- Embed and upsert children to Pinecone with `parent_id` in metadata.
- Store parents in a key-value store or database table.
- Query Pinecone, collect unique parent IDs from the top children, and load those parents.
- Optionally merge adjacent children into a parent only when several of them match, the auto-merging idea.

LangChain's ParentDocumentRetriever and LlamaIndex's auto-merging retriever implement this pattern with any vector store.

# Pinecone vs Supabase for vector search: how each works, RAG in Supabase, and keys
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/pinecone-vs-supabase/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Pinecone and Supabase solve vector search differently. Pinecone is a managed, vector-only database built for similarity search at scale. Supabase is a backend platform on PostgreSQL, with auth, storage and APIs, that does vector search through the pgvector extension. If your app already needs a database, Supabase keeps everything together; if vector search is the main workload at large scale, Pinecone removes operations work. I build RAG on PostgreSQL, so this page compares them and covers Supabase RAG, Python, self-hosting and keys. Pinecone vs Supabase: which should I use? Use Supabase when you want embeddings next to your application data, with SQL joins, auth-based access control and one bill. Use Pinecone when you have very large vector collections, need managed scaling without tuning Postgres, or want a dedicated vector service. Comparison: Model: Pinecone is vector-first; Supabase is Postgres with pgvector. Filtering: Pinecone uses metadata filters; Supabase uses full SQL. Hybrid search: Pinecone supports sparse-dense vectors; Supabase combines pgvector with Postgres full-text search. Access control: Supabase applies Row Level Security to vectors; Pinecone uses namespaces and API keys. Operations: both are managed; Supabase can also be self-hosted. For most student and startup RAG apps, Supabase is simpler. How does Pinecone work? You create an index with a dimension and distance metric, upsert vectors with IDs and metadata, and query with a vector to get the nearest matches. Pinecone manages storage, indexing, replication and scaling behind an API. Also asked as: when is pinecone season Its serverless architecture separates storage from compute, so you pay for what you store and query rather than provisioning servers. Namespaces partition an index, which suits multi-tenant apps where each customer's data must stay separate. Queries can include metadata filters, and Pinecone offers hosted embedding and reranking models in some configurations. You cannot see or tune the internal index algorithms, which is the trade-off for not running anything yourself. What is a Pinecone index? A Pinecone index is the top-level container for your vectors, defined by vector dimension, distance metric such as cosine or dot product, and deployment type. All vectors in an index share the same dimension, matching your embedding model. Also asked as: what is pinecone index Inside an index, namespaces divide data, for example one per user or document set, and every vector has an ID, values and optional metadata. You can create separate indexes for different embedding models or environments, such as development and production. Changing embedding models means creating a new index and re-embedding your data, so record which model produced each index. Pinecone vs Chroma: when should I use each? Use Chroma for local development, prototypes, notebooks and small applications, because it is open source and runs in-process with no setup. Use Pinecone for production workloads that need managed scaling, high availability and multi-tenant isolation. A common path is starting with Chroma while you design chunking and prompts, then moving to a managed or database-backed store when the app has users. To make that move painless, put retrieval behind a small interface in your code with functions such as add, query and delete. Chroma also offers a hosted cloud service, so the line between them has narrowed; evaluate on your own data, cost and operational needs. How does Supabase store data? Supabase stores application data in a PostgreSQL database, files such as images and PDFs in S3-compatible object storage, and user accounts in Postgres tables managed by its auth service. Vectors are stored in Postgres columns using pgvector. Because everything is Postgres, you can join user records with documents and embeddings in one query, apply Row Level Security policies to every table, and use standard tools for backups and migrations. Supabase auto-generates REST and GraphQL APIs from your schema, and Realtime streams database changes to clients. Your data is portable: you can dump the database and move to any Postgres host. Can I use Supabase with Python? Yes. Install the official client with pip install supabase, create a client with your project URL and key, then query tables, call database functions, upload files and manage auth from Python. You can also connect directly to Postgres with drivers such as psycopg. Also asked as: can you use supabase with python from supabase import create_client sb = create_client(SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_KEY) rows = sb.rpc(&quot;match_chunks&quot;, {&quot;query_embedding&quot;: emb, &quot;match_count&quot;: 5}).execute() For backend services, such as a FastAPI app, use a server-side key kept in environment variables, never in front-end code. Async support exists for high-concurrency apps; check the client documentation for current options. How do I build strong RAG retrieval in Supabase with three files? Three pieces cover it: a SQL migration that creates a chunks table with an embedding column, a full-text search column and indexes; a hybrid search function that merges vector and keyword results with reciprocal rank fusion; and an ingestion script that chunks, embeds and inserts documents. Also asked as: how i created superior rag retrieval with 3 files in supabase Details: Migration: enable pgvector, add vector and tsvector columns, an HNSW index and a GIN index. Function: run both searches, rank each, fuse by summing one over rank plus a constant, return top results. Ingestion: split by headings, embed in batches, store source and page metadata. Supabase's documentation includes a hybrid search example. This mirrors the hybrid design in RAG.NextUpgrad, where keyword and vector retrieval are fused before reranking. Can I self-host Supabase? Yes. Supabase is open source, and its repository includes a Docker Compose setup that runs Postgres, the API gateway, auth, storage, realtime and the dashboard on your own server. Self-hosting suits data residency needs or full control. Also asked as: can you self host supabase Plan for operations: secure secrets and keys, configure HTTPS and SMTP for auth emails, back up Postgres regularly, monitor resources, and apply updates. Some managed-platform features may differ or require extra setup when self-hosting. For most teams starting out, the managed service is easier; self-host when you have a specific reason and the capacity to run it reliably. Should the Supabase anon key be public? Yes, the anon key, or newer publishable key, is designed to be used in browsers and mobile apps, so it is effectively public. It is safe only if Row Level Security is enabled on every table with correct policies. Never expose the service role or secret key. Also asked as: should supabase anon key be public The anon key lets clients call your API as an unauthenticated or logged-in user, and RLS policies decide what each request can read or write. Without RLS, anyone with the key can read or modify your tables. Check every table in the dashboard's security advisor, test policies with different users, and keep privileged keys only on servers. When is pine cone season? Outside software, pine cones mature and fall mostly in autumn, roughly September to November in the northern hemisphere, depending on the pine species and climate. Many species take about two years to mature their cones. Collectors gather fallen cones for crafts and decorations, and some species' cones release seeds only after fire or heat. The database company borrowed the name, and its logo nods to the pine cone's ordered spiral pattern, which follows Fibonacci numbers, a fitting image for a product built on mathematical structure. For search, check whether results refer to the trees, crafts or the vector database.

# Best pitch deck template: slides, structure, Canva, and presenting a pitch
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/pitch-deck-template-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

The best pitch deck template is a simple structure that tells one clear story: the problem, your solution, a demo or proof, the market, how you make money or create impact, traction, the team and what you are asking for. Design matters less than clarity and evidence. I have pitched and won Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025 with BrandHive, along with two other hackathon first prizes, and judged other teams, so this page covers what a deck includes, slide counts and length, creating one, investor versus hackathon decks, Canva, format and how to present. What is the best pitch deck template? The best template follows a proven order and keeps one idea per slide: title, problem, solution, demo or product, market, business model or impact, traction, competition, team, and the ask. Many founders adapt the structures published by well-known investors and accelerators. A template that works for students and early founders: Title: name, one-line description, logo. Problem: a specific user and their pain, with evidence. Solution: what you built, in one sentence. Demo: screenshots or a live demo. Market: who and how many. Business model or impact. Traction: users, pilots, results. Competition: why you are different. Team: why you can build it. Ask: funding, mentorship, partnership or next step. Large, readable text and one strong visual per slide beat crowded designs. What does a pitch deck include? A pitch deck includes the problem, solution, product or demo, target market, business model, traction, competition, team and the ask. For hackathons, replace business details with impact, technical approach and next steps as the judging criteria require. Also asked as: what does pitch deck include Each slide should answer a question the audience has: why does this matter, why now, why you, how will it grow, and what do you want from us. Include real evidence where you have it: user quotes, pilot results, a working prototype. Avoid long paragraphs, tiny charts and jargon; if a slide needs a long explanation, it needs to be simpler. How many slides should a pitch deck have? For investors, ten to twelve main slides, with extra details in an appendix. For a hackathon pitch of three to five minutes, five to eight slides, because each slide needs time to land. Also asked as: how many slides pitch deck A rule of thumb is roughly one slide per thirty to sixty seconds of speaking. Fewer, stronger slides are better than many rushed ones. Keep backup slides for likely questions, such as technical architecture, data privacy or detailed financials, and show them only if asked. Judges and investors remember the story and the demo, not the slide count. How long should a pitch be? Hackathon pitches are usually three to five minutes plus questions; investor pitches commonly run ten to twenty minutes; a quick verbal pitch should be under a minute. Always confirm the time limit and rehearse to fit it with margin. Also asked as: how long pitch deck Plan time deliberately: about a fifth on the problem, the largest share on the solution and demo, and a short close on impact, traction and the ask. Rehearse with a timer at least three times; most first drafts run long. Cut slides rather than speaking faster. Leaving time for questions often helps, because questions show what the audience cares about. How do I create a pitch deck? Write the story first, then build slides. Draft a one-paragraph narrative, outline one slide per point, gather evidence and visuals, design simply, and rehearse with feedback. Also asked as: how to create pitch deck Steps: Write the problem and solution in one sentence each. List the questions your audience will ask and answer each on a slide. Add proof: demo screenshots, user feedback, data. Use a clean template with large fonts and consistent colours. Practise aloud, get feedback from someone outside your team, and simplify. Use AI tools to tighten wording or suggest structure, but make sure every claim is true and you can explain every number. How do I make a pitch deck for investors? Focus on the opportunity and your ability to capture it: a painful problem, a solution customers want, evidence of traction, a large enough market, a credible business model, a strong team, and a clear funding ask with how you will use it. Also asked as: how to make pitch deck for investors Investor-specific tips: Lead with traction if you have it; it is the strongest evidence. Show market size with a clear, bottom-up calculation. Explain how you will acquire customers and what it costs, in principle. Address competition honestly and state your advantage. State the round size and the milestones it will reach. Send a PDF version that reads well without you presenting, and keep a separate, more visual version for live pitches. Can I create a pitch deck on Canva? Yes. Canva has many pitch deck templates and makes it easy to design clean slides, add images and charts, collaborate with teammates, and present or export to PDF or PowerPoint. Tips for Canva decks: pick a minimal template and remove decorative elements, use one or two fonts, keep text large, and use your own product screenshots rather than stock images where possible. Export a PDF for sharing, and test the presentation on the actual screen or projector if you can. PowerPoint, Google Slides and Keynote work equally well; choose the one your team collaborates in most easily. Is a pitch deck a PPT? A pitch deck is a presentation, and it can be made in PowerPoint, which saves files as PPTX, or in Google Slides, Keynote or Canva. "PPT" is often used loosely to mean any slide presentation. Also asked as: is pitch deck a ppt When sharing, a PDF is usually best, because it looks the same on every device and cannot be accidentally edited. Some competitions, such as Smart India Hackathon, specify a template and format for idea submissions, so follow official instructions exactly. For live pitches, keep the presentation file and a PDF backup on your laptop and a USB drive or cloud link. How do I give a pitch? Open with a hook about the problem, keep eye contact, tell the story slide by slide in your own words, show the demo confidently, close with your impact and ask, then handle questions calmly and concisely. Also asked as: how to give pitch deck Presenting tips from the judge's table: Start with the user and their problem, not your technology stack. Rehearse the demo many times; have a recorded backup. Assign speaking parts so transitions are smooth. Do not read slides; slides support you. Answer questions directly, admit unknowns, and say how you would find out. Teams that clearly explain what they built and why it matters usually outscore teams with more features and a confusing story. Is pitch deck one word or two words? "Pitch deck" is two words. It means a short slide presentation used to pitch a business, product or idea to investors, judges, customers or partners. You will also see "pitch presentation" or simply "deck" used in startup conversations, such as "send us your deck". In writing, keep it as two words without a hyphen when used as a noun, as in "our pitch deck", and some writers hyphenate it when used before another noun, as in "pitch-deck template", though "pitch deck template" without a hyphen is common and acceptable.
