# What is privacy and security? The difference, and what it means for AI
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/privacy-and-security-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Privacy is about who is allowed to collect, see and use information about a person, and for what purpose. Security is the set of technical and organisational controls that keep information safe from people who are not allowed. They overlap but are not the same: a system can be very secure and still misuse your data. This page explains the difference, why both matter, what they mean for data, apps, social media and iPhones, how they apply to AI systems including inference attacks, and what the HIPAA privacy and security rules cover.

## What is privacy and security?

Privacy is a person's right to control how information about them is collected, used and shared. Security is the protection of information and systems against unauthorised access, change or loss.

Put simply, privacy answers "should this data be collected and used this way?", and security answers "is this data protected from those who should not have it?". A privacy decision is limiting a sign-up form to the fields you actually need. A security control is encrypting the database that stores those fields and requiring two-factor authentication for the admins. Good systems design both together: collect less, protect what you keep, and delete it when the purpose is over.

## Do privacy and security mean the same thing?

No. Security is about protection; privacy is about appropriate use. You can have security without privacy, but you cannot have privacy without security.

Two examples make the difference clear. A company that encrypts all its data perfectly but sells your browsing history to advertisers has strong security and poor privacy. A company with a strong privacy policy that leaves its database open on the internet has good intentions and no real privacy, because anyone can read the data. Security is necessary for privacy but not enough. Privacy adds questions security does not ask: do you have consent, is this the minimum data needed, how long will you keep it, and can the person see or delete it?

## Why is privacy and security important?

They protect people from harm such as fraud, identity theft, stalking, discrimination and embarrassment, and they protect organisations from breaches, fines and lost trust. Laws in most countries now require both.

For individuals, leaked phone numbers, ID details and passwords lead directly to scams and account takeovers. For organisations, a single breach can mean regulatory penalties, legal claims and customers who never return. For engineers, privacy and security are also design quality: systems that collect less data are simpler to secure and cheaper to run. In India, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets duties for anyone processing personal data, so these are now legal requirements, not just good practice.

## What is data privacy and security?

Data privacy is the set of rules and practices for handling personal data properly: consent, purpose, minimisation, retention and individual rights. Data security is the protection of that data through encryption, access control, monitoring and backups.

A practical checklist for any app that stores user data:

- Collect only the fields you need and record why you need each one.
- Encrypt data in transit with TLS and at rest in the database.
- Give each person and service the least access they need.
- Log access to sensitive data and review the logs.
- Set retention periods and actually delete old data.
- Let users see, correct and delete their data.

Most data breaches come from ordinary failures: weak passwords, exposed storage buckets and unpatched software.

## What is digital privacy and security?

Digital privacy and security is the same idea applied to your online life: controlling what your devices, apps and accounts reveal about you, and protecting them from being hacked or misused.

The basics give most of the protection. Use a password manager and unique passwords, turn on two-factor authentication for email and banking, keep your phone and laptop updated, and install apps only from official stores. Review app permissions for location, contacts, camera and microphone, and remove the ones an app does not need. Be careful with public Wi-Fi for sensitive accounts, and treat unexpected links in messages as suspicious, because phishing is still the most common way accounts are lost. Your email account is the master key to the rest, so protect it most.

## What is privacy and security in AI?

In AI, privacy means controlling what personal data goes into training, prompts, logs and outputs. Security means protecting models and AI apps from attacks such as prompt injection, data leakage and model theft.

AI adds new risks to old ones. Models can memorise and repeat training data. Users paste personal or confidential information into prompts that may be logged. Prompt injection can trick an AI app into revealing data or taking actions it should not. Good practice is to minimise personal data, mask it before it reaches a model, restrict what tools an AI agent can call, and review the OWASP list of risks for LLM applications. In FaceVision I designed for this: recognition runs in the browser and the server stores face embeddings only, never images.

## What is a privacy inference attack in AI security?

A privacy inference attack tries to learn private information from a trained model's outputs, for example whether a specific person's record was in the training data, or a sensitive attribute about them.

The main types:

- **Membership inference**: deciding whether a given record was used in training, often because models are more confident on data they have seen.
- **Attribute inference**: predicting a sensitive attribute, such as a health condition, from other known features.
- **Model inversion and data extraction**: reconstructing training examples, or getting a language model to repeat memorised text.

Defences include differential privacy during training, which adds calibrated noise so no single record changes the model much, limiting how much detail outputs reveal, removing duplicates and personal data from training sets, and testing models with these attacks before release.

## What is privacy and security in online social media?

On social media, privacy is about who can see your posts, profile and contacts, and what the platform does with your data. Security is about protecting your account from takeover and your information from scraping and scams.

Steps worth taking on every platform: review who can see your posts and contact you, turn off location tagging, hide your phone number and email from your profile, and enable two-factor authentication. Be careful what you share: your college, daily routine and photos of documents give attackers more than you think. Check which third-party apps are connected to your account and remove old ones. Remember that "private" posts can still be screenshotted, and that the platform itself sees everything you post.

## What is privacy and security on iPhone?

On iPhone, Privacy & Security is the section of Settings where you control which apps can access your location, contacts, photos, camera, microphone and other data, and where security features such as Safety Check and Lockdown Mode live.

Useful settings to review:

- **Location Services**: set apps to "While Using" or "Never", and turn off precise location where it is not needed.
- **Tracking**: refuse app tracking requests so apps cannot follow you across other apps.
- **Photos and contacts**: give limited access instead of full access.
- **Safety Check**: review and reset who has access to your information.
- **Lockdown Mode**: an extreme protection mode for people facing targeted attacks.

Keep iOS updated, because many updates fix actively exploited security flaws.

## What are the HIPAA privacy and security rules?

HIPAA is a United States law for health information. Its Privacy Rule sets when protected health information may be used or disclosed; its Security Rule sets the safeguards required to protect electronic health information.

The Privacy Rule covers patients' rights, such as access to their records, and limits on how hospitals, insurers and their partners share data. The Security Rule requires administrative, physical and technical safeguards: risk analysis, access controls, audit logs, encryption where appropriate and staff training. A third piece, the Breach Notification Rule, requires notice when protected data is exposed. If you build a health app for US clients you will meet HIPAA. In India, health data falls under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and sector rules, so check the requirements for each market you serve.

# What is Qdrant Cloud? Qdrant URL, who built it, and Qdrant vs Pinecone and OpenSearch
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/qdrant-cloud-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Qdrant is an open-source vector database, written in Rust, for storing embeddings with metadata and running fast similarity search with filtering; Qdrant Cloud is the company's managed service that runs Qdrant clusters for you. It is a popular choice for RAG, semantic search and recommendations. This page explains Qdrant Cloud and how to use it, finding the Qdrant URL, who builds and uses Qdrant, and how it compares with OpenSearch, Pinecone, Chroma and PostgreSQL with pgvector. What is Qdrant Cloud? Qdrant Cloud is the managed, hosted version of the Qdrant vector database. It creates and runs clusters on major cloud providers, handling setup, scaling, backups and upgrades, and offers a free tier for small projects alongside paid plans. You create a cluster in the Qdrant Cloud console, get a URL and API key, and connect from your application with Qdrant's client libraries, exactly as you would to a self-hosted instance. This suits teams who want Qdrant's features without operating infrastructure. Because the core database is open source, you can also self-host the same software with Docker if you need full control or data residency on your own servers. How do I use Qdrant Cloud? Sign up, create a cluster, copy its URL and create an API key, then connect with a Qdrant client, create a collection with the right vector size and distance metric, upsert points with payloads, and query. Also asked as: how to use qdrant cloud from qdrant_client import QdrantClient from qdrant_client.models import VectorParams, Distance, PointStruct client = QdrantClient(url=&quot;https://YOUR-CLUSTER-URL&quot;, api_key=&quot;YOUR_KEY&quot;) client.create_collection(&quot;notes&quot;, vectors_config=VectorParams(size=384, distance=Distance.COSINE)) client.upsert(&quot;notes&quot;, points=[PointStruct(id=1, vector=[0.1] * 384, payload={&quot;subject&quot;: &quot;os&quot;, &quot;page&quot;: 3})]) hits = client.query_points(&quot;notes&quot;, query=[0.1] * 384, limit=3).points Keep the API key in environment variables, match the vector size to your embedding model, and add payload indexes for fields you filter on. What is the Qdrant URL? For a local Qdrant instance, the default URL is http://localhost:6333 for the REST API, with gRPC on port 6334. For Qdrant Cloud, each cluster has its own HTTPS URL shown in the console, used together with an API key. Also asked as: what is qdrant url The REST URL also serves a web dashboard at /dashboard on local instances, useful for inspecting collections. In Docker, map the ports with -p 6333:6333 -p 6334:6334 and mount a volume for storage so data persists. When your app runs in another container, use the Qdrant service name as the host, such as http://qdrant:6333, rather than localhost. Where do I find my Qdrant URL? For Qdrant Cloud, open the cloud console, select your cluster, and copy its endpoint URL from the cluster details; create or copy an API key from the same area. For self-hosted Qdrant, the URL is your server's address with port 6333. Also asked as: where to find qdrant url Common mistakes: using localhost from inside a different container, forgetting the port, using HTTP instead of HTTPS for cloud clusters, and missing the API key. If connection fails, test the URL with a simple request in the browser or with curl, check firewall rules, and confirm the cluster is running. Never expose a self-hosted Qdrant to the internet without authentication. Who developed Qdrant? Qdrant is developed by Qdrant, a company founded in 2021 that maintains the open-source database under the Apache 2.0 licence and runs Qdrant Cloud. The core is written in Rust for performance and memory safety. The open-source project has an active community on GitHub, with client libraries for Python, JavaScript and TypeScript, Rust, Go, Java and .NET. Because it is open source, you can inspect the code, self-host freely, and contribute. The company funds development through its cloud and enterprise offerings, a common model for open-source infrastructure. Who uses Qdrant? Qdrant is used by startups, enterprises and developers building RAG systems, semantic search, recommendation engines, anomaly detection and AI agents' memory. The company publishes case studies and the open-source project has a large community of users. Typical users choose it for fast filtered search, where vector similarity is combined with conditions on metadata, such as user, language or date, and for the option to self-host. It integrates with LangChain, LlamaIndex and other frameworks, so it appears in many tutorials. For your own decision, what matters is how it performs on your data and operational needs, not who else uses it. What is the difference between Qdrant and OpenSearch? Qdrant is a dedicated vector database focused on similarity search with rich filtering. OpenSearch is a search and analytics engine that combines strong keyword search, aggregations and logs with vector search. Also asked as: qdrant vs opensearch Choose Qdrant when vectors are the core workload and you want a lean, fast, specialised engine with excellent filtering. Choose OpenSearch when you need full-text search, BM25 relevance tuning, analytics and vectors in one system, or already run OpenSearch for logs or search. Hybrid search is possible in both: Qdrant supports sparse and dense vectors together, and OpenSearch combines BM25 with vector queries. Test retrieval quality on your own queries. Qdrant vs Pinecone: how do they compare? Both are vector databases with fast similarity search and metadata filtering. Qdrant is open source and can be self-hosted or used through Qdrant Cloud; Pinecone is a proprietary, fully managed service with no self-hosting option. Feature-wise, both support namespaces or collections, filtering and hybrid search with sparse and dense vectors. Differences show in deployment control, data residency options, pricing models and operational responsibility. Qdrant lets you run the same software locally for development and in production on your own infrastructure; Pinecone minimises operations by being serverless. Benchmark both on your data, latency targets and expected scale. Which is better, Pinecone or Qdrant? Neither is better universally. Choose Pinecone if you want zero infrastructure work and a fully managed serverless service. Choose Qdrant if you want open source, self-hosting options, strong filtering and the flexibility to move between local, self-hosted and cloud. Also asked as: which is better pinecone or qdrant Decision factors: Control and residency: Qdrant can run on your own servers. Operations: Pinecone requires none; self-hosted Qdrant requires some. Lock-in: open-source Qdrant reduces it. Cost: compare on your expected data size and query volume. Developer experience: try both SDKs on a small prototype. For most RAG projects, retrieval quality depends more on chunking, hybrid search and reranking than on this choice. Which is better: Qdrant, Chroma or Postgres? For small projects and prototypes, Chroma is the simplest. If you already use PostgreSQL, pgvector keeps vectors with your data and is often enough. Qdrant is the strongest of the three as a dedicated vector database for larger workloads with heavy filtering. Also asked as: which is better qdrant chroma or postgres A rough guide: Chroma: notebooks, prototypes, small local apps. Postgres with pgvector: apps already on Postgres; joins, transactions, row-level security. Qdrant: larger vector workloads, high query volume, complex payload filters, multi-tenant setups. RAG.NextUpgrad runs hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval in about 220 MB on a free tier, a reminder that the simplest store that meets your needs is usually the right one. Measure recall and latency on your data before switching.

# What is quantization of charge? Meaning, who discovered it, Class 12, and ignoring it
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/quantization-of-charge/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Quantization of charge is the principle that electric charge comes in discrete packets: any free charge equals a whole number times the elementary charge e, the magnitude of an electron's charge, about 1.602 × 10^-19 coulomb. You can have 3e or minus 5e, but never 2.5e on a free particle. In AI, "quantization" means something different, storing model weights in fewer bits, which I use in FineTune Studio. This page covers the physics: meaning, reasons, history, the Class 10 and 12 syllabus, implications, and when to ignore it. What is quantization of charge? Quantization of charge means electric charge exists only in integral multiples of a basic unit, the elementary charge e. Mathematically, q = ne, where n is an integer, positive or negative, and e is approximately 1.602 × 10^-19 C. Also asked as: what does quantization of charge means · why charge is quantization in nature · what does quantization of charge implies So a body's charge changes in jumps of e, by gaining or losing whole electrons. A body that loses three electrons has a charge of plus 3e. Since 2019, the SI system defines e as exactly 1.602176634 × 10^-19 coulomb, making it a fundamental constant. Quantization is one of the basic properties of charge, alongside additivity and conservation. What does quantization of charge mean in simple words? It means charge comes in tiny, fixed-size pieces, like coins rather than water. You can add or remove only whole electrons or protons, so charge always changes by a whole number of these smallest units. An analogy: money in paise can only change in whole paise, never half a paisa. Similarly, an object's charge can be 1e, 2e or 1,000,000e, but not 1.5e. Because one electron's charge is so small, everyday objects carry billions of these units, so charge appears smooth even though it is grainy at the smallest scale. Why is charge quantized in nature? Charge is quantized because it is carried by particles, electrons and protons, that each have a fixed charge of minus e or plus e. Objects become charged only by transferring whole particles, so total charge is always a whole multiple of e. Why the fundamental particles have exactly these charges is a deeper question. Quarks inside protons and neutrons carry fractional charges of plus or minus one-third and two-thirds of e, but they are never found free; they combine into particles with whole-number charges. Some theories link charge quantization to the existence of magnetic monopoles, as Dirac proposed, but no monopole has been observed. Who proposed quantization of charge? The idea grew from Michael Faraday's laws of electrolysis in the 1830s, which suggested electricity comes in definite amounts per atom. George Johnstone Stoney proposed a natural unit of charge in 1874 and named it the "electron" in 1891. Faraday found that a fixed quantity of electricity deposits a fixed amount of substance during electrolysis, implying that each ion carries a definite charge. Hermann von Helmholtz also argued in 1881 that electricity is divided into elementary portions. These proposals set the stage for experiments that identified the electron and measured its charge. Who discovered quantization of charge? J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 through cathode ray experiments, identifying the particle that carries the basic unit of negative charge. Robert Millikan later measured the elementary charge precisely, confirming that charge is quantized. Thomson measured the charge-to-mass ratio of cathode ray particles and showed they were much lighter than atoms, establishing the electron as a subatomic particle. This explained Faraday's and Stoney's ideas: charge comes in electron-sized units. Thomson received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906 for his work on conduction of electricity in gases. Who proved quantization of charge? Robert Millikan proved it experimentally with his oil drop experiment, published from 1909 to 1913, with Harvey Fletcher's assistance. He measured charges on tiny oil drops and found they were always whole-number multiples of one basic value, e. In the experiment, charged oil drops were suspended between two metal plates, balancing gravity against an adjustable electric force. From each drop's motion, Millikan calculated its charge, and every value was an integer multiple of about 1.6 × 10^-19 C. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1923 partly for this work. Modern values of e are far more precise. Later analysis of his notebooks showed he excluded some drops, which historians still discuss, but repeated experiments by others confirmed the result. What is quantization of charge in Class 12? In Class 12 Physics, quantization of charge is covered in Chapter 1, Electric Charges and Fields, as a basic property of charge: q = ne, where n is an integer and e is the elementary charge, about 1.6 × 10^-19 C. Also asked as: what is quantization of charge class 12 Students learn it alongside additivity and conservation of charge, and solve numericals such as finding how many electrons must be removed to give a body a certain charge, using n = q / e. The chapter also explains why quantization can be ignored at macroscopic scales. Expect short-answer questions on its meaning and numericals on electron counts in board exams. A typical question: how many electrons must be removed from a neutral body to give it a charge of 1.6 × 10^-12 C? Dividing by e gives 10^7 electrons, a clean example of q = ne. Is quantization of charge in Class 10? Not as a formal topic. Class 10 Science's Electricity chapter introduces electric charge, current and the coulomb, and mentions the electron's charge, but quantization of charge as a named property is taught in Class 12 Physics. Class 10 students may meet related ideas, such as current being the flow of electrons and one coulomb corresponding to about 6 × 10^18 electrons, which hints that charge is made of tiny units. If a Class 10 question involves counting electrons, it uses the same relation as Class 12: number of electrons equals total charge divided by the charge of one electron. What does quantization of charge imply? It implies that charge cannot be divided indefinitely: there is a smallest free charge, e, and every observed charge on a free body is a whole multiple of it. It also implies that charging happens by transferring whole particles. Consequences include the ability to count electrons from a measured charge, the discrete energy and charge effects seen in very small devices such as single-electron transistors, and a check on theories of particle physics. Combined with conservation of charge, quantization means the total number of elementary charges in an isolated system stays balanced through any process. Why can one ignore quantization of charge? At everyday, macroscopic scales, charges involve enormous numbers of electrons, so the step size e is negligible compared with the total. Adding or removing one electron from a charge of a microcoulomb changes it by a tiny fraction, so charge behaves as continuous. A charge of one microcoulomb contains about 6 × 10^12 elementary charges, so treating it as continuous causes no practical error in circuits, capacitors or electrostatics problems. Quantization matters only at microscopic scales, such as individual atoms, ions, nanoscale devices and experiments like Millikan's, where charges involve only a few electrons.

# Why chunking matters in RAG: strategies, best chunk size, PDFs and legal documents
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-chunking-strategy/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Chunking is splitting documents into smaller pieces, chunks, that a RAG system embeds, indexes and retrieves. It matters because retrieval can only return what chunking created: chunks too large blur meaning, chunks too small lose context, and splits in the wrong place separate a question's answer from its explanation. I build RAG.NextUpgrad and document-scoped RAG with page citations, so this page covers chunking strategies, why RAG needs them, chunk size, production practices, PDFs and legal documents, hybrid search, a tutorial, and chunking as a study method. What is a chunking strategy? A chunking strategy is the rule for splitting documents into chunks: by fixed length, by sentences or paragraphs, by document structure such as headings, by meaning with semantic chunking, or hierarchically with small chunks linked to larger parents. Also asked as: what is chunking strategy Common strategies: Fixed-size: every N tokens with overlap; simple but cuts across ideas. Recursive: split on paragraphs, then sentences, then words until chunks fit. Structure-aware: follow headings, sections, tables and list items. Semantic: split where embedding similarity between sentences drops. Parent-child: retrieve small chunks, return their larger parent section. Structure-aware chunking with recursive fallback is a strong default for most documents. Why do we need chunking in RAG? RAG needs chunking because a single embedding of a long document is too vague to match specific questions, and language models can only take limited context. Chunks let retrieval find the precise passage that answers a question and send only that to the model. Also asked as: why we need chunking in rag Without chunking, a 50-page manual becomes one vector that loosely matches everything and precisely matches nothing. With chunks, a question about refund timelines retrieves the refund section. Chunking also controls cost and latency, since fewer, relevant tokens go into each prompt, and enables citations: each chunk carries its source and page, so answers can point to exact locations, as in the page citations of the OCR and Speech Workspace. What is the best chunk size for RAG? There is no universal best size. A practical starting range is about 300 to 800 tokens with 10 to 15 percent overlap, adjusted for your documents and questions. Smaller chunks suit precise facts; larger ones suit explanations. Also asked as: best chunking size for rag Tune with evaluation, not intuition: build a set of real questions with known answer locations, try two or three sizes, and measure retrieval recall at your top-k and answer quality. FAQ-style content works with small chunks, one question each; narrative reports need larger chunks or parent-child retrieval. Your embedding model's input limit sets a hard maximum, and very small chunks can lose the context that makes them meaningful. What are chunking best practices for RAG? Split on document structure, keep chunks self-contained, attach metadata, add a little overlap, treat tables and code specially, and evaluate. Most improvements come from respecting how the document is organised. Best practices: Keep headings with their content, and prepend section titles to chunk text. Never split mid-sentence; avoid splitting lists and tables. Store metadata: document title, section, page, date, access level. Add short context to each chunk describing where it comes from, as in contextual retrieval. Deduplicate repeated boilerplate such as headers and footers. Re-chunk and re-embed when you change strategy, and version indexes. What are RAG chunking best practices for production systems? In production, make chunking deterministic, versioned and observable: the same document always produces the same chunks, every chunk has a stable ID and source, and you can trace any answer back to the exact chunks retrieved. Additional practices: process documents incrementally so updates re-chunk only changed files; delete old chunks when documents change; monitor retrieval quality with a fixed evaluation set after each change; log retrieved chunks with answers for debugging; handle failures in parsing, such as scanned PDFs needing OCR; and enforce access control at the chunk level using metadata. In RAG.NextUpgrad, a confidence gate declines to answer when retrieved chunks are weak, which protects users when chunking misses. What is the best chunking strategy for PDFs? Parse the PDF into structure first, headings, paragraphs, tables and pages, then chunk by section with recursive fallback, keeping page numbers in metadata. Scanned PDFs need OCR before any chunking. PDF challenges include multi-column layouts, headers and footers repeated on every page, tables broken into fragments, and hyphenated words across lines. Use a layout-aware parser or OCR that outputs Markdown, then chunk the Markdown by headings. Convert tables into Markdown or row-level text so values stay with their column names. For page citations, keep a mapping from chunk to page. Test retrieval on questions about tables and footnotes specifically, because these fail most often. What is the best chunking strategy for legal documents? Chunk legal documents along their natural structure: articles, sections, clauses and sub-clauses, keeping numbering and headings with each chunk, and storing hierarchy in metadata so a clause can be returned with its parent section. Legal text relies on definitions and cross-references, so add the defined terms section to context or retrieve it alongside clauses, and preserve clause numbers for precise citations. Avoid fixed-size chunks that split a clause from its exceptions. Hybrid search is essential because users search exact terms such as section numbers and defined phrases. Always cite the exact clause, and treat answers as research aids rather than legal advice. Why does RAG often fail, and how do chunking and hybrid search fix it? Most disappointing RAG systems fail at retrieval, not generation: chunks split answers apart or lack context, and pure vector search misses exact names, codes and numbers. Better chunking and hybrid search fix most of these failures. Also asked as: why your rag sucks: the art and science of chunking and hybrid search Hybrid search runs keyword search such as BM25 alongside vector search and merges results with reciprocal rank fusion, then a reranker reorders the top candidates. That is the design of RAG.NextUpgrad. Combined with structure-aware chunks and metadata, it finds both semantic matches and exact terms. Diagnose by checking whether the right chunk was retrieved before blaming the model; if it was not, fix chunking and retrieval first. What is a simple RAG chunking tutorial? Load a document, split it with a recursive splitter that respects paragraphs, attach metadata, embed the chunks, store them in a vector index, and test retrieval with real questions before adding a language model. from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=150) chunks = splitter.create_documents([text], metadatas=[{&quot;source&quot;: &quot;handbook.pdf&quot;}]) Then embed each chunk, store it, and query with ten questions whose answers you know. Inspect the retrieved chunks, adjust size, overlap and separators, and repeat. Only add generation once retrieval reliably finds the right chunks. Why is chunking an effective study strategy? In learning, chunking means grouping information into meaningful units, such as remembering a phone number as three groups instead of ten digits. It works because working memory holds only a few items at once, and chunks let each item carry more information. Psychologist George Miller's 1956 paper popularised the idea that short-term memory is limited, and later research suggests around four chunks is a more typical limit. Students use chunking by grouping related concepts, building acronyms, and learning patterns rather than isolated facts. The idea is related to RAG chunking in spirit: both organise information into meaningful units so it can be found and used effectively.

# When was RAG invented? The RAG approach, roadmaps, agentic RAG and RAG status
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-history-and-roadmaps/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) was introduced in 2020 in a paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI Research and partner universities, which combined a neural retriever with a text generator so answers could draw on an external knowledge source. Today RAG is the standard way to ground language models in your own documents. I built RAG.NextUpgrad, a production RAG platform, so this page covers RAG's origin and definition, the approach, why it and embeddings matter, roadmaps for RAG pipelines, chatbots and agentic RAG, and the unrelated RAG assessment in project management. When was RAG invented? RAG was introduced in 2020 by Lewis and colleagues in the paper "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks", which showed that retrieving Wikipedia passages and generating answers from them improved factual tasks compared with models relying only on their parameters. Also asked as: when rag was invented The idea built on earlier work in open-domain question answering, such as dense passage retrieval, and on decades of information retrieval research. The term became widespread after 2022, when large language models such as ChatGPT made it practical to build RAG applications with an off-the-shelf model and a vector index. Modern RAG differs from the original paper, which trained retriever and generator together; most systems today combine separate components. What is the definition of RAG? In AI, RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation: a technique where a system retrieves relevant information from external sources and supplies it to a language model so the model's answer is grounded in that information. In project management, RAG means Red, Amber, Green status ratings. Also asked as: do rag definition The AI definition has three parts: retrieval, finding relevant passages from documents, databases or the web; augmentation, adding those passages to the model's prompt; and generation, producing the answer, ideally with citations. RAG lets models use private, recent or specialised knowledge without retraining, and makes answers verifiable. What is the RAG approach? The RAG approach is to retrieve first, then generate: search a knowledge source for passages relevant to the question, place the best ones in the prompt with instructions to answer only from them, and have the model write a cited answer, declining if the evidence is insufficient. Also asked as: what is rag approach A production RAG approach adds layers: clean ingestion and chunking, hybrid retrieval with keyword and vector search, reciprocal-rank fusion, a reranker, prompt rules for citations, a confidence threshold for refusing weak-evidence answers, and evaluation. This is the shape of RAG.NextUpgrad, which also streams answers and falls back across model providers. The approach keeps knowledge in documents you control rather than in the model's weights. Why is RAG important? RAG is important because it makes language models useful for real organisations: answers can use private and current information, cite sources, and be updated by changing documents, while reducing hallucinations compared with relying on the model's memory. It also lowers cost and risk compared with fine-tuning for knowledge, supports access control at retrieval time, and works with smaller models when retrieval is good. Most enterprise AI assistants, from customer support bots to internal knowledge search, are built on RAG. For engineers, RAG skills, retrieval, evaluation and grounding, are among the most requested in GenAI roles. Why are embeddings important in RAG? Embeddings make semantic retrieval possible: they represent the meaning of questions and passages as vectors, so the system can find relevant passages even when wording differs. Without good embeddings, a RAG system misses answers phrased differently from the question. Embedding quality directly affects retrieval recall, and therefore answer quality. Choose a model suited to your language and domain, use the same model for documents and queries, and evaluate with real questions. Embeddings have limits: they blur exact identifiers such as codes and names, which is why combining them with keyword search in hybrid retrieval improves results. Chunking also matters, because each embedding represents one chunk's meaning. What is a roadmap for building a RAG pipeline? Build a simple pipeline end to end first, measure it, then improve the weakest stage. The order matters: ingestion, chunking, embeddings and indexing, retrieval, prompting with citations, then evaluation and iteration. Also asked as: rag pipeline roadmap A roadmap: Basics: Python, an LLM API, an embedding model, a vector store such as pgvector or Chroma. Version 1: load documents, chunk by headings, embed, retrieve top 5, answer with citations. Evaluation: 50 real questions with known answers; measure recall and faithfulness. Retrieval: add BM25 hybrid search, fusion and a reranker. Robustness: refusal threshold, handling of tables and scanned PDFs, updates. Production: API, logging, monitoring, cost control and access control. What is a roadmap for building a RAG chatbot? Start with a reliable single-turn question-answering RAG, then add conversation: rewriting follow-up questions into standalone queries, keeping short conversation memory, and streaming answers with citations in a chat interface. Also asked as: rag chatbot roadmap Steps: Build and evaluate single-turn RAG first. Add query rewriting so "what about the fees for that?" becomes a full question using chat history. Stream answers and show source citations users can click. Add guardrails: stay on topic, decline politely, never invent policies. Collect feedback with thumbs up or down and review failures weekly. Deploy behind authentication if documents are private. Most chatbot failures are retrieval failures in disguise, so keep measuring retrieval as you add features. What is a roadmap for agentic RAG? Agentic RAG lets an agent decide how to retrieve: which sources to search, whether to search again with a refined query, and when it has enough evidence to answer. Learn it after standard RAG is solid. Also asked as: agentic rag roadmap A roadmap: Master standard RAG and evaluation. Expose retrieval as tools, such as search_docs and search_web, with clear descriptions. Let the agent plan multi-step retrieval for complex questions. Add limits on steps and cost, and require citations in final answers. Evaluate on multi-hop questions that need several searches. Monitor for loops and irrelevant tool calls. Use agentic RAG where questions are complex or span sources; for simple document Q&amp;A, a fixed pipeline is cheaper and more predictable. When was agentic RAG introduced? Agentic RAG emerged around 2023 to 2024 as language models gained reliable tool calling and agent frameworks matured, letting models control retrieval steps instead of following a fixed pipeline. Surveys describing it as a distinct approach appeared from 2024 onwards. It builds on research such as ReAct, which interleaves reasoning and actions, and on iterative retrieval methods that refine queries based on intermediate results. In practice, products such as deep research modes in AI assistants use agentic retrieval: they search, read, decide what is missing, search again and then write. The concept will keep evolving as agents become more capable. What is a RAG assessment? In project and programme management, a RAG assessment rates status as Red, Amber or Green: green means on track, amber means at risk or minor issues, and red means serious problems needing action. It is unrelated to retrieval-augmented generation. Also asked as: what is rag assessment RAG assessments appear in status reports, dashboards and reviews for schedule, budget, scope, risks and quality. Good practice is to define each colour clearly, report amber early with a recovery plan, and explain causes rather than just colours. If you see "RAG assessment" in an AI context, check whether it refers to evaluating a retrieval-augmented generation system, which uses metrics such as retrieval recall and answer faithfulness.

# What is RAG testing? How to test a RAG pipeline, and where RAG fails
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-testing-and-failures/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


RAG testing is evaluating a retrieval-augmented generation system in two parts: whether retrieval finds the right passages for each question, and whether the generated answer is correct and faithful to those passages. Testing them separately tells you which half to fix. I built RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid retrieval, re-ranking and a confidence gate, and testing is what made each change safe. This page covers how to test a pipeline and the answers, RAG architecture, how a RAG system differs from a model, why RAG is needed, where it fails and hurts, rerankers, and the unrelated "RAG status" in project management.

## What is RAG testing?

RAG testing measures how well a retrieval-augmented system answers questions from its documents. It checks retrieval quality, such as recall of the right passages, and generation quality, such as faithfulness, correctness and citation accuracy.

A RAG system can fail at either stage. If retrieval misses the passage with the answer, no model can answer correctly. If retrieval succeeds but the model ignores or misreads the passage, the answer is wrong anyway. Testing covers both with a fixed set of questions, known relevant passages and reference answers, scored automatically and spot-checked by people. Run the same tests after every change to chunking, embeddings, retrieval settings, prompts or models, so you know whether a change helped or hurt.

## How do I test a RAG pipeline?

Build a test set of real questions with the source passage that answers each, then measure retrieval recall at k, the share of questions where the right passage appears in the top k results, before you look at answers at all.

A practical process:

- Collect 50 to 100 real user questions, including hard and unanswerable ones.
- Mark the document and passage that answers each.
- Run retrieval and compute recall at 5 and at 10, and mean reciprocal rank.
- Inspect failures: was the passage chunked badly, missing, or ranked too low?
- Change one thing at a time, chunk size, hybrid search or reranker, and re-run.

Retrieval metrics are cheap and deterministic, so they are the fastest feedback loop you have.

## How do I test the RAG model's answers?

Score generated answers for faithfulness, meaning every claim is supported by the retrieved passages, correctness against a reference answer, and citation accuracy. Use an LLM as a judge for scale, and check a sample by hand.

Frameworks such as RAGAS compute faithfulness, answer relevance and context precision automatically. Include unanswerable questions in the test set and check that the system declines instead of inventing an answer, which is the behaviour a confidence gate enforces. Track latency and cost per query too. When an LLM judge and a human disagree, trust the human and adjust the judge's instructions. Keep the test set versioned alongside the code.

## What is RAG architecture?

RAG architecture has an indexing pipeline and a query pipeline. Indexing loads documents, splits them into chunks, embeds them and stores them in an index. At query time, the system retrieves relevant chunks, often reranks them, and gives them to a language model to write a grounded answer.

A production version usually adds:

- **Hybrid retrieval**: BM25 keyword search plus vector search, merged with reciprocal-rank fusion.
- **Reranking**: a cross-encoder reorders the top candidates by relevance.
- **Prompting with citations**: the model must cite chunk IDs or pages.
- **Confidence gate**: refuse when retrieval scores are weak.
- **Fallbacks and monitoring**: switch providers on failure, log every query.

That is the shape of RAG.NextUpgrad, which runs in about 220 MB on a free tier.

## How is an AI model different from a RAG system?

An AI model, such as a language model, answers from what it learned during training. A RAG system is an application that combines a model with a retrieval step, so answers come from documents you supply at question time.

The practical differences: a model alone cannot know your private documents or events after its training cutoff, and cannot point to sources; a RAG system can, and you can update its knowledge by updating documents, without retraining. "RAG model" is a loose phrase; the original RAG paper trained a retriever and generator together, but most systems today combine an off-the-shelf model with a separate search index. Fine-tuning changes the model itself, and is better for style and format than for adding facts.

## Why is RAG needed?

RAG is needed because language models do not know your private or recent information, cannot cite sources from memory, and sometimes invent facts. Retrieval supplies the right facts at question time, which makes answers current, specific and checkable.

Typical uses are company knowledge assistants, customer support over product documentation, college and policy question answering, legal and research search, and chat over a user's own files. RAG is usually cheaper and easier to keep current than fine-tuning for knowledge, because updating a document is enough. It also improves trust: users can click a citation and read the source, which a plain chatbot cannot offer.

## Where does RAG fail?

RAG fails most often at retrieval: documents are missing or outdated, chunking splits the answer across pieces, embeddings miss exact terms such as codes and names, or the right passage ranks below the cut-off. Generation fails when the model ignores context or answers beyond it.

Common failure points:

- **Missing content**: the answer is not in the index at all.
- **Bad chunks**: tables, lists and headings separated from their meaning.
- **Exact-match misses**: product codes and error messages lost by vector search.
- **Ranking**: the right chunk retrieved but too low to be used.
- **Context overload**: too many chunks, with key facts lost in the middle.
- **Unsupported answers**: the model fills gaps from its own knowledge.

Hybrid search, rerankers, better chunking and a refusal path address most of them.

## When does RAG hurt?

RAG hurts when retrieval brings back irrelevant or misleading passages, because the model then answers confidently from the wrong context. It can also hurt on questions the model already handles well, such as general reasoning, by adding noise, latency and cost.

Signs RAG is the wrong tool: questions need reasoning across a whole corpus, such as "what are the trends across all reports", which needs aggregation rather than top-k retrieval; the documents are low quality or contradictory; or the task is about style or format rather than facts, where fine-tuning or better prompts work better. Route queries: retrieve only when the question needs your documents, and let the model answer directly otherwise.

## What are the best reranking models for RAG?

Cross-encoder rerankers give the biggest quality gain: open models such as the BGE rerankers and MS MARCO cross-encoders from the sentence-transformers library, and hosted options such as Cohere Rerank and Jina's rerankers.

A reranker scores each query-passage pair together, which is more accurate than comparing separate embeddings, but slower, so you apply it only to the top 20 to 100 candidates from first-stage retrieval. Choose by language support, latency and licence, and measure recall before and after on your own test set. In RAG.NextUpgrad, re-ranking on top of hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion fixed many wrong answers cheaply, because the right passage was usually retrieved, just ranked too low.

## What is RAG status?

In project management, RAG status means Red, Amber, Green: a traffic-light rating of a project's health. Green is on track, amber has risks or minor delays, and red has serious problems needing action. It is unrelated to retrieval-augmented generation.

Teams report RAG status on dashboards and in status meetings for schedule, budget, scope and risks. Useful practice is to define clearly what each colour means for your project, report amber early rather than staying green until things turn red, and attach a short note on the cause and the next step. If you see "RAG" in an engineering context about AI, it almost always means retrieval-augmented generation instead.

A good RAG tutorial walks you through building retrieval-augmented generation end to end: load documents, split them into chunks, embed and index them, retrieve relevant chunks for a question, and have a language model answer from them with citations, then evaluate and improve. I built RAG.NextUpgrad, a production RAG platform with hybrid search and reranking, so this page gives a practical tutorial path, Python and LlamaIndex examples, GitHub projects, free courses and certificates, what RAG analysis means, and, for sewers, the rag quilt. What is a good RAG tutorial path? Build the simplest working pipeline first, measure it, then improve the weakest stage. Most learners go wrong by adding advanced techniques before their basic retrieval works. Also asked as: tutorial rag A tutorial path: Step 1: answer questions over one PDF with chunking, embeddings and top-5 retrieval. Step 2: add citations and an instruction to refuse when context is missing. Step 3: create 30 test questions with known answers and measure retrieval recall. Step 4: add keyword search with BM25 and fuse results. Step 5: add a reranker and compare metrics. Step 6: wrap it in a FastAPI service with streaming. Each step should improve a measured number, not just add code. What is RAG analysis? In AI, RAG analysis means evaluating a retrieval-augmented generation system: whether retrieval finds the right chunks, whether answers are faithful to them, and where failures come from. In project management, RAG analysis is a Red, Amber, Green status review. For AI systems, analyse each stage: retrieval recall at k, precision of retrieved chunks, answer faithfulness, answer relevance and citation accuracy. In project reporting, a RAG analysis colours each workstream's status and explains the reasons and recovery plans. How do I build RAG in Python? Embed your chunks, embed the question, find the most similar chunks with cosine similarity, and put them in a prompt for a language model. A minimal version needs only a few libraries. Also asked as: tutorial rag python from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer import numpy as np model = SentenceTransformer(&quot;all-MiniLM-L6-v2&quot;) chunks = open(&quot;handbook.txt&quot;, encoding=&quot;utf-8&quot;).read().split(&quot;\n\n&quot;) emb = model.encode(chunks, normalize_embeddings=True) q = model.encode([&quot;What is the attendance rule?&quot;], normalize_embeddings=True)[0] top = [chunks[i] for i in np.argsort(emb @ q)[::-1][:4]] prompt = &quot;Answer only from these passages and cite them:\n&quot; + &quot;\n---\n&quot;.join(top) Send prompt plus the question to any chat model. Then replace the list with a vector store and add evaluation. How do I build RAG with LlamaIndex? Next steps: persist the index to disk or a vector database, set a node parser for chunk sizes, return source nodes for citations, and evaluate with LlamaIndex's evaluation modules. How do I make a rag quilt? A rag quilt is a cosy quilt with exposed seams that fray into a soft, ragged texture. Cut squares of flannel or cotton in layers, sew them with seams facing outward, snip the seam allowances, and wash so the edges fluff up. Also asked as: tutorial rag quilt Steps: Cut matching squares for top, middle and back layers. Stack each set and sew an X through it to hold layers. Sew squares together with seam allowances on the front side. Sew around the outer edge, leaving an allowance. Snip every allowance at short intervals without cutting stitches. Wash and dry to fray the edges. This rag has nothing to do with AI, but it shares the search term.

# RAG vs fine-tuning: when to use each for LLMs, with examples
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-vs-fine-tuning-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and fine-tuning solve different problems. RAG gives a model the right information at question time by retrieving passages from your documents; fine-tuning changes the model's weights so it behaves differently, such as following a format, a tone or a narrow task. Most products need RAG for knowledge and only sometimes fine-tuning for behaviour. I have built both: RAG.NextUpgrad for grounded answers and FineTune Studio for QLoRA fine-tuning, so this page answers the common questions with practical examples.

## Is it "fine tuning" or "fine-tuning"?

Both spellings appear, and they mean the same thing. "Fine-tuning", with a hyphen, is the more standard form in technical writing as a noun and adjective, as in "fine-tuning a model" or "a fine-tuned model".

You will see "finetuning" as one word in some papers and code, such as library names, and "fine tuning" in casual writing and search queries. In documentation and reports, pick one form and use it consistently; "fine-tuning" is the safe choice. The concept is the same in every spelling: continuing to train a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset so it adapts to your use case.

## Fine-tuning LLMs vs RAG: what is the difference?

RAG keeps the model as it is and supplies relevant documents with each question. Fine-tuning trains the model further on examples, changing its weights so it behaves differently without needing those examples in the prompt.

Compare them on what matters:

- **Knowledge**: RAG handles private and changing facts; fine-tuning bakes in knowledge poorly.
- **Updates**: RAG updates by editing documents; fine-tuning needs retraining.
- **Citations**: RAG can cite sources; fine-tuned models cannot.
- **Behaviour and format**: fine-tuning is strong; RAG does not change style.
- **Cost**: RAG costs more per query because of longer prompts; fine-tuning costs up front.

They also combine well: a fine-tuned model that follows your format, with RAG for the facts.

## When should I use fine-tuning vs RAG?

Use RAG when answers depend on documents, especially private, large or frequently changing ones. Use fine-tuning when you need consistent behaviour that prompts cannot achieve: a strict output format, a specific tone, a narrow classification task, or a smaller, cheaper model that matches a larger one on one job.

Decision rules I use:

- Answer must cite a source or reflect today's documents: RAG.
- Output must always follow a complex structure: try structured outputs first, then fine-tune.
- High-volume narrow task where cost and latency matter: fine-tune a small model.
- Domain jargon the model misreads: RAG with good examples, then consider fine-tuning.
- Both knowledge and behaviour: RAG plus a fine-tuned model.

Measure on a test set either way.

## Why does fine-tuning not work as well as RAG for knowledge?

Fine-tuning teaches patterns more readily than facts. A model trained on your documents may pick up their style without reliably recalling specific details, may mix them with what it already knew, and cannot show where an answer came from.

There are practical problems too. Every document change needs a new training run. Verifying which facts the model has learned is hard. Fine-tuning on new facts can increase hallucination, because the model learns to answer confidently about things it only partly absorbed. RAG avoids these: the exact passage is in the prompt, the answer can quote it, and updating knowledge means updating the index. That is why RAG.NextUpgrad grounds answers in retrieved passages with citations and refuses when evidence is weak, rather than relying on a model's memory.

## What is the difference between prompt engineering, RAG and fine-tuning?

Prompt engineering changes the instructions and examples you send; RAG adds retrieved information to the prompt; fine-tuning changes the model itself. They form a ladder from cheapest and fastest to most involved.

Start at the bottom:

- **Prompt engineering**: clear instructions, examples, output format. Minutes to try, no infrastructure.
- **RAG**: an index of your documents and a retrieval step. Days to build well, easy to update.
- **Fine-tuning**: a dataset of examples and a training run. Days to weeks, needs evaluation and re-training for changes.

Move up a rung only when the one below demonstrably fails on your test set. Many teams fine-tune when better prompts or retrieval would have solved the problem faster.

## What are some examples of fine-tuning?

Good fine-tuning targets are behaviours: classifying support tickets into your categories, extracting fields into a strict schema, writing in a brand's voice, generating SQL for your database schema, or making a small model match a larger one on one task.

Concrete examples:

- A sentiment or intent classifier trained on a few thousand labelled messages.
- A model that turns invoice text into a fixed JSON format every time.
- A customer-support model that answers in your company's tone and structure.
- A small open model distilled from a larger model's outputs for cheaper inference.
- A model adapted to Indian-English phrasing for a specific domain.

FineTune Studio runs this loop from the browser: upload a dataset, train a QLoRA adapter, watch the loss curve live, and compare base and tuned outputs side by side.

## How long does fine-tuning take?

With parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA or QLoRA, fine-tuning a small open model on a few thousand examples takes from minutes to a few hours on a single GPU. Full fine-tuning of large models takes far longer and needs many GPUs.

Time depends on model size, dataset size, sequence length, number of epochs and hardware. A 7B or 8B model with QLoRA on a few thousand short examples commonly trains within an hour or two on one modern GPU, including free or low-cost cloud options for small runs. Hosted fine-tuning services queue and run jobs for you, typically finishing within minutes to hours. Preparing a clean dataset and an evaluation set usually takes longer than training itself, and matters more for the result.

## What type of fine-tuning does the OpenAI API use?

OpenAI's API offers supervised fine-tuning on example conversations, preference fine-tuning with Direct Preference Optimization using preferred and rejected answers, and reinforcement fine-tuning for reasoning models using graders. Vision fine-tuning with images is also supported on some models.

Supervised fine-tuning is the common starting point: you upload JSONL examples of input messages and ideal assistant replies. Preference fine-tuning helps when you can say which of two answers is better more easily than writing the perfect one. Reinforcement fine-tuning suits tasks with checkable answers. OpenAI hosts the training and serves the resulting model through the same API; you do not get the weights. Which models can be fine-tuned changes, so check the fine-tuning guide.

## Why is a vector database required for fine-tuning or RAG?

A vector database is required for RAG, not for fine-tuning. RAG stores document embeddings in a vector index so it can find relevant passages by meaning; fine-tuning trains on a dataset file and never needs a vector store.

The confusion comes from both being ways to "teach a model about your documents". For RAG, the vector store, or PostgreSQL with pgvector, or a library such as FAISS, holds embeddings and returns the nearest chunks. Many production systems also add keyword search such as BM25, because embeddings miss exact terms. For fine-tuning, you need training examples in a format such as JSONL, a training framework or hosted service, and an evaluation set. If someone says you need a vector database to fine-tune, they are describing RAG.

## How does fine-tuning work for question answering on custom documents?

You create question-and-answer pairs from your documents and train the model on them, so it learns to answer in that domain and format. It works for consistent style and common questions, but it is unreliable for exact facts, so it is usually combined with RAG.

A better recipe for document Q&A is RAG first: index the documents, retrieve passages for each question, and answer with citations. If answers are correct but the style or format is wrong, fine-tune on examples where the input includes retrieved passages and the output is the ideal grounded answer, which teaches the model to use context well. Evaluate on held-out questions, including ones the documents cannot answer, and check that the model declines rather than inventing.


---

# RAG vs fine-tuning vs prompt engineering: which one your problem actually needs, with a decision tree and real costs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-vs-fine-tuning/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## RAG vs fine-tuning: what is the difference?

**RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, changes what the model reads: at answer time it retrieves passages from your documents and answers from them, with citations. Fine-tuning changes what the model is: it trains the weights on your examples so the model's behaviour, style, format or skill shifts permanently. RAG is for knowledge the model lacks or that changes. Fine-tuning is for behaviour no prompt can produce. They solve different problems, and the most common mistake is using one for the other's job.**


I built both kinds of system in the same six months of 2026: RAG.NextUpgrad, a production retrieval platform with hybrid search, reranking and a confidence gate [9], and FineTune Studio, a QLoRA fine-tuning platform with live telemetry and base-versus-tuned evaluation [10]. Clients asked me the same question about both, and this page is the answer I now give before writing any code.

> Knowledge or behaviour? Answer that in one word and you have chosen your architecture. Everything after is engineering.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## When should I use RAG?

**When the answer depends on information the model does not have: your documents, your database, anything after its training cutoff, anything private. When answers must cite their source. When content changes often, because re-indexing a document takes seconds while retraining takes hours. When different users may see different documents, because retrieval can filter by permission and a model's weights cannot. When you need to ship this week, because a RAG prototype is an afternoon.**


Lewis et al. introduced the pattern for knowledge-intensive tasks precisely because a model's parameters are a poor place to store facts that must be exact and current [1]. Ovadia et al. compared knowledge injection by fine-tuning against retrieval directly and found retrieval consistently better at giving models new factual knowledge [3].

## When should I use fine-tuning?

**When the problem is how the model behaves, not what it knows: a consistent voice, a strict output format, a domain's phrasing, a classification or extraction skill the base model does poorly, or a narrow task you want a small, cheap, fast model to do well. When you have hundreds to thousands of clean examples of the right output. When the requirement is stable enough that retraining every month would not be needed. When prompting with examples has been tried and still falls short.**


LoRA made this affordable by training small adapters instead of all weights [2], and LIMA showed how few examples alignment needs when they are clean: a thousand, not a hundred thousand [4]. Both papers point the same way: fine-tuning is a scalpel for behaviour, not a container for facts.

## Where does prompt engineering fit?

**First. A prompt is free to change, takes effect instantly and often solves the problem: a clear task, an output format, a few examples, a rule for the not-enough-information case. Few-shot examples in the prompt were the original demonstration that models can learn a task without training [7]. Every RAG system still needs a well-engineered prompt that says "answer only from these passages and cite them", and every fine-tuning project should start by proving that prompting was insufficient.**



The official prompting guides are free and current; read one before spending on anything else [8].

## RAG vs fine-tuning: side by side

**The comparison, on the dimensions that decide real projects.**



## Can I combine RAG and fine-tuning?

**Yes, and mature systems usually do. RAG supplies the facts; a fine-tune supplies the behaviour: the house voice, a strict answer format, better use of retrieved passages, or a smaller model that follows citation rules reliably. You can also fine-tune the embedding model or the reranker on your own query-passage pairs to improve retrieval itself. Add the fine-tune after the RAG system works and is measured, never before, so you can see what the training actually changed.**



## Can fine-tuning add knowledge to a model?

**Weakly, unreliably and expensively. A model fine-tuned on facts may repeat some of them, but it cannot cite them, it does not know when they changed, and it blends them with prior beliefs. Ovadia et al. found retrieval outperformed fine-tuning for injecting new knowledge, and that repeated exposure to facts was needed for fine-tuning to teach them at all [3]. Luo et al. document the forgetting that aggressive fine-tuning causes [5]. If the fact must be right and traceable, retrieve it.**


This is the expensive mistake I see most: a team fine-tunes a model on their product manual, the manual changes, and the model confidently describes the old version with no way to show where it got it.


## What does each approach cost?

**RAG costs are in retrieval engineering up front, chunking, embeddings, indexing, evaluation, and then per query, because every answer sends retrieved passages as tokens. Fine-tuning costs are up front in the dataset, weeks of a person's time to write and clean examples, plus a few GPU hours that are cheap or free, and then again with every requirement change. Per-query, a fine-tuned small model is cheaper than a large model with a long RAG prompt. Total cost depends on volume and how often things change.**



## What are the failure modes of each?

**RAG fails when retrieval returns the wrong passage, when chunks lose context, when the prompt lets the model ignore the documents, or when passages conflict. Fine-tuning fails when the dataset is inconsistent, when the model overfits and memorises, when it forgets general ability, when the chat template is wrong, or when facts in the training data go stale. Prompting fails when phrasing breaks across model versions and when a task genuinely exceeds the model's ability. Each failure has a specific fix, and none of the fixes is "switch approaches" without measuring first.**



## Which is easier for a beginner or a student project?

**RAG. A retrieval system over documents you know is an afternoon to prototype, runs on a laptop with a free model API or a local model, and teaches chunking, embeddings, prompting, evaluation and hallucination in one project. Fine-tuning is a strong second project once you have a dataset you understand; QLoRA on a small model fits a free GPU. Doing both, and being able to say which problem each solved, is what interviewers want to hear.**



## RAG vs fine-tuning interview questions

**Define both and state the one-line rule. Give an example that needs RAG, one that needs fine-tuning and one that needs both. Explain why fine-tuning is a poor way to add facts, citing forgetting and the inability to cite. Explain how you would prove prompting was insufficient before training. Estimate the cost shape of each. Describe a system you built and which approach it used, and why.**



## Where to go from here

**Build the RAG version first, measure recall on twenty questions, and write down what it cannot do. That list is your fine-tuning specification, if you need one at all.** My longer decision write-up with client examples is on the portfolio [11]. For a session at your college on choosing and building these systems, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Redis and caching strategies for LLM apps: exact-match caching, semantic caching, and what to cache when every model call costs money and time
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/redis-and-caching-strategies-for-llm-apps/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Why does caching matter so much for LLM applications?

**Because an LLM call is both slow, often one to several seconds, and billed by the token, unlike a typical database query that is usually fast and free at the margin. A cache hit for a repeated or near-duplicate question skips both costs entirely: no tokens billed, no round trip to the provider, an answer in milliseconds instead of seconds. For any application with real traffic, a meaningful fraction of questions repeat or nearly repeat, which makes caching one of the highest-leverage, lowest-risk optimisations available.**


Every production system I run treats caching as part of the architecture from day one, not a later optimisation, because the cost and latency gap between a cache hit and a fresh model call is too large to leave on the table.

> The fastest, cheapest LLM call is the one you don't make. Caching is how you make fewer of them without answering fewer questions.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is exact-match caching, and how do I set it up with Redis?

**Exact-match caching stores the response for a specific input, and returns it instantly if the exact same input is seen again, typically keyed by a hash of the normalised prompt plus relevant parameters, model name, temperature, system prompt version [1]. Redis fits this well because it is a fast in-memory key-value store with built-in expiry, so a cache entry can be set to expire after a sensible time-to-live. This catches genuinely repeated questions, the same FAQ asked verbatim, but misses near-duplicates that are worded differently.**



## What is semantic caching, and when does it help?

**Semantic caching catches near-duplicate questions that are not worded identically: "what is RAG" and "can you explain retrieval augmented generation" mean the same thing but would miss an exact-match cache entirely. It works by embedding the incoming query, searching a small vector index of previously cached queries, and returning the cached response if a past query is similar enough, above a chosen similarity threshold [2][3]. This catches far more repeats than exact matching, at the cost of needing an embedding call per request and careful threshold tuning to avoid returning a cached answer to a subtly different question.**




## What should I never cache, and what needs careful scoping?

**Never cache anything containing per-user private data under a key shared across users; a cache is a way to leak one user's private answer to another user if scoped incorrectly. Never cache a response that depends on real-time information, current stock levels, today's date-sensitive content, without a very short TTL matched to how fast that information actually changes. Scope any cache key that includes personalised context, a user's name, their account data, their specific documents, to that user or session specifically, never globally.**



## How does caching interact with RAG, and how do I invalidate it correctly?

**A RAG answer's correctness depends on the documents it was generated from, so a cache entry must be invalidated the moment a source document changes, not just after a fixed TTL expires. The reliable pattern is to tie the cache key, or a cache-validity check, to a version identifier of the underlying document set, a hash or a last-updated timestamp, so a document update naturally invalidates every cache entry that depended on the old version, rather than serving a stale answer until an arbitrary timer runs out.**



## What is provider-side prompt caching, and how is it different?

**Some providers offer their own prompt caching, where a long, repeated prefix of a prompt, a large system prompt or a big block of retrieved context, is cached on the provider's side across calls, so you are billed less and served faster for the repeated portion even though the full request still goes to the model [4][5]. This is different from application-side caching like Redis: it does not skip the model call entirely, it makes the unavoidable model call cheaper and faster when large parts of the prompt repeat across requests, which stacks well alongside your own exact-match and semantic caching layers.**


## How do I know if my caching setup is actually worth it?

**Measure the real cache hit rate in production, not an assumption. A cache with a ten percent hit rate is complexity added for a small saving; a cache with a fifty percent hit rate on a high-traffic FAQ-style application is a major cost and latency win. Track hit rate, cost saved, and latency saved separately, and revisit the caching strategy, exact-match only, add semantic, adjust the similarity threshold, if the measured hit rate does not match what the traffic pattern suggested it should be.**



## Caching interview questions for AI applications

**Explain the difference between exact-match and semantic caching. Describe how you would scope cache keys to avoid leaking one user's data to another. Explain how you would invalidate a RAG cache when source documents change. Describe provider-side prompt caching and how it differs from an application cache. Explain how you would measure whether a caching layer is actually worth its complexity. The strongest answer includes a real hit-rate number you measured.**



## Where should I start?

**Add a simple exact-match Redis cache in front of your most repeated LLM call this week, measure the hit rate for a few days, and only add semantic caching if the traffic pattern shows enough near-duplicate questions to justify it.** For a hands-on session on cost and latency optimisation for LLM applications, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
