# What is text to speech and speech to text? AI voice tools compared
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/text-to-speech-and-speech-to-text/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Text to speech (TTS) converts written text into spoken audio, and speech to text (STT), also called automatic speech recognition, converts spoken audio into written text. Both now use AI: neural networks trained on large amounts of recorded speech. This page explains how they work, how to convert speech to text on any device, the best converters, how OpenAI's Whisper compares with cloud services, what Gemini can do with audio, how to create an AI voice, and how to use the Microsoft tools, including dictation in Word.

## What is text to speech (TTS)?

Text to speech is technology that reads text aloud in a synthetic voice. Modern TTS uses neural networks that generate natural-sounding speech with realistic rhythm and intonation, in many languages and voices.

A TTS system first analyses the text, expanding numbers and abbreviations and working out pronunciation, then a neural model generates the audio. Uses include screen readers for visually impaired users, voice assistants, audiobook and video narration, navigation apps and language learning. Quality is now high enough that synthetic voices can be hard to tell from real ones, which is why responsible services restrict cloning a real person's voice without consent. When you use TTS in a project, label it as synthetic where listeners might be misled.

## Does speech to text use AI?

Yes. Modern speech to text uses deep learning models, typically transformers, trained on very large amounts of transcribed audio. Older systems used statistical models with separate acoustic and language components.

Today's models map audio directly to text and handle accents, background noise and natural speech far better than earlier systems. Some, like Whisper, were trained on hundreds of thousands of hours of multilingual audio from the web. Accuracy still depends on conditions: clear microphones, one speaker at a time and common vocabulary work best, while cross-talk, heavy noise, code-switching between languages and technical jargon cause errors. In the OCR & Speech Workspace I built live speech-to-text into the same workspace as document chat, because once speech is text, search and summaries work on it too.

## Can you convert speech to text?

Yes, on almost any device for free. Phones have voice typing in the keyboard, Windows has voice typing with Windows key plus H, macOS has Dictation, and Word, Google Docs and most messaging apps support dictation.

For recordings rather than live speech, options include:

- **Transcription in apps**: Microsoft Word's Transcribe on the web, meeting tools such as Teams and Google Meet, and voice recorder apps.
- **Open-source models**: Whisper runs on your own computer, privately and free.
- **Cloud APIs**: Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, Azure AI Speech, Amazon Transcribe and others for apps and large volumes.
- **AI assistants**: Gemini and ChatGPT can transcribe uploaded audio within their limits.

Always proofread names, numbers and technical terms, the most common error points.

## What is the best speech to text converter?

There is no single best one; it depends on the job. For dictation, your device's built-in voice typing is best. For recordings and privacy, Whisper. For apps, live captions and scale, a cloud API such as Google, Azure or Amazon.

How to choose:

- **Accuracy on your audio**: test three short clips in your accent, with your vocabulary and noise.
- **Live or recorded**: live captions need streaming support.
- **Languages**: check support for Indian languages and mixed Hindi-English speech if you need it.
- **Speaker labels and timestamps**: needed for meetings and interviews.
- **Privacy**: sensitive recordings are safer on a local model.

For a student transcribing lectures, Whisper on your own laptop or Word's Transcribe is usually enough.

## Whisper vs other speech to text: which is better?

Whisper is a free, open-source speech recognition model from OpenAI that is accurate across many languages and runs on your own hardware. Cloud speech services add real-time streaming, speaker separation, custom vocabularies and managed scale.

Choose Whisper when you want privacy, no per-minute cost and offline use, and you can provide a GPU or accept slower transcription on a CPU; faster community implementations make it practical on laptops. Choose a cloud service for live captions, call-centre volumes, guaranteed uptime or features like speaker diarisation built in. Accuracy differs by language and audio, so benchmark on your own samples:

```bash
pip install -U openai-whisper
whisper lecture.mp3 --model small --language en
```

That writes text and subtitle files you can compare against a cloud service's output.

## Can Gemini do speech to text?

Yes. Gemini models accept audio input, so they can transcribe recordings, and also summarise them, answer questions about them or translate them. You can do this in the Gemini app, in Google AI Studio or through the Gemini API.

Upload an audio file and ask for a transcript with timestamps, or ask directly for meeting notes and action items. Because Gemini understands the content, it can also label speakers and clean up filler words if you ask. For long recordings, the API's file upload handles large files better than pasting. For precise, verbatim transcripts at scale with live streaming, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text is the more specialised option. Check the Gemini API audio documentation for supported formats and length limits.

## How do I create an AI voice with text to speech?

Choose a TTS tool, paste your script, pick a voice, adjust speed and style, and export the audio. Most tools offer many ready-made voices; cloning a specific voice needs that person's consent and a service that supports it.

Tips for natural results:

- Write for the ear: short sentences, contractions and clear punctuation for pauses.
- Spell out tricky names phonetically or use the tool's pronunciation settings.
- Use style controls or prompts, such as "calm and friendly", where available.
- Generate one paragraph at a time and listen before continuing.
- Export WAV or high-quality MP3 for video editing.

Free options include the Gemini API's speech generation in Google AI Studio, Microsoft Edge's Read Aloud for listening, and video editors such as Clipchamp with built-in TTS.

## How do I use text to speech in Google AI Studio?

Open Google AI Studio, choose the speech generation option, select a model that supports audio output, enter your text and a style instruction, pick a voice, and run it. You can play the audio and download it, or get the code to do the same through the Gemini API.

Gemini's speech generation lets you steer delivery with natural-language instructions, such as "read this like an excited sports commentator", and supports multiple speakers for dialogue, with each speaker assigned a different voice. It is a quick way to prototype narration for a project demo or a podcast-style explainer. Usage is subject to AI Studio's free limits and the API's pricing, and models with audio output may be in preview, so check the speech generation documentation for current model names.

## Which Microsoft text to speech should I use?

For listening to documents and web pages, use Read Aloud in Microsoft Edge or the Immersive Reader in Word. For video narration, use Clipchamp's built-in text to speech. For apps and developers, use Azure AI Speech, which offers many neural voices and languages.

Windows also has Narrator, a full screen reader for accessibility. Azure AI Speech provides a text-to-speech API with standard neural voices, control over pronunciation and pauses through SSML, a markup language for speech, and options for custom voices with consent and approval. Many Indian English and Indian-language voices are available. For a student project, Edge's Read Aloud is enough to test how text sounds, and the Azure free tier is enough to build a small voice feature.

## How do I use speech to text in Microsoft Word?

Open your document, select Home, then Dictate, and start speaking. Word types what you say and supports voice commands for punctuation such as "comma", "full stop" and "new line". Select Dictate again to stop.

Dictate needs a Microsoft 365 account and an internet connection, and you can change the spoken language in its settings. To transcribe a recording instead, Word for the web has Transcribe, which uploads an audio file and produces a transcript with speakers and timestamps that you can insert into the document. On Windows you can also press Windows key plus H in any text box to use system voice typing. Proofread afterwards, especially names and numbers.

# What does tuning mean in machine learning? Fine-tuning, GPUs and GPU tuning
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/tuning-fine-tuning-gpus/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Tuning means adjusting something to make it work better. In machine learning it has two common meanings: hyperparameter tuning, choosing settings such as learning rate before or during training, and fine-tuning, continuing to train a pretrained model on your own data. "GPU tuning" is different again: adjusting a graphics card's clocks, power and fans. This page explains each meaning, whether fine-tuning retrains the whole model, which GPUs and clouds suit LLM fine-tuning, whether and how to tune an NVIDIA GPU, and vLLM on AMD, drawing on building FineTune Studio, a browser-based QLoRA fine-tuning tool. What is the meaning of tuning? Tuning means making small adjustments to improve performance or fit a purpose, like tuning a guitar, an engine or a radio. In computing, it means adjusting settings of software or hardware to run faster, more accurately or more efficiently. In AI, you will meet several kinds: hyperparameter tuning, fine-tuning a model, prompt tuning, performance tuning of databases and inference servers, and GPU tuning. They share the idea of adjusting a system against a measurable goal. The key habit in all of them is measurement: change one thing, measure the effect, keep what helps. What is the meaning of fine-tuning? Fine-tuning means taking a model that has already been trained on a large general dataset and training it further on a smaller, specific dataset, so it adapts to a particular task, domain, format or style. Also asked as: what is the meaning of fine tuning For example, a general language model can be fine-tuned on support tickets to classify them into your categories, or on examples of your reports to follow your format. Fine-tuning is much cheaper than training from scratch because the model already knows language; you only teach the specifics. It changes behaviour well, but is weaker for adding facts, where retrieval-augmented generation is usually better. What is tuning in machine learning? In machine learning, tuning usually means hyperparameter tuning: finding the best values for settings that are not learned from data, such as learning rate, batch size, number of trees, regularisation strength or model depth, by testing combinations on validation data. Methods include grid search, which tries every combination; random search, which samples combinations and is often more efficient; and Bayesian optimisation, which uses past results to choose promising settings. Always tune on a validation set and report final results on a separate test set, or you overfit to your evaluation. Libraries such as scikit-learn and Optuna make this straightforward. For LLM fine-tuning, the important hyperparameters are learning rate, number of epochs, LoRA rank and batch size. Does fine-tuning require retraining the entire model? No. Full fine-tuning updates all weights, but parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA freeze the original model and train only small added matrices, often well under one per cent of the parameters. QLoRA also loads the frozen model in 4-bit precision to save memory. The benefits: far less GPU memory, faster training, tiny adapter files that can be swapped on one base model, and less risk of damaging the model's general abilities. Quality is close to full fine-tuning for many tasks. Full fine-tuning still makes sense for large changes in behaviour or domain when you have lots of data and compute. FineTune Studio uses QLoRA through Transformers, PEFT and TRL so fine-tuning fits on modest GPUs. What is the best GPU for fine-tuning LLMs? The most important factor is GPU memory. With QLoRA, 7B to 8B models fit on GPUs with 16 to 24 GB; larger models need 40 to 80 GB data-centre GPUs or several GPUs. NVIDIA GPUs have the broadest software support. Also asked as: best gpu for fine tuning llm Rough guidance: Learning and small models: free cloud GPUs in Google Colab or Kaggle notebooks. 7B to 8B models with QLoRA: consumer GPUs with 24 GB, or cloud GPUs such as the L4. 13B to 34B models: 40 to 80 GB GPUs such as A100 or H100 class, or multi-GPU setups. Very large models: multiple data-centre GPUs and distributed training. Memory also depends on sequence length and batch size; long contexts need much more. Measure peak memory on a short run before a long one. Big vs small GPU clouds for fine-tuning LLMs: which is better? Large cloud providers offer reliability, enterprise security, many regions and integration with other services, at higher prices and with quota hurdles for GPUs. Smaller GPU clouds often offer cheaper, easier access to GPUs by the hour, with fewer extra services. Also asked as: big vs. small gpu clouds for fine-tuning llms For students and individual experiments, smaller GPU clouds and notebook platforms are usually the most practical: quick to start, pay only for training time. For companies with compliance needs or data already in a major cloud, the big providers simplify security and data transfer. Whichever you use, save checkpoints to persistent storage, shut instances down when finished, set budget alerts, and keep training scripts reproducible so you can move between providers. What is GPU tuning? GPU tuning means adjusting a graphics card's operating settings, such as core and memory clock speeds, voltage, power limit and fan curve, to get more performance, lower temperatures, less noise or better efficiency. There are two directions. Overclocking raises clocks for more performance, at the cost of heat, power and possible instability. Undervolting or power limiting lowers voltage or power for nearly the same performance with less heat and noise, which is often ideal for long machine learning runs. Tools include vendor utilities and third-party apps. Changes should be small and tested for stability, because an unstable GPU can crash a training run after hours. Should I tune my GPU? For machine learning, modest power limiting or undervolting is often worth it: it reduces temperature, noise and power draw, usually with little loss of speed, which helps on long training runs. Aggressive overclocking is rarely worth the instability risk for training. Before tuning, make sure drivers are up to date, cooling and airflow are good, and dust is cleared, since these often matter more. Change one setting at a time and run a stress test or a short training job to check stability. On laptops, manufacturer power modes are safer than manual tuning. If you are not comfortable, leave defaults; modern GPUs already manage boost clocks and thermals automatically. How do I tune an NVIDIA GPU? Use NVIDIA's own app or a third-party tool to adjust power limit, clocks and fan curve, or nvidia-smi on the command line to set a power limit, then test stability with a real workload. Also asked as: how to tune nvidia gpu A cautious approach for machine learning: Check current power, temperature and clocks with nvidia-smi. Lower the power limit step by step, for example in small percentages, and measure training speed. Keep the setting where speed barely drops but temperature and noise fall clearly. Adjust the fan curve if temperatures stay high. Run a full training epoch to confirm stability. Setting power limits may need administrator rights and resets after reboot unless made persistent. Does vLLM support AMD GPUs? Yes. vLLM supports AMD GPUs through AMD's ROCm software platform, in addition to NVIDIA GPUs with CUDA, and it also has support for other accelerators. Check the documentation for supported AMD models, ROCm versions and installation steps. On AMD, installation typically uses ROCm-specific Docker images or builds, and some features may arrive later than on NVIDIA. Before committing, verify that your exact GPU and ROCm version are supported, and benchmark throughput with your model and settings. vLLM's strengths, efficient memory management and continuous batching, apply on both platforms, which makes it a good choice for serving open models to many users.

# Turning a student project into a startup: the real signal to look for, what changes, and what most student founders get wrong first
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/turning-a-student-project-into-a-startup/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## When does a student project actually deserve to become a startup?

**When strangers use it without being asked to, repeatedly, for a problem that costs them real time or money. Not when you are proud of the code, not when it won a hackathon, not when friends say it's a good idea. The signal that separates a project worth pursuing from one that should stay a project is unprompted, repeated use by people who owe you nothing, because that is the only signal that is hard to fake and hard to talk yourself into.**


Annapurna, a food-sharing platform I built for a hackathon, won first prize and then kept running as a real tool afterward, and the difference between it and other hackathon projects that stopped the day after judging was exactly this signal, not the idea's cleverness or the demo's polish [7].

> A hackathon prize measures whether judges liked your demo in three minutes. A startup measures whether a stranger comes back on their own, for weeks, with nobody grading them for it.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Why do most student projects, including good ones, not deserve this?

**Because most student projects are built to demonstrate a skill or win a specific evaluation, a grade, a hackathon prize, an interview portfolio piece, and that goal is fully achieved the moment the evaluation ends. A project built to impress a judge for three minutes was never tested against the much harder question of whether a stranger would choose to keep using it a month later with no one watching. Most good projects are good demonstrations, not good businesses, and there is nothing wrong with that; the mistake is assuming every good demonstration is secretly a startup waiting to happen.**



## What actually changes when you move from project to startup attempt?

**You need users who did not choose you out of friendship, loyalty, or a grading relationship, which means finding and convincing strangers, the hardest part most student founders underestimate [2]. You need a reason to keep working without a deadline, grade or judging panel forcing progress, which most people discover they do not actually have once the artificial deadline disappears. You need to survive being told no, or being ignored, repeatedly, by people who have no obligation to engage with you at all. None of this is about the code getting harder; the code is often the easy part.**




## Is a hackathon win a signal that a project should become a startup?

**A hackathon win is a strong signal of judged execution: you built something that worked, demoed well, and impressed a panel in a short, high-pressure window. It is not a signal of market demand, which is measured over weeks by whether people choose to keep using the thing without a judge, a prize, or a room full of attention pushing them toward it. Some hackathon-winning projects do have real demand underneath, Annapurna did, but the win itself is not the evidence; what happens in the weeks after, with no one watching, is the evidence [7].**



## What is the honest test before committing real time?

**Would you keep working on this for a stranger who owes you nothing, with no deadline, no grade, and no one watching, for the next month? Not "is the idea good" or "do I believe in it", both of which are easy to answer yes to for almost anything you built. The honest test is behavioural: are you actually still doing the unglamorous work, talking to users, fixing the boring bug, following up on a lead, once the applause from the demo has faded. Most ideas fail this test quietly, and that is useful information, not failure.**


## What mistakes do student founders make first?

**Pursuing every reasonably good project as a potential startup, diluting effort across ideas instead of concentrating it on the one with a real signal. Confusing a hackathon prize or a good grade with market validation. Building for months in isolation before showing it to a single stranger outside their circle [3]. Assuming the hard part is the code, when for most consumer and small-business ideas the hard part is finding and keeping the first real users. Quitting a real signal too early because the early weeks of any real attempt are slow and unglamorous, indistinguishable from the early weeks of one that will fail.**



## Interview and pitch questions this topic prepares you for

**"Why did you stop working on that project" or "why did you keep going" comes up naturally once you have a project with real signal or a clear decision to move on from one without it. The strongest answer names the specific evidence, user behaviour, not vibes, that drove the decision either way, which reads as founder judgement whether or not you ultimately built a company.**



## Where should I start?

**Take your best finished project and show it to five strangers outside your immediate circle this week. Watch what they actually do, not what they politely say. That is the whole test.** For a session on evaluating student projects for real founder potential, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Who is a web developer? Full stack skills, course length and portfolio ideas
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/web-developer-skills-portfolio/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A web developer is someone who builds and maintains websites and web applications. Front-end developers build what users see and interact with in the browser, back-end developers build the servers, databases and APIs behind it, and full stack developers do both. This page explains the role, what to learn to become full stack, how long courses take, and how to build a portfolio and personal website that win jobs and freelance clients, with ideas and examples, plus whether course profiles belong on a resume.

## Who is a web developer?

A web developer is a programmer who creates websites and web apps: they turn designs into working pages, connect them to data and services, and keep them fast, secure and reliable. They work in agencies, product companies, startups, as freelancers and in-house for businesses.

Day to day, web developers write code in HTML, CSS and JavaScript or TypeScript, use frameworks such as React and Next.js, build APIs, work with databases, fix bugs, review code and deploy changes. Specialisations include front end, back end, full stack, performance and accessibility. AI tools now handle much routine code, so valuable developers are those who understand the whole system, make good design decisions, and ship reliable products.

## What would you learn to become a full stack web developer?

You learn the front end, the back end, a database, and how to ship: HTML, CSS, JavaScript or TypeScript, a framework such as React or Next.js, a server language and framework, SQL, Git, authentication, testing and deployment.

A practical stack and order:

- **Foundations**: HTML, CSS, responsive design, accessibility basics.
- **JavaScript and TypeScript**: the language, async code, the DOM.
- **Front-end framework**: React, then Next.js for full-stack routing and rendering.
- **Back end**: Node.js, or Python with FastAPI; REST APIs and authentication.
- **Database**: PostgreSQL and SQL; an ORM later.
- **Tools**: Git, GitHub, the command line, testing.
- **Deployment**: Vercel, Render or a cloud platform; environment variables and logs.

Build a project at each stage instead of finishing all the theory first.

## How long does an online web developer course take?

Most self-paced web development courses take three to nine months part-time to complete; intensive bootcamps run about three to six months full-time. Becoming job-ready usually takes six to twelve months of consistent practice and project work.

Course length matters less than output. Someone who spends six months building and deploying three real projects is better placed than someone who finishes a twelve-month course of exercises. Free, well-regarded options include The Odin Project, freeCodeCamp, MDN's learning area and web.dev. Paid courses can add structure and mentorship, but check their projects and reviews first. Plan a daily routine: an hour of learning and an hour of building beats weekend marathons.

## What are good web developer portfolio ideas?

Build projects that solve real problems and show different skills: a full-stack app with authentication and a database, a fast, accessible business website, a dashboard that uses a public API, and one project with an AI feature.

Ideas that impress more than to-do apps:

- A booking or appointment system for a local clinic or salon.
- An events site for your college fest with registrations and a QR check-in.
- A dashboard visualising public data, such as air quality or cricket stats.
- A study tool that answers questions from your notes with an AI API.
- A redesigned website for a small business you know, with their permission.

Each project should be live, have a clean README, and explain your decisions.

## What are some web developer portfolio examples?

Strong portfolios share a pattern: a clear headline saying who you are and what you build, three to five featured projects with screenshots, live links and short case studies, a brief about section, and an easy way to contact you.

What a good project card includes:

- The problem and who it is for, in one or two sentences.
- Your role and the stack.
- A screenshot or short video.
- Links to the live site and the code.
- One interesting challenge and how you solved it.
- A result: users, speed, or feedback.

My own portfolio, at pranjulrathour.scult.in, follows this idea: shipped products first, each with what it does and how it was built. Keep design simple and fast; a slow, flashy portfolio works against a web developer.

## What do the top web developer portfolios have in common?

The best ones are fast, clear and focused on evidence. They load quickly, work well on phones, make the developer's specialty obvious in seconds, and lead with a few excellent projects that have real write-ups.

Common traits:

- A one-line positioning statement at the top.
- Few projects, each deep, with case studies.
- Good performance and accessibility scores, since the portfolio itself is a project.
- Personality in writing, not in heavy animations.
- Visible proof: client logos, testimonials, open-source contributions or hackathon results.
- Clear calls to action: email, GitHub, LinkedIn, resume.

Look at portfolios of developers you admire, note what you remember after thirty seconds, and apply that.

## What is the best way to build a web developer portfolio website?

Build it yourself with the stack you want to be hired for, such as Next.js, and deploy it on a free host with your own domain. A hand-built portfolio is itself a project that shows your skill.

Practical steps:

- Start from a simple layout: hero, projects, about, contact.
- Write project case studies in Markdown or MDX so they are easy to update.
- Optimise images, use good metadata and test on a phone.
- Add analytics to see which projects visitors open.
- Buy a domain with your name for credibility.

Website builders such as Webflow or Framer are fine for designers, but for developers, a well-built custom site sends a stronger signal. Keep it updated; a portfolio last touched two years ago suggests you stopped building.

## How do I build the best personal website as a web developer?

Make it fast, personal and useful: introduce yourself clearly, show your best work, and add writing, such as short articles about problems you solved. Writing gives visitors and search engines a reason to return.

A personal site can do more than a portfolio: host a blog, notes on what you are learning, talks or workshop slides, and project pages that rank in search for the problems they solve. Use structured data and good titles so your name and projects appear properly in search results. Link it from GitHub, LinkedIn and your resume. Over time, a personal site with consistent writing becomes one of the strongest assets in a developer's career.

## What are good freelance web developer website examples?

A freelance web developer's site should sell outcomes to clients, not technologies to developers: who you help, what results you deliver, examples of past work, a clear process, and an easy way to start a conversation.

Elements that convert visitors into clients:

- A headline aimed at clients, such as "Fast websites for clinics and local businesses".
- Case studies with before and after results: speed, enquiries, bookings.
- Services listed clearly: new websites, redesigns, maintenance.
- Testimonials with names and businesses, with permission.
- A simple process: call, proposal, build, launch, support.
- A contact form or WhatsApp link with a quick response promise.

Keep pricing discussions for the call. Show local or industry examples relevant to the clients you want.

## Is a Khan Academy profile resume-worthy for a web or game developer?

As a line in a learning section, it can show initiative, but it is not strong evidence for a developer role. Employers want to see what you built: deployed projects, code on GitHub and, for games, playable builds.

Use course platforms to learn, then convert that learning into projects. For web development, build and deploy two or three sites or apps. For game development, publish small playable games on a site such as itch.io, with source code. On your resume, list projects first with links, then skills, then education and courses. If you include course platforms, keep it brief and name the specific skills learned. A single good project outweighs many completed course badges.

# What is a website developer? Hiring one, and building a developer portfolio website
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/website-developer-and-portfolio/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

A website developer is someone who builds and maintains websites, writing the code for what visitors see, the front end, and often the servers, databases and integrations behind it, the back end. Some also design; others work from a designer's mockups. I build web products with Next.js, FastAPI and PostgreSQL and run my own site at pranjulrathour.scult.in, so this page covers what developers do, when a business needs one, how to find and hire one, and how to build a developer portfolio website. What is a website developer? A website developer writes and maintains the code that makes websites work. Front-end developers build the interface with HTML, CSS and JavaScript frameworks; back-end developers build servers, APIs and databases; full-stack developers do both. Also asked as: what is website developer Typical work includes turning designs into responsive pages, connecting forms and payments, building content management, optimising speed and search visibility, ensuring accessibility, deploying to hosting, and fixing issues over time. A web designer focuses on layout, visuals and user experience, though many professionals combine both roles. Developers also make decisions about security, performance and maintainability that visitors never see but that determine whether a site keeps working. Does a small business need a website developer? Not always. Many small businesses can start with a website builder such as Wix, Squarespace, Shopify or WordPress.com and do it themselves. A developer becomes worthwhile when you need custom features, integrations, better performance, or a site that must scale. Also asked as: does small business need a website developer Signs you need one: booking or ordering flows that builders cannot handle, integration with your CRM or inventory system, slow pages hurting conversions, accessibility requirements, multilingual content, or custom web applications. A good middle path is having a developer set up a solid template, analytics and search basics, then editing content yourself. Whatever you choose, make sure you own the domain and have admin access to everything. How do I find a website developer? Look for developers through referrals from businesses whose sites you like, freelance platforms such as Upwork and Toptal, local tech communities and college clubs, LinkedIn and GitHub, and agencies for larger projects. Also asked as: how to find website developer Shortlist three to five people whose past work matches what you need, such as e-commerce or booking sites. Check that their sites are fast on mobile, look professional and still work. Ask previous clients about communication, deadlines and support after launch. Student developers can be a good fit for small, well-scoped projects, with clear expectations; I have seen strong work come out of hackathon teams and student communities when the brief is clear. How do I hire a website designer and developer? Write a clear brief, compare proposals from a few candidates, review live work and references, agree on scope, milestones and ownership in writing, and start with a small paid milestone before committing to the whole project. Also asked as: how to hire website designer and developer Your brief should include goals, pages, features, examples you like, content responsibilities, deadline and budget range. In interviews, ask how they handle design approval, testing, hosting, security updates and handover. Insist that you own the domain, hosting account, code repository and design files. Agree on support after launch, since websites need updates. Avoid choosing purely on lowest cost; poorly built sites often cost more to fix later. How do I find and evaluate a website developer's portfolio? Most developers link portfolios from their LinkedIn, GitHub or freelance profiles, or share them when asked. Evaluate by opening the live sites, checking them on a phone, and asking what exactly the developer built on each. Also asked as: how to find website developer portfolio What to check: Live, working links rather than only screenshots. Speed and layout on mobile. Variety relevant to your project, such as e-commerce or booking. Case studies explaining problems, decisions and results. Code samples on GitHub for technical roles. Ask the developer to walk you through one project; clear explanations of trade-offs show real ownership of the work. How do I build a developer portfolio website? Pick three to five of your best projects, write a short case study for each, build a simple, fast site with a clear introduction, projects, about and contact sections, and deploy it free on GitHub Pages, Vercel or Netlify with your own domain if possible. Also asked as: example developer portfolio website Steps: Write content first: who you are, what you build, your best work. For each project: the problem, your role, stack, key decisions, results, live and code links. Use a framework you know, such as plain HTML, React or Next.js. Make it responsive, accessible and fast. Add a clear way to contact or hire you. My own site has project pages plus separate invite and hire pages, so visitors with different goals each find a clear next step. What makes the best developer portfolio website? The best developer portfolios are clear, fast and specific: within seconds a visitor knows who you are, what you build, and can see working projects with evidence of impact. Design polish helps, but content and proof matter most. Strong portfolios share traits: a one-line positioning statement, three to five deep projects instead of twenty shallow ones, case studies with real numbers such as users, speed gains or awards, visible contact details, and up-to-date work. Weak portfolios have broken links, tutorial clones presented as original projects, slow animations and no explanation of the developer's role. Recruiters often spend under a minute, so make the first screen count. What are good examples of developer portfolio websites? Good examples are easy to find through curated lists such as the "awesome developer portfolios" collections on GitHub, discussions of well-designed personal sites on Hacker News, and the personal sites of engineers you admire. When studying examples, look past the visuals and note structure: how they introduce themselves, how many projects they show, how they write case studies, and how they invite contact. Some engineers use minimal text-first sites with writing; others build interactive experiences that demonstrate front-end skill. Choose a style that matches the work you want. Never copy someone's site directly; adapt ideas and make the content yours. What are good ideas for a software developer portfolio website? Good ideas make the portfolio itself show your skills: a blog with technical write-ups, interactive demos of your projects, a "now" page about current work, a uses page listing your tools, and case studies with architecture diagrams. Also asked as: software developer portfolio website ideas More ideas: An AI chat that answers questions about your work, grounded in your own content. Live project status or GitHub activity. A talks and community section with events and slides. A timeline of your journey with milestones. A resume page that is also downloadable. Pick ideas that support your goal, such as getting hired, finding clients or speaking invitations, rather than adding features for their own sake. Where can I find a free developer portfolio website template? Free templates are available from Vercel's template gallery, Netlify and GitHub Pages themes, open-source repositories on GitHub tagged "portfolio template", HTML5 UP, and starter themes for frameworks such as Astro, Next.js and Hugo. Also asked as: developer portfolio website template free Choose a template that is lightweight, responsive and easy to edit, check its licence, and customise colours, fonts and layout so it does not look identical to thousands of others. Deploy free with GitHub Pages, Vercel or Netlify. Templates save time, but the content, your projects, explanations and results, is what earns interviews. Update it whenever you finish something meaningful.

# ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot: what each one actually is, who makes it, what it's for, and how to tell them apart
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-chatgpt-claude-gemini-copilot/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is the difference between ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot?

**ChatGPT is OpenAI's consumer and developer assistant, built on OpenAI's GPT models [1]. Claude is Anthropic's assistant, built on Anthropic's own Claude models [2]. Gemini is Google's assistant, built on Google's Gemini models [4]. Copilot is Microsoft's brand for AI assistance across its products, historically built on OpenAI models under a partnership, now increasingly mixing in Microsoft's own [5]. All four are chat interfaces to an underlying large language model; the differences that matter are which company controls the model, what each is tuned for, and where each shows up, in a browser tab, an IDE, or Office.**


I use several of these daily in production work and teach students to choose deliberately rather than defaulting to whichever name they heard first. My longer framework for choosing a model provider for an actual application, not a chat tab, is on the portfolio [11].

> These are four companies' front doors to their own models. The chat window is the least interesting part; the model behind it is what actually differs.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is ChatGPT, and who makes it?

**ChatGPT is OpenAI's assistant product, the interface most people first meet a large language model through [1]. It runs on OpenAI's GPT-series models and has grown from a text chat window into a multimodal assistant that reads images, browses, runs code, and increasingly acts as an agent. "Is ChatGPT down" usually means an OpenAI-side outage or degraded service, checkable on OpenAI's own status page rather than guessed at [7], though a browser extension conflict or a regional network issue can look identical from the user's side.**


## What is Claude, and what is Claude Code?

**Claude is Anthropic's assistant, built on Anthropic's own Claude model family, generally positioned around careful reasoning, longer documents, and steerable behaviour [2][9]. Claude Code is a distinct product from the chat assistant: an agentic coding tool that runs in a terminal or editor, reads and edits a real codebase, runs commands, and works through multi-step engineering tasks rather than just answering questions in a chat window [3]. Anthropic's newer "Claude Cowork"-style collaborative features extend this agent pattern to broader work tasks beyond code.**



## What is Gemini, and what is Copilot?

**Gemini is Google's assistant, built on Google's own Gemini models, integrated across Google Search, Workspace and Android [4]. Copilot is Microsoft's umbrella brand for AI assistance woven through Windows, Office, and GitHub; GitHub Copilot specifically is the coding-completion and chat assistant inside an IDE, historically powered substantially by OpenAI's models under the Microsoft-OpenAI partnership, with Microsoft's own models increasingly part of the mix [5]. "Why is Copilot down" or "not working" is almost always a GitHub or Microsoft service issue, an extension needing a restart, or an expired sign-in, checkable the same way as any outage, on the provider's status page first.**



## What is Codex, and how does it compare to Claude Code?

**Codex is OpenAI's agentic coding product, in the same category as Claude Code: an AI system that works directly in a codebase, running commands and making multi-file changes rather than only chatting [6]. The comparison that matters for choosing between them is less "which is smarter" in the abstract and more which integrates with your existing workflow, editor, and CI, and which model family's coding behaviour you have personally found more reliable on your kind of codebase, since both improve on overlapping but not identical benchmarks release to release.**


## Is Ollama a competitor to these, and is it free?

**Not directly. Ollama is a tool for running open-weight models, Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen and others, on your own machine, entirely free and offline [8]. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot are hosted products built on closed or semi-closed models you access through an account and, for heavy use, a subscription or API bill. Ollama is the local, self-hosted alternative to all of them for tasks where privacy, cost, or offline access matter more than having the single most capable model available.**



## How do I choose which one to use for a task?

**For coding inside a real project, a coding agent, Claude Code or Codex, beats a general chat window because it can actually read and run your code. For long documents or careful step-by-step reasoning, compare Claude and the others on the specific document, since strengths shift by release. For anything tied into Google's ecosystem, Gemini's integration wins on convenience. For anything tied into Microsoft's ecosystem, Copilot wins the same way. For a quick one-off question, whichever is already open in a tab is the right answer; the differences matter for sustained work, not a single query.**



## What mistakes do people make comparing these assistants?

**Assuming "AI" is one thing and any assistant should behave like any other. Blaming your account for what is a provider-wide outage, or the reverse, assuming an outage when the problem is a browser extension. Using a general chat assistant for a coding agent's job, pasting code back and forth by hand when a coding agent would read the repository directly. Picking a favourite once and never re-checking as models change every few months. The fix for all of these is the same: know which product you are actually using and what it is built for.**



## Where should I start?

**Try the same real task, a piece of code, a document, a question you actually have, on two of these assistants this week and compare the answers yourself rather than trusting a ranking.** For a workshop that teaches students to evaluate AI tools rather than default to whichever is trending, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What are Copilot agents? Uses, memory, privacy, credits and SharePoint agents
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-copilot-agents/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Copilot agents are focused AI assistants inside Microsoft 365 Copilot, each with its own instructions, knowledge sources and actions for a specific job, such as answering HR policy questions, helping new hires, or handling IT requests. Microsoft provides some built-in agents, and organisations build their own with Agent Builder or Copilot Studio. This page explains what agents are used for, when to use one, whether they learn or remember, how credits apply, privacy and where they run, how good they are in practice, and how agents work in SharePoint.

## What are Copilot agents?

Copilot agents are specialised assistants built on Microsoft 365 Copilot. Each one combines instructions that define its role, knowledge it can search, and optionally actions it can take in other systems, so it handles one kind of task better than general Copilot.

There are a few kinds. Retrieval agents answer from specific knowledge, such as a policy site. Task agents take actions, such as creating a ticket or updating a record. Autonomous agents run on triggers or schedules without a user starting a chat. Microsoft also ships prebuilt agents, such as research and analysis agents, and agents in Teams and SharePoint. You find agents in the Copilot app or Teams, and you can mention them in a chat to call them in.

## What are Copilot agents used for?

Organisations use Copilot agents to answer recurring questions, guide people through processes and automate routine tasks: HR and policy questions, employee onboarding, IT helpdesk, sales preparation, project status and customer support.

Examples that work well:

- An onboarding agent that answers new joiners' questions from the handbook and links the right forms.
- An IT agent that resolves common issues and opens a ticket when it cannot.
- A sales agent that summarises an account from CRM data before a call.
- A project agent that reports status from a SharePoint site and task lists.
- A college department agent that answers questions about syllabus, deadlines and lab rules.

The common pattern is a clear audience, trusted sources and a defined hand-off to a person.

## When should I use a Copilot agent?

Use an agent when the same kind of question or task keeps coming up, the answers live in known sources, and a focused assistant would be more accurate than general Copilot. Use general Copilot for one-off, varied requests.

Signals an agent is worth building: a team answers the same twenty questions every week; a process has steps people often get wrong; information is scattered across sites and documents; or a task needs data from another system. Signals it is not: the questions are rare or completely different each time, the source documents are outdated or contradictory, or nobody will own and maintain the agent. Clean, current knowledge matters more than clever instructions.

## Do Copilot agents learn?

Not in the sense of retraining themselves. Agents do not update the underlying model from your conversations. They improve when their owners update instructions, add or fix knowledge sources, and refine actions based on what users ask.

That is by design: a model that changed itself from every conversation would be unpredictable and could absorb wrong or sensitive information. What looks like learning comes from fresh knowledge: when a policy document is updated in SharePoint, the agent's next answer reflects it. Owners should review conversation analytics regularly, note questions the agent answered poorly, and fix the source content or instructions. That loop is the real way agents get better over time.

## Do Copilot agents have memory?

Within a conversation, yes: an agent remembers what has been said in that chat. Across conversations, memory is limited and depends on the agent and Microsoft's features; agents generally do not carry details from one user's chats into another's.

Microsoft 365 Copilot has been adding personalisation and memory features for individual users, controlled by user and admin settings. Agents built in Copilot Studio can store and use variables during a conversation and can save information to systems such as Dataverse or a SharePoint list through actions, which acts as explicit, controlled memory. If an agent must remember something, such as a user's preferences or a case history, store it deliberately in a system of record rather than relying on chat history.

## Do Copilot agents use credits?

It depends on the agent and licensing. Agents built in Copilot Studio consume Copilot Credits for their interactions and actions, especially when used by people without a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence, on external channels or when running autonomously.

Users with a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence can use many agents within Microsoft 365 as part of that licence, while organisations without it pay for agent usage through Copilot Studio capacity or pay-as-you-go billing. Actions that call generative AI, search knowledge or run autonomously typically consume more. Microsoft updates these rules, so admins should check the current Copilot Studio licensing guide and monitor consumption in the Power Platform admin centre.

## Are Copilot agents private?

Agents follow Microsoft 365's security model: they only access content that the user, or the configured identity for autonomous agents, is allowed to see, and data stays within your organisation's Microsoft 365 environment under enterprise data protection.

Privacy risks come from configuration, not the platform. An agent with an uploaded file shares that file's content with everyone who can use the agent. An agent using a service account can expose data the end user should not see. SharePoint sites with overly broad permissions make agents surface documents widely. Before sharing an agent, check its knowledge and actions against its audience, and ask your admin about policies for agent creation and sharing.

## Where do Copilot agents run?

Copilot agents run in Microsoft's cloud, within your organisation's Microsoft 365 tenant and Power Platform environments. You use them through Microsoft 365 Copilot, Teams, SharePoint, websites or other channels where they are published.

Copilot Studio agents live in a Power Platform environment, which sets the region where their data is stored. Agent Builder agents are stored with Microsoft 365. The language models run in Microsoft's data centres under the same commitments as Microsoft 365 Copilot. Nothing runs on your laptop, except the app or browser you use to chat. For data residency questions, admins can check environment regions and Microsoft's data boundary commitments for their geography.

## Are Copilot agents any good?

They are good when the scope is narrow, the knowledge is clean and current, and someone owns them. They disappoint when built as general "ask me anything" bots over messy, outdated document collections.

What separates useful agents from poor ones:

- A specific audience and purpose written into the instructions.
- A small set of authoritative sources, with duplicates and old versions removed.
- Clear behaviour when the answer is not found: say so and hand over.
- Tested with real questions before launch.
- Reviewed regularly using analytics and feedback.

The same lesson shaped RAG.NextUpgrad: retrieval quality and a refusal path when evidence is weak matter more than the model. An honest "I do not know" beats a confident wrong answer.

## How do Copilot agents work in SharePoint?

SharePoint agents answer questions grounded in the content of a specific site, document library, folder or set of files. Every site can offer a ready-made agent, and site members can create custom agents scoped to chosen content.

To create one, select the files or library, choose to create an agent, give it a name, instructions and starter prompts, and save it; it becomes an item in the library that you can share and use in Teams chats. The agent searches only its scoped content, within each user's permissions, and cites the documents it used. This works well for project sites, policy libraries and course material. Keep the scoped content tidy: archive old versions and use clear titles so the agent finds the right document.

# What are embeddings in AI? Text embeddings, vector similarity, choosing a model, and how embeddings power RAG and semantic search
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-embeddings-in-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What are embeddings in AI?

**An embedding is a list of numbers, a vector, that a model produces to represent the meaning of an input: a sentence, a paragraph, an image, a sound clip. The model is trained so that inputs with similar meaning produce vectors that are close together and dissimilar inputs produce vectors far apart. Once text is a vector, meaning becomes geometry: you can measure similarity with a distance, search by nearest neighbour, cluster, and feed vectors to other models.**


Word2vec showed in 2013 that simple training objectives produce vectors where analogies work as arithmetic [1]. BERT produced contextual vectors for every token [2], and Sentence-BERT trained networks so that a whole sentence's vector could be compared with cosine similarity directly, which is the form every RAG system uses [3]. Dense passage retrieval then showed embeddings beating keyword search for question answering [4].

In every retrieval system I have built, the embedding model is chosen once, early, and it decides what "similar" means for the life of the index. This page is how I make that choice, and what I tell students who confuse embeddings with tokens.

> An embedding model is a definition of similarity, frozen into numbers. Pick the one whose idea of similar matches your users' idea of relevant.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How do embedding models work?

**A transformer reads the input and produces a vector for every token; a pooling step, usually the mean or a special token's vector, collapses them to one vector for the whole input; a final normalisation makes it unit length. Training uses pairs: a query and a passage that answers it, or two sentences that mean the same, pushed together, with unrelated pairs pushed apart, a contrastive objective. Millions of such pairs teach the model which differences matter and which do not.**



Two terms collide here. An "embedding layer" inside any neural network maps token ids to vectors as the first step of processing; an "embedding model" is a whole network whose output is a vector for the input. The second is what RAG and search use.

## What is the difference between embeddings and tokens?

**Tokens are the pieces of text a model reads, word fragments mapped to integer ids; there are as many tokens as pieces. An embedding is one vector representing an entire input's meaning. A 500-word passage might be 650 tokens and exactly one embedding. Tokens are how language models consume text; embeddings are how retrieval systems compare it. People search for this distinction often because both are "numbers that represent text", and they are not the same numbers.**



## What do dimensions mean, and how many do I need?

**Dimensions are the length of the vector, commonly 384, 768, 1,024 or 1,536, sometimes 3,072 or more. More dimensions can capture more nuance and cost more storage and search time. The right number is whatever your chosen model produces; it is not a knob to maximise. Matryoshka-trained models let you truncate a long vector to a shorter prefix with graceful quality loss, which is useful when storage matters [7]. Test truncation on your own retrieval set before relying on it.**


A 1,536-dimension vector for a million chunks is about six gigabytes in 32-bit floats before any index overhead. A 384-dimension model is a quarter of that. Whether it retrieves worse for your documents is an empirical question, and it is often closer than the size suggests.

## How is similarity between embeddings measured?

**By a distance or similarity function between two vectors. Cosine similarity, the cosine of the angle between them, is the standard for text; on unit-length vectors it equals the dot product and ranges from minus one to one. Euclidean distance is common in image search. Use the metric the model's documentation specifies, normalise vectors at index time, and never mix metrics or models within one index.**


There is no universal "good" cosine score. The same model can put unrelated texts at 0.6 and paraphrases at 0.85; another model spreads them differently. Thresholds come from your own labelled pairs, not from a blog post.

## Which embedding model should I use?

**Shortlist by the retrieval task on the MTEB leaderboard, filtered for your language and a size you can run [5][6]. Prefer models trained on query-to-passage pairs for RAG. Then evaluate two or three on twenty of your own questions against your own documents, measuring recall at k. Choose the smallest model that meets your target. For Hindi and mixed-language content, check multilingual models specifically; English-only leaders can collapse.**



The MTEB paper explains the benchmark's tasks and why a single average hides large differences between tasks [5]. Sentence Transformers is the library most open models ship with [10]; commercial APIs document their models and dimensions [11]. My own decision notes on switching models in a production RAG system are on the portfolio [13].


## How are embeddings used in RAG and semantic search?

**At index time, each document chunk is embedded and stored in a vector index. At query time the question is embedded with the same model and the nearest chunks are retrieved, then reranked and passed to the language model as context. Semantic search is the same retrieval without the generation step: the results are the chunks or documents themselves. Embeddings make "how do I reset my password" match a passage titled "Credential recovery" even though they share no words.**



That table is why every retrieval system I ship is hybrid: dense retrieval for meaning, BM25 for exact terms, fused with reciprocal rank fusion [12].

## What else can I do with embeddings?

**Deduplicate near-identical documents by finding pairs above a similarity threshold. Cluster support tickets or feedback into themes. Classify text by nearest labelled examples, which needs no training run. Recommend items whose descriptions are close to what a user liked. Detect topic drift in a conversation. Match resumes to job descriptions by section. Anything that reduces to "which of these is most like that" is an embedding problem.**


## What are multimodal, image and code embeddings?

**Multimodal models place images and text in the same vector space, so a text query can retrieve images and an image can retrieve captions; CLIP established the approach [8]. Image embeddings power visual search and duplicate detection. Code embeddings, trained on code and natural language pairs, let you search a codebase by describing what a function does. Each is a separate model with its own space; a text embedding and an image embedding from unrelated models cannot be compared.**


## What are the limitations of embeddings?

**They compress meaning, so they lose detail, especially exact strings, numbers and negation: "no refund" and "refund" can land close. They inherit their training data's biases and domain, so a general model can misjudge medical or legal text. They are model-specific, so switching models means re-embedding everything. They cannot be reversed into the original text, which is a privacy advantage and an interpretability limit. Late-interaction methods such as ColBERT keep per-token vectors to recover some lost precision, at higher storage cost [9].**



## What are common embedding interview questions?

**Explain what an embedding is to a non-engineer. Explain why cosine similarity is used and why vectors are normalised. Compare tokens and embeddings. Describe how you would choose an embedding model for a RAG system and how you would evaluate it. Explain why keyword search is still needed. Say what happens when you switch models. If you have built one retrieval system, these are all stories rather than definitions.**



## Where should I start with embeddings?

**Install Sentence Transformers, embed a hundred sentences you wrote, and print the nearest neighbours of a few. Then embed a real document set, ask twenty questions, and measure how often the right chunk is in the top five. Swap the model and measure again. That afternoon teaches everything above.** If your college wants a hands-on session on retrieval, embeddings and RAG, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What are hackathons? Origins, types, judging, India events, pay, and how many to do
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-hackathons/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Hackathons are events, usually 24 to 48 hours long, where small teams build a working prototype of a software or hardware idea and present it to judges, often around a theme such as AI, health or climate. They combine learning, competition and networking. I have won first prizes at Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee, Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025 and BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats, and mentored at more than ten hackathons, so this page covers what they are, origins, Indian events, types, judging, pay, how many to do, and regional exclusions. What are hackathon events? Hackathon events bring together developers, designers and domain experts to build prototypes in a fixed time, usually one to three days. Teams pick or receive a problem, build, then demo to judges, who award prizes based on published criteria. Also asked as: what are hackathons events A typical event has an opening session with themes and rules, team formation, building time with mentors, meals and short workshops, a submission deadline, and final presentations. Sponsors offer prizes, technology credits and sometimes job interviews. Beyond winning, people attend to learn new tools quickly, meet collaborators and recruiters, and build portfolio projects under real constraints. Where did hackathons start? The term and format began in 1999. The OpenBSD project held a developer event in Canada that June focused on intensive coding, and Sun Microsystems ran a hackathon around its JavaOne conference, challenging developers to build software for a new device. Intensive collaborative coding sessions existed before, in university computer labs and early software culture, but 1999 gave the format its name. Through the 2000s, companies like Facebook made internal hackathons part of their culture, and student hackathons grew rapidly in the 2010s with organisations such as Major League Hacking. Today they run worldwide, including national programmes like Smart India Hackathon. The format has also spread beyond software to journalism, healthcare, government and design. What are the upcoming hackathons in India? Upcoming hackathons in India are listed on Devfolio, Unstop, Major League Hacking, Devpost and college tech fest websites. Recurring large events include Smart India Hackathon, company challenges, Web3 and AI hackathons, and IIT and NIT tech fest competitions. How to stay informed: Create profiles on Devfolio and Unstop and follow events. Follow college tech fests and student communities on social media. Join developer communities and campus clubs that share announcements. Watch company careers pages for hiring hackathons. Ask seniors which events were well organised. Registration often closes weeks before events, so check listings regularly rather than looking only when you are free. Do online hackathons exist? Yes. Online hackathons run entirely over the internet, with teams collaborating remotely through chat, video calls and shared repositories, then submitting demo videos and code. They became common during the pandemic and remain popular. Advantages: no travel, global participation, flexible timing and often longer durations, such as one or two weeks. Disadvantages: less networking, harder team coordination and more competition. Devpost hosts many online hackathons, and MLH runs online seasons. For beginners, online events are a low-pressure way to start; for networking and mentorship, offline events usually give more. If you join one, set up a shared repository and a daily video check-in on the first day, agree on time zones and roles, and record your demo video early so a last-minute bug does not leave you without a submission. How many types of hackathons are there? There is no fixed number, but common types include themed hackathons, such as AI, health or fintech; corporate internal hackathons; hiring hackathons; social impact hackathons; hardware hackathons; online and offline events; and related formats like ideathons, datathons and designathons. Other variations: student-only events, open events, government challenges like Smart India Hackathon, sponsor-specific challenges using one company's technology, and long-running innovation challenges spanning weeks. Each type rewards different strengths: hiring hackathons emphasise coding skill, social impact events emphasise problem understanding, and hardware events need physical prototypes. If you are new, start with a beginner-friendly themed event with mentors, then try hiring or hardware hackathons once you know how you work under time pressure. How are hackathons judged? Judges typically score against published criteria: problem relevance, working solution, technical execution, innovation, impact or feasibility, and presentation. Many events weight the live demo heavily, because a working prototype separates real progress from slides. Judging formats vary: some have preliminary rounds where judges visit tables, then finalists present to a panel; others review demo videos. Questions test whether the team understands its own choices. From judging and mentoring, I have seen that teams who state their limitations honestly and explain trade-offs earn more trust than teams claiming everything works perfectly. Do hackathons pay? Participants are not usually paid, but hackathons can be rewarding: prizes, sponsor credits, internships, job interviews, incubation offers and grants. Some corporate and government challenges award significant prizes or follow-on funding. Prize details vary, so read rules carefully: eligibility, taxes, intellectual property terms, and how prizes are distributed. Many events also cover meals, travel or accommodation for selected teams. Beyond prizes, the value is in skills, network and portfolio projects. Several of my hackathon projects became talking points in interviews and led to collaborations, which outlast any prize. How many hackathons should I do? Do enough to learn and build a portfolio, but not so many that you never finish projects. For students, three to six per year is a reasonable range, mixing online and offline events, and continuing your best project after the event. Quality beats quantity: one project developed further after a hackathon, with real users, is worth more than ten abandoned prototypes. Choose events aligned with your interests and target career. After each event, write a short reflection: what worked, what broke, what you learned. If hackathons start hurting your studies or health, cut back. Do hackathons matter? Yes, for learning, networking and proof of skills. Hackathons show you can build under pressure, work in a team and present clearly, which employers value. Wins and strong projects stand out on resumes, especially for freshers. They matter less if they only produce slide decks or unfinished code. Recruiters care about what you built and can explain, not just participation certificates. Use hackathons as accelerators: learn new tools, meet collaborators, and turn the best ideas into real projects. KrishGyan started at a hackathon and won first prize because it solved a real problem in a demo judges could see working. Why are Quebec and some countries excluded from hackathons? Many hackathon rules exclude places such as Quebec, Brazil and some other jurisdictions because their laws regulate prize contests, requiring registration, fees, translations or government authorisation. Organisers exclude them to avoid compliance costs and legal risk. Also asked as: why is quebec excluded from hackathons Quebec, for example, has rules requiring certain contests open to its residents to be registered with a provincial regulator, and Brazil regulates promotional prize distributions. Sanctions laws also bar participants from some countries. These exclusions are about legal compliance, not the participants. If you live in an excluded region, check whether the event allows participation without prizes, or look for events organised locally. Organisers usually list excluded regions in the official rules, so read them before investing time.

# What are large language models? How LLMs work, training, and small vs large
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-large-language-models/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks, usually transformers with billions of parameters, trained on huge amounts of text and code to predict the next token. From that one objective they learn grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and coding, which is why one model can answer questions, write, translate and program. This page explains how they work, what they are trained on, how many exist, how small and large models differ, what instruction tuning changes, why pretrained models already handle many tasks, what vLLM does for serving, and where to read more.

## What are large language models?

Large language models are AI models trained on very large text datasets to understand and generate language. "Large" refers to their size, from a few billion to hundreds of billions of parameters, and to the scale of their training data.

GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, Qwen and DeepSeek are all LLM families. They power chat assistants, coding tools, search features, translation and document analysis. An LLM on its own only generates text; products add tools, retrieval, memory and safety layers around it. In my own work, RAG.NextUpgrad wraps LLMs with hybrid retrieval and a confidence gate, and FineTune Studio adapts open models with QLoRA, which shows the two main ways engineers shape an LLM: give it the right context, or change its weights.

## How do large language models work?

An LLM splits text into tokens, turns each into a vector, and passes the sequence through many transformer layers whose attention mechanism lets each token draw on every earlier token. The final layer outputs a probability for every possible next token.

Generation repeats that step: pick a next token from the probabilities, append it, and predict again. Settings such as temperature control how adventurous the choice is. The model's knowledge lives in its parameters, learned during training; it does not look things up unless a tool or retrieval system gives it documents. That is why LLMs can be fluent and wrong at the same time: they produce the most plausible continuation, which usually, but not always, matches the truth.

## What are large language models trained on?

LLMs are pretrained on very large collections of text and code: filtered web pages, books, encyclopedias, academic papers, code repositories and other licensed or public data. Later stages use smaller curated datasets of instructions, conversations and human preference ratings.

Training data is cleaned heavily: duplicates, low-quality pages and some personal or harmful content are filtered out, and mixtures are balanced across languages and domains. Model makers rarely publish full data details, and the use of copyrighted material is the subject of ongoing legal debate. Training data has a cutoff date, so models lack knowledge of later events unless connected to search or retrieval. The quality of data matters more than raw quantity, which is why curated datasets and synthetic data now play a large role.

## How many large language models are there?

Thousands. Major labs release a few flagship families, while open-weight models and their fine-tuned variants number in the many thousands on Hugging Face, which hosts over a million models of all kinds.

The landscape has three layers. Frontier proprietary models, such as those from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, available through apps and APIs. Open-weight base models from Meta, Mistral, Alibaba's Qwen team, Google's Gemma, DeepSeek and others, which anyone can download. And the long tail of community fine-tunes and quantised versions built on those bases. For practical choices, you rarely need more than a shortlist: one strong hosted model, one fast cheap model, and one open model you can run or fine-tune yourself.

## What is the difference between small and large language models?

Small language models, typically from under one billion to a few billion parameters, are cheaper, faster and can run on laptops and phones. Large models, from tens to hundreds of billions of parameters, handle complex reasoning, long documents and broad knowledge much better.

Small models are good at focused tasks: classification, extraction, simple summaries and autocomplete, especially after fine-tuning on a specific job. They also keep data on the device. Large models are better at open-ended questions, multi-step reasoning, coding across files and following complex instructions. Size is not everything: training quality, data and fine-tuning let today's small models beat much larger models from a few years ago.

## When should I use a small vs a large language model?

Use a small model when the task is narrow, volume is high, latency matters or data must stay on the device. Use a large model when the task is open-ended, mistakes are costly, or it needs reasoning across long context.

A practical approach is routing: send easy requests to a small, cheap model and hard ones to a large model, based on rules or a quick classifier. Another is distillation: use a large model to label data or generate examples, then fine-tune a small model on them for production. With QLoRA, fine-tuning a small open model fits on a single consumer GPU, which is what FineTune Studio makes possible from the browser. Always measure on your own test set before choosing.

## What is the difference between instruction-tuned and non-instruction-tuned LLMs?

A base, non-instruction-tuned model only continues text; give it a question and it may continue with more questions. An instruction-tuned model has been further trained on examples of instructions and good responses, so it follows requests and answers helpfully.

Instruction tuning, shown at scale in Google's FLAN work and OpenAI's InstructGPT, trains the model on many tasks phrased as instructions, often followed by preference tuning with human or AI feedback. Chat assistants are instruction-tuned. Base models are still useful: for further fine-tuning on your own format, for text completion and for research. When downloading open models, choose the "instruct" or "chat" variant for assistants and the base variant only if you plan to fine-tune it into something specific.

## Do large pretrained language models already "know" NLP tasks?

Largely, yes. Pretraining on huge text teaches models to perform many tasks, such as translation, summarisation, question answering and classification, from a prompt alone, without task-specific training. GPT-2 and GPT-3 demonstrated this zero-shot and few-shot ability.

The knowledge is latent: the model has seen enough examples of summaries, translations and answers in its data that a well-phrased prompt or a few examples activate the behaviour. Instruction tuning makes this much more reliable. It is not perfect, though: performance varies by task and language, and specialised tasks, such as medical coding or a company's document format, still benefit from retrieval of examples or fine-tuning. Always evaluate on your own data instead of assuming the model already knows.

## What is vLLM?

vLLM is an open-source library for serving large language models efficiently. Its PagedAttention technique manages the memory for attention keys and values in blocks, like virtual memory pages, so many requests share the GPU with little waste.

Combined with continuous batching, which adds new requests to a running batch instead of waiting for it to finish, vLLM achieves much higher throughput than naive serving on the same hardware. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, supports many open models, quantisation and multiple GPUs. Use vLLM when you host open models for many users on a GPU server. For a single user on a laptop, simpler tools such as Ollama or llama.cpp are easier.

## Is there a good PDF that explains how large language models work?

Yes. Jurafsky and Martin's Speech and Language Processing, whose third-edition draft chapters on transformers and large language models are free online as PDFs, is a clear academic introduction. The original Transformer paper and the GPT-3 paper are free on arXiv.

A reading path:

- The transformer and LLM chapters of Speech and Language Processing for foundations.
- "Attention Is All You Need" for the architecture.
- "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners" for why scale and prompting matter.
- The FLAN and InstructGPT papers for instruction tuning.
- The PagedAttention paper for serving.

Read with a notebook open and implement a tiny transformer; building one, even small, makes the papers much easier to follow.
