# What is an AI product manager? Role, skills, coding, demand and a roadmap
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-ai-product-manager/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

An AI product manager is a product manager who leads products or features powered by AI: deciding which problems AI should solve, defining what good output looks like, working with engineers and data scientists to build and evaluate it, and owning its quality, safety and business impact. The role combines classic product skills with fluency in data, models and their limits. This page covers the role, how it differs from regular PM and data science, whether it needs coding or is technical, demand and career prospects, a roadmap, certifications and pay. What is an AI product manager? An AI product manager owns AI-powered products or features end to end: identifying user problems where AI helps, defining success metrics and quality bars, prioritising work, coordinating engineering, data and design, and making launch decisions based on evaluations and risks. Also asked as: what is ai product manager · difference between ai product manager and product manager · does ai product manager require coding Typical responsibilities include writing specifications that describe desired model behaviour with examples, deciding between approaches such as prompting, retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning with engineers, planning evaluation sets, setting guardrails and human review for risky outputs, tracking cost per request, and communicating limitations honestly to users and stakeholders. They also handle feedback loops, so the product improves from real usage. How is an AI product manager different from a product manager? All product managers decide what to build and why. AI product managers additionally manage probabilistic behaviour: outputs that can be wrong, data dependencies, evaluation, model costs and AI-specific risks such as hallucination, bias and prompt injection. Practical differences: Specs: describe quality with examples and evaluation sets, not only features. Uncertainty: plan for wrong answers with fallbacks, citations and human review. Data: understand what data the model sees and how it is protected. Costs: track cost per request and latency as product metrics. Iteration: improve through evaluation and prompt or retrieval changes, not only new screens. A regular PM building a checkout flow can test deterministic behaviour; an AI PM must manage a system that is right most of the time. Does an AI product manager need to code? Usually not as a job requirement, but basic technical skills make AI PMs much more effective. Being able to call an LLM API, build a quick prototype, read evaluation results and understand system design lets you make better decisions and earn engineers' trust. Useful technical skills for AI PMs: Prompting and writing clear model specifications. Basic Python or a no-code tool to prototype ideas. Understanding of RAG, embeddings, fine-tuning and agents at a conceptual level. Reading metrics: accuracy, recall, latency, cost. SQL for analysing usage data. With AI coding tools, PMs can now prototype far more than before; use that to test ideas before asking engineers to build them. Is AI product manager a technical role? It is a technical-leaning product role. AI PMs are not expected to train models, but they must understand how AI systems work well enough to define behaviour, judge feasibility, interpret evaluations and weigh trade-offs with engineers. Some AI PM roles are deeply technical, such as product managers for AI platforms, developer tools or model APIs, where customers are engineers. Others are closer to traditional product work, adding AI features to consumer apps. Read job descriptions closely: phrases like "experience with LLM evaluation" or "familiarity with RAG architectures" signal a more technical role. Is AI product manager in demand? Demand is growing as companies add AI features to products and build new AI-first products, and employers increasingly ask product managers for AI experience. Competition is also strong, because many PMs are moving into AI. What stands out to employers: evidence that you have shipped or prototyped AI features, can define quality and evaluation, understand costs and risks, and communicate clearly with technical teams. Experience in a domain, such as education, health, finance or developer tools, combined with AI fluency, is especially valuable. For students, entry usually goes through associate product manager programmes, product analyst roles, or engineering roles followed by a move into product. Is AI product manager a good career? It can be an excellent career for people who enjoy understanding users, making decisions under uncertainty and working across disciplines, and who are curious about technology. It offers high impact and visibility, but also responsibility for products that can fail in unusual ways. Consider the trade-offs: PMs spend much of their time communicating, prioritising and resolving conflicts, with less hands-on building. AI products bring extra ethical and quality responsibilities. If you love building, engineering roles with product ownership may suit you better; if you love deciding what to build and why, AI product management is a strong fit. Many successful AI PMs started as engineers, designers or analysts. Data scientist vs AI product manager: which should I choose? Choose data science if you enjoy analysis, statistics, modelling and experiments; choose AI product management if you enjoy defining problems, prioritising, coordinating teams and owning outcomes. The roles work closely together. Data scientists explore data, build and evaluate models and run experiments, going deep on technical questions. AI product managers decide which problems matter, define success, and make trade-offs across users, business and technology. Data scientists often move into product roles later, bringing strong analytical skills. Try both through projects: build a model and analyse results, then write a product specification for an AI feature, and notice which you enjoy more. What is a roadmap to become an AI product manager? Build product fundamentals, AI fluency and evidence. Learn how products are discovered, prioritised and measured, learn how modern AI systems work and fail, and ship at least one AI prototype with an evaluation plan and a product write-up. Also asked as: roadmap to become ai product manager A practical roadmap: Product basics: user research, problem framing, prioritisation, metrics, writing specifications. AI fluency: LLMs, prompting, RAG, agents, fine-tuning, evaluation, costs and risks. Hands-on: build a small AI feature, such as a document Q&amp;A assistant with citations. Evaluation: create a test set, measure quality, and iterate. Portfolio: a case study covering the problem, decisions, results and what you would change. Experience: associate PM roles, product internships, or leading AI features in your current role. What is the best AI product manager certification? There is no single standard certification. Some universities, online platforms and companies offer AI product management courses with certificates, and broader product management certifications cover fundamentals. Choose programmes with hands-on projects and practitioner instructors. Certificates help a little for career switchers, but hiring managers look for evidence: a shipped or prototyped AI feature, an evaluation approach, and clear product thinking. Free resources, such as Google's People + AI Guidebook and Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, teach valuable principles for designing AI products. Pair any course with a real project and a written case study. What is the salary of an AI product manager? Pay varies widely with company, location, seniority and how technical the role is, so there is no single figure. AI product roles are generally paid in line with or above comparable product management roles at the same company. Also asked as: what is ai product manager salary To understand current pay for roles you target, compare listings and verified reports on job platforms for your country and level, and talk to people in those roles. For students, focus on getting the first product role, often through associate PM programmes, internships or a move from engineering or analytics, since early experience drives later earnings more than any certificate.

# What is an AI agent? Definition, examples, tools, and how to build one free
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-an-ai-agent-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


An AI agent is a system in which a language model works towards a goal in a loop: it decides the next step, calls a tool such as search, a database query or code execution, reads the result, and continues until the task is done or it needs a person. That loop is what separates an agent from a chatbot that only replies. This page defines agents with examples, separates agents from agentic AI, explains tools, skills and harnesses, and shows how to build one for free and which frameworks and builders to consider.

## What is an AI agent?

An AI agent is software that uses an AI model to choose and take actions towards a goal, observing the results of each action before deciding the next. It typically has a model, instructions, a set of tools, memory of what it has done, and a loop that runs until the goal is reached.

The key word is decide. In a fixed workflow, the developer writes every step. In an agent, the model chooses which tool to call and with what inputs, based on the situation. That flexibility handles messy, varied tasks, such as researching a question or fixing a failing test, but it also makes agents less predictable. Good agents limit that freedom with clear instructions, a small set of well-described tools, step limits and approval for risky actions.

## What is an AI agent, explained with an example?

Take a support agent for a college's admissions office. A student asks "has my application fee been received, and when is the counselling date?". The agent looks up the application in the database, checks the payment status, searches the admissions notice for dates, and replies with both answers and links.

Step by step:

- The model reads the question and decides it needs two lookups.
- It calls `get_application(student_id)` and reads the payment status.
- It calls `search_notices("counselling date")` and reads the passage.
- It writes the answer, citing the notice.
- If the record is missing, it hands over to a staff member instead of guessing.

A chatbot would answer from general knowledge; the agent acts on real systems.

## What is the difference between an AI agent and agentic AI?

Agentic AI is the broad approach of giving AI systems autonomy to plan and act towards goals. An AI agent is a specific system built that way. Agentic describes the quality; an agent is the thing.

In practice, "agentic" also describes a spectrum. A chatbot with search that decides when to search is slightly agentic. A coding agent that plans a change, edits ten files, runs tests and fixes failures is highly agentic. Many production systems sit in between: mostly fixed workflows with a few agentic steps where judgement helps. That middle ground is often the best design, because each added degree of autonomy adds failure modes. Choose the least autonomy that solves the problem.

## What are AI agent tools?

Tools are functions an agent can call: search the web, query a database, read a file, run code, send an email, call an API. Each tool has a name, a description and an input schema, and the model chooses tools based on those descriptions.

A tool definition looks like a function signature with documentation: `search_orders(customer_email: string)`, "Find a customer's recent orders; use when the user asks about an order". The quality of descriptions decides how well the agent picks tools, so write them as you would for a new teammate. Tools should validate inputs, return compact results and fail with clear error messages the model can act on. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for packaging tools so many agents and apps can use them.

## What are AI agent skills?

Skills are packaged know-how an agent loads when a task needs it: instructions, examples, templates and sometimes scripts for a specific job, such as creating a report in your company format or following your testing procedure.

The agent first sees only a short description of each skill and loads the full contents when relevant, which keeps its context small even with many skills available. That differs from tools, which are actions it can take, and from the system prompt, which is always loaded. Skills are supported in Claude's apps and API, Claude Code and other agent environments. Write a skill like a good checklist for a colleague: when to use it, the exact steps, and an example of the expected output.

## What is an AI agent harness?

The harness is the code around the model that turns it into an agent: it runs the loop, sends the model its instructions and context, executes the tools it asks for, enforces limits and permissions, manages memory and logs everything.

The model only produces text, including tool requests; the harness does the actual work. A good harness handles errors and retries, caps the number of steps and cost, asks a person before risky actions, trims or summarises context as it grows, and records every step for debugging. Claude Code and other coding agents are harnesses around models; frameworks such as LangGraph and agent SDKs help you build your own. Much of an agent's reliability comes from its harness, not the model.

## Can I build an AI agent?

Yes. If you can write basic Python and call an API, you can build a simple agent in an afternoon: a model API, two or three tools as Python functions, and a loop that runs the model's tool calls until it gives a final answer.

A sensible first project is an agent that answers questions about your own documents and can look up one live data source, such as a timetable or an API. Log every step so you can see how it decides. Then add evaluation: twenty test questions with expected answers, run after every change. Agents look impressive in demos and fail in subtle ways in real use; the evaluation set is how you find and fix those failures.

## How do I make an AI agent for free?

Use a free-tier model API, such as Google's Gemini API through AI Studio, or a local model with Ollama, and write a small agent loop in Python with an open-source framework or none at all.

A minimal agent with free tools:

- **Model**: Gemini's free tier, or a local model such as a Llama or Qwen model in Ollama.
- **Tools**: plain Python functions, such as a calculator, a search over your notes, a weather API with a free key.
- **Loop**: send the conversation and tool definitions, run any tool calls, append results, repeat with a step limit.
- **Interface**: a terminal, or Streamlit for a quick web page.
- **Hosting**: run locally, or a free tier on Hugging Face Spaces.

Keep API keys in environment variables and never let a free agent take irreversible actions without confirmation.

## What is the best AI agent framework?

There is no single best one. LangGraph suits complex, stateful workflows with explicit control; the OpenAI Agents SDK and the Claude Agent SDK are lightweight and close to their providers' models; CrewAI and AutoGen focus on multi-agent setups; LlamaIndex suits document-heavy agents.

Choose by your needs: control and observability for production, provider flexibility if you may switch models, and a community large enough to find answers. Many experienced builders start with no framework at all, a plain loop over the model's tool-calling API, because it is easier to debug and understand. Add a framework when you need what it offers, such as persistence, branching or human-in-the-loop steps, not before.

## What is the best AI agent builder?

For no-code and low-code agents, Microsoft Copilot Studio suits Microsoft 365 organisations, OpenAI's agent tools and custom GPTs suit ChatGPT users, and workflow tools such as n8n and Zapier offer agent steps for automations. For developers, code frameworks give more control.

Pick by where the agent will live and what it must reach: Teams and SharePoint point to Copilot Studio; Google Workspace points to Google's agent tools; many SaaS integrations point to n8n or Zapier; custom products point to code. Whatever you choose, judge it on how well you can test, monitor and limit the agent, not on how quickly the demo appears. The builder that makes failures visible is the better one.

# What is an AI agent? Agentic AI explained: tools, function calling, MCP, frameworks, and why most agents fail
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-an-ai-agent/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is an AI agent?

**An AI agent is a language model running in a loop with tools. Given a goal, the model decides on an action, your code executes it, a search, a database query, an API call, a file edit, the result is fed back, and the model decides the next action, until it judges the goal met or a stopping rule fires. The model supplies judgement; the tools supply reach; the loop supplies persistence. Without the loop it is a chatbot; without tools it is a planner that cannot act.**


The pattern was named ReAct by Yao et al., reasoning and acting interleaved, with the model writing a thought, an action and reading an observation on each turn [1]. Toolformer showed models could learn when to call tools [2], Reflexion added self-critique between attempts [3], and the survey by Wang et al. maps the many variants that followed [4]. Anthropic's practitioner guide distinguishes fixed workflows, where code decides the steps, from true agents, where the model does, and argues for the simplest design that works [5].

I ship both kinds. My publishing pipeline is a workflow: code decides the order, models write the text. The coding assistant that helped build it is an agent: it reads, edits and runs tests until the tests pass. The distinction is the first thing to get right, because a workflow is cheaper, more predictable and easier to test, and most "agent" products are workflows that would be better admitted as such.

> Every agent I have built started as a workflow that needed one decision I could not write as an if-statement. That decision is where the model belongs. Everywhere else, write code.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is agentic AI, and how is it different from generative AI?

**Generative AI produces content on request: text, images, code, audio. Agentic AI uses a generative model to pursue a goal through actions over multiple steps, using tools and reacting to results. The same model can do both; the difference is the harness around it. A chat window is generative. A system that reads your inbox, drafts replies, checks your calendar and books the meeting is agentic.**



## How do AI agents work?

**Each turn, the agent's context holds the goal, the tool definitions, the history of previous actions and their results. The model reads it and outputs either a final answer or a tool call: the tool's name and arguments as structured data. Your code validates the call, runs the tool, appends the result to the context, and calls the model again. Guardrails sit around the loop: a maximum number of steps, a budget, permissions per tool, and confirmation for irreversible actions.**



The whole loop is under a hundred lines in any language. The frameworks add memory management, retries, streaming, tracing and multi-agent orchestration on top; none of that changes the loop.

## What is tool calling or function calling?

**Tool calling, also called function calling, is the API feature that lets a model request an action in a machine-readable form instead of free text. You describe each tool with a name, a description and a JSON schema for its arguments. When the model decides a tool is needed it returns a call object with the tool name and arguments; your code runs the function and returns the result as a tool message. It is what makes agents reliable enough to build on, because you never parse prose to find the action.**


The shape, in the form both major providers use [7][8]:

```json
{
  "name": "search_docs",
  "description": "Search the company knowledge base. Use for any question about policies or products.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "query": {"type": "string", "description": "What to search for, in the user's words"},
      "top_k": {"type": "integer", "default": 5}
    },
    "required": ["query"]
  }
}
```

Two rules that decide whether the model picks the right tool: the description says when to use it, not just what it does, and the tools do not overlap. Ten tools with fuzzy boundaries produce worse agents than three tools with sharp ones.

## What is MCP, the Model Context Protocol?

**The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for exposing tools, data sources and prompt templates to AI applications through a common interface, so that a tool server written once can be used by any client that speaks the protocol, a coding assistant, a chat app, an agent framework, without a custom integration each time [6]. An MCP server declares its tools with schemas; the client lists them, the model calls them, the server executes. It turns "integrate this API with this agent" into "run this server".**


I run a public MCP server at tools.scult.in that exposes the same free tools and prompt library the website offers, so an agent can call the schema generator or pull a stamped prompt with one line of configuration and no signup [12]. Building it taught me the practical value of the protocol: the client side is finished by other people, so a server is the whole product.


## How do I build an AI agent from scratch?

**Pick one task with a verifiable outcome, define one to three tools with tight descriptions and schemas, write the loop with a step limit and a budget, log every call, and run it on twenty real cases before adding anything. Only then decide whether it needs memory, more tools, a planner or a second agent. Most successful agents in production have fewer than five tools and a very clear stopping condition.**


The loop, in plain Python against a tool-calling API:

```python
def run_agent(goal: str, tools: dict, max_steps: int = 12) -> str:
    history = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
    for step in range(max_steps):
        reply = llm(history, tools=[t.schema for t in tools.values()])
        if reply.tool_calls is None:
            return reply.text                      # final answer
        for call in reply.tool_calls:
            tool = tools[call.name]
            if tool.needs_confirmation and not confirm(call):
                return "Stopped: action needs approval"
            result = tool.run(**call.arguments)    # validated by the schema
            history.append(tool_result(call.id, result))
            log(step, call, result)
    return "Stopped: step limit reached"
```

Everything a framework gives you is a refinement of those lines. Write them once yourself; you will debug every framework faster afterwards.


### Which AI agent framework should I use?

**For a first agent, none: the loop above and your provider's SDK. When you need branching, retries, persistence and human-in-the-loop steps, LangGraph models the agent as a graph with explicit state and is the most widely used [9]. Provider SDKs from Anthropic and OpenAI now include agent loops and tool handling. For non-developers, n8n and similar automation tools wire models and APIs visually [11]. Choose by how much control you need over state and failure, not by popularity.**


## What are multi-agent systems?

**A multi-agent system splits a task across several agents with different tools or roles, a researcher, a writer, a reviewer, coordinated by a planner or a fixed handoff. It helps when the task decomposes cleanly and each part needs a different context, and it hurts when the coordination overhead, cost and failure surface outgrow the benefit. Start with one agent; move to several only when one agent's context or tool set becomes unmanageable.**


Anthropic's guide makes the same recommendation from a larger sample of deployments than I have: composable patterns first, prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers, and autonomous agents only for open-ended problems where the model's judgement is needed at every step [5].

## Why do AI agents fail?

**Agents fail for predictable reasons: the goal was vague, so the model optimised the wrong thing; too many overlapping tools, so it picked badly; no stopping rule, so it looped; a tool returned an error the model could not interpret; the context filled with history and it forgot the goal; it took an irreversible action nobody confirmed; or a document it read contained instructions and it followed them. Almost all of these are design failures, fixed in the harness rather than the model.**



OWASP lists excessive agency and prompt injection among the top risks for LLM applications, and agents are where both bite hardest, because an injected instruction can now cause an action, not just a bad sentence [10].

## What is agent memory?

**Agent memory is whatever the agent can consult beyond the current context: the conversation so far, a scratchpad of notes it writes to itself, a vector store of past interactions or documents it can retrieve from, and structured facts in a database. Short-term memory is the context window; long-term memory is retrieval. Most agents need less memory than their builders assume and more discipline about what to forget.**


## Are AI agents worth learning, and what jobs use them?

**Yes. Agents are how language models get connected to real systems, and every AI engineering role I see in 2026 expects familiarity with tool calling, at least one orchestration pattern and the safety basics. Learn them by building one that does a job you actually have, connect it to a real API, and measure how often it finishes the task. That measured number, on a public repository, is worth more than any course certificate.**


I will not quote an "agentic AI engineer salary" because I have no measured source for one; job posts in India in 2026 mostly list it under AI engineer or GenAI engineer roles, and pay tracks those roles in the same city and company tier.



## What are common AI agent interview questions?

**Explain the agent loop and where the model's judgement is actually needed. Compare a workflow with an agent and say when you would choose each. Describe how tool calling works and how you write a tool description. Explain how you would stop an agent from taking a harmful action, and how you would measure whether it works. Describe a failure you debugged. If you have built even one agent with a real tool, you can answer all five.**



## Where can I try an agent for free?

**Point any MCP-capable client at the server at tools.scult.in and you have an agent with a working tool set in a minute, no signup [12].** Then build your own with one tool. If your college or hackathon wants a hands-on session on agents, tool calling and MCP, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is an AI hackathon? Rules, project ideas and tools, from a winner
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-an-ai-hackathon/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


An AI hackathon is a time-boxed competition, usually 24 to 48 hours, where teams build a working prototype that uses artificial intelligence to solve a problem, then present it to judges. The theme might be generative AI, machine learning or agents, and the best projects pair a real user problem with a demo that works. I have won three hackathon first prizes and judged and mentored others, so this page draws on both sides of the table: what each kind of AI hackathon is, whether AI tools are allowed, the projects and tools that win, and the big hackathons to aim for.

## What is an AI hackathon?

An AI hackathon is an event where teams of two to five people build, in a fixed time, a prototype that uses AI to solve a problem, and pitch it with a live demo. Judges score the problem, the solution, technical depth and the presentation.

Hackathons run in colleges, at companies and online, often with themes such as healthcare, agriculture, education or sustainability. You usually get a problem statement or an open theme, mentors to unblock you, and food and sleep in short supply. The output is not a finished product; it is a convincing proof that an idea works. KrishGyan, which won Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee, was exactly that: farming advice delivered in the farmer's own voice and language over WhatsApp, demonstrated live.

## What is a GenAI hackathon?

A GenAI hackathon focuses on generative AI: projects built with large language models, image, audio or video generation. Typical builds are chat assistants over documents, content tools, voice interfaces and copilots for a specific job.

Organisers often provide API credits from model providers and judge how well teams go beyond a plain chatbot. Strong GenAI projects ground the model in real data with retrieval, use structured outputs so results can drive actions, and handle failure honestly, for example by refusing to answer when evidence is weak. Judges have seen many "chat with your PDF" demos, so a clear user, a specific workflow and a measurable result stand out more than the model you used.

## What is an AI/ML hackathon?

An AI/ML hackathon covers both generative AI and classic machine learning: prediction, classification, recommendation, computer vision and analytics. Some are data challenges where you train models on a provided dataset and are scored on accuracy.

There are two formats. In build hackathons, you create an application and the model is one part of it. In data challenges, closer to Kaggle competitions, a leaderboard ranks your predictions on hidden test data. For build formats, use pre-trained models and focus on the product. For data challenges, invest in clean features, solid validation and a few well-tuned models rather than exotic architectures. Read which format you are entering before the event, because the winning strategies are completely different.

## What is an agentic AI hackathon?

An agentic AI hackathon asks teams to build AI agents: systems that plan and take multi-step actions with tools, such as searching, calling APIs, filling forms or writing code, rather than only answering questions.

Judges look for agents that complete a real task end to end, show their steps, and stay safe: asking for confirmation before irreversible actions, staying within permissions, and recovering from errors. Good agent projects keep scope narrow, for example "an agent that books a lab slot and emails the confirmation", and give the agent a few well-described tools. Standards such as the Model Context Protocol make it quicker to connect tools. Log every step the agent takes; a visible trace makes the demo more convincing and helps you debug at 3 a.m.

## Is AI allowed in hackathons?

Usually yes. Most hackathons now allow AI coding assistants and AI APIs, but some restrict pre-written code, require code written during the event, or ban specific tools. Always read the rules and ask organisers when unsure.

Even where AI is allowed, judges test understanding. Expect questions such as "why did you choose this approach?" or "what happens if the model returns an empty answer?". As a judge, I trust teams that can explain their architecture and trade-offs, and I am wary of polished demos the team cannot explain. Use AI tools to move faster, keep a Git history that shows your work during the event, and disclose generated assets where the rules ask for it.

## What are the best AI hackathon projects?

The best AI hackathon projects solve a specific problem for a specific person, use AI where it adds something people cannot easily do, and work live in front of judges. Social impact and a clear user story score well.

Patterns that win:

- **Voice and local language access**: like KrishGyan, AI that serves people who cannot use English apps.
- **Coordination problems**: like Annapurna, which won BYTEBATTLE by matching surplus food with people who need it.
- **Document automation**: extracting fields from forms, invoices or certificates with validation.
- **Grounded assistants**: answers from a trusted source, with citations, for a college, clinic or government scheme.
- **Accessibility**: tools for people with visual, hearing or learning difficulties.

Pick one user, one painful task and one wow moment in the demo.

## What are the best AI tools for a hackathon?

Use hosted model APIs, a quick front end, a simple backend and free deployment. Training models during a hackathon rarely pays off; integrating good ones well does.

A practical stack:

- **Models**: an API from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or Groq for fast inference; open models through Hugging Face when needed.
- **Speech**: speech-to-text and text-to-speech APIs for voice features.
- **Retrieval**: a small vector index or pgvector for document Q&A.
- **Backend**: FastAPI or Node.js.
- **Front end**: Next.js, React or Streamlit for the fastest UI.
- **Deployment**: free tiers on Vercel, Render or Hugging Face Spaces.
- **Coding help**: an AI coding assistant, used with care.

Set up keys, a repository and a deployed "hello world" before the clock starts if the rules allow it.

## What do you see at an AI hackathon?

You see teams split between ambitious ideas and working demos, last-minute integration problems, and a final hour where most of the outcome is decided by who has a stable demo and a clear story.

From the judge's table, the patterns repeat. Many teams build similar chatbots; the ones that stand out have spoken to a real user, narrowed the problem and show one feature working end to end. Live demos fail more often from network and API key problems than from bad ideas, so the winners rehearse and keep a recorded backup. Mentors are underused: ten minutes with one early can save hours. And the best teams stop adding features a few hours before the end to polish the demo and the pitch.

## What is India's biggest AI hackathon?

There is no single official title, but Smart India Hackathon, run with the Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell, is among the largest hackathons in India, and many of its problem statements involve AI and machine learning.

Beyond it, large AI-themed hackathons in India are run by technology companies, cloud providers and startups, and listed on platforms such as Devfolio and Unstop, along with college tech festivals at IITs, NITs and other institutes. Sizes and themes change every year, so check the current season's listings. For a student, the "biggest" hackathon matters less than a well-run one in your area with good mentors, where you can finish a project and meet people.

## What is a global AI hackathon?

A global AI hackathon is an online or multi-city event open to participants from many countries, often run by AI companies, cloud providers or communities, with remote judging and prizes such as cash, credits or incubation support.

They are a good option if there are few events near you: you can join from anywhere, team up with people from other countries and get feedback from international judges. The trade-offs are time zones, less mentoring and a very large number of submissions, so a short, sharp demo video and a clear README matter more than at in-person events. Find them on Devfolio, Devpost, Major League Hacking and the developer pages of AI companies. Treat each one as a deadline to ship a portfolio project.

# What is BM25 search? How it works, how to cite it, hybrid search, and key release dates
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-bm25-search/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

BM25 is a keyword ranking function: it scores how well a document matches a query by counting how often the query's words appear in it, giving rare words more weight and adjusting for document length. It has been the default ranking in search engines such as Lucene, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch for years. RAG.NextUpgrad combines BM25 with dense vector search through reciprocal rank fusion and reranking, so this page explains BM25, citing it, its history, hybrid search, its future, MongoDB, and when FAISS and Llama arrived. What is BM25 search? BM25 search ranks documents for a keyword query using the BM25 formula, short for Best Matching 25, from the Okapi information retrieval system. Documents containing more of the query's rarer words, in shorter or typical-length text, rank higher. It needs no training data or model, is fast with inverted indexes, and works well for many search tasks, which is why it remains a strong baseline even against neural methods. It powers search in tools from website search bars to log analysis. In RAG, BM25 catches exact matches, such as product codes, section numbers and names, that embedding search can miss. How does BM25 search work? For each query term, BM25 multiplies the term's inverse document frequency, which rewards rare terms, by a saturating function of how often the term appears in the document, normalised by document length. It sums these scores across query terms. Two parameters tune it: k1, usually between 1.2 and 2.0, controls how quickly repeated occurrences stop adding score, so a word appearing fifty times is not fifty times better; b, usually 0.75, controls how strongly long documents are penalised. An inverted index maps each word to the documents containing it, so only relevant documents are scored. Text processing, such as lowercasing, stemming and stop-word removal, strongly affects results. What is BM25 lexical search? Lexical search matches the actual words in a query to words in documents, as opposed to semantic search, which matches meaning. BM25 is the most widely used lexical ranking method, which is why "BM25 search", "keyword search" and "lexical search" are often used interchangeably. Lexical search is precise and explainable: you can see exactly which words matched. Its weakness is vocabulary mismatch: "car" does not match "automobile" unless you add synonyms. Semantic search fixes that but can blur exact identifiers. That complementary strength is why hybrid search, combining lexical and semantic retrieval, has become standard in production RAG systems. How do I cite BM25? Cite the original Okapi work and, for a full treatment, the later review. The commonly cited original is: Robertson, S. E., Walker, S., Jones, S., Hancock-Beaulieu, M. M., and Gatford, M. (1995). "Okapi at TREC-3". In Proceedings of the Third Text REtrieval Conference (TREC-3). Also asked as: how to cite bm25 For the theory and variants, cite: Robertson, S., and Zaragoza, H. (2009). "The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond". Foundations and Trends in Information Retrieval, 3(4). Many papers cite both: the 1995 paper for origin and the 2009 review for explanation. If you used a specific implementation, such as Lucene or rank_bm25 in Python, mention it and its parameter settings in your methods section. When did BM25 come out? BM25 emerged from the Okapi retrieval system developed at City University London in the 1980s and 1990s, and was presented through the TREC evaluations in 1994, with the proceedings published in 1995. The name refers to the 25th in a series of "best match" weighting functions. It built on earlier probabilistic retrieval models by Stephen Robertson and Karen Spärck Jones from the 1970s. Variants followed, such as BM25F for documents with multiple fields like title and body. Decades later, it remains a default in major search engines and a standard baseline in research, a rare longevity in computing. How do I combine BM25 and vector search? Run BM25 and vector search in parallel for each query, merge the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion, which scores each document by the sum of one over its rank plus a constant, then rerank the top merged results with a cross-encoder. Also asked as: how to combine bm25 and vector search Steps: Index each chunk for both BM25 and embeddings. Retrieve the top 20 to 50 from each method. Fuse with reciprocal rank fusion, using the common constant of 60. Rerank the top 20 to 30 with a reranker model. Send the best few chunks to the language model with citations. This is the RAG.NextUpgrad pipeline. Fusion by rank avoids comparing BM25 scores and cosine similarities, which are on different scales. Will BM25 and TF-IDF keyword search be replaced by neural search? Not entirely. Neural search improves meaning-based retrieval, but BM25 remains competitive, cheap, explainable and robust across domains, and often beats neural models on unfamiliar data. The trend is hybrid search, not replacement. Also asked as: will keyword (bm25, td-idf) be replaced for search by neural search Benchmarks such as BEIR showed that BM25 is a hard baseline for zero-shot retrieval across diverse domains, and that combining it with dense retrieval gives the best results on many tasks. Learned sparse models, such as SPLADE, blend both ideas. In practice, keyword search will remain essential for exact terms, filters and transparency, while neural methods handle paraphrase and meaning. How do I run top-k BM25 queries with MongoDB search indexes? In MongoDB Atlas, create an Atlas Search index on your collection, then use the $search aggregation stage with a text operator, followed by $limit for your top k. Atlas Search is built on Apache Lucene and scores results with BM25. Also asked as: top-k queries with mongodb search indexes (bm25 db.docs.aggregate([ { $search: { index: &quot;default&quot;, text: { query: &quot;refund policy&quot;, path: &quot;body&quot; } } }, { $limit: 5 }, { $project: { title: 1, score: { $meta: &quot;searchScore&quot; } } } ]) For hybrid search, combine $search with Atlas Vector Search's $vectorSearch, using MongoDB's documented hybrid patterns or rank fusion. Check the current documentation for supported stages in your version. When did FAISS come out? FAISS, Facebook AI Similarity Search, was released as open source by Facebook AI Research in 2017. It provided fast similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, with GPU acceleration, and became a foundation for many vector search systems. Its accompanying paper, "Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs", appeared the same year. For context on the modern retrieval stack: HNSW was published in 2016, pgvector arrived in 2021, and dedicated vector databases grew from around 2019. FAISS remains widely used for research, offline indexing and as a component inside other systems. When did Llama come out? Meta released the first LLaMA models in February 2023, initially to researchers. Llama 2 followed in July 2023 with a licence allowing commercial use, and Llama 3 arrived in April 2024, with further versions since. Llama's open weights helped create the local AI ecosystem: Ollama, which launched in 2023, made running models such as Llama on a laptop a single command, and frameworks such as LangChain, released in late 2022, connected these models to retrieval and tools. DocuLens AI uses Llama models hosted on Groq for fast document analysis, a typical pattern for open models in production.

# What is BM25? How the BM25 algorithm works, vs TF-IDF, and using it in RAG
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-bm25/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

BM25, short for Best Match 25, is a ranking function used by search engines to score how relevant a document is to a keyword query. It rewards documents that contain the query terms, especially rare terms, while preventing very frequent repetitions and very long documents from dominating. It is the default scoring in Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Lucene-based search, and the keyword half of hybrid retrieval in RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad. This page explains how it works, how it relates to TF-IDF, why Elasticsearch adopted it, and how to use it in Python and RAG. What is the BM25 algorithm? BM25 is a probabilistic ranking function that scores each document for a query by summing, over the query terms, a weight based on how rare the term is across documents and how often it appears in the document, adjusted for document length. Also asked as: what is bm25 algorithm It came out of the probabilistic relevance framework developed by Stephen Robertson and colleagues, with the "Okapi" BM25 version becoming standard in the 1990s. Despite its age, it remains a strong baseline that neural methods are compared against, and it is fast, needs no training and works in any language with a tokenizer. In modern AI systems, it is used alongside embeddings because it handles exact words reliably. How does the BM25 algorithm work? For each query term, BM25 multiplies the term's inverse document frequency (IDF), which is high for rare terms, by a saturating function of how many times the term appears in the document, normalised by document length. The document's score is the sum over query terms. Also asked as: how does bm25 algorithm work In formula form, for each term: score += IDF(term) * tf * (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 * (1 - b + b * doc_len / avg_doc_len)) Here tf is the term's count in the document, k1 controls how quickly extra repetitions stop adding score, typically between 1.2 and 2.0, and b controls length normalisation, typically 0.75. A document mentioning "pgvector" twice scores well; mentioning it fifty times scores only a little more. What is a BM25 retriever? A BM25 retriever is a retrieval component that returns the top-ranked documents or chunks for a query using BM25 scoring. In RAG frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex, it is the keyword-based counterpart to a vector store retriever. Also asked as: what is bm25 retriever It indexes your chunks by their terms, then for each query returns the highest-scoring chunks. It needs no embedding model or GPU and is fully explainable: you can see which words matched. Its weakness is vocabulary mismatch: it will not match "car" to "automobile" or a paraphrased question to its answer. That is why it is usually paired with a dense retriever in an ensemble or hybrid retriever. Why use BM25? Use BM25 because it is fast, cheap, transparent and excellent at exact matching: product codes, error messages, names, acronyms and technical terms that embeddings often blur. It is also a strong baseline to compare any fancier retrieval against. Specific advantages: No training or GPU: works immediately on any text. Exact terms: finds "ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED" or "BCA301" reliably. Explainable: scores come from visible word matches. Robust across domains: no embedding model mismatch. Cheap at scale: inverted indexes are mature and fast. In hybrid RAG, BM25 often rescues questions where vector search returns topically similar but wrong passages. Is BM25 the same as TF-IDF? No, but they are related. Both weight terms by frequency in a document and rarity across documents. BM25 adds term-frequency saturation and document-length normalisation, and comes from a probabilistic model rather than a heuristic. Also asked as: is bm25 the same as tf idf With classic TF-IDF, a term appearing twenty times counts roughly twenty times as much as appearing once, and long documents gain an advantage because they contain more words. BM25 limits the benefit of repetition through the k1 parameter and corrects for length with b, producing rankings that match human relevance judgements better in most collections. You can think of BM25 as a carefully tuned evolution of the TF-IDF idea. Does BM25 use TF-IDF? BM25 uses the same two ingredients, term frequency and inverse document frequency, but combines them differently from the classic TF-IDF formula. So it uses TF and IDF concepts, not the TF-IDF score itself. Also asked as: does bm25 use tf idf The IDF part in BM25 is typically a smoothed log ratio of documents without the term to documents with it, which gives rare terms more weight. The TF part is saturating and length-normalised. In practice this means BM25 behaves like a smarter TF-IDF: rare query words still dominate, but spamming a word or writing a very long document does not unfairly boost the score. Why is BM25 better than TF-IDF? BM25 usually ranks better because it models diminishing returns from repeated terms and normalises document length, both of which match how relevance works in real text. Its two parameters can also be tuned for a collection. Also asked as: why is bm25 better than tf idf In evaluations on standard information retrieval datasets, BM25 consistently outperforms basic TF-IDF ranking, which is why it became the default in modern search engines. TF-IDF vectors still have uses, for example as features for classifiers or for quick document similarity, but for ranking documents against queries, BM25 is the standard choice. If you need semantic matching, add embeddings rather than tweaking TF-IDF. What is BM25, and why did Elasticsearch choose it from version 5? BM25 is a keyword relevance scoring function, and Elasticsearch, through Apache Lucene, made it the default similarity from version 5 because it gives better relevance than the older TF-IDF-based scoring on most data, with sensible parameters. Also asked as: what is bm25 and why elasticsearch chose this algorithm for scoring in version 5 and above The older Lucene scoring tended to over-reward term repetition and handled document length less well. BM25's saturation and length normalisation fix those issues, and its k1 and b parameters can be tuned per field if needed. For users, the change meant better default search quality without configuration. OpenSearch inherits the same default, and many vector databases now implement BM25 too, so hybrid search is easier than ever. How do I use BM25 in RAG? Index your chunks with BM25 alongside your vector index, retrieve top candidates from both for each question, merge the lists with reciprocal-rank fusion, rerank the merged candidates, and give the best passages to the LLM. Also asked as: how to use bm25 in rag Practical tips: Tokenise consistently: lowercase, handle punctuation, keep codes and numbers intact. Retrieve more candidates than you need, such as 20 from each, before fusion. Use reciprocal-rank fusion, which merges by rank rather than incompatible scores. Add a cross-encoder reranker on the fused list. Measure recall at 5 with and without BM25 on your test questions. This exact pipeline, dense plus BM25 with fusion and re-ranking, is how RAG.NextUpgrad retrieves before generating cited answers. How do I use BM25 in Python? The rank_bm25 library provides BM25 in a few lines: tokenise your documents, build the index, and score a tokenised query. Also asked as: how to use bm25 in python # pip install rank_bm25 from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi docs = [&quot;pgvector adds vector search to PostgreSQL&quot;, &quot;BM25 ranks documents by keyword relevance&quot;, &quot;FAISS is a library for similarity search&quot;] tokenized = [d.lower().split() for d in docs] bm25 = BM25Okapi(tokenized) query = &quot;keyword ranking bm25&quot;.lower().split() print(bm25.get_top_n(query, docs, n=2)) For larger collections, use a search engine such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, PostgreSQL full-text search, or a vector database with built-in BM25. LangChain also offers a BM25 retriever for quick experiments.

# What is ChatGPT Codex? How it works, limits, and when to use it
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-chatgpt-codex/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


ChatGPT Codex is OpenAI's software engineering agent. Unlike chatting about code, Codex works on your actual repository: it reads the code, edits files, runs commands and tests in a sandbox, and gives you a diff or pull request to review. You can use it from ChatGPT in the browser, from the Codex CLI in your terminal, or from an IDE extension. This page explains how it works, which models power it, when to use it instead of ChatGPT, how memory and limits differ, which plans include it, and how to start.

## What is ChatGPT Codex?

Codex is OpenAI's coding agent. You give it a task such as "fix the failing date parser test", and it works in a copy of your repository, makes the change, runs the tests and presents the result for review.

It is available in several places that share one account: the Codex section of ChatGPT, which runs tasks in OpenAI's cloud on a connected GitHub repository; the open-source Codex CLI, which runs on your own machine; and extensions for editors such as VS Code. Cloud tasks can run in parallel, so you can hand off several small tasks and review them later. The name Codex was first used in 2021 for an earlier code model; today it refers to the agent and its coding-tuned models.

## How does ChatGPT Codex work?

Codex runs a loop: it reads your request and the relevant code, plans the change, edits files, runs commands such as tests and linters, reads the results and repeats until the task is done or it needs your input.

For cloud tasks, Codex starts a sandboxed container with your repository, installs dependencies using setup steps you can configure, and works inside it, so it cannot touch your machine. When finished, it shows the diff, a summary and the commands it ran, and you can open a pull request. With the CLI it works in your local folder, and you choose how much freedom it has, from asking before every command to working automatically inside the project. Instructions in an `AGENTS.md` file at the repository root tell it how to build, test and style the code.

## What are the GPT Codex models?

Codex models are versions of OpenAI's GPT models tuned for software engineering: writing code, following repository conventions, running tests and working through long agentic tasks. The Codex agent uses them by default.

The first Codex model, released in 2021 and described in OpenAI's paper on evaluating code models, powered the original GitHub Copilot and was later retired. The current generation is built on OpenAI's GPT-5 family, with coding-specialised variants such as GPT-5-Codex, and newer versions arrive regularly. You can usually choose the model and reasoning level in the Codex settings or CLI: higher reasoning is slower but better for hard changes. Developers can also call coding models through the OpenAI API. Check OpenAI's model list for the current names.

## When should I use ChatGPT vs Codex?

Use ChatGPT to learn, explain, brainstorm and design. Use Codex when you want a change made in a real codebase, tested and delivered as a diff or pull request.

A simple rule:

- **ChatGPT**: "Explain how JWT authentication works", "compare FastAPI and Flask for my project", "review this function I pasted".
- **Codex**: "Add JWT authentication to this FastAPI app with tests", "upgrade the project to the new library version and fix the breaking changes".

ChatGPT sees only what you paste, so its code suggestions do not know your project structure. Codex sees the whole repository and can run it, which makes its changes far more likely to work. Many developers use both: design in ChatGPT, implement with Codex.

## Should I use Codex or ChatGPT for work?

For engineering work in a team repository, Codex is the better fit because it works on the code, follows the repository's rules and produces reviewable pull requests. ChatGPT is better for documents, analysis, emails and thinking through problems.

On business and enterprise plans, admins control which repositories Codex can access and how its environments are configured, which matters for company code. Keep the usual review process: Codex output goes through code review and continuous integration like any teammate's work. Never paste secrets into ChatGPT or Codex prompts, and keep API keys in your environment configuration. If your employer restricts AI tools on its code, follow that policy; using a personal account on company code is a common way to break it.

## Do ChatGPT and Codex share memory?

No. Codex does not use ChatGPT's memory of your past conversations. It learns about your project from the repository itself and from instructions you write, usually in an `AGENTS.md` file.

This is deliberate. A coding agent should behave the same for everyone working on a repository, so project knowledge belongs in files that are versioned with the code, not in one person's chat history. A good `AGENTS.md` covers how to install dependencies, run tests and lint, the project's structure, coding conventions, and things to avoid. You can add more specific files in subfolders for parts of a large project. Your account settings, such as connected repositories, are shared across ChatGPT and Codex, but conversation memory is not.

## Are ChatGPT and Codex limits different?

Yes. Codex has its own usage limits, separate from ChatGPT message limits, and they vary by plan. Local CLI use and cloud tasks are counted, and limits reset over rolling time windows.

Heavier tasks and higher reasoning levels use more of the allowance than small ones, so a long refactor counts for more than a one-line fix. OpenAI publishes the current limits for each plan in its help centre, and they have changed several times since launch. If you hit limits often, split work into smaller tasks, choose a lower reasoning level for routine changes, and avoid asking Codex to explore a huge repository without pointing it at the right folder. Developers can also run the CLI with an API key and pay per use instead.

## Does ChatGPT Plus give unlimited use of Codex?

No. ChatGPT Plus includes Codex with usage limits, and higher plans such as Pro raise them substantially. No plan gives truly unlimited Codex use.

For a student or solo developer, Plus limits are usually enough for regular coding sessions if tasks are well scoped. If you hit the limit, you wait for the window to reset, upgrade, or switch to API-key usage in the CLI. Treat any claim of "unlimited" access through a third-party site as a red flag: shared or resold accounts break OpenAI's terms and can expose your code. Check the plan comparison page for the current inclusion and limits before you decide.

## Does ChatGPT Go have Codex?

ChatGPT Go is OpenAI's lower-cost plan, offered first in India and then in other countries. Its features differ from Plus, and whether Codex is included, and with what limits, depends on OpenAI's current plan details.

Codex has been included in Plus and higher individual plans and in business plans. Plan features change, so check OpenAI's pricing page or help centre for what Go includes in your country today rather than relying on a forum post. If Go does not include enough Codex use for you, the alternatives are the Codex CLI with an API key, paying per use, or other coding agents with free tiers. For learning to code, the chat itself on any plan is already a strong tutor.

## Is there a ChatGPT Codex tutorial?

Yes. OpenAI's Codex documentation and the Codex CLI repository have setup guides. The fastest way to learn is one small task in a repository with tests, done end to end.

A first session with the CLI:

```bash
npm install -g @openai/codex
cd my-project
codex
```

Sign in with your ChatGPT account, then:

- Ask "explain the structure of this project and how to run the tests".
- Add an `AGENTS.md` with the test command and coding rules.
- Give a narrow task: "add input validation to the signup route and a test for it".
- Approve commands one by one, read the diff, run the tests yourself.
- Commit, then try a cloud task from ChatGPT on the same repository.

# What is Chroma DB? How it works, install, run locally, and is it open source
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-chroma-db/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Chroma DB is an open-source vector database built for AI applications. It stores text chunks, their embeddings and metadata, and finds the most similar items to a query, which makes it a popular retrieval layer for RAG chatbots and semantic search. It runs inside a Python process, as a standalone server, or as a hosted service. This page covers why to use it, how it works and what it is built on, whether it is local and open source, who makes it, and how to install, run and delete it.

## What is Chroma DB?

Chroma DB is a vector database, sometimes called an embedding database, that lets applications store embeddings and search them by similarity. It is designed to be simple for developers: a few lines of Python give you a working semantic search.

Data lives in collections, each holding documents, their embeddings, metadata and IDs. Chroma can compute embeddings with a built-in or configured embedding function, or accept embeddings you compute yourself. Queries return the nearest items with their distances, optionally filtered by metadata, such as subject or date. Chroma integrates with LangChain, LlamaIndex and other frameworks, which is why it appears in many RAG tutorials.

## Why use Chroma DB?

Use Chroma when you want a fast, free, easy way to add semantic search or RAG to a project, especially in Python. It needs no separate infrastructure to start, and the same code can later point to a Chroma server or hosted service.

It suits prototypes, student projects, internal tools and small to medium production apps. Reasons to choose something else: you already run PostgreSQL and prefer one database, so pgvector is simpler; you need a managed service at very large scale; or you need strong keyword search alongside vectors, where engines with built-in BM25 help. Whichever store you choose, retrieval quality depends more on chunking, hybrid search and reranking than on the database.

## How does Chroma DB work?

When you add documents, Chroma stores each document's text, metadata and embedding, and adds the embedding to an approximate nearest-neighbour index. When you query, it embeds the query with the same function and returns the closest items.

The search index uses HNSW, a graph-based method that finds near neighbours quickly without comparing every vector. Metadata filters narrow results before or during search. Distances are computed with a configurable metric such as cosine or L2; use the one recommended for your embedding model. Because results are approximate, very large collections may need tuning of index parameters, and measuring recall on real queries tells you whether results are good enough.

## What is Chroma DB built on?

Chroma's core has been rewritten in Rust in recent versions, with Python and JavaScript clients. In local mode it stores data on disk, using SQLite for metadata and records, and an HNSW index for vector search.

The architecture supports three ways of running: embedded in your process for simplicity, a client-server mode where a Chroma server holds the data and many clients connect, and a distributed cloud service run by the company. For most users, the details matter only for performance tuning and deployment; the API stays the same. Check the documentation for the current architecture, as the project has evolved quickly.

## Is Chroma DB local?

It can be. Chroma can run entirely on your machine, either in memory or persisted to a local folder, with no data leaving your computer. It can also run as a server on your own infrastructure, or be used as a hosted cloud service.

Local mode is ideal for development, privacy-sensitive data and offline work: use `chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./store")` to save data between runs. Note that embedding functions may still call external APIs if you configure a hosted embedding model; for a fully local setup, use a local embedding model, for example through sentence-transformers or Ollama. For apps with several processes or servers, run Chroma as a server so all instances share one database.

## Is Chroma DB open source?

Yes. Chroma is open source under the Apache 2.0 licence, with its code on GitHub. You can use it in personal and commercial projects, self-host it and modify it.

The company behind it also offers a hosted cloud product with its own terms and pricing, while the open-source database remains free to self-host. Because it is open, you can inspect how indexing and querying work, which helps when debugging retrieval quality or performance. Check the repository's releases and changelog before upgrading, since fast-moving projects sometimes change storage formats or APIs between versions.

## Who owns Chroma DB?

Chroma DB is developed by Chroma, a company founded in 2022 that builds the open-source database and a hosted cloud service. The open-source code is licensed under Apache 2.0, so the community can use and contribute to it.

For users, ownership matters mainly for support and longevity: the open-source licence means your ability to use the database does not depend on buying anything, while the company funds ongoing development. If you use the hosted service, its terms, data location and pricing apply. For critical systems, keep your source documents and a way to rebuild the index, so you are never locked into one vector store.

## How do I install Chroma DB?

Install the Python package with pip, then import it. For a JavaScript project, install the JavaScript client and run a Chroma server.

```bash
pip install chromadb
```

```python
import chromadb
client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_store")
col = client.get_or_create_collection("docs")
col.upsert(ids=["a1"], documents=["Chroma stores embeddings for semantic search."])
print(col.query(query_texts=["what does chroma store?"], n_results=1)["documents"])
```

Use a virtual environment, and pin the version in `requirements.txt`. If installation fails on an older system or unusual CPU, check the troubleshooting section of the documentation for build requirements.

## How do I run Chroma DB as a server?

Use the Chroma command-line tool to start a server with a data folder, or run the official Docker image, then connect from your app with an HTTP client.

```bash
chroma run --path ./chroma_data      # starts a local server
```

```python
import chromadb
client = chromadb.HttpClient(host="localhost", port=8000)
```

Server mode lets several app instances, or apps in different languages, share one database. In Docker, mount a volume for the data directory so it persists across restarts. Do not expose the server to the internet without authentication; put it on a private network or behind an authenticated proxy, and back up the data directory.

## How do I delete a Chroma DB collection or database?

Delete a collection with `client.delete_collection("name")`, delete specific items with `collection.delete(ids=[...])` or a metadata filter, and remove the whole local database by deleting its persistence folder while no process is using it.

```python
client.delete_collection("docs")                         # whole collection
col.delete(where={"source": "old_policy.pdf"})            # items by metadata
```

Before deleting, make sure you can rebuild from source documents. In tests, use a temporary folder or an in-memory client so each test starts clean. If you change the embedding model, deleting and rebuilding the collection is required, since old and new vectors are not comparable.

# What is chunking in RAG? Chunk size, overlap, structure-aware splitting and the experiments that actually decide retrieval quality
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-chunking-in-rag/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is chunking in RAG?

**Chunking is splitting documents into passages, chunks, that are embedded and indexed individually so retrieval can return the piece of a document relevant to a question rather than the whole document. Every later stage of a RAG system, embedding, retrieval, reranking, generation, can only choose among the chunks you created, so chunking sets the ceiling on answer quality. A chunk that lost its context cannot be recovered by a better model.**


Most RAG quality problems I have debugged were chunking problems in disguise. The model looked like it was hallucinating; the retriever was handing it half a table, or a paragraph whose subject lived in the previous chunk. Barnett et al. list missing content and wrongly ranked passages among the seven failure points of RAG systems, and both usually trace back to how documents were split [3].

> Before you tune prompts or switch models, print the chunks your retriever returned. Nine times out of ten, the bug is sitting right there in plain text.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building RAG.NextUpgrad</cite>

## Why does chunking matter so much?

**Three reasons. Embeddings represent one meaning per vector, so a chunk mixing several topics produces a blurred vector that matches nothing well. Retrieval returns whole chunks, so a chunk with the answer buried in unrelated text wastes the model's context and attention, and models attend poorly to the middle of long contexts [4]. And chunks are the unit of citation, so a chunk without its heading or page cannot be pointed at. Good chunks are precise, self-contained and traceable.**


## What are the chunking strategies?

**Fixed-size chunking splits every N tokens with an overlap and ignores structure; it is a baseline, not a strategy. Recursive splitting tries paragraph, then sentence, then word boundaries to hit a size. Structure-aware chunking splits on the document's own units, headings, paragraphs, list items, table rows, code blocks, and keeps them whole. Semantic chunking groups sentences by embedding similarity. Parent-child chunking indexes small chunks for precise retrieval but returns their larger parent for context. Most production systems use structure-aware splitting with a size cap and parent-child retrieval.**



LangChain and LlamaIndex ship implementations of each [7][8]; Unstructured partitions PDFs, Word files and HTML into typed elements you can chunk structurally [9]. The survey by Gao et al. covers these and the research variants [2].

## What is the best chunk size for RAG?

**Whatever size lets a chunk answer a realistic user question on its own, and that differs by corpus. Policy documents and manuals often work at a few hundred tokens; API references at one function signature plus its description; legal clauses at the clause; support tickets at the ticket. Anyone quoting one number without asking about your documents is guessing. Pick three candidate sizes, index each, run twenty real questions, measure recall at k, and keep the winner.**



My own experiments on this, with the numbers for the corpora I tested, are written up separately [12]. The pattern that repeated: smaller chunks retrieve more precisely but need a parent or a heading to be understood; larger chunks are understood alone but retrieve less precisely. Parent-child gets both.

## How much overlap should chunks have?

**Small: enough to catch a sentence that straddles a boundary, roughly ten to fifteen percent of the chunk, and none at all when you split on structure that already respects sentence and paragraph ends. Large overlaps duplicate text, inflate the index, and make the reranker see the same passage twice. If you find yourself increasing overlap to fix retrieval, the real problem is where the boundaries fall, and the fix is structure-aware splitting.**


## Should I add context to each chunk?

**Yes. Prepend the document title and the section heading path to every chunk, so a passage that says "the limit is 5 requests per second" is indexed and retrieved as "API Reference, Section 4.2 Rate limits: the limit is 5 requests per second". This single change did more for retrieval accuracy in RAG.NextUpgrad than any embedding model swap [13]. Contextual retrieval goes further by having a model write a short situating sentence for each chunk before embedding, at index-time cost [6].**



## How do I chunk PDFs, tables and code?

**PDFs: extract with layout awareness so columns, headers and footers are handled, then split on headings and paragraphs, keeping page numbers on every chunk; PyMuPDF and Unstructured both expose structure [9][10]. Tables: keep each table whole, or split by row groups while repeating the header row in every chunk, and consider a text summary of the table as an extra chunk. Code: split on functions, classes and files, never mid-function, and include the file path and imports as context. Slide decks: one slide per chunk with the title.**




## What is parent-child or hierarchical chunking?

**Index small chunks for precise matching, but store a pointer from each to a larger parent, the section or the page, and return the parent to the model at generation time. Retrieval is precise because small chunks have sharp embeddings; generation has context because the model reads the whole section. RAPTOR takes the idea further by building a tree of summaries over the corpus and retrieving at multiple levels [5]. For most systems, two levels, child and section, capture most of the benefit.**


## How do I evaluate chunking?

**Directly, at the retrieval stage, before any generation: build a set of real questions each labelled with the passage that answers it, and measure recall at k for your chunking configuration. Then read the misses. Was the answer split across two chunks? Was it retrieved but ranked low because the chunk was diluted? Was the heading lost? Each miss points at a specific chunking change. Generation metrics come later; you cannot generate a correct answer from a chunk that was never retrieved.**



## What are common chunking mistakes?

**Copying a chunk size from a tutorial. Splitting mid-sentence, mid-table or mid-function. Dropping the heading. Chunking a PDF's text in extraction order on a two-column page. Overlap so large that the reranker sees duplicates. No page or source metadata, so citations are impossible. Re-chunking without re-embedding. Never reading the retrieved chunks by eye. Every one of these produces a system that looks like it hallucinates and is actually retrieving garbage.**



## Chunking interview questions

**Explain why chunking matters more than the model. Compare fixed, recursive and structure-aware splitting. Say how you would choose a chunk size and defend the method, not the number. Explain parent-child retrieval. Describe how you would chunk a PDF with tables. Explain what metadata a chunk needs and why. These are stories if you have built a RAG system, definitions if you have not.**



## Where should I start?

**Take one real document set, write twenty questions and mark their answers, and index the corpus three ways: fixed 512 tokens, structure-aware, and structure-aware with headings prepended. Measure recall at 10 for each. The third will win, and you will understand why in a way no article can teach.** My longer guide and the experiment write-up are on the portfolio [11][12]. For a hands-on retrieval session at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
