# What is overfitting in machine learning, and how do you actually prevent it? Train/validation/test splits, regularization, and catching it early
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-overfitting-and-how-to-prevent-it/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is overfitting?

**Overfitting is when a model learns the specifics of its training data, including its noise and quirks, instead of the general pattern underneath it, so it performs very well on the data it was trained on and measurably worse on new data it has not seen. The model has effectively memorised answers rather than learned to reason from inputs to outputs, and the gap between training performance and validation or real-world performance is the tell.**


Every training run I evaluate, classic model or LLM fine-tune, gets checked against this exact failure before I trust a good-looking training metric.

> A model that aces its training data and stumbles on anything new hasn't learned. It has memorised the answer key.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How is overfitting different from underfitting?

**Overfitting is too much capacity relative to the signal in the data, or too little regularization, so the model fits noise as if it were signal. Underfitting is the opposite: the model is too simple, or trained too little, to capture even the real pattern, and performs poorly on both training and new data. Overfitting shows a large gap between training and validation performance; underfitting shows both scores mediocre and close together. The fixes are opposite too: overfitting needs less capacity or more regularization, underfitting needs more capacity or more training.**



## How does a train/validation/test split actually catch overfitting?

**Training data is what the model learns from. Validation data is held out and checked periodically during training, specifically to notice when validation performance stops improving or starts getting worse while training performance keeps improving, which is overfitting happening in real time. Test data is held out entirely until the very end, used exactly once, to report a final, honest number that was never used to make any decision during development. Without this separation, you have no way to distinguish a model that generalises from one that has simply memorised what you are checking it against.**




## What actually prevents overfitting?

**Regularization techniques such as L1 and L2 penalties discourage the model from relying too heavily on any single feature or weight [1]. Dropout randomly disables a fraction of neurons during training, forcing the network to not depend on any one path through it [2]. Early stopping halts training the moment validation performance stops improving, rather than training until training performance maxes out. More data, and more varied data, reduces the model's ability to memorise specifics because there are simply more specifics than it has capacity to memorise. Simplifying the model, fewer parameters or a shallower architecture, directly reduces its capacity to overfit in the first place.**



## What does overfitting look like when fine-tuning an LLM specifically?

**The model starts repeating training examples' exact phrasing verbatim, even in contexts where it does not quite fit, a strong sign it has memorised specific training completions rather than learned the underlying behaviour. Validation loss on held-out examples rises while training loss keeps falling, the same signature as classic overfitting, but often appearing faster than in classic ML because fine-tuning datasets are typically much smaller than pretraining corpora. The standard fixes shift accordingly: fewer training epochs, a lower learning rate, more varied examples per behaviour rather than many near-duplicates, and parameter-efficient methods like LoRA, which constrain how much the model's weights can shift in the first place [5].**



My longer walkthrough of reading a fine-tuning loss curve specifically, including what a healthy one looks like against an overfitting one, is on the portfolio [9].

## How do I catch overfitting early rather than after the fact?

**Watch the training and validation loss curves together from the first epoch, not just the final metric. The moment validation loss stops improving while training loss keeps dropping, that gap is overfitting starting, and it is far cheaper to stop or adjust there than to discover it only after evaluating a finished model. Set up automatic checkpointing at the point of best validation performance, not the last epoch, so the model you actually keep is the one before the overfitting started, not after.**



## What mistakes do people make with overfitting?

**Reporting training accuracy as if it were the model's real performance. Peeking at the test set during development and unconsciously tuning toward it, which quietly turns the test set into a second validation set and inflates the final number's honesty. Training for a fixed number of epochs regardless of what the validation curve says. Assuming more data always fixes overfitting, when sometimes the actual fix is a simpler model or a smaller learning rate. Ignoring that a small, over-repeated fine-tuning dataset can cause the exact same failure a huge classic-ML model shows with too little data.**



## Overfitting interview questions

**Define overfitting and contrast it with underfitting. Explain why a validation set is necessary and what leaking the test set into development actually breaks. Name three concrete techniques to prevent overfitting and what each one limits. Explain how overfitting shows up differently when fine-tuning an LLM compared with training a classic model. Describe how you would catch it early in a real training run. The strongest answer includes a loss curve you actually read and a decision it drove.**



## Where should I start?

**Look at the training and validation loss curves from your last training run, classic model or fine-tune, side by side. If you cannot find that plot, that is the first thing to fix before the next run.** For a hands-on session on training and evaluating models honestly, from loss curves to held-out test sets, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is personal branding? Why it matters, examples, and how to build one online
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-personal-branding/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Personal branding is the reputation you build on purpose: what people know you for, why they trust you, and where they can see your work. For a student or engineer, it might be "the person who builds AI tools for farmers" or "the one who explains system design clearly". It matters because many opportunities, internships, speaking invitations, clients and jobs, come through people who already know your work. I have built mine around shipping GenAI products, hackathons and teaching, so this page covers the definition, why and what for, how to build it online, examples, branding in business, and long-term tips. What is personal branding? Personal branding is the deliberate practice of shaping how others perceive you professionally: identifying what you want to be known for, doing work that proves it, and sharing that work consistently so the right people notice. Also asked as: how to make personal branding · how to get online personal branding Everyone has a reputation; personal branding means managing it rather than leaving it to chance. It is not about self-promotion for its own sake or pretending to be someone else. Strong personal brands are built on substance: projects shipped, problems solved, people helped, ideas explained well. Visibility amplifies substance; it cannot replace it. What is the definition of personal branding? Personal branding is the process of establishing and promoting a distinct professional identity, based on your skills, experience, values and personality, so that you are recognised and trusted for a specific area of expertise. Also asked as: what is personal branding definition The key elements in this definition are distinctiveness, expertise and trust. Distinctiveness means a clear focus, not "good at everything". Expertise means evidence: work others can see. Trust comes from consistency over time and honesty about what you know and do not know. A useful test: if someone mentions your name in a room, what would people say you are good at? What is personal branding and why is it important? Personal branding is how you are known professionally, and it is important because it makes opportunities find you: recruiters, collaborators, clients and event organisers prefer people whose work they have already seen. For students in India competing for internships and jobs, a visible track record, such as projects on GitHub, writing on LinkedIn or a personal site, talks at college events, and hackathon results, sets you apart from candidates with similar degrees. It also compounds: each project and post adds to a body of work that keeps working for you. Being known for something specific makes it easier for people to recommend you. What is the purpose of personal branding? The purpose is to connect your skills with the people who need them: to make it easy for the right audience to discover, understand and trust your work, so that opportunities come to you more often. Practical purposes include getting interviews and offers, attracting freelance clients, being invited to speak or judge, finding collaborators for projects or startups, and building a community around a topic. For me, sharing what I build and teach led to campus sessions and hackathon judging; the brand is the bridge between the work and the opportunities. Keep the purpose in mind: it decides which platforms and content matter. How do I build my personal brand? Choose a focus, do real work in it, document and share that work consistently, and engage genuinely with others in the field. Repeat for months; branding is a compound effect. Steps: Focus: pick one area, such as GenAI apps, web development or data analysis. Proof: build projects, write case studies, contribute to open source. Home base: a personal website plus LinkedIn and GitHub. Share: post what you learn and build, with specifics and lessons. Community: help others, join communities, speak at events. Consistency: same name, photo and positioning everywhere. Be honest: never claim results or credentials you do not have; credibility is the whole point. How do I step up my personal branding? Move from occasional posts to a system: a clear positioning line, a content plan around your focus, regular publishing, public projects with write-ups, speaking at events, and collaborations with others in your field. Also asked as: how to step up your personal branding Ways to level up: Turn each project into a short case study: problem, approach, result, lessons. Teach: workshops, college sessions, recorded tutorials. Write longer pieces on your own site that answer real questions. Engage thoughtfully with others' posts, not just your own. Track what resonates and do more of it. Founding TechVerse Enclave and speaking at college sessions helped me more than any single post, because teaching creates trust that content alone cannot. How do I build a personal brand online? Create a consistent online presence: a personal website as your hub, a complete LinkedIn profile, a GitHub with pinned projects for technical work, and one or two content channels where your audience already spends time. Practical steps: Use the same name, photo and one-line headline everywhere. Write a clear LinkedIn headline and about section focused on what you do. Publish project write-ups and lessons regularly. Link everything from your website, and your website from every profile. Make your work findable: descriptive titles and clear writing help search engines. Choose depth over breadth: doing two platforms well beats being inactive on ten. What are some examples of personal branding? Examples include a developer known for clear tutorials on a specific framework, a student known for building AI tools for local problems, a designer known for accessibility, or an engineer known for open-source contributions to a popular library. Also asked as: what is personal branding examples What these examples share: a specific focus, visible work, consistent sharing and a community around them. In tech, many strong brands started small: a blog solving one recurring problem, a GitHub repository many people use, a talk that got shared, or a hackathon project that solved a real need. Study people you admire, notice what they are known for, and how they made it visible, then apply the pattern to your own focus rather than copying their style. What is personal branding in business? In business, personal branding refers to founders, executives and professionals building public reputations that support their companies: a founder known for expertise attracts customers, investors and talent to the business. Founders often become the face of early-stage companies, sharing the journey, insights and product progress. Professionals inside companies build personal brands that also strengthen their employer's reputation, through talks, articles and community work. Balance matters: keep confidential information private, follow company policies, and ensure your personal brand aligns with your values and your organisation's. What are the best long-term personal branding tips? Focus on substance, consistency and generosity: keep doing good work, share it regularly for years, help others, stay honest about what you know, and let your focus evolve gradually rather than chasing trends. Also asked as: best long term personal branding tips Long-term principles: Build on platforms you own, such as your website, not only on rented social feeds. Keep a record of your work: projects, talks, articles. Prioritise relationships over follower counts. Update your positioning as you grow, but keep a thread of continuity. Never fabricate achievements; reputations are slow to build and fast to lose. Ten years of consistent, honest work is the most reliable personal brand strategy there is.

# What is pgvector in PostgreSQL? Install on Windows, HNSW, and estimating RAM
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-pgvector/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

pgvector is an open-source extension for PostgreSQL that adds a vector data type, distance operators and approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, so you can store embeddings next to your relational data and run similarity search with SQL. It is the most common way to add vector search to Postgres. PostgreSQL is a core part of my stack, so this page covers what pgvector is, the pgvector store, who owns it, installing and enabling it including on Windows, using it, HNSW, and estimating memory. What is pgvector in PostgreSQL? pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension for storing vectors and querying them by similarity. It adds vector column types, operators for L2 distance, inner product, cosine distance and L1 distance, and IVFFlat and HNSW indexes for fast approximate search. Because vectors live in normal tables, you get joins, transactions, backups, replication and row-level security, and you can filter by any column in the same query. It also supports half-precision vectors, binary vectors and sparse vectors for different storage and search needs. Most managed Postgres services, including those from major cloud providers, offer pgvector, so you can often enable it without installing anything. What is the pgvector store? "PGVector store" usually refers to the vector store integration in frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex that uses PostgreSQL with pgvector as the backend for storing document chunks, embeddings and metadata for retrieval. Also asked as: what is pgvector store In LangChain, the PGVector vector store, in the langchain-postgres package, creates tables for collections and embeddings and lets you add documents and run similarity searches with metadata filters through the standard retriever interface. It is convenient for prototypes. For production, many teams design their own tables, indexes and SQL for full control over schema, migrations, filters and hybrid search with Postgres full-text search. Who owns pgvector? pgvector was created by Andrew Kane, a developer known for many open-source libraries, and is maintained as an open-source project on GitHub with community contributions. It is released under the PostgreSQL licence, a permissive licence. No company owns it in a commercial sense; anyone can use, modify and distribute it, including in commercial products. Cloud providers and database companies contribute improvements and package it for their services. When using a managed service, check which pgvector version it offers, because features such as HNSW indexes, half-precision vectors and iterative index scans arrived in specific versions. How do I install pgvector? Use your platform's package manager or a ready-made Docker image. On Debian or Ubuntu with the PostgreSQL repository, install the package for your Postgres version; on macOS, use Homebrew; or run the pgvector/pgvector Docker image. Also asked as: how to install pgvector Examples: sudo apt install postgresql-16-pgvector # Debian or Ubuntu, Postgres 16 brew install pgvector # macOS with Homebrew docker run -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev -p 5432:5432 pgvector/pgvector:pg16 You can also compile from source with make and make install. On managed databases, you usually only need to enable the extension. Match the package to your exact PostgreSQL major version. How do I install pgvector in PostgreSQL on Windows? On Windows, build pgvector from source using Visual Studio's C++ build tools: open the x64 Native Tools Command Prompt as administrator, set PGROOT to your PostgreSQL install folder, then run nmake with the Windows makefile and install. Also asked as: how to install pgvector in postgresql windows set &quot;PGROOT=C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\16&quot; cd %TEMP% git clone https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector.git cd pgvector nmake /F Makefile.win nmake /F Makefile.win install Then enable the extension in your database. If building is inconvenient, run PostgreSQL with pgvector in Docker Desktop or WSL, which avoids compiling. Check the repository's README for the current version tag to clone. How do I enable pgvector in PostgreSQL? Connect to your database and run CREATE EXTENSION vector;. You need permission to create extensions, and the extension must be installed on the server. Enable it in each database where you need it. Also asked as: how to enable pgvector in postgresql Verify with SELECT extversion FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'vector';. On managed services, you may need to allow the extension in settings first, depending on the provider. To upgrade after installing a newer version, run ALTER EXTENSION vector UPDATE;. Note the extension's SQL name is vector, not pgvector, which is a common source of "extension does not exist" errors. How do I use pgvector in PostgreSQL? Create a table with a vector column of your embedding's dimension, insert embeddings from your model, create an HNSW index, and query with a distance operator ordered by nearest first, with a limit. Also asked as: how to use pgvector in postgresql CREATE TABLE chunks (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, content text, embedding vector(768)); CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops); SELECT id, content FROM chunks ORDER BY embedding &lt;=&gt; $1 LIMIT 5; The &lt;=&gt; operator is cosine distance, &lt;-&gt; is L2 distance and &lt;#&gt; is negative inner product. Add WHERE clauses for metadata filters, and combine with Postgres full-text search for hybrid retrieval. Does pgvector support HNSW? Yes. pgvector added HNSW indexes in version 0.5.0 in 2023, alongside its earlier IVFFlat indexes. HNSW generally gives better speed and recall trade-offs than IVFFlat and does not need a training step, though it builds more slowly and uses more memory. Tune with m, the number of connections per node, and ef_construction when building, and hnsw.ef_search at query time for higher recall. Build indexes after bulk loading data for speed, and increase maintenance_work_mem so the graph fits in memory during builds. Newer versions support parallel index builds and iterative scans that help when filters remove many results. Does pgvector use Lucene-based HNSW? No. pgvector implements HNSW itself, in C, inside PostgreSQL's index access method framework. Lucene, the library behind Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, has its own separate HNSW implementation. Also asked as: does pgvector use lucene based hnsw Both follow the same algorithm from the 2016 HNSW paper by Malkov and Yashunin, with multi-layer graphs of nearest neighbours, but implementations differ in storage, concurrency, filtering and tuning parameters. pgvector's index is stored in PostgreSQL pages, uses its buffer cache and benefits from write-ahead logging and replication. So performance comparisons between pgvector and Lucene-based engines depend on configuration and workload, not the algorithm name. How do I calculate the RAM needed for N vectors of D dimensions with pgvector HNSW? Start with raw vector size: N times D times 4 bytes for standard vectors, plus a small per-row overhead. The HNSW index stores the vectors again plus graph links, so budget roughly the same again or more for the index, then measure. Also asked as: how to calculate amount of ram required for serving x n-dimensional vectors with pgvector (hnsw Example: one million 768-dimension vectors take about 3 GB as raw data, and the HNSW index adds a similar amount or more, depending on m. For fast queries, the index should fit in RAM, so plan for shared buffers and the operating system cache to hold it. Reduce memory with half-precision halfvec, which halves storage, or binary quantisation with re-ranking. Build an index on a sample and check pg_relation_size to extrapolate accurately.

# What is prompt engineering? How it works, examples, courses and jobs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-prompt-engineering-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Prompt engineering is the practice of designing the instructions, context and examples you give an AI model so that it produces accurate, useful and consistent output. For everyday users it means writing clearer requests; for developers it means system prompts, structured outputs and evaluation inside applications. This page defines it, explains how and why it works, gives examples, points to the best courses and official guides, estimates how long it takes to learn, where to practise, what the jobs look like, and whether it still matters as models improve.

## What is prompt engineering?

Prompt engineering is the process of crafting and refining inputs to a generative AI model, including instructions, context, examples and output format, to get reliable results for a specific task.

It covers simple techniques, such as stating the goal and audience, and engineering practices, such as writing system prompts, giving few-shot examples, requiring JSON that matches a schema, splitting tasks into steps, and testing prompts against a set of cases. In applications, prompts are part of the code: versioned, reviewed and evaluated. Good prompt engineering is less about magic phrases and more about clear communication plus measurement.

## How does AI prompt engineering work?

A language model generates text based on everything in its input. Prompt engineering shapes that input: clear instructions, relevant context and examples make the desired answer the most likely continuation, and format rules constrain the output.

Common techniques:

- **Role and goal**: who the model should act as and what success looks like.
- **Context**: the documents, data or code the answer must use.
- **Few-shot examples**: two or three input-output pairs showing the format.
- **Decomposition**: break complex tasks into steps or separate calls.
- **Reasoning**: ask the model to think through the problem before answering.
- **Output contracts**: a JSON schema or exact template.

Then test on varied examples and adjust based on failures.

## Why does prompt engineering work?

It works because models condition every word they generate on the input. Specific instructions and examples narrow the range of likely outputs towards what you want, while vague prompts leave the model to guess.

Research showed early on that large models can learn tasks from a few examples in the prompt, called few-shot learning, and that asking for step-by-step reasoning improves results on maths and logic, known as chain-of-thought prompting. Instruction tuning makes modern models follow directions well, so clear directions matter more than tricks. Context is the biggest lever: giving the model the right document turns a guess into a grounded answer, which is the principle behind retrieval-augmented generation.

## What are some prompt engineering examples?

Examples range from everyday requests to production patterns. A weak prompt is "summarise this"; a strong one is "Summarise this lecture transcript for a first-year student in five bullet points, each under 20 words, then list three terms to revise."

More patterns:

- **Extraction**: "Extract name, date and amount from this invoice as JSON matching this schema. Use null if missing."
- **Classification**: "Label this support email as billing, technical or other. Reply with the label only."
- **Grounded Q&A**: "Answer only from the passages below and cite passage IDs. If the answer is not there, say so."
- **Code review**: "Review this function for bugs and security issues. List each with a line number and a fix."
- **Tutoring**: "Ask me one question at a time on recursion and explain my mistakes."

## What are the best prompt engineering courses?

Start with free resources: DeepLearning.AI's short course on ChatGPT prompt engineering for developers, and the official prompting guides from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Then learn by building and evaluating a small application.

Choose courses that teach transferable skills: structured outputs, evaluation with test sets, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use and safety, not lists of "magic prompts". Paid courses can help with structure, but the material changes quickly as models improve, so prefer recently updated content. A practical self-course: pick one task, such as extracting fields from receipts, build a test set of fifty examples, and improve the prompt until accuracy stops rising, logging every change.

## Where is OpenAI's prompt engineering guide?

OpenAI publishes a prompt engineering guide in its platform documentation, covering clear instructions, providing reference text, splitting complex tasks, giving the model time to think, using tools and testing changes systematically.

Read it alongside Anthropic's and Google's guides, since the core advice overlaps and each adds model-specific tips, such as how to use system messages, XML-style tags or structured outputs. Guides are updated as models change, so check the date and prefer official documentation over older blog posts. The most valuable advice in all of them is the same: be specific, give context and examples, and evaluate.

## How long does it take to learn prompt engineering?

The basics take a few days of practice: clear instructions, context, examples and format. Using prompts well inside real applications takes weeks to months, because it involves evaluation, structured outputs, retrieval, tool use and handling edge cases.

A realistic path for a developer: one week to learn techniques and build a few prompts; two to four weeks to build a small app with a test set and measure improvements; ongoing practice as models change. For non-technical users, a few hours of deliberate practice with real tasks, such as emails, summaries and study notes, already makes a big difference. Speed comes from writing many prompts and examining failures, not from reading lists of templates.

## Where can I practise prompt engineering?

Practise in the free tiers of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for everyday tasks, and in developer playgrounds such as Google AI Studio, the OpenAI Playground and Anthropic's Console for system prompts, parameters and structured outputs.

Good practice tasks:

- Turn messy notes into a structured study guide.
- Extract fields from ten real receipts into JSON, then measure accuracy.
- Build a classifier for messages into three categories with a test set.
- Write a grounded Q&A prompt over a document and test unanswerable questions.
- Compare two models on the same prompts.

Keep a prompt log: the prompt, the model, the result and what you changed. That log is how you improve.

## What are prompt engineering jobs?

Dedicated "prompt engineer" roles exist but are uncommon; prompt engineering is now mostly a skill within roles such as AI engineer, GenAI developer, ML engineer, AI product manager, conversation designer, technical writer and domain experts who build AI workflows.

Employers hiring for GenAI work expect prompt skills plus software engineering: APIs, retrieval, evaluation, deployment and cost control. Domain experts, such as lawyers, doctors and teachers, with strong prompting skills are also valuable for building and testing AI tools in their fields. To show the skill, build a project with a measurable result, such as "improved extraction accuracy from 78 to 95 per cent on 200 documents by restructuring the prompt and adding validation", documented in a README.

## Does prompt engineering still matter?

Yes, but its form has changed. Models now follow plain instructions well, so tricks matter less, while clear specifications, good context, structured outputs and evaluation matter more than ever, especially in products and agents.

What has faded: elaborate magic phrases and fragile hacks. What remains: clearly defining the task, supplying the right information, setting output contracts, and testing systematically. In agentic systems, writing tool descriptions and system instructions is prompt engineering under another name. As models improve, the bottleneck shifts from wording to knowing exactly what you want and giving the model what it needs to do it.

# What is public speaking? Definition, types, why it matters, and how to start
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-public-speaking/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Public speaking is the act of presenting a structured message, live or recorded, to an audience, with the aim of informing, persuading, demonstrating or celebrating. It ranges from a class presentation to a conference keynote. I have spoken at more than 20 campus sessions, including the VSICS induction for over 100 first-year students in July 2025, so this page covers the definition, what counts, its types and origins, why it matters, whether it suits everyone, and how to start, practise and build a speaking career. What is the definition of public speaking? Public speaking is the process of communicating information, ideas or stories to a live audience in a structured, deliberate way, adapted to that audience's needs, with the goal of informing, persuading, inspiring or entertaining. Also asked as: what is public speaking definition · why public speaking matters · how to practice public speaking The key elements are a speaker, a message, an audience, a purpose and a context. Unlike conversation, public speaking is planned, mostly one-to-many, and usually has a defined time and structure. It is sometimes called oratory or presentation skills. The core skills are organising ideas, connecting with listeners, using voice and body language well, and managing nerves. What counts as public speaking? Any time you present a prepared message to a group counts: class presentations, project vivas, team meetings, interviews, webinars, conference talks, hackathon pitches, wedding toasts, and increasingly recorded videos and live streams. Informal settings count too: introducing yourself in a meeting, explaining an idea to a group, or answering questions after a demo. Recognising this helps beginners, because it means you already practise public speaking in daily life and can improve through those small moments. Hackathon pitches are a good example: three minutes, a live demo and questions from judges, which is public speaking under pressure. How many types of public speaking are there? Most frameworks describe four main types: informative speaking, which explains; persuasive speaking, which changes beliefs or actions; demonstrative speaking, which shows how to do something; and special occasion or ceremonial speaking, such as toasts and tributes. Other classifications add entertaining speeches, impromptu speaking, panel discussions and debates. Many real talks blend types: a technical talk informs and demonstrates, then persuades the audience to try a tool. My campus sessions on careers in AI combine an informative roadmap with persuasion to start building projects early. Knowing the primary purpose helps you choose structure and tone. Who invented public speaking? No single person invented it; people have spoken to groups since language began. The formal study of public speaking, rhetoric, developed in ancient Greece in the fifth century BCE, with Corax and Tisias in ancient Sicily often credited as early teachers. Aristotle's "Rhetoric" defined lasting ideas: persuasion through ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, emotion; and logos, logic. Roman orators such as Cicero and teachers such as Quintilian further developed the discipline. Many cultures, including India, have rich traditions of oratory, debate and storytelling. Modern speaking advice still largely builds on these ancient foundations. Why does public speaking matter? Public speaking matters because ideas spread through people who can explain them clearly. It affects careers, leadership, education and civic life: job interviews, team leadership, pitching projects, teaching and advocating for causes all depend on it. Strong speakers get more opportunities, because visibility follows people who can share their work. In tech, engineers who can explain their projects in demos and talks progress faster than equally skilled peers who cannot. Speaking also spreads knowledge: a single session can change how many students approach their first year. That is why I keep giving campus talks alongside building products. What does public speaking help with? Public speaking builds confidence, clear thinking, persuasion, leadership and networking. It helps in interviews, presentations, meetings, sales, teaching and any role where you need others to understand or act on your ideas. Preparing a talk forces you to understand a topic deeply and organise it logically, which improves your writing and problem solving too. Speaking at events creates connections: people approach speakers afterwards with questions, opportunities and collaborations. It also helps you handle pressure, think on your feet during questions, and receive feedback gracefully, skills that transfer to every part of professional life. Is public speaking for everyone? Yes, in the sense that almost anyone can learn to speak clearly and confidently with practice. Fear of public speaking is very common, and many skilled speakers started nervous. Styles differ: quiet, thoughtful speakers can be just as effective as energetic ones. Not everyone needs to become a keynote speaker, but everyone benefits from being able to explain their work, ask for what they need and present ideas in meetings. Introverts often prepare more thoroughly, which is an advantage. If anxiety is severe, start with very small, supportive audiences and build gradually; professional support is worth seeking if fear significantly limits your life. How do I start public speaking? Start small and low-stakes: speak up in class or meetings, present a short topic to friends, join a club such as Toastmasters or your college's tech community, and volunteer for brief talks, like a five-minute demo of your project. Also asked as: how to start public speaking A beginner's path: Pick a topic you know well, ideally something you built. Prepare a simple structure: problem, story or demo, key points, takeaway. Practise out loud several times, timing yourself. Give the talk to a small, friendly group and ask for feedback. Speak again within a few weeks to build momentum. Each talk becomes easier. My first sessions were to small groups of juniors; that is where confidence started. How do I practise public speaking? Practise out loud, not just in your head, ideally standing up, with a timer, and record yourself on video to review pace, filler words and body language. Get feedback from friends or a speaking club, and repeat. Effective practice habits: Rehearse the opening and closing until they are natural. Practise with your slides or demo exactly as you will present. Do one run for a friend and ask what was unclear. Practise answering likely questions. Practise impromptu speaking: one minute on a random topic daily. Record your actual talks too; reviewing a real session teaches more than rehearsals alone. How do I start a public speaking career? Build expertise in a topic, speak for free at colleges, meetups and communities to gain experience, record your talks, create a speaker page with topics and past sessions, and grow through referrals. Paid speaking usually follows a track record and visibility. Also asked as: how to start public speaking career Steps: Choose two or three topics where you have real experience. Create a short speaker bio and talk descriptions. Speak at local communities, colleges and online events. Collect recordings, photos and testimonials. Publish writing or videos on your topics to build visibility. Make it easy to invite you, with a clear contact or invite page. My own site has an invite page for campus sessions, which turns interest into actual bookings.

# What is Qdrant? How it works, who made it, vs Elasticsearch and Milvus, installing
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-qdrant/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Qdrant is an open-source vector database, written in Rust, for storing embeddings and searching them by similarity with fast metadata filtering. It runs as a single service you can self-host or use through Qdrant Cloud, and is a popular choice for RAG, semantic search and recommendations. I build RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid retrieval, so this page explains what Qdrant is, how it works and stores data, who made it and when, how it compares with Elasticsearch and Milvus, images, and installation. What is Qdrant DB? Qdrant is a vector database and similarity search engine. You store vectors, such as text or image embeddings, with JSON payloads, then query for the nearest vectors to a query vector, optionally filtered by payload fields such as category, date or user. Also asked as: how qdrant db works It supports dense vectors, sparse vectors for keyword-style hybrid search, multiple named vectors per record, and multi-vector representations. It offers REST and gRPC APIs with client libraries for Python, JavaScript, Rust, Go, Java and .NET. It is licensed under Apache 2.0. Typical use cases include RAG retrieval, semantic product search, recommendations, duplicate detection and anomaly detection. How does Qdrant work? Qdrant organises data into collections of points. Each point has an ID, vectors and a payload. It builds an HNSW graph index over vectors for fast approximate search, and payload indexes for filtering, applying filters during graph traversal so results stay accurate. When you query, Qdrant walks the HNSW graph towards the query vector while skipping points that fail the filter, then returns the top matches with scores and payloads. It supports cosine, dot product, Euclidean and Manhattan distances. Quantisation options compress vectors to cut memory, with rescoring on original vectors for accuracy. For hybrid search, it can combine dense and sparse results with fusion in a single query. Distributed mode shards and replicates collections across nodes. How does Qdrant store data? Qdrant stores each collection in segments containing vectors, payloads and indexes. Writes go first to a write-ahead log for durability, then into segments, which are optimised and merged in the background. You can keep vectors in memory for speed or on disk with memory-mapped files to handle collections larger than RAM, and similarly choose where payloads live. Snapshots let you back up and restore collections. When self-hosting, mount the storage directory on persistent disk, otherwise data disappears when a container is removed. Quantised vectors can stay in memory while full-precision originals stay on disk, a common way to balance speed and cost. Who made Qdrant? Qdrant was created by Andre Zayarni, the company's chief executive, and Andrey Vasnetsov, its chief technology officer, who began it as an open-source project. Qdrant the company, based in Germany, develops the database and runs Qdrant Cloud. The project is developed in the open on GitHub, with contributions from the community. The company is venture-backed and offers managed cloud, hybrid cloud and enterprise options alongside the free open-source version. For users, this means a commercially supported product with an open-source core, so you can self-host without licence fees or move to managed hosting later. When was Qdrant founded? Qdrant the company was founded in 2021; the open-source project started a little earlier, around 2020, with early releases on GitHub. It grew quickly as RAG made vector search a mainstream need after 2022. Since then, it has added features such as sparse vectors, hybrid queries, multi-vector support, quantisation, distributed deployment and a managed cloud. Vector databases as a category are young, so features change rapidly; check the release notes and documentation for current capabilities rather than relying on older comparisons. Qdrant vs Elasticsearch: which should I use? Use Elasticsearch when full-text search, aggregations and log analytics are central and vector search is an addition. Use Qdrant when vector similarity with filtering is the core workload and you want a lighter, specialised engine. Elasticsearch has mature BM25 search, analysers for many languages, aggregations and a huge ecosystem, plus dense-vector kNN search. It is heavier to run and tune. Qdrant is purpose-built for vectors, efficient with filtered search and quantisation, and simpler to operate, with sparse vectors for keyword-style signals. Many RAG teams pair a keyword engine with a vector engine, or use one that does both well enough; measure on your own queries before deciding. Qdrant vs Milvus: what is the difference? Both are open-source vector databases. Milvus is a distributed, cloud-native system built for very large scale, with separate components and GPU index options. Qdrant is a single Rust service that is simpler to run, with optional distributed mode. Milvus suits teams expecting billions of vectors and willing to operate a more complex architecture, or using Zilliz Cloud. Qdrant suits teams wanting quick setup, strong filtering and efficient resource use, scaling out when needed, or using Qdrant Cloud. Performance comparisons depend heavily on dataset, recall target and configuration, so run your own benchmark with your vectors and filters rather than trusting vendor charts. Can Qdrant store images? Qdrant stores image embeddings, not image files. You compute vectors with an image model such as CLIP, store them in Qdrant with a payload containing the image's URL or storage path, and keep the actual images in object storage or a file system. Payloads can technically hold encoded image data, but it bloats the database and slows queries, so avoid it. This pattern enables image search by text, finding similar images and duplicate detection. It also helps privacy: FaceVision follows the same principle, storing face embeddings and never the images themselves. If you need image and text search together, store multiple named vectors per point. How do I install Qdrant locally? The simplest way is Docker: pull the image and run it with ports 6333 for REST and 6334 for gRPC, mounting a folder for storage. The dashboard is then available on port 6333 in your browser. Also asked as: how to install qdrant locally docker pull qdrant/qdrant docker run -p 6333:6333 -p 6334:6334 \ -v &quot;$(pwd)/qdrant_storage:/qdrant/storage&quot; qdrant/qdrant Then pip install qdrant-client and connect to localhost on port 6333. For quick experiments without any server, the Python client has a local mode that runs in memory or saves to a folder. Enable an API key before exposing Qdrant beyond your machine. How do I install Qdrant on Windows? On Windows, install Docker Desktop with the WSL 2 backend, then run the same Docker command as on other systems, using a Windows path or named volume for storage. Alternatively, use the Python client's local mode for development without running a server. Also asked as: how to install qdrant in windows In PowerShell, mount storage with a full path such as -v ${PWD}/qdrant_storage:/qdrant/storage, or use a named Docker volume to avoid path issues. Qdrant also publishes release binaries; check the GitHub releases page for current Windows support. For production, run Qdrant on Linux servers or a managed cloud, and treat Windows setups as development environments.

# What is quantization in LLMs? 4-bit and 8-bit models, GGUF vs AWQ vs GPTQ, quality loss, and running big models on small hardware
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-quantization-in-llms/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is quantization in LLMs?

**Quantization is storing a model's weights, and sometimes its activations, in fewer bits than they were trained in: 8-bit or 4-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats. Each weight is mapped to a small grid of values with a scale factor per block, so the model takes a half or a quarter of the memory and often runs faster, at the cost of a small approximation error. It is why a 7-billion-parameter model that needs about 14 GB in 16-bit runs on a laptop with 8 GB in 4-bit.**


Quantization is the reason open models became usable outside data centres. LLM.int8() showed 8-bit inference at scale with almost no loss [1]; the k-bit scaling-law paper argued that for a fixed memory budget, 4-bit weights on a bigger model usually beat 16-bit weights on a smaller one [5]. QLoRA then made 4-bit the basis for training, not just inference [2].

I quantize every model that leaves FineTune Studio, because a fine-tuned adapter is only useful once it is running somewhere, and "somewhere" is usually a machine smaller than the one that trained it [12].

> Quantization is the difference between a model that impressed you in a notebook and a model your users can actually run.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does quantization work?

**Weights are grouped into blocks, typically 32 to 128 values. For each block, the largest magnitude sets a scale, and every weight is rounded to the nearest point on a small integer grid, 256 points for 8-bit, 16 for 4-bit. At inference, the integers are multiplied back by the scale, exactly or approximately, before the matrix multiplication. Smarter methods choose the grid or the rounding to minimise error on real activations rather than on the weights alone.**



### What is NF4?

**NF4, NormalFloat4, is the 4-bit data type QLoRA introduced: instead of an evenly spaced grid, its 16 levels are placed where normally distributed weights actually cluster, so the same 4 bits capture more of the distribution [2]. It is a training-time quantization for the frozen base model, held in memory while adapters train; it is not a serving format. When people fine-tune "in 4-bit", this is usually what they mean.**


## What are GGUF, AWQ and GPTQ?

**GGUF is a file format used by llama.cpp that packages a quantized model with its metadata for fast loading on CPUs, Apple Silicon and consumer GPUs; its quantization schemes are named like Q4_K_M and Q8_0 [6]. GPTQ is a post-training method that quantizes weights layer by layer using calibration data to minimise output error, aimed at GPU inference [3]. AWQ observes that a small fraction of weights matter far more, protects them by scaling, and quantizes the rest, also for GPUs [4]. Same goal, different trade-offs and runtimes.**



The rule of thumb I give: GGUF if it runs on a laptop or a phone, AWQ or GPTQ if it runs on a GPU server behind vLLM [10], NF4 through bitsandbytes if you are training [7]. The Transformers quantization guide covers loading each [8].

## How much quality do you lose with quantization?

**Little at 8-bit, usually within noise on most benchmarks. Modest at 4-bit for chat, summarisation and extraction, and more noticeable on arithmetic, code generation and long multi-step reasoning, where small errors compound. Below 4 bits the drop steepens quickly. Larger models tolerate quantization better than small ones, so a 4-bit 13B usually beats a 16-bit 7B in the same memory [5]. Measure on your own task before trusting any of these generalisations.**




## How is quantization related to QLoRA and fine-tuning?

**QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model to NF4 so it fits in memory while small adapters train in higher precision [2]. That is quantization for training. After training you merge the adapter into the 16-bit base weights and then quantize the merged model for serving with GGUF, AWQ or GPTQ. Do not quantize before merging, and do not merge into a 4-bit base for serving; reload the base in 16-bit, merge, then quantize.**



My own notes on this pipeline, with the commands, are on the portfolio [11].


## How much memory does a quantized model need?

**Roughly parameters in billions times bytes per weight, plus a few gigabytes for activations and the KV cache that grows with context length and concurrent users. Two bytes per weight at 16-bit, one at 8-bit, about half a byte at 4-bit. So 7B is about 14, 7 and 4 to 5 GB; 13B about 26, 13 and 8 GB; 70B about 140, 70 and 40 GB. Long contexts add memory fast, which is why a model that "fits" can still run out at 32,000 tokens.**



## How do I quantize a model myself?

**For local use: convert the merged model to GGUF with llama.cpp's conversion script and quantize to a variant such as Q4_K_M or Q8_0, then run it with llama.cpp or Ollama [6][9]. For GPU serving: quantize with AWQ or GPTQ using a few hundred calibration samples that resemble your real inputs, then serve with vLLM [10]. For loading in Transformers without a conversion step: bitsandbytes 8-bit or 4-bit at load time [7]. Always keep the 16-bit merged model as the source of truth.**


## Which quantization should I choose?

**Decide by where the model runs and what it does. Laptop or phone: GGUF Q4_K_M as the default, Q8_0 if memory allows. GPU server: AWQ or GPTQ 4-bit behind vLLM, 8-bit if quality on hard tasks matters. Training: NF4 via bitsandbytes. Maths, code or long reasoning as the main task: prefer 8-bit or a bigger 4-bit model. Then confirm on your eval set. The wrong answer is to skip the measurement.**



## Quantization interview questions

**Explain what quantization does and why it saves memory. Compare 8-bit and 4-bit loss. Explain the difference between GGUF, AWQ and GPTQ and where each runs. Explain NF4 and its role in QLoRA. Describe the adapter-to-serving pipeline. Estimate the memory of a 13B model at 4-bit. Each is answered above; the strongest evidence is a model you quantized and measured.**



## Where should I start?

**Pull a 7B model in GGUF through Ollama at Q4_K_M and at Q8_0, ask each the same twenty questions including some arithmetic and code, and note where they differ. Then quantize a model you fine-tuned yourself and run the same comparison against the 16-bit merged version.** For a hands-on session on fine-tuning and deploying models on modest hardware, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is RAG in AI? Retrieval-augmented generation, explained from a production system
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-rag-in-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is RAG in AI?

**RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, is a way of building AI answers in two moves: first search a store of your own documents for the passages most relevant to the question, then hand those passages to a large language model and have it write the answer from them, with citations.** The model no longer answers from memory alone. It answers from evidence you chose, which is why RAG is the default architecture for chatbots over company documents, support desks, legal and medical search, and any product where "I'm not sure" beats a confident guess.


The term comes from a 2020 paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI Research, which combined a dense retriever with a sequence-to-sequence generator and showed the pair beat purely parametric models on knowledge-intensive tasks while producing more specific, factual language [1]. The idea has since grown into an entire engineering discipline, catalogued in surveys such as Gao et al. [2].

The one-sentence version I give students: a plain LLM is a very well-read person answering with the library door locked. RAG unlocks the door, walks them to the right shelf, and asks them to quote the page.

> A RAG demo works on the one document you tested it with. A RAG product works on the document a stranger uploads at 2 a.m. Everything in this guide is about closing that gap.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building RAG.NextUpgrad</cite>

## How does RAG work?

**RAG runs in two phases. Offline, you split documents into chunks, turn each chunk into an embedding vector and store it in an index. Online, you embed the user's question, pull the closest chunks, optionally rerank them, and prompt the model with the question plus those chunks so it answers from them.**



The offline phase is where most quality is won or lost, because everything downstream can only choose among the chunks you created. The online phase is where latency and cost live, since each question costs an embedding call, a search, possibly a reranker pass and a generation.

In RAG.NextUpgrad, the platform I built at NextUpgrad in 2026, the online path looks like this: the query is embedded and also tokenised for BM25, both retrievers return candidates, reciprocal rank fusion merges them, a cross-encoder reranks the top set, a confidence gate checks whether the evidence actually supports an answer, and only then does the model stream a response with inline citations [17].

### What is a RAG pipeline?

**A RAG pipeline is the chain of components that turns a raw document collection and a user question into a cited answer: loaders, a chunker, an embedding model, a vector index, usually a keyword index, a retriever, a reranker, a prompt template, the LLM and an evaluation harness.** Frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex give you each piece; the engineering is in choosing and tuning them for your documents.


### What is a RAG model?

**There is no separate "RAG model". RAG is a system pattern that wraps an ordinary language model, open or closed, with a retriever.** The original paper trained the retriever and generator jointly [1], but almost every production system today uses an off-the-shelf embedding model for retrieval and an off-the-shelf LLM for generation, connected by code.


## Why do we need RAG? Why is it important?

**RAG solves three problems a plain LLM cannot: it knows nothing after its training cutoff, it knows nothing about your private data, and when it lacks facts it invents plausible text. Retrieval supplies current, private, checkable facts at answer time, so the model can quote instead of guess.**


The practical benefits, in the order clients care about them:

- **Grounding and citations.** Every sentence can point at the passage it came from, which makes answers auditable. This matters more than raw accuracy in regulated work.
- **Freshness without retraining.** Add a document to the index and it is answerable a minute later. Retraining or fine-tuning a model for new facts takes hours and still does not cite.
- **Access control.** Retrieval can filter by user, tenant or clearance before the model ever sees the text. A fine-tuned model has no such boundary.
- **Cost.** Retrieval is cheap compared with training, and with a small model plus good retrieval you often match a much larger model answering from memory.

The limit is just as important: RAG helps with what the model knows, not how it reasons or writes. If your problem is tone, format or a specialised skill, retrieval will not fix it. That is where fine-tuning belongs.

## What is the difference between RAG and fine-tuning?

**RAG changes what the model can see at answer time; fine-tuning changes the model's weights, so it changes how the model behaves. Use RAG when the answer depends on facts, documents or anything that changes. Use fine-tuning when you need a consistent style, a strict output format, a niche skill, or lower latency and cost on a narrow task. Many production systems do both.**




I have built both kinds of platform in the same year, RAG.NextUpgrad and FineTune Studio, and the question I ask clients is one word: is the problem *knowledge* or *behaviour*? Knowledge is retrieval. Behaviour is training. A support bot that must know your refund policy is a knowledge problem. A model that must write incident reports in your house format is a behaviour problem. A bot that must do both is RAG for the policy and a small fine-tune for the voice.

### What is the difference between RAG and prompt engineering?

**Prompt engineering writes better instructions for the model; RAG adds a retrieval system that supplies evidence to those instructions. Prompt engineering alone cannot give the model facts it never saw, but every RAG system still needs a well-engineered prompt that tells the model to answer only from the passages and to say so when they are insufficient.**


## What is chunking in RAG, and what is the best chunking strategy?

**Chunking is splitting documents into passages that can be embedded and retrieved on their own. The best strategy respects the document's structure, headings, paragraphs, table rows and code blocks, keeps chunks small enough to be precise and large enough to be understood alone, and prepends the section heading to each chunk so a passage carries its context.**


There is no universal chunk size, and anyone quoting one without asking about your documents is guessing. What holds across the projects I have shipped:

1. **Chunk for the question, not the document.** A chunk should be able to answer a realistic user question by itself. For policy documents that is often a few hundred tokens; for API references it can be one function signature plus its description.
2. **Overlap is insurance, not a strategy.** A small overlap catches sentences that straddle a boundary. Large overlaps duplicate what the reranker sees and inflate the index.
3. **Never split inside a structure.** Tables, code blocks, numbered procedures, and a heading with its first paragraph belong together. Splitting them yields chunks that are individually meaningless.
4. **Carry the heading.** Prepending "Section 4.2, Rate limits" to a chunk that says "the limit is 5 requests per second" did more for answer accuracy in RAG.NextUpgrad than any embedding model change.


Barnett et al. list missing content and wrongly ranked chunks among the seven failure points of RAG systems, and both usually trace back to chunking decisions [10].

## What are embeddings, and which embedding model is best for RAG?

**An embedding is a list of numbers, a vector, that represents the meaning of a piece of text so that texts about the same thing end up close together. RAG uses embeddings to find chunks that are semantically similar to the question even when they share no keywords. The best model is the one that scores well on retrieval for your language and domain on the MTEB benchmark and fits your latency and cost budget; test two or three on your own questions before committing.**


Dense retrieval with learned embeddings was shown to beat traditional keyword retrieval for open-domain question answering by Karpukhin et al. in 2020 [3], and that result is why almost every RAG system starts with a vector index. Three practical notes:

- **Dimensions are a trade-off, not a score.** A 1,536-dimension vector costs more storage and search time than a 384-dimension one. Whether it retrieves better for you is an empirical question.
- **Embeddings are not tokens.** Tokens are the pieces a model reads; an embedding is a single vector summarising a whole chunk. People search for the difference often enough that it deserves saying plainly.
- **Switching models means re-embedding everything.** Vectors from two models are not comparable. Budget for a full re-index when you upgrade.

The MTEB leaderboard on Hugging Face ranks open and commercial embedding models on retrieval and other tasks [14]. Use it to shortlist, then evaluate on your own documents, because leaderboard corpora are not your corpus.

## What is a vector database, and do I need one?

**A vector database stores embeddings and answers "which stored vectors are closest to this one" quickly, usually with an approximate nearest-neighbour index. You need one when your index outgrows memory, needs filtering by metadata, or must serve many concurrent users. For a prototype or a few hundred thousand chunks, a library such as FAISS or the pgvector extension inside the Postgres you already run is enough.**



FAISS is described in Johnson, Douze and Jégou's 2017 paper and remains the reference implementation for in-process search [7]. pgvector adds vector columns and indexes to PostgreSQL [15]. Qdrant is documented at qdrant.tech [16]. My default for a new client project is pgvector, because the vectors then live next to the metadata, the permissions and the audit log, and "one more database to operate" is a real cost for a small team.

## What is hybrid search in RAG?

**Hybrid search runs two retrievers on every question, a keyword retriever such as BM25 and a dense embedding retriever, then merges their ranked lists. Keywords catch exact terms, product codes, names and rare words that embeddings blur; embeddings catch paraphrases and meaning that keywords miss. Fusing them, most simply with reciprocal rank fusion, gives better recall than either alone.**


BM25 is the classic probabilistic ranking function, described in full by Robertson and Zaragoza [4]. Reciprocal rank fusion, from Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher, scores each document by the sum of 1 divided by (a constant plus its rank) in every list, which needs no score normalisation and was shown to outperform more complex fusion methods [5]. It is a dozen lines of code and it is in RAG.NextUpgrad exactly because of that paper.

The pattern I see in support corpora: users ask with the product's own words ("error E-4021", "Form 16"), and dense retrieval alone often returns something semantically nearby but wrong. BM25 nails the exact token. The reverse happens for how-do-I questions phrased in plain language, where BM25 misses and embeddings win. Hybrid is not a luxury; it is the fix for both.

## What is reranking in RAG?

**Reranking is a second scoring pass over the top retrieved candidates using a model that reads the question and the passage together, a cross-encoder, and outputs a relevance score. Retrievers compare vectors computed separately for speed; a reranker looks at the pair, which is far more accurate, so you retrieve, say, 30 candidates and rerank to the best 5 before generation.**


Passage reranking with BERT-style cross-encoders was introduced by Nogueira and Cho in 2019 and remains the standard recipe [6]. It also addresses a known weakness of long prompts: Liu et al. showed that models use information at the start and end of a long context far better than information in the middle [8], so sending five well-ordered passages beats sending thirty in a heap.

## How do I build a RAG chatbot?

**Start with one document type and ten real questions. Load and chunk the documents with structure-aware splitting, embed with a model you shortlisted from MTEB, index in pgvector or FAISS, add BM25, retrieve with both and fuse with reciprocal rank fusion, rerank with a cross-encoder, and prompt the model to answer only from the passages and to cite them. Measure retrieval recall on your ten questions before touching the prompt. Then add streaming, a confidence gate and logging.**


The skeleton of the query side, without any framework, is short enough to read:

```python
def answer(question: str) -> dict:
    q_vec = embed(question)                       # same model used at index time
    dense = vector_index.search(q_vec, k=30)      # pgvector / FAISS / Qdrant
    sparse = bm25_index.search(question, k=30)    # keyword retriever
    fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion([dense, sparse], k=60)
    top = rerank(question, fused[:30])[:5]        # cross-encoder scores the pairs
    if confidence(question, top) < THRESHOLD:     # evidence too weak
        return {"answer": None, "reason": "no supporting passages", "sources": []}
    prompt = build_prompt(question, top)          # "answer only from these passages, cite [n]"
    return {"answer": llm(prompt), "sources": [c.source for c in top]}
```

Everything else, ingestion jobs, a UI, authentication, tenant filters, is ordinary software engineering. In RAG.NextUpgrad that engineering includes Docker, CI/CD, structured logging, and a test suite of 196 tests, and the whole service runs in about 220 MB of RAM on a free tier, which is a useful reminder that RAG is not inherently heavy [17].


### Which framework should I use, LangChain or LlamaIndex, or none?

**Use a framework to prototype and to borrow loaders, then own the retrieval code yourself once you know what your system needs.** Both LangChain and LlamaIndex are excellent for getting to a first answer in an afternoon. The trouble comes later, when a bug sits under three layers of abstraction. The query path above is a few hundred lines; you can read all of it.


## How do I evaluate a RAG pipeline?

**Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. For retrieval, build a set of real questions with the passages that should be returned and measure recall at k, the share of questions where a correct passage is in the top k. For generation, measure faithfulness, whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved passages, and answer relevance. Frameworks such as RAGAS automate the generation metrics with an LLM judge, but the retrieval set you must build by hand.**


RAGAS, from Es et al., defines faithfulness, answer relevance and context relevance as reference-free metrics scored by a model [9]. They are useful, and they are not a substitute for a human-labelled retrieval set, because a system can be perfectly faithful to the wrong passage.


The metric that changed my own systems most was the simplest: for each question, was the right chunk anywhere in the top 30? When it was not, no prompt or model could help, and the fix was always upstream, in chunking or in adding keyword retrieval.

## Why does RAG fail, and how do I fix it?

**RAG fails for a small number of repeatable reasons: the answer was never in the index, it was in the index but chunked so it lost its meaning, retrieval ranked the right chunk too low, the model ignored the passages and answered from memory, or the passages contradicted each other and the model picked wrong. Each has a specific fix, and the fix is almost never "a bigger model".**



Barnett et al. catalogue seven failure points from three case studies, from missing content to incomplete answers, and their central observation matches my experience: you only discover most failures in operation, so logging every retrieval and every answer is part of the architecture, not an add-on [10].

## What is a confidence gate, and why did I build one?

**A confidence gate is a check between retrieval and generation that measures how strongly the retrieved passages support an answer, and refuses to generate when support is weak. Instead of a fluent hallucination the user sees "I could not find this in the documents", with the option to rephrase or upload more. It turns the most dangerous RAG failure, a confident wrong answer, into an honest non-answer.**


In RAG.NextUpgrad the gate looks at reranker scores and the agreement between passages before any tokens are generated. The threshold is tuned on the evaluation set so that it rarely blocks answerable questions. This is the single feature clients noticed most, and I wrote up the reasoning in a separate article [18]. Research is moving the same way: Self-RAG trains a model to decide when to retrieve and to critique its own output with reflection tokens [12].

> The model is never allowed to guess. If the evidence is not there, the honest answer is that the evidence is not there, and the product says so out loud.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, RAG.NextUpgrad design note</cite>

## What is agentic RAG, and what is Graph RAG?

**Agentic RAG puts a planning loop around retrieval: the model decides whether to retrieve, rewrites the query, calls several retrievers or tools, checks the results, and retrieves again if needed, instead of doing one fixed search. Graph RAG builds a knowledge graph of entities and relationships from the documents and retrieves over that graph, which helps with questions that need connections across many documents, such as "what are the main themes in this corpus".**



Microsoft's Graph RAG paper describes building an entity graph with community summaries and shows gains on global, sense-making questions over a corpus [13]. HyDE, another retrieval upgrade, has the model write a hypothetical answer first and embeds that to search, which helps when questions are short and vague [11]. My advice to students is to climb the levels above in order. Agentic loops and graphs are level-eight problems; most systems I audit are stuck at level two.

## Is RAG still relevant with long context windows?

**Yes. Long context windows let you paste more into a prompt, but they do not tell you which of a million documents to paste, they cost per token on every question, and models still attend unevenly across long inputs. Retrieval is how you choose what deserves the context window. Longer windows make RAG easier, because you can send more and better passages, not unnecessary.**


Liu et al.'s finding that accuracy drops when relevant information sits in the middle of a long context is the empirical reason retrieval and reranking still matter [8]. The economics are the practical reason: a 200-page manual is hundreds of thousands of tokens; five reranked passages are a few thousand.

## What are common RAG interview questions?

**Expect to explain the two phases, to compare RAG with fine-tuning, to describe chunking trade-offs, to justify hybrid search and reranking, to define recall and faithfulness, and to walk through a failure you debugged. Interviewers are testing whether you have operated a RAG system, not whether you can recite the paper.**


The questions that separate candidates, from the interviewing I have done for SCULT INDIA and from the sessions I run for students:

1. How do you know your retrieval is working before you look at the answers?
2. A user says the bot gave a wrong answer. Walk me through your debugging, in order.
3. Why would you add BM25 to a system that already has embeddings?
4. What happens when two retrieved passages disagree?
5. How do you stop the model answering when the documents do not contain the answer?

If you can answer those five from experience, you can build the system. The rest of this guide is the experience, compressed.


## Where can I learn RAG properly?

**Read the original paper and the 2023 survey for the map, build one pipeline by hand without a framework so you understand every stage, then evaluate it on your own questions. That order, paper, build, measure, teaches more than any course, and it is exactly what I ask of students who want to work on retrieval systems with me.**


A good first project is a RAG system over your own college's notes, syllabus and previous-year papers, because you can judge the answers yourself and the documents are messy in exactly the ways real client documents are. I mentor students through TechVerse Enclave on projects like this, and the ones who finish have something no certificate gives them: a system they can explain failure by failure. If you want to talk RAG at your college or hackathon, my email is pranjulrathour41@gmail.com and the invite page is at pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
