# What is RAG in LLMs? How RAG works, building it, and fixing bad results
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-rag-in-llm/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, is a way of using a large language model where the system first retrieves relevant passages from your own documents and then has the LLM answer from them. It gives LLMs knowledge they were not trained on, keeps answers current without retraining, and lets every answer cite its source. I built RAG.NextUpgrad, a production RAG platform with hybrid retrieval, re-ranking and a confidence gate, so this page explains RAG in LLMs from practice: how it works, how to build and update it, how to evaluate it on a budget, and why results go wrong.

## What is RAG in LLMs?

RAG in LLMs means retrieval-augmented generation: before the model answers, a retriever searches a document collection for passages relevant to the question, and those passages are added to the prompt so the LLM answers from them.

The term comes from a 2020 research paper that combined a neural retriever with a generator. Today it describes a broad pattern used in company knowledge bots, customer support, document Q&A and research assistants. The LLM provides language understanding and fluent answers; retrieval provides the facts. Done well, users get specific answers with citations they can check, instead of the model's general and possibly outdated memory.

## What is a RAG system?

A RAG system is the full application that implements retrieval-augmented generation: document ingestion and chunking, an index such as a vector store with keyword search, a retrieval and reranking step, a prompt that grounds the LLM, and evaluation and monitoring.

Components in a production system:

- **Ingestion**: load PDFs, web pages and databases; clean text; keep metadata.
- **Chunking**: split into passages that keep meaning together.
- **Indexing**: embeddings in a vector index plus a keyword index.
- **Retrieval**: hybrid search, merged with reciprocal-rank fusion.
- **Reranking**: a cross-encoder reorders the top candidates.
- **Generation**: grounded prompt, citations, refusal on weak evidence.
- **Operations**: updates, logging, evaluation, cost control.

## How does RAG work with an LLM?

The user's question is turned into a search, the most relevant chunks are retrieved and ranked, and the top few are placed into the LLM's prompt with instructions to answer only from them and cite them. The LLM writes the answer.

Step by step: embed the question; search the vector index and the keyword index; merge and rerank results; select the top passages within the context budget; build a prompt with the passages labelled by ID; generate the answer with citations; check that citations point to real passages; and decline if the evidence was weak. Streaming the answer keeps the experience fast. Logging the retrieved passages for every query is what lets you debug wrong answers later.

## How does RAG enhance an LLM?

RAG gives an LLM access to private, recent and specific information, reduces hallucinations by grounding answers in sources, enables citations, and lets you update knowledge by updating documents instead of retraining the model.

It also lowers cost and risk compared with fine-tuning for knowledge: smaller models can answer well when given the right passages, and access control can be applied at retrieval time so users only get answers from documents they are allowed to see. The limits are equally important: RAG cannot fix bad source documents, and if retrieval misses the right passage, the model has nothing correct to work with. That is why retrieval quality is the main lever.

## What is the difference between RAG and an LLM?

An LLM is a trained model that generates text from its input. RAG is a system design that adds a retrieval step before the LLM, so the model's input includes relevant documents. RAG uses an LLM; it is not an alternative to one.

Without RAG, the LLM answers from what it learned in training, with no access to your files and no sources. With RAG, it answers from passages your system chose. That changes accuracy, freshness and trust. RAG is also different from fine-tuning, which changes the model's weights; RAG changes only what the model reads at question time, which makes it far easier to update and audit.

## How do I build a RAG-based LLM application?

Start with a small, real document set and a list of real questions, build a simple pipeline end to end, measure retrieval and answer quality, then improve the weakest part. Resist adding complexity before you can measure it.

A build order that works:

- Collect 50 real questions with known answers in your documents.
- Ingest and chunk documents by structure, such as headings, with page numbers in metadata.
- Index with embeddings and BM25; merge results with reciprocal-rank fusion.
- Add a cross-encoder reranker on the top candidates.
- Prompt the LLM to answer only from passages, with citations.
- Add a confidence gate that declines on weak evidence.
- Evaluate after every change.

RAG.NextUpgrad follows this design and runs in about 220 MB on a free tier.

## How do I keep information updated in a RAG system?

Re-index incrementally: detect new, changed and deleted documents, re-chunk and re-embed only what changed, and delete outdated chunks so old versions never reach the model. Store document versions and timestamps in metadata.

Practical habits:

- Give every chunk an ID derived from its document and position, so updates replace rather than duplicate.
- Track a hash of each document to detect changes cheaply.
- Schedule syncs from source systems, or trigger them on changes.
- Filter or boost by date for time-sensitive questions.
- Show the source date in citations so users see how current an answer is.

If you change the embedding model, re-embed everything; vectors from different models are not comparable.

## How do I evaluate a RAG system with a local or free-tier model?

Build a test set, measure retrieval with simple metrics that need no model, and use a local model through Ollama or a free API tier as a judge for answer faithfulness, checking a sample by hand to confirm the judge agrees with you.

Steps:

- Write 50 questions with the passage that answers each.
- Compute recall at 5 and 10 for retrieval: free, fast and deterministic.
- Generate answers and ask a judge model: is every claim supported by the passages?
- Include unanswerable questions and measure how often the system declines.
- Hand-check 20 judged answers to calibrate.

Small local judges are less reliable than large ones, so keep the rubric simple, binary where possible, and trust retrieval metrics most.

## Why do RAG hallucinations often start at ingestion?

Because bad ingestion corrupts what the model reads: broken PDF extraction, tables flattened into nonsense, headers repeated in every chunk, lost page structure, or chunks that split a fact from its context. The LLM then faithfully answers from garbled or misleading text.

Fixes at ingestion:

- Use layout-aware extraction or OCR for scanned and complex PDFs.
- Keep tables as tables, or convert them to clear text rows.
- Strip repeated headers, footers and navigation.
- Chunk by headings and paragraphs, with overlap where meaning spans boundaries.
- Carry titles and section names into each chunk.

Inspect random chunks by eye before indexing; many "model" problems disappear once the text is clean.

## Why does a large FAISS RAG system return irrelevant results?

With many chunks, pure semantic search tends to surface passages that are topically similar but not relevant, especially when chunks are noisy, embeddings are mismatched, or the index uses approximate settings that trade recall for speed.

Common causes and fixes:

- **Mixed or mismatched embeddings**: use one model for indexing and queries, and normalise vectors for cosine similarity.
- **Noisy chunks**: remove boilerplate and duplicates.
- **Approximate index settings**: raise `nprobe` for IVF or `efSearch` for HNSW and measure recall.
- **No keyword search**: add BM25 and fuse results.
- **No reranking**: rerank the top 50 with a cross-encoder.
- **Wrong scope**: filter by metadata such as document type or date.

Measure recall at 10 before and after each change.

# What is RLHF, instruction tuning and DPO? How base models become assistants, what alignment training actually does, and when a small team should use it
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-rlhf-instruction-tuning-and-dpo/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is RLHF?

**Reinforcement learning from human feedback is the training stage that turns an instruction-following model into one whose answers people prefer. Humans compare pairs of model answers to the same prompt and pick the better one; a reward model is trained to predict those preferences; the language model is then optimised with reinforcement learning, classically PPO, to produce answers the reward model scores highly, with a penalty for drifting too far from the starting model [1][2]. It is how InstructGPT and the first ChatGPT were trained, and it is why assistants sound the way they do [1][3].**


Fine-tune Studio, the training platform I built, stops at supervised fine-tuning for a reason that this page explains: for most teams, the preference stage costs more in data than it returns in quality, and knowing where it does pay off is the useful part [14].

> Every alignment method is a way to spend human judgement efficiently. The algorithm is a detail; the comparisons are the product.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is a base model, and what is instruction tuning?

**A base model is trained only to predict the next token over a huge corpus, so given "What is the capital of France?" it may continue with another question rather than an answer, because that is what documents look like. Instruction tuning, also called supervised fine-tuning or SFT, trains the base model on demonstrations: prompts paired with good responses, in a chat format, so it learns to answer rather than continue [1][9]. FLAN showed instruction-tuned models generalise to unseen tasks [9]; LIMA showed a thousand very good demonstrations can be enough for the format [10].**



## How does RLHF work step by step?

**Start from an instruction-tuned model. Sample several answers per prompt. Have humans rank or compare them. Train a reward model, usually a copy of the language model with a scalar head, to predict which answer wins. Then run reinforcement learning: the policy generates an answer, the reward model scores it, and the policy is updated to increase the score while a KL penalty keeps it close to the SFT model so it does not collapse into reward-gaming gibberish [1]. Iterate with fresh comparisons as the policy changes.**



## What is DPO, and why did it replace much of RLHF?

**Direct preference optimisation skips the reward model and the reinforcement learning. It takes the same comparison data, preferred and rejected answer per prompt, and trains the language model directly with a loss that raises the likelihood of the preferred answer relative to the rejected one, measured against a frozen reference model [4]. The paper shows this is mathematically equivalent to optimising the RLHF objective under the usual reward model assumptions, with none of the instability or infrastructure of PPO. It became the default for open models because a fine-tuning script can run it.**



## What are ORPO, KTO and GRPO?

**Variants that change what data or memory the preference stage needs. ORPO folds preference learning into the SFT stage with an odds-ratio term, so no reference model is needed and one training run does both [6]. KTO works from single answers labelled good or bad instead of pairs, which is much cheaper to collect from real users, who give thumbs up or down rather than comparing two answers [7]. GRPO is a reinforcement learning method that estimates the baseline from a group of sampled answers rather than a value model, used to train reasoning models on verifiable rewards such as maths answers [8].**



## What is RLAIF and Constitutional AI?

**Reinforcement learning from AI feedback replaces some or all of the human comparisons with judgements from a model, guided by written principles. Constitutional AI is the best-known form: the model critiques and revises its own answers against a set of principles, the revisions become SFT data, and a model-generated preference set trains the reward model [5]. It makes preference data cheap and scalable, at the cost of inheriting the judging model's biases. Most current open preference datasets are at least partly model-judged.**



## What does preference data look like, and how much do I need?

**A prompt, a chosen answer and a rejected answer, in the model's chat format, with the difference between them being the behaviour you want to teach: more accurate, better formatted, more concise, safer, more on-brand. Quality dominates quantity; a few thousand clean pairs where the preference is unambiguous beat fifty thousand noisy ones. The cheapest real source is your own product: two generations, a user choice, or thumbs up and down for KTO. The most common mistake is pairs where the rejected answer is obviously broken, which teaches the model nothing about the hard cases.**



## What goes wrong in RLHF and DPO?

**Reward hacking: the policy finds outputs the reward model over-scores, such as longer answers, confident tone or particular phrases, without being better. Sycophancy: models learn that agreeing with the user is preferred, and start agreeing when the user is wrong [11]. Over-refusal: safety preferences push the model to decline reasonable requests. Mode collapse: the model's answers become samey. Length bias is the most common of all, because raters prefer longer answers slightly and the optimiser amplifies it. Each is a data or reward problem and shows up in evals before users notice, if you have evals.**



## Should a student or small team do RLHF or DPO?

**Usually not yet. Supervised fine-tuning with LoRA on a few thousand good examples captures most of what a small team needs: format, tone, domain vocabulary, task behaviour. Preference tuning pays off when you have real comparisons from users, a measured quality gap that SFT could not close, and an eval set to prove the gap closed. If you have those, DPO or KTO with the TRL library on a LoRA adapter is a weekend of work on a rented GPU [12][13]. If you do not, the time is better spent on data and evals.**



## How do I run DPO in practice?

**Start from your SFT model. Build the preference set in the chosen and rejected format. Use the TRL DPO trainer with a LoRA adapter, a small learning rate, one to three epochs, and the SFT model as the frozen reference [13]. Evaluate against the SFT model on a held-out set with a model judge and with your task metrics. Check for length inflation explicitly. Keep the adapter that wins the eval, and log everything so the run can be reproduced.**



## RLHF and DPO interview questions

**Explain the three training stages. Describe how a reward model is trained and why the KL penalty exists. Derive or sketch why DPO needs no reward model. Compare DPO, KTO and ORPO by the data each needs. Name three failure modes and their causes. Explain what GRPO changes and where verifiable rewards apply. Say when you would not do preference tuning. The strongest answer includes an SFT run you evaluated and a reason you did or did not go further.**



## Where should I start?

**Read the DPO paper's first four pages, then run the TRL DPO example on a small model with a public preference set for one epoch and compare outputs against the starting model. An evening, and the abstractions become concrete.** For a workshop on fine-tuning and alignment for students, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is semantic search? Meaning, engines, vs RAG, Python, testing and tuning
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-semantic-search/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Semantic search means searching by meaning rather than exact words: a query like "laptop gets hot when gaming" finds an article titled "managing thermal throttling on notebooks" even though they share no keywords. It works by converting queries and documents into embeddings and finding the closest matches. It is the retrieval step in RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad, where I pair it with keyword search. This page covers the meaning, semantic search engines, similarity search, whether it is NLP or uses LLMs, how it relates to RAG, building it in Python, testing and improving it, and the Semantic Scholar academic search engine. What is semantic search? Semantic search is a search technique that tries to understand the intent and meaning of a query and return results that are relevant in meaning, not just results that contain the same words. Also asked as: what is semantic search meaning · what is semantic search and similarity search Traditional keyword search matches terms, so synonyms, paraphrases and natural-language questions often fail. Semantic search uses language models to represent text as vectors in which similar meanings are close together, so it handles "how do I fix a slow laptop" and "speed up my computer" as related. Its weakness is exact details: specific codes, names and numbers are better handled by keyword search, which is why production systems combine both. What is a semantic search engine? A semantic search engine is a search system that ranks results by meaning, typically using embedding models to encode documents and queries and a vector index to find nearest matches, often combined with keyword search, filters and reranking. Also asked as: what is semantic search engine Examples range from web search engines, which use semantic understanding heavily, to site search, e-commerce product search, documentation search and enterprise knowledge search. Building blocks include an embedding model, a vector database or library, a keyword index for hybrid search, a reranker for precision, and an interface that may show snippets or generated answers. Many search platforms now offer semantic features built in. What is the difference between semantic search and similarity search? Similarity search is the technical operation: finding vectors nearest to a query vector by cosine similarity or distance. Semantic search is the application: using similarity search over meaning-based embeddings to return relevant results to people. Similarity search can be used for many things beyond text meaning, such as finding similar images, songs, products or fraud patterns. Semantic search specifically aims at relevance to a user's intent, which often requires more than raw similarity: query understanding, hybrid keyword matching, filters such as language or date, and reranking. In short, similarity search is a tool; semantic search is a product built with it. Is semantic search NLP? Yes. Semantic search is an application of natural language processing: it uses NLP models, especially transformer-based embedding models, to understand the meaning of queries and documents. It sits at the intersection of NLP and information retrieval. NLP provides the models that represent meaning; information retrieval provides indexing, ranking and evaluation methods. Related NLP techniques often support it, such as query expansion, named entity recognition for filters, and language detection. Semantic search also extends beyond text: multimodal models can match text queries to images, which uses the same principles. Does semantic search use LLMs? Not necessarily. Semantic search usually uses embedding models, which are smaller transformer encoders, not large generative LLMs. LLMs can be added to rewrite queries, generate hypothetical answers to search with, rerank results or produce a summarised answer. A basic semantic search system needs only an embedding model and a vector index, which is fast and cheap. Adding an LLM increases cost and latency, so use it where it helps: rephrasing vague questions, generating answers with citations in RAG, or reranking a small set of candidates. Many embedding models are themselves derived from language models, which is why the line can seem blurry. Is semantic search the same as RAG? No. Semantic search finds and returns relevant documents. RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, uses retrieval, often semantic search, to find passages and then has an LLM generate an answer from them. Also asked as: is semantic search same as rag So semantic search is a component of most RAG systems. Search results alone let users read sources directly; RAG adds a synthesised answer, ideally with citations. RAG quality depends heavily on search quality: if the right passage is not retrieved, the answer cannot be right. That is why improving semantic search, through hybrid retrieval and reranking, is the most effective way to improve a RAG system. How do I do semantic search in Python? Use the sentence-transformers library to embed documents and queries, then compute cosine similarity and return the top matches. For larger collections, store embeddings in a vector index such as FAISS, Chroma or pgvector. Also asked as: how to do semantic search in python # pip install sentence-transformers from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util model = SentenceTransformer(&quot;all-MiniLM-L6-v2&quot;) docs = [&quot;Paging splits memory into fixed-size pages.&quot;, &quot;A deadlock occurs when processes wait on each other forever.&quot;, &quot;Thermal throttling slows a laptop when it gets too hot.&quot;] doc_emb = model.encode(docs, convert_to_tensor=True) q = model.encode(&quot;why does my laptop slow down when gaming&quot;, convert_to_tensor=True) best = util.semantic_search(q, doc_emb, top_k=1)[0][0] print(docs[best[&quot;corpus_id&quot;]], round(best[&quot;score&quot;], 2)) Swap in a stronger or multilingual embedding model for production. How do I test semantic search? Create a set of real queries with known relevant documents, run your search, and measure metrics such as recall at k, precision at k and mean reciprocal rank. Also review results by hand for a sample of queries. Also asked as: how to test semantic search A simple process: Collect 50 to 100 real queries from users or logs. Label the relevant documents for each. Compute recall at 5 and 10: how often a relevant document appears in the top results. Include hard cases: exact codes, synonyms, misspellings and multi-part questions. Re-run after every change to embeddings, chunking or ranking. Track failures by type, such as exact-term misses or wrong-topic matches, to choose the right fix. How do I improve semantic search? The biggest improvements usually come from hybrid search, adding keyword ranking such as BM25 to vector search, better chunking of documents, a stronger or domain-suited embedding model, metadata filters, and a reranker on the top results. Also asked as: how to improve semantic search Checklist: Hybrid retrieval merged with reciprocal-rank fusion. Chunking by structure, with titles and headings included in each chunk. Embedding model chosen by tests on your own queries. Query handling: rewrite vague queries, expand acronyms. Reranking with a cross-encoder on the top 20 to 50. Feedback: log clicks or ratings to find weak queries. Measure each change; some ideas that sound good do not help on a given dataset. How do I search on Semantic Scholar? Semantic Scholar is a free academic search engine from the Allen Institute for AI. Enter keywords, a paper title or an author's name in the search box, then filter by year, field of study, publication type and venue. Also asked as: how to search semantic scholar Useful features: paper pages show abstracts, citations, references and AI-generated short summaries; "highly influential citations" highlight important follow-up work; you can create a library and set alerts for new papers; and an API supports programmatic access. For literature reviews, start with a few key papers, follow their citations and references, and save relevant ones to your library. Always open and read the actual paper before citing it.

# What is the Supabase database? Postgres, connection URL, backups, reset and security
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-supabase-database/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

The Supabase database is a full PostgreSQL database that Supabase hosts and manages for you, with auto-generated REST and GraphQL APIs, a dashboard, extensions such as pgvector, and built-in backups. Supabase wraps it with authentication, file storage, realtime updates and edge functions, making it a complete backend. PostgreSQL is central to my stack for products like FaceVision's embedding store, so this page covers what Supabase's database is, how it works, connection URLs, backups and exports, resets and security. What is the Supabase database? Every Supabase project includes a dedicated PostgreSQL database. You can create tables with the dashboard's table editor or SQL, and Supabase instantly exposes them through APIs your front end can call with client libraries. Also asked as: what is supabase database · how to backup supabase database Because it is real Postgres, you get SQL, joins, transactions, views, functions, triggers and extensions, including pgvector for embeddings and PostGIS for location data. Supabase adds conveniences: a visual editor, SQL editor, database migrations through its CLI, connection pooling, logs and performance advisors. It is used for SaaS apps, mobile back ends, internal tools and AI applications that need structured data and vectors together. Which database does Supabase use? Supabase uses PostgreSQL, the open-source relational database. It is not a custom database; your data lives in standard Postgres, so any Postgres tool, driver or ORM can connect to it. Also asked as: which database supabase use This is a key difference from Firebase, which uses NoSQL document databases. Using Postgres means your data model is relational, with tables, foreign keys and SQL queries, and your data is portable: you can export it with standard tools and move it to any Postgres host. Supabase keeps its Postgres versions reasonably current and supports a wide range of extensions, which you enable from the dashboard. Is Supabase a database or a backend? Both. At its core is a Postgres database, and around it Supabase provides backend services: authentication, file storage, realtime subscriptions, edge functions and auto-generated APIs, so many apps need no separate server. Also asked as: is supabase a database or backend Developers often describe Supabase as a backend-as-a-service or an open-source Firebase alternative. You can use just the database, connecting from your own server like any Postgres host, or use the full platform from front-end code with Row Level Security protecting data. For complex business logic, many teams pair Supabase with their own API, such as a FastAPI service, using Supabase for data, auth and storage. Is Supabase a relational database? Yes. Supabase's database is PostgreSQL, a relational database, so data lives in tables with columns and types, related through keys, and queried with SQL. It also supports JSON columns for flexible, document-style data when needed. Also asked as: is supabase relational database Relational structure suits most applications: users, orders, posts and comments relate naturally through foreign keys, and constraints keep data consistent. Postgres's JSONB type lets you store semi-structured data, such as settings or metadata, without giving up relational features. Design your schema thoughtfully, with indexes on columns you filter by, because a well-designed relational schema scales far better than one that stores everything as JSON. How does the Supabase database work? Your app talks to Postgres either through Supabase's auto-generated APIs, using client libraries with a project key and user session, or directly with a Postgres connection string from servers. Row Level Security policies decide what each user can access. Also asked as: how does supabase database work When a logged-in user queries through the API, Supabase passes their identity to Postgres, and policies such as "users can read only their own rows" are enforced inside the database. Realtime streams changes to subscribed clients. Database functions can be called as remote procedures, and triggers can run logic on inserts or updates. Migrations, managed with the Supabase CLI, version your schema changes like code. How do I get the Supabase database URL? Open your project in the Supabase dashboard and click Connect, or look under the project's database settings, to find connection strings for direct connections and for the connection pooler. Replace the password placeholder with your database password. Also asked as: how to get supabase database url Which string to use: Direct connection: for long-running servers and migrations. Pooler in transaction mode: for serverless functions and many short connections. Pooler in session mode: for clients that need session features over IPv4. The project URL and API keys used by client libraries are different from the database connection string; find them in the API settings. Keep the database password and service keys in environment variables, never in front-end code or public repositories. How do I back up a Supabase database? Supabase runs automatic daily backups on paid plans, with point-in-time recovery available as an add-on. For your own copies, use the Supabase CLI's supabase db dump or standard pg_dump with your connection string, and store dumps securely off-platform. A practical routine: Rely on managed backups for quick restores. Schedule your own dumps, for example nightly through a CI job. Back up files in storage separately; database dumps do not include them. Test restoring a backup into a new project occasionally. Encrypt and restrict access to backup files. Free plan projects have limited backup options, so take your own dumps if your data matters. Can I export a Supabase database? Yes. Because it is PostgreSQL, you can export the whole database with pg_dump or the Supabase CLI, export individual tables as CSV from the dashboard's table editor, or copy data with any Postgres-compatible tool. Also asked as: can i export supabase database Exports include schema, data, functions and policies when using full dumps; choose schema-only or data-only options as needed. To migrate elsewhere, restore the dump into another Postgres server, then reconfigure auth and storage, which are separate services. Supabase's documentation includes migration guides to and from other platforms. This portability is a major advantage over proprietary databases that lock data into one vendor. How do I reset a Supabase database? For local development, run supabase db reset, which recreates your local database and reapplies all migrations and seed data. For a hosted project, there is no single button to wipe data; drop and recreate schemas or tables carefully, restore a backup, or create a fresh project. Also asked as: how to reset supabase database Before any reset of a hosted project, take a backup, because deletions are permanent. If you only need a clean database password, use the dashboard option to reset the database password, which does not touch data. Managing schema through migrations makes resets safe and repeatable: your database can always be rebuilt from versioned files. Is the Supabase database secure? Supabase encrypts data at rest and in transit, runs on major cloud infrastructure, and offers compliance options for organisations. Real-world security, though, depends mostly on configuration: Row Level Security, key handling and access policies you set. Also asked as: is supabase database secure Essential practices: Enable Row Level Security on every table exposed to clients, with tested policies. Never expose the service role or secret key in front-end code. Use strong database passwords and restrict network access where possible. Review the dashboard's security and performance advisors. Keep auth settings strict, such as email confirmation and rate limits. Most Supabase data leaks come from tables without RLS, not from platform breaches.

# What is system design? Interviews, examples, AI system design, and preparation
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-system-design/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


System design is the process of deciding how a software system is built to meet its requirements: which components it has, how data flows between them, where data is stored, how it scales, and what happens when parts fail. It is also a standard interview round for software engineers. This page explains system design and how it differs from architecture, what interviews test and how to prepare, works through an example, covers AI and agentic system design, asks whether it is AI-proof, and clears up two other meanings: VLSI system design and UI design systems.

## What is system design?

System design is planning the structure of a software system: its components, such as services, databases, caches and queues, the interfaces between them, and the trade-offs that let it meet functional needs and goals such as scale, latency, reliability and cost.

A system design starts from requirements: what users must be able to do, and how many users, how fast, how reliable. Then you choose components and data models, estimate load, plan for failure, and decide on trade-offs, such as consistency versus availability, or cost versus speed. Good designs are as simple as the requirements allow and evolve as the product grows. The skill combines knowledge of building blocks with judgement about which ones fit.

## What is a system design interview?

A system design interview asks you to design a system, such as a URL shortener, a chat app or a news feed, in about 45 to 60 minutes, explaining your reasoning aloud. Interviewers assess how you clarify requirements, structure the problem and reason about trade-offs.

A typical flow: clarify functional and non-functional requirements, estimate scale, sketch a high-level design, define APIs and data models, then go deep on one or two parts, such as storage or caching, and discuss bottlenecks, failures and improvements. There is no single correct answer. Interviewers look for structured thinking, sensible choices with reasons, awareness of trade-offs and good communication. For junior roles, expect simpler problems and more focus on fundamentals; for senior roles, more depth on scale and reliability.

## How do I prepare for system design?

Learn the building blocks, practise a set of classic designs out loud with a fixed structure, and connect it all to your own projects. Six to eight weeks of steady practice is enough for most junior and mid-level interviews.

A preparation plan:

- **Concepts**: load balancers, caching, databases and indexing, replication and sharding, queues, CDNs, consistency, rate limiting.
- **Estimation**: requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth.
- **Classic problems**: URL shortener, chat, news feed, file storage, rate limiter, notification system.
- **Structure**: requirements, estimates, high-level design, deep dive, trade-offs.
- **Mock interviews**: practise with a friend or record yourself.

Read The System Design Primer and Designing Data-Intensive Applications for depth.

## What is an example of system design?

A URL shortener is the classic example: users submit a long URL and get a short code; visiting the short link redirects to the original. It is simple to describe but raises real design questions about IDs, storage, caching and scale.

A sketch:

- **API**: `POST /shorten` returns a code; `GET /{code}` redirects.
- **ID generation**: base62-encode a unique counter or a random ID, checking for collisions.
- **Storage**: a key-value store or database table mapping code to URL.
- **Caching**: popular codes in an in-memory cache, since reads vastly outnumber writes.
- **Scale**: stateless app servers behind a load balancer; replicate the database for reads.
- **Extras**: analytics through an asynchronous queue, expiry, abuse checks.

Practise explaining each choice and its alternatives.

## What is the difference between system design and software architecture?

They overlap heavily. Software architecture usually refers to the high-level structure and principles of a system and the decisions that are expensive to change; system design is the broader activity of designing a specific system, from architecture down to data models, APIs and capacity planning.

In practice, architecture answers questions like "monolith or services, synchronous or event-driven, which data stores", and system design also covers "this table, this index, this cache policy, this API contract, this number of servers". Architects focus on long-term structure across many systems and teams; system design interviews test whether you can design one system end to end. Both depend on understanding requirements and trade-offs.

## What is system design in AI?

AI system design adds machine learning concerns to classic design: data pipelines, feature or document processing, model training or selection, serving and scaling inference, retrieval for LLM apps, evaluation, monitoring for quality drift, and cost per request.

For an LLM application, a design might include document ingestion and chunking, an embedding model and vector index, hybrid retrieval and reranking, an LLM call with a grounded prompt, guardrails, caching, fallbacks across providers, and evaluation and logging. RAG.NextUpgrad is a compact example: hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion, re-ranking, cited streaming answers, a confidence gate that refuses weak evidence, multi-provider fallback, and a small enough footprint, about 220 MB, to run on a free tier. Interviews for AI roles increasingly include designs like this.

## What is agentic AI system design?

Agentic AI system design is designing systems where a model plans and takes actions with tools. Beyond normal design, it covers the agent loop, tool definitions and permissions, state and memory, limits on steps and cost, human approval for risky actions, evaluation and observability.

Key decisions include how much autonomy to grant, since workflows with a few agentic steps are often more reliable than fully autonomous agents; how tools authenticate and what they may change; how to persist state so long tasks can resume; how to defend against prompt injection from content the agent reads; and how to trace every step for debugging. Designs should define failure behaviour clearly: when unsure, the agent asks or stops rather than guessing.

## Is system design AI-proof?

No skill is entirely AI-proof, but system design is among the most durable. AI tools can suggest components and draw diagrams, but deciding trade-offs for a specific business, team, budget and risk tolerance requires judgement and accountability that remain human responsibilities.

AI actually raises the value of design skills. As coding becomes faster with AI assistance, the bottleneck shifts to deciding what to build and how pieces fit together, and to reviewing AI-generated code against that design. Engineers who can design systems, including AI systems, evaluate trade-offs and explain decisions clearly are well placed. Use AI tools to explore alternatives faster, but own the decisions.

## What is system design in VLSI?

In VLSI, very large-scale integration, system design means designing electronic chips: defining the architecture of a chip or system-on-chip, then implementing it in hardware description languages, verifying it, and taking it through synthesis, layout and fabrication.

The flow typically goes from specification and architecture, to register-transfer level design in Verilog or VHDL, functional verification, logic synthesis, physical design including placement and routing, timing analysis and sign-off checks. It is a different field from software system design, though both involve architecture, trade-offs and verification. Electronics students interested in it should learn digital design, HDLs and verification, and get familiar with EDA tools from vendors such as Cadence, Synopsys and Siemens.

## How do I use a design system?

A design system, in UI and product design, is a shared library of components, styles and guidelines, such as buttons, colours, typography and spacing, used to build consistent interfaces. Use it by building screens from its components instead of styling from scratch.

To use one well: learn its tokens for colours, spacing and type; use existing components before creating new ones; follow its accessibility and usage guidelines; and contribute improvements back rather than making one-off variations. Popular examples include Google's Material Design and many open-source React component libraries. Despite the similar name, it is unrelated to system design interviews, which are about software architecture and scale.


---

# What is tool calling in AI? Tool vs function calling, LangChain, MCP and Gemma
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-tool-calling/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Tool calling is how a language model uses external tools: you describe tools to the model, it decides when one is needed and returns a structured request with arguments, your application runs the tool, and the result goes back to the model so it can continue. Tools can be anything code can do: search, calculators, databases, APIs, file operations or other agents. This page explains tool calling in AI and how it works, how it relates to function calling, tool-calling models, LangChain, agentic AI, MCP, and whether Gemma supports it. What is tool calling? Tool calling is a capability of language models to request the use of external tools by producing a structured call, usually a tool name and JSON arguments, instead of plain text. The application executes the tool and returns the result to the model. Also asked as: how tool calling works This bridges the gap between language and action. A model cannot check today's train timings or query your database by itself, but with a search_trains(from, to, date) tool it can request exactly that, then answer from real data. Tool calling also makes structured output reliable, because arguments must match a schema. It is the foundation of AI agents and of integrations such as coding assistants that edit files and run tests. What is tool calling in AI? In AI, tool calling extends a model's abilities beyond its training data and text generation, letting it retrieve live information, compute precisely and take actions in other systems, under the control of the application. Examples include chatbots that look up orders, assistants that schedule meetings, coding agents that read files and run commands, research agents that search the web, and data assistants that run SQL queries. In each, the model decides what to call and with what arguments, and the application decides what is allowed. Good systems keep sensitive actions behind confirmations and log every call for review. How does tool calling work? You send the model the conversation plus tool definitions with names, descriptions and input schemas. The model either answers or returns one or more tool calls. Your code validates and runs them, adds the results to the conversation, and calls the model again. The loop in steps: Define tools clearly: what each does and when to use it. Send the user message and tool list to the model. If the model returns tool calls, validate arguments and execute. Return results to the model, marked as tool results. Repeat until the model gives a final answer, with a step limit. Tool descriptions are the most important prompt in this process: models choose tools by reading them. What is the difference between tool calling and function calling? They mean essentially the same thing. "Function calling" was the name OpenAI used when it launched the feature in 2023; "tool calling" or "tool use" is the broader term now used by most providers, since tools also include built-in capabilities such as web search and code execution. In practice, a "function" is one kind of tool: a custom operation you define with a JSON schema. Providers also offer server-side tools they run themselves, such as search or code interpreters, alongside your functions. APIs and frameworks use both terms, sometimes interchangeably, so do not let naming confuse you: the concept is the model requesting a structured action that the system performs. What are tool-calling models? Tool-calling models are language models trained to decide when to use tools and to produce correctly formatted tool calls. Most current major models support it, including models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Mistral, and many open-weight models. Also asked as: what are tool calling models Quality differs in choosing the right tool, producing valid arguments, handling many tools, and calling tools in sequence for multi-step tasks. Frontier models are generally most reliable; smaller open models work for simple tool sets. Leaderboards for function calling compare models, but testing with your own tools and tasks is essential. When running open models locally, check that the model and serving tool, such as Ollama or vLLM, support tool calling. What is tool calling in LangChain? In LangChain, tool calling means defining tools, often with the @tool decorator on a Python function, binding them to a chat model with bind_tools, and handling the tool calls the model returns, either manually or through an agent that runs the loop. from langchain_core.tools import tool from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model @tool def add(a: int, b: int) -&gt; int: &quot;&quot;&quot;Add two integers.&quot;&quot;&quot; return a + b llm = init_chat_model(&quot;anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5&quot;).bind_tools([add]) msg = llm.invoke(&quot;What is 19 + 23?&quot;) print(msg.tool_calls) # [{'name': 'add', 'args': {'a': 19, 'b': 23}, ...}] LangChain standardises tool calls across providers, so the same code works with different models. Check the docs for current model names. What is tool calling in agentic AI? In agentic AI, tool calling is the mechanism through which agents act: the agent repeatedly reasons about the goal, calls tools, observes results and decides the next step, until the task is complete or it needs a person. The quality of an agent depends heavily on its tools: a small set of well-designed, clearly described tools with good error messages works far better than many overlapping ones. Agents also need guardrails around tool calls: permission checks, confirmation for destructive actions, limits on steps and cost, and defences against prompt injection from tool results. Logging every call makes debugging and auditing possible. Is tool calling agentic? A single tool call is not agentic by itself; it is one structured request. A system becomes agentic when the model uses tool calls in a loop, choosing which tools to use and when, to pursue a goal across multiple steps. For example, a chatbot that always calls a weather API for weather questions is tool use, not an agent. A system that plans a trip by searching trains, checking hotels, comparing options and asking you to confirm bookings is agentic. Many useful products sit in between: mostly fixed workflows with one or two model-chosen tool calls, which are easier to test and more reliable than fully autonomous agents. Is MCP tool calling? MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is not tool calling itself; it is a standard way to provide tools, resources and prompts to AI applications. The model still uses tool calling to invoke MCP tools, while the MCP client handles talking to MCP servers. In practice: an MCP server exposes tools such as query_database; the AI application, as an MCP client, lists them to the model as available tools; the model returns a tool call; the client forwards it to the server and returns the result. MCP's value is reuse: build a tool once as an MCP server and use it from many assistants and agents, instead of writing separate integrations for each. Can Gemma do tool calling? Gemma models can be used for function calling: Google's newer Gemma releases support it through prompting and structured outputs, and serving tools that run Gemma, such as Ollama or Hugging Face libraries, can expose tool calling depending on the model version and template. Results are best with clear function descriptions, few tools and strict JSON schemas, and with validation in your code. Smaller Gemma sizes make more mistakes on complex tool use than larger hosted models. For production agents needing many tools, test carefully or use a larger model; for simple local tasks, such as routing requests or extracting fields, Gemma can work well. Check Google's Gemma documentation for the current function-calling guidance.

# What is vector data? GIS vector data, vector database data, storage, and why vector DBs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vector-data/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

"Vector data" means two different things. In geography and GIS, vector data represents real-world features as points, lines and polygons with attributes, such as wells, roads and district boundaries. In AI, vector data means embeddings: lists of numbers that represent the meaning of text, images or audio so software can search by similarity. I work with the AI kind in RAG.NextUpgrad and FaceVision, so this page covers both meanings, examples, how vector databases store data, why and how to use one, LangChain, and initialisation vectors in encryption. What is vector data? In GIS, vector data stores geographic features as geometry, coordinates forming points, lines or polygons, plus attribute tables describing them. In machine learning, vector data is numerical arrays, embeddings, representing items in a high-dimensional space. Also asked as: example of vector database data The two share the mathematical idea of vectors but serve different purposes. GIS vector data answers "where is it and what is it?", such as the boundary of a farm and its crop type. AI vector data answers "what is similar to this?", such as finding documents related to a question. Context usually makes the meaning clear: shapefiles and GeoJSON are GIS; embeddings and vector databases are AI. What is the vector data model? In GIS, the vector data model represents the world as discrete features: points for single locations, lines for linear features such as rivers and roads, and polygons for areas such as lakes and administrative boundaries. Each feature links to attributes in a table. Also asked as: what is vector data model It contrasts with the raster model, which represents the world as a grid of cells, suited to continuous data such as elevation, rainfall or satellite imagery. Vector data is precise, compact for discrete features and good for network analysis and maps with sharp boundaries. Common formats include shapefiles, GeoJSON, GeoPackage and spatial databases such as PostGIS. What are some vector data examples? GIS examples: schools and hospitals as points, roads, railways and rivers as lines, and state boundaries, land parcels and lakes as polygons. AI examples: sentence embeddings for search, image embeddings for visual similarity, and face embeddings for recognition. Concretely, a GeoJSON file of bus stops is GIS vector data, each stop a point with a name and route attributes. A 384-number embedding of the sentence "How do I apply for a scholarship?" is AI vector data. In FaceVision, each enrolled face becomes an embedding vector, stored without the original image, and recognition compares a new face's vector against stored ones. What does data in a vector database look like? Each record typically has an ID, a vector of numbers, metadata such as source, title, page and date, and often the original text chunk. For example: ID "handbook-p12-c3", a 768-number embedding, metadata about the hostel rules section, and the chunk text. {&quot;id&quot;: &quot;handbook-p12-c3&quot;, &quot;vector&quot;: [0.021, -0.113, 0.087, &quot;...&quot;], &quot;metadata&quot;: {&quot;source&quot;: &quot;student-handbook.pdf&quot;, &quot;page&quot;: 12, &quot;section&quot;: &quot;Hostel rules&quot;}, &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Students must return to the hostel by 10 pm...&quot;} Queries send a vector, plus optional metadata filters, and receive the most similar records with scores. How do vector databases store data? Vector databases store vectors with IDs and metadata in segments on disk or in memory, and build approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, commonly HNSW graphs or inverted-file indexes, so searches check only promising candidates instead of every vector. Many also compress vectors with quantisation to save memory, keep payload or metadata indexes for filtering, and use write-ahead logs for durability. Database extensions such as pgvector store vectors in ordinary table columns, with indexes managed by PostgreSQL. Storage design trades off memory, speed and accuracy, so most systems let you tune index parameters and choose in-memory or disk-based storage. Does a vector database keep the original chunked text for RAG? It can, and for RAG it usually should. Most vector databases let you store the chunk text and metadata alongside each vector, so retrieval returns the text needed for the prompt. Alternatively, store only IDs and fetch text from another database. Also asked as: does a vector database maintain pre-vector chunked data for rag systems Storing text with vectors is simpler; keeping text in a separate store suits large documents, strict access control or existing databases. Either way, keep the original documents and chunk text somewhere durable, because you will need to re-embed everything when you change embedding models. Vectors alone cannot be reliably turned back into exact text, and you need the text for citations. Why do we need a vector database? We need vector databases to search large collections by meaning quickly, with filtering, updates and persistence. Comparing a query against millions of vectors one by one is too slow; vector indexes make it fast. Also asked as: why do we need vector db You may not need a dedicated one: for small collections, an in-memory library or a few thousand vectors in a NumPy array works; for apps already on PostgreSQL, pgvector is often enough. Dedicated vector databases help with very large scale, heavy filtering, multi-tenancy and high query volumes. Choose based on data size, latency needs and what your team already operates. How do I use a vector database? Choose an embedding model, embed your data in chunks, insert vectors with IDs, metadata and text, create an index, then embed each query with the same model and search for the nearest vectors, optionally with filters. Also asked as: how to use vector db Steps for a RAG app: Chunk documents and embed each chunk. Upsert vectors with metadata such as source and page. Create an HNSW or similar index. At query time, embed the question and retrieve the top 5 to 20. Optionally combine with keyword search and rerank. Pass the best chunks to a language model with citation instructions. Record the embedding model name with your index so you never mix models. Does LangChain have a vector database? LangChain is not a vector database, but it provides a common vector store interface with integrations for many databases, including pgvector, Chroma, FAISS, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate and Milvus, plus a simple in-memory store for testing. Also asked as: does langchain have vector db This lets you write retrieval code once and switch backends with minimal changes. For production, choose the underlying database deliberately for scale, filtering and operations, and consider writing direct queries when you need features the abstraction does not expose, such as hybrid search tuned in SQL. LangChain's retriever interface then connects the store to chains and agents. What is the difference between an initialisation vector and a key in encryption? The key is the secret that encrypts and decrypts data and must be protected. The initialisation vector, or IV, is a random or unique value used with the key so the same plaintext encrypts differently each time; it is not secret but must not be reused improperly. Also asked as: encryption: use of initialization vector vs key For example, with AES in GCM mode, each message needs a unique nonce or IV with the same key; reusing one can break security badly. The IV is usually stored or sent alongside the ciphertext. This "vector" is simply a block of bytes and has nothing to do with embeddings or GIS vector data. Use well-tested libraries rather than implementing encryption yourself.

# What is a vector embedding? Embedding models, search, and long texts
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vector-embedding/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A vector embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of data, such as a word, sentence, image or document, so that similar things have vectors close together. Embedding models produce these vectors, and vector search uses them to find the most similar items to a query, which is the retrieval step in RAG systems like RAG.NextUpgrad. This page explains embeddings and embedding models, how search works, terminology, building an embedding layer from scratch, long texts, embeddings versus TF-IDF, rerankers, and choosing a model.

## What is a vector embedding?

A vector embedding is a fixed-length list of numbers, often hundreds or thousands long, that encodes the meaning or features of an input. Inputs with similar meaning map to vectors that are close in that space, measured by cosine similarity or distance.

For example, "How do I reset my password?" and "I forgot my login" have different words but similar embeddings, so a search using embeddings matches them. Embeddings exist for text, images, audio and code, and multimodal models can place images and text in the same space. They power semantic search, recommendations, clustering, duplicate detection and classification, and they are the backbone of retrieval-augmented generation.

## What is an embedding model?

An embedding model is a neural network that converts input, such as text, into an embedding vector. Text embedding models are trained so that related sentences or passages produce nearby vectors and unrelated ones produce distant vectors.

You can use hosted embedding models through APIs from providers such as OpenAI, Google and others, or open models from Hugging Face, such as sentence-transformers and newer open embedding families, run locally or through Ollama. Important properties are the vector dimension, maximum input length, supported languages and quality on retrieval benchmarks. The rule that matters most in practice: use the same embedding model for indexing documents and for embedding queries, or the vectors will not be comparable.

## How does an embedding model work?

Modern text embedding models are transformer encoders. They tokenise the text, process tokens with attention so each token's representation reflects its context, and pool the token vectors, for example by averaging, into one vector for the whole text.

They learn useful vectors through contrastive training: pairs of related texts, such as a question and its answer passage, are pulled together, while unrelated texts are pushed apart. Training on millions of such pairs teaches the model which meanings are similar. Sentence-BERT popularised this approach for sentence embeddings. Some models also accept instructions, such as "represent this query for retrieval", which improves search quality, so follow each model's usage notes on its model card.

## How does vector embedding search work?

You embed every document chunk once and store the vectors in an index. At query time, you embed the query with the same model and find the stored vectors nearest to it, returning their chunks as results.

Comparing a query with every vector works for small collections but becomes slow at scale, so vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, such as HNSW graphs or inverted-file indexes, that return nearly the best matches in milliseconds. Normalise vectors and use cosine similarity or inner product as the model recommends. In production, combine vector search with keyword search, merge the lists with reciprocal-rank fusion, and add metadata filters, because embeddings alone often miss exact terms such as IDs and error codes.

## Are "vector embedding" and "embedding vector" interchangeable?

Yes, in practice they mean the same thing: the vector produced by an embedding model. "Embedding" alone is also common. Strictly, "embedding" can mean the mapping itself, while "embedding vector" is one output of it.

You will also see "dense vector" or "dense representation", in contrast to sparse vectors from keyword methods such as BM25 or TF-IDF, where most values are zero. In vector database documentation, "vectors" usually refers to embeddings. When writing documentation or reports, pick one term and use it consistently, and say which model produced the vectors, because embeddings from different models are not interchangeable.

## How can I create an embedding layer from scratch?

An embedding layer is a lookup table: a matrix with one row per word in your vocabulary, initialised randomly and learned during training. In PyTorch, `nn.Embedding` provides it; training the network on a task updates the rows so useful word relationships emerge.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn
vocab = {"<pad>": 0, "ai": 1, "model": 2, "data": 3}
emb = nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=len(vocab), embedding_dim=8, padding_idx=0)
ids = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 3]])
vectors = emb(ids)          # shape (1, 3, 8)
```

To learn word vectors without a downstream task, train word2vec-style: predict surrounding words from a word, or the reverse, which makes words in similar contexts get similar vectors. For real projects, pre-trained sentence embedding models are far better than training from scratch.

## How do you create embeddings for long texts?

Split long texts into chunks, embed each chunk, and store them separately with a reference to the source document. A single vector for a 32,000-character document averages away detail, and many embedding models cannot accept that much text anyway.

Chunking guidelines:

- Split by structure, such as headings and paragraphs, to keep ideas together.
- Use chunks of a few hundred tokens, with small overlap where meaning spans boundaries.
- Include the document title and section heading in each chunk's text.
- Keep page numbers and IDs in metadata for citations.

If you need one vector per document, for example for clustering, average the chunk embeddings or use a long-context embedding model, but retrieve at chunk level for question answering.

## Vector embeddings vs TF-IDF: which is better for document similarity?

Embeddings usually perform better when meaning matters and wording differs, such as paraphrases and questions versus answers. TF-IDF and BM25 perform better for exact terms, rare names, codes and specialised jargon. Combining both usually beats either alone.

TF-IDF and bag-of-words count words, so "car" and "automobile" do not match, but "error 0x80070005" matches exactly. Embeddings capture semantics but can blur specific identifiers. TF-IDF is also cheap, transparent and needs no model. A sound approach is to evaluate both on your own data with labelled similar pairs or search queries, then use hybrid retrieval: run both, and merge results with reciprocal-rank fusion, as RAG.NextUpgrad does with dense retrieval and BM25.

## What is the difference between an embedding model and a reranking model?

An embedding model encodes the query and each document separately into vectors, which makes search over millions of documents fast. A reranking model, usually a cross-encoder, reads the query and one document together and outputs a relevance score, which is more accurate but too slow to run over everything.

So they work in two stages: embeddings, often with keyword search, retrieve the top 50 to 100 candidates quickly, and the reranker reorders those candidates by true relevance. Adding a reranker is one of the most effective ways to improve RAG answers, because the right passage is often retrieved but ranked too low to reach the prompt. Measure retrieval recall at 5 before and after adding one.

## What is the best embedding model for semantic search?

There is no universal best. Check the MTEB leaderboard for retrieval scores, then test two or three candidates on your own queries, considering language support, maximum input length, vector size, speed and cost.

Practical guidance:

- **Hosted and easy**: embedding APIs from major providers.
- **Open and local**: strong sentence-transformers and newer open embedding models, runnable with Ollama or Hugging Face.
- **Indian languages or mixed Hindi-English**: choose a multilingual model and test on your own data.
- **Large scale**: smaller dimensions reduce storage and speed up search.

Build a test set of 50 real queries with known relevant passages, and pick the model with the best recall at 5 for your data, not the best leaderboard score.

# What is vibe coding? Origin, best platforms, Claude and GitHub, and jobs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vibe-coding-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Vibe coding is building software by describing what you want to an AI tool in plain language, running what it produces, and steering by results rather than writing or reading every line yourself. Andrej Karpathy coined the term in February 2025, and it spread quickly with app builders and coding agents. It is a fast way to prototype and a risky way to ship. This page covers its origin, the main apps and platforms, how to do it with Claude and GitHub Copilot, Power Apps, when to use it, whether it helps you get a job, and its future.

## What is vibe coding in AI?

Vibe coding is a style of AI-assisted programming where you describe the app or feature you want, let an AI generate the code, test it by using it, and keep asking for changes until it works, focusing on the result rather than the code itself.

It differs from traditional AI-assisted coding, where a developer reads and owns every line the assistant suggests. In vibe coding the human acts more like a product owner: "add a login page", "make the button blue", "fix this error". It lowers the barrier to building, letting non-programmers create working tools. The trade-off is hidden problems: security holes, duplicated logic, fragile code and dependencies nobody understands, which surface later.

## When was vibe coding coined?

Andrej Karpathy, an AI researcher who co-founded OpenAI and led AI at Tesla, coined "vibe coding" in a post in February 2025, describing coding where you "give in to the vibes" and let the AI handle the code.

The term caught on quickly because it named something many people were already doing with tools such as Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT and app builders. Within months, it was used in product marketing, job posts and debates about software quality. It describes a practice made possible by much stronger coding models and agentic tools in 2024 and 2025, which could write and fix whole features rather than single lines.

## What are vibe coding apps?

Vibe coding apps let you build software from natural language. Browser-based app builders such as Lovable, Bolt, v0 by Vercel and Replit generate and host full apps from prompts; coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot's agent mode and Codex work inside real codebases.

The two groups suit different people. App builders give the fastest path from idea to a running web app with hosting included, ideal for non-developers and prototypes. Coding agents work with your own repository, tools and tests, ideal for developers who want speed with control. Many builders start a prototype in an app builder, export the code, and continue in a coding agent when the project becomes serious.

## Which vibe coding platform is best?

For non-developers building a web app prototype, Lovable, Bolt, v0 and Replit are the easiest. For developers working on real projects, Claude Code, Cursor and GitHub Copilot's agent mode give more control and better results on existing codebases.

How to choose:

- **Speed to a hosted demo**: an app builder.
- **Your own stack and repository**: a coding agent.
- **Team on GitHub with enterprise controls**: GitHub Copilot.
- **Long, multi-file changes**: Claude Code or Cursor's agent.
- **Free start**: free tiers of several tools, which change often.

Try two on the same small project, such as a hackathon registration app, and compare how much you had to fix.

## How do I vibe code with Claude?

Use Claude Code in your terminal or IDE for real projects, or artifacts on claude.ai for quick prototypes. Describe the feature, let Claude build it, run it, and ask for fixes with exact error messages.

A workflow with Claude Code:

- Start a project folder with Git, and add a `CLAUDE.md` describing the stack and rules.
- Ask for a plan first: "Plan a Next.js app for hackathon registrations with a form and admin list."
- Build feature by feature, running the app after each step.
- Ask for tests alongside features.
- Commit after every working step so you can roll back.
- Ask Claude to review the code for security issues before sharing.

Keep API keys in `.env` files and never paste secrets into prompts.

## How do I vibe code with GitHub?

Use GitHub Copilot's agent mode in VS Code to build features from natural language, and the Copilot coding agent on GitHub to hand off issues and review the pull requests it opens. GitHub then gives you version history, reviews and continuous integration.

Steps:

- Create a repository and open it in VS Code with Copilot.
- Add `.github/copilot-instructions.md` with your stack and conventions.
- In agent mode, describe a feature and review each change before accepting.
- Set up GitHub Actions to run tests on every push.
- For small tasks, write an issue with clear acceptance criteria and assign it to Copilot.

Version control is what makes vibe coding safe: every change is reviewable and reversible.

## What is vibe coding in Power Apps?

In Power Apps, Microsoft's low-code platform, vibe coding refers to building business apps by describing them in natural language with Copilot, which generates the app's screens, data tables and logic for you to refine.

You describe something like "an app for tracking lab equipment loans with a form, a list and an approval step", and Copilot proposes the data structure and screens, which you then adjust conversationally or in the editor. Because it runs on the Power Platform, the result inherits Microsoft 365 sign-in, Dataverse data storage and admin governance, which suits organisations. Microsoft's natural-language app-building features have been changing quickly, so check current Power Apps documentation for what is available.

## When should I use vibe coding?

Use vibe coding for prototypes, hackathon builds, internal tools, personal scripts and exploring ideas, where speed matters more than long-term maintainability. Avoid pure vibe coding for production systems that handle money, personal data or security-sensitive operations.

Signs it fits: a short-lived project, a demo, a tool only you use, or a first version to test with users. Signs it does not: payments, authentication, health or legal data, or code that a team must maintain for years. For those, use AI as a pair programmer instead: generate code, but read it, test it and understand it. Security basics, such as input validation and access control, are where vibe-coded apps fail most often.

## Can vibe coding get you a job?

Not on its own. Employers hire people who can build reliable software and explain how it works. Vibe coding can help you ship more projects faster, which helps, but only if you understand and can defend what you built.

How to make it count: use AI tools to build real projects, then study the code, refactor it, add tests and write a README explaining design decisions. In interviews, you will be asked why you chose an approach, how you handled errors and what you would change. Hackathon judges ask the same, and I have seen teams lose points for polished demos they could not explain. Skill with AI coding tools is now expected; understanding is what sets you apart.

## Why is vibe coding the future?

Because building software through natural language makes creation accessible to far more people and makes developers much faster. The future is likely a mix: vibe coding for exploration and simple apps, and engineering discipline for systems people depend on.

As models improve, more of the code will be written by AI, and the human role shifts to defining requirements, designing systems, reviewing changes, testing and taking responsibility for quality and security. That favours people who combine product sense with engineering judgement. Students should learn to use AI coding tools fluently while building strong fundamentals, because when the vibes fail, someone has to debug the system.
