# What is vLLM? vLLM vs Ollama vs llama.cpp vs SGLang, and how to actually serve an LLM in production
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vllm-ollama-and-llm-inference-serving/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is vLLM?

**vLLM is an open-source inference server for large language models built around PagedAttention, a memory-management technique that lets many concurrent requests share a GPU's memory efficiently by managing the attention key-value cache the way an operating system manages virtual memory, in pages, rather than reserving one large contiguous block per request [1][2]. The practical result is much higher throughput on the same hardware compared with naively calling a model's `generate()` method for each request, which is why vLLM is the default choice for serving open-weight models at real request volume.**


Every production system I run that serves an open model sits on some form of batched serving; the difference between "it works in a notebook" and "it serves five hundred requests a minute without falling over" is almost entirely this layer.

> A model that answers one request beautifully and a service that answers a thousand requests a minute are different engineering problems. vLLM, SGLang and friends are the answer to the second one.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Why can't I just call `model.generate()` for production traffic?

**Because it processes one request, or a small fixed batch, at a time, and each request occupies GPU memory for its full duration even while it is producing tokens slowly one at a time. Real traffic arrives as many concurrent requests of different lengths, and naive batching either wastes memory reserving worst-case space for every request or wastes GPU time waiting for a batch to fill before starting. Continuous batching solves the second problem, starting and finishing requests within a batch as they arrive and complete rather than waiting for a fixed batch to fill [8]. PagedAttention solves the first, sharing memory pages between requests instead of reserving a contiguous block per request [1].**



## What is Ollama, and how is it different from vLLM?

**Ollama is a tool for running open-weight models easily on a laptop or a single machine, wrapping llama.cpp with a simple CLI, a model library, and an API that feels like calling a hosted service [3]. It optimises for ease of local use, quantized models that fit on consumer hardware, and a good single-user experience, not maximum concurrent throughput. Running Ollama to serve many simultaneous users at scale is possible but is not what it is built or tuned for; vLLM is built specifically for that case.**


## What is llama.cpp, and where does it fit?

**llama.cpp is a C++ inference engine for running LLMs efficiently on CPUs and consumer GPUs, using quantized model formats such as GGUF to shrink memory use [4]. It underlies Ollama and many other local-inference tools. Its strength is portability and running well on hardware without a data-centre GPU, phones, laptops, Raspberry Pi-class devices; it is not designed around maximising throughput for many concurrent server requests the way vLLM is.**



## What is SGLang, and how does it compare to vLLM?

**SGLang is an inference framework that combines fast serving, similar in spirit to vLLM's continuous batching and paged memory, with a structured-generation front end that lets you express constrained outputs, branching, and reused prompt prefixes efficiently [5][6]. Its RadixAttention technique caches shared prompt prefixes across requests, which is particularly effective for workloads with repeated system prompts or few-shot examples, agents calling the same tools repeatedly. Benchmarks between vLLM and SGLang shift with every release of both; the honest answer is to benchmark your own workload rather than trust either project's numbers alone.**



## How do I decide what I actually need?

**Count your expected concurrent requests per second and your latency budget, then pick backward from that. A weekend project or an internal tool with a handful of users rarely needs more than Ollama on a single GPU or even a good CPU. A product with real concurrent traffic needs vLLM or SGLang on dedicated GPU serving from day one, because retrofitting proper batching after launch under load is a much worse day than provisioning for it up front.**



## What does this cost, and how does quantization fit in?

**Serving throughput and quantization are separate levers that stack: a quantized model uses less memory and can run on smaller GPUs, while a serving engine like vLLM uses that freed memory to run more concurrent requests rather than only fitting a bigger model [9]. The cheapest production setup is usually a quantized model served through vLLM or SGLang on the smallest GPU that hits your latency target, re-benchmarked whenever a new quantization method or a smaller strong model appears, since the frontier moves every few months.**



## LLM serving interview questions

**Explain what problem continuous batching solves. Describe PagedAttention in your own words. Compare vLLM, SGLang, Ollama and llama.cpp and say when you would choose each. Explain how quantization and serving throughput interact. Describe how you would capacity-plan a serving setup for a given requests-per-second target. The strongest answer includes a real throughput number you measured, not a number you read.**


## Where should I start?

**Stand up vLLM on a rented GPU with a small open model and hit it with a simple load-testing script, then repeat with Ollama on the same hardware and compare throughput yourself. The gap will be obvious within the first ten minutes.** For a hands-on session on serving LLMs in production, from a notebook to real concurrent traffic, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is workflow automation? How it works, with AI, and versus RPA
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-workflow-automation/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Workflow automation is using software to run a repeatable sequence of business steps, such as approving a leave request, onboarding a customer or processing an invoice, automatically instead of by hand. A trigger starts the workflow, and the software moves data between apps, applies rules and takes actions. With AI, workflows can also read documents, classify messages and draft replies. This page explains how it works, which tools to use, examples, how it differs from RPA, how to add AI safely, and how to learn it.

## What is workflow automation?

Workflow automation is the use of software to carry out a series of tasks, decisions and hand-offs that people used to do manually, following defined rules, so that work moves from start to finish with little human effort.

Typical candidates are tasks that are frequent, rule-based and boring: copying form responses into a spreadsheet, sending welcome emails, routing support tickets, creating invoices from orders, or posting alerts to a team chat. Automating them saves time, removes copy-paste errors and makes the process consistent and auditable. People stay in the loop for exceptions and decisions that need judgement. The aim is not to remove people but to stop them doing work a machine does better.

## How does workflow automation work?

A workflow starts with a trigger, then runs a series of steps: fetch or transform data, check conditions, and take actions in other systems through their APIs. Each run is logged so failures can be seen and retried.

A simple example: a trigger fires when a new row is added to a Google Sheet; a step formats the data; a condition checks whether the amount is above a threshold; an action creates a record in the CRM and another sends a message to the sales channel. Under the hood, the tool calls each app's API with stored credentials. Good workflows also handle errors: retries with back-off, alerts when a step fails, and idempotency so that a retry does not create duplicates. That last point is where most homemade automations break.

## What is a workflow automation tool?

A workflow automation tool is software that lets you build, run and monitor automated workflows, usually with a visual editor of triggers and steps and ready-made connectors to common apps. Zapier, Make, n8n and Microsoft Power Automate are popular examples.

They suit different people. Zapier is the easiest for non-developers connecting popular SaaS apps. Make offers more complex visual logic. n8n is popular with developers because it can be self-hosted, runs custom JavaScript or Python steps and has strong AI nodes. Power Automate fits organisations on Microsoft 365. For data and engineering pipelines, developers use code-first orchestrators such as Apache Airflow or Temporal instead, because they need versioning, testing and scale.

## What are some workflow automation examples?

Common examples include lead capture into a CRM, employee onboarding, invoice processing, support ticket routing, social media scheduling, report generation and alerts when a metric crosses a threshold.

Examples a student or small team can build this week:

- A contact form that saves to a sheet, emails a confirmation and notifies you on Telegram or Slack.
- A daily job that pulls yesterday's sales or website visits and emails a summary.
- An inbox rule that labels invoices, extracts amounts and adds them to a spreadsheet.
- A GitHub workflow that runs tests and deploys on every push.
- A hackathon registration flow that checks team sizes and sends welcome kits.

Pick one you do by hand every week; that is the best first automation.

## What is the difference between workflow automation and RPA?

Workflow automation connects systems through their APIs and data. Robotic process automation (RPA) uses software robots that operate an application's user interface like a person, clicking buttons and typing into fields.

Use RPA when a system has no API, such as an old desktop application or a government portal, because it is the only way in. Its weakness is fragility: a moved button or a changed page layout can break the robot. API-based workflow automation is faster, more reliable and easier to maintain. In practice, mature teams combine them: workflow tools orchestrate the process and call an RPA bot only for the one legacy step that needs it. UiPath and Power Automate Desktop are common RPA tools.

## What is workflow automation using AI?

AI workflow automation adds steps that need judgement, such as reading an email, extracting fields from a document, classifying a request or drafting a reply, to workflows that used to handle only fixed rules.

A classic workflow can route an email if the subject contains "invoice". An AI workflow can read any email, decide whether it is an invoice, a complaint or a meeting request, extract the amount and due date, and draft a response. AI agents go further, choosing which tools to call to reach a goal. This is powerful but less predictable than rules, so the AI step must be constrained: structured output, validation, confidence thresholds, and a human review queue for uncertain cases. Deterministic rules should still make the final decision on anything with money or legal effect.

## How do I use AI for workflow automation?

Put the model where judgement is needed and keep everything else deterministic. Give it a narrow job, require structured JSON output, validate it against a schema, and route low-confidence results to a person.

That is the design I used in DocuLens AI: a Groq-hosted Llama model extracts fields from invoices and contracts, the output is validated against a schema, and compliance scoring is deterministic code, not the model's opinion. A practical starting pattern in n8n or Make: trigger on a new email, send the text to an LLM with a prompt that returns `{"type", "amount", "due_date", "confidence"}`, check the JSON, then branch: high confidence goes to the spreadsheet, low confidence goes to a review list. Log every input and output so you can measure accuracy.

## What is the best AI workflow automation platform?

There is no single best one. n8n is a strong choice for developers who want AI agents, custom code and self-hosting; Zapier for the fastest setup with popular apps; Make for complex visual flows; Power Automate for Microsoft 365 organisations.

Choose by four questions. Where does your data live: Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or your own database? Who will maintain it: a developer or a non-technical team? Do you need self-hosting for data control? How many runs a month will you need, since pricing usually scales with runs or tasks? For custom AI products, a code-first approach with Python, a queue and an orchestrator gives the most control. Prototype the same flow on two platforms before committing.

## Is there an AI workflow automation tutorial?

Yes. The official documentation of n8n, Zapier, Make and Power Automate includes step-by-step tutorials, including AI steps. The fastest way to learn is to build one real automation end to end.

A one-evening tutorial with n8n:

- Run n8n locally or use its cloud trial, and create a workflow with a Gmail or IMAP trigger.
- Add an AI step that classifies each email and returns JSON.
- Add an IF node that checks the class and confidence.
- Send high-confidence results to a Google Sheet and the rest to a Slack or Telegram message for review.
- Add an error workflow that alerts you when a step fails.

Then run it for a week and read the logs.

## What is the best AI workflow automation course?

The best course is the official learning material of the tool you choose, plus a project you build yourself. n8n, Zapier and Microsoft Learn for Power Automate all have free tutorials and learning paths.

Look for courses that cover more than the visual editor: APIs and webhooks, JSON, authentication with OAuth and API keys, error handling, and how to evaluate AI steps. Those skills transfer between tools, while button-by-button lessons date quickly. If you know some Python, learning to call an LLM API and validate its output teaches more than a no-code course alone. A finished automation on your GitHub or in a short demo video is worth more to an employer or client than a certificate.

# What is YOLO in machine learning? Uses, versions and commercial licensing
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-yolo-machine-learning/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


YOLO, short for You Only Look Once, is a family of deep learning models for real-time object detection: given an image, it predicts boxes around objects and labels them, such as person, car or helmet, in a single pass of the network. That speed made it the default choice for video, robotics and edge devices. This page explains why YOLO is used, how the versions differ, whether it can classify, segment and work on video, the commercial licensing question, how it relates to vision-language models, how it compares with MediaPipe, and how to train one in Colab.

## What is YOLO in machine learning?

YOLO is an object detection model that divides an image into a grid and predicts, in one forward pass, bounding boxes, confidence scores and class labels for objects. It was introduced by Joseph Redmon and colleagues in 2016.

Earlier detectors first proposed many candidate regions and then classified each one, which was slow. YOLO framed detection as a single regression problem from image pixels to boxes and classes, trading a little accuracy for a large gain in speed. Later versions improved accuracy with better backbones, multi-scale features, anchor-free heads and training tricks, while keeping real-time performance. The output is a list of boxes with class and confidence, usually cleaned up with non-maximum suppression to remove duplicates.

## Why is YOLO used?

YOLO is used because it is fast, accurate enough for most practical tasks, easy to train on custom data and easy to deploy, from GPUs to phones and edge devices.

Typical uses:

- Traffic and vehicle counting from CCTV.
- Safety compliance, such as helmet and vest detection on construction sites.
- Retail shelf monitoring and product counting.
- Crop, pest and fruit detection in agriculture.
- Robotics and drones that must see in real time.

Its ecosystem matters too: tools such as Ultralytics provide training, evaluation and export in a few lines of code, and models export to formats such as ONNX and TensorRT. In FaceVision I ran vision models in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web, and the same export path lets YOLO run client-side.

## What is the difference between YOLO versions?

Versions differ in architecture, accuracy, speed and tooling, and they come from different authors. The original author released v1 to v3; later versions came from other researchers and from Ultralytics, which maintains the most widely used library.

A rough map:

- **v1 to v3** (2016 to 2018): the original design, adding anchors and multi-scale prediction.
- **v4** (2020): many training and architecture improvements.
- **v5 and v8**: Ultralytics' popular, easy-to-use releases; v8 added an anchor-free head and multiple tasks.
- **v6, v7, v9, v10**: research and industry releases with their own trade-offs.
- **YOLO11 and later**: newer Ultralytics models with better accuracy per computation.

For a new project, start with the latest stable Ultralytics model and compare two sizes on your own data.

## Can YOLO be used for image classification?

Yes. Ultralytics YOLO models include classification variants that predict a single label for a whole image, alongside detection, segmentation and pose models. Use classification when you only need "what is in this image", not where.

For example, classifying leaf images as healthy or diseased is a classification task; finding every diseased leaf in a field photo is detection. Classification models are smaller and faster, and need simpler labels: just a folder per class. If you might later need locations or counts, label boxes from the start, because converting a classification dataset into a detection dataset means relabelling everything. For pure classification, other architectures, such as EfficientNet or vision transformers, are also strong options.

## Can YOLO be used for segmentation?

Yes. YOLO segmentation models predict a pixel mask for each detected object as well as its box, which is instance segmentation. Ultralytics provides segmentation versions of its models.

Segmentation helps when the shape matters: measuring the area of a crack, counting overlapping fruits, separating people from background, or cutting out products. It needs polygon or mask labels, which take longer to create than boxes, though annotation tools with AI assistance speed this up. Segmentation models are a bit slower than detection models of the same size. If boxes are enough for your decision, use detection; add segmentation only when you need precise outlines.

## Can YOLO detect objects in video?

Yes. YOLO processes each video frame as an image, fast enough for real-time video on a GPU and often on edge devices with smaller models. Tracking links detections across frames so each object keeps an ID.

With Ultralytics, running on a video is one line, and tracking is another:

```python
from ultralytics import YOLO
model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt")
model.predict(source="traffic.mp4", save=True)          # boxes on every frame
model.track(source="traffic.mp4", save=True)            # adds persistent IDs
```

For counting objects crossing a line, use tracking IDs rather than raw detections, or you will count the same car many times. Lower resolution and smaller models increase frame rate.

## Can YOLO be used commercially?

It depends on the model's licence. Ultralytics YOLO models are released under AGPL-3.0, which requires releasing your source code if you distribute or offer the software as a service; closed-source commercial use needs an Ultralytics enterprise licence.

Other YOLO implementations have different licences, some more permissive, so check the licence of the exact repository and weights you use, including any pretrained weights and datasets. For college projects, research and open-source work, AGPL is usually fine. For a startup product or client work, decide on licensing before you build, because switching models late means retraining and re-validating. When unsure, ask the licensor or a lawyer; this page is not legal advice.

## Can YOLO be used with vision-language models?

YOLO itself is not a vision-language model; it predicts boxes for a fixed set of classes. But open-vocabulary detectors such as YOLO-World accept text prompts for classes, and YOLO is often combined with vision-language models in pipelines.

Two common patterns: use YOLO to find and crop objects quickly, then ask a vision-language model to describe or reason about each crop; or use a vision-language model to label images automatically, then train a fast YOLO model on those labels for real-time deployment. Open-vocabulary models let you detect "red helmet" or "fire extinguisher" without training a new model, at some cost in speed and accuracy compared with a custom-trained detector.

## MediaPipe vs YOLOv8: which should I use?

Use MediaPipe for ready-made, highly optimised on-device solutions such as face detection, face mesh, hand tracking and pose estimation. Use YOLOv8 or newer when you need to detect your own custom objects or want to train and tune the model yourself.

MediaPipe, from Google, provides pipelines that run in real time on phones and in browsers with little setup, and it offers some customisation through model training tools. YOLO gives you more control: custom classes, model sizes, training options and export targets. For a fitness app that counts squats, MediaPipe's pose solution is the quick path. For detecting helmets on a site or pests on leaves, train a YOLO model. Some projects use both.

## How do I train YOLOv8 in Google Colab?

Open a Colab notebook with a GPU, install Ultralytics, upload a labelled dataset in YOLO format with a `data.yaml` file, train a small model, then evaluate and export it.

```python
!pip install ultralytics
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt")                       # small pretrained model
model.train(data="data.yaml", epochs=50, imgsz=640)
metrics = model.val()                            # mAP on the validation set
model.export(format="onnx")                      # for deployment
```

Label a few hundred images per class with an annotation tool, keep a separate test set, and check predictions visually, not only the mAP number. Save weights to Google Drive, because Colab sessions reset.

# What problems does RAG solve? How it works, implementing it, and is it dead
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-problems-does-rag-solve/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Retrieval-augmented generation primarily solves four problems with language models: their knowledge is frozen at training time, they do not know your private data, they can make up confident answers, and they cannot show where an answer came from. RAG retrieves relevant documents at question time and makes the model answer from them, with citations. I built RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid search, reranking and a confidence gate, so this page covers RAG's purpose and name, how it works, implementing and improving it, SQL, ChatGPT, NVIDIA and its future. What problems does RAG primarily solve? RAG solves stale knowledge, missing private or specialised data, hallucination and lack of traceability. Instead of relying on what the model memorised, it grounds answers in documents you supply and update. Also asked as: what problems does retrieval augmented generation rag primarily solve Concretely: a college chatbot can answer from this year's fee and exam rules; a support assistant can use the latest product manuals; a legal research tool can cite exact clauses. Updating knowledge means updating documents, not retraining models. RAG also supports access control, since retrieval can respect who may see which documents. It does not eliminate errors, but evidence plus citations lets users verify, and a refusal rule can stop answers when evidence is weak. Why is it called retrieval-augmented generation? The name describes the method: the generation of text by a language model is augmented with information obtained by retrieval from an external source. It comes from the 2020 paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues that introduced the approach. Also asked as: why is it called retrieval augmented generation Lewis has said in interviews that the team would have chosen a more appealing name had they known how widely it would be used. The acronym stuck anyway, and "RAG" now names a whole family of techniques. It is unrelated to "RAG" in project management, which means Red, Amber, Green status. How does retrieval-augmented generation work? Documents are split into chunks, embedded and indexed. When a question arrives, the system retrieves the most relevant chunks, inserts them into the prompt with instructions to answer only from them, and the model generates an answer citing those chunks. Also asked as: how does retrieval augmented generation (rag) work Production systems add steps: query rewriting for follow-up questions, hybrid retrieval combining keyword and vector search, fusion of result lists, reranking with a cross-encoder, a confidence threshold, streaming output, and logging for evaluation. In RAG.NextUpgrad, dense and BM25 results are fused with reciprocal rank fusion, reranked, and answered with streamed citations, with multi-provider fallback if a model provider fails. Is retrieval-augmented generation a model? No. RAG is a technique and system architecture that combines a retriever, such as a search index, with a generator, a language model. You can build RAG with many different models and search engines. Also asked as: is retrieval augmented generation a model The original 2020 paper trained a retriever and generator together as one model, which is why some people still describe RAG as a model. Today's systems usually combine separately chosen components: an embedding model, a vector or hybrid search index, a reranker and a chat model. Changing any component keeps the system "RAG". This modularity is a strength: you can upgrade the model or search without rebuilding everything. How do I implement retrieval-augmented generation? Start simple: parse your documents, chunk them by structure, embed and index them, retrieve the top chunks for each question, and prompt a model to answer with citations. Then evaluate and improve retrieval before anything else. Also asked as: how to implement retrieval augmented generation Implementation checklist: Parse documents, using OCR for scans. Chunk by headings with metadata such as title and page. Index for both vector and keyword search. Retrieve, fuse and rerank. Prompt with rules: answer only from context, cite, refuse if unsure. Build 30 to 100 test questions with expected answers. Serve through an API with streaming and logging. Frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex speed this up, but understand each step. How do I improve retrieval in RAG? Fix chunking first, then add hybrid search, reranking and query rewriting, measuring each change on a fixed evaluation set. Retrieval quality, not the language model, causes most RAG failures. Also asked as: how to improve retrieval in rag Proven improvements: Chunk along document structure and prepend section titles. Add BM25 keyword search alongside vectors, fused with reciprocal rank fusion. Rerank the top 20 to 50 candidates with a cross-encoder. Rewrite follow-up questions into standalone queries. Use metadata filters for date, product or department. Add short contextual descriptions to chunks. Try a better or domain-tuned embedding model. Track recall at k: whether the right chunk appears in the retrieved set. Why use SQL for retrieval-augmented generation? SQL databases such as PostgreSQL can store chunks, embeddings, full-text indexes, metadata and permissions together, so one query can combine vector similarity, keyword matching, filters and access control. Much business knowledge also already lives in SQL tables. Also asked as: why sql for retrieval-augmented generation (rag With pgvector and Postgres full-text search, hybrid retrieval runs in a single database with transactions, backups and row-level security. For structured questions, such as "How many orders were delayed last week?", text-to-SQL retrieval queries the data directly instead of searching documents. Many strong RAG systems combine both: document retrieval for policies and explanations, SQL for numbers and records. Does ChatGPT use retrieval-augmented generation? Yes, in several features. ChatGPT's search retrieves web pages and answers with cited sources, uploaded files and custom GPT knowledge use retrieval over your documents, and connectors retrieve from linked apps. Plain chat without these relies on the model's trained knowledge. Also asked as: does chatgpt use retrieval augmented generation When ChatGPT shows citations to web pages, it is using a form of RAG. Answer quality then depends on which sources were retrieved. For your own organisation's data, a dedicated RAG system gives you control over sources, permissions, evaluation and refusal behaviour that general assistants cannot fully provide. What is retrieval-augmented generation according to NVIDIA? NVIDIA describes RAG as a technique for enhancing the accuracy and reliability of generative AI models with facts fetched from external sources, and offers tools to build it: NeMo Retriever for embedding and reranking, NIM microservices for deploying models, and reference blueprints for RAG pipelines. Also asked as: what is retrieval augmented generation nvidia Its widely read explainer compares RAG to a court clerk fetching precedents for a judge. NVIDIA's focus is enterprise RAG on GPU infrastructure, with fast embedding, retrieval and inference at scale. The underlying concepts are the same as any RAG system; NVIDIA's offerings are one implementation option, alongside open-source frameworks and cloud services. Is retrieval-augmented generation dead? No. Claims that long-context models or agents make RAG obsolete misread the problem. Even very long context windows cannot hold an organisation's entire knowledge base, and stuffing huge contexts is slow, costly and less accurate than retrieving relevant parts. Also asked as: is retrieval augmented generation dead What is changing is the form: agentic RAG lets models decide when and where to search, long context lets them read more retrieved material, and tools like file search and grep complement vectors. All of these are still retrieval feeding generation. As long as models need current, private and verifiable information, retrieval will remain central.

# When to use Ollama: vs vLLM, production, VS Code, Copilot, n8n and LlamaIndex
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/when-to-use-ollama/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Use Ollama when you want to run open language models on your own machine with minimal setup: local development, prototypes, privacy-sensitive documents, offline work and small internal tools. For serving many users at high throughput on GPU servers, a dedicated serving engine such as vLLM is the better fit. This page covers when Ollama fits, Ollama versus vLLM, production use, choosing a model, and using Ollama with VS Code, GitHub Copilot, n8n and LlamaIndex, plus Gemini and NPU questions. When should I use Ollama? Use Ollama when data must stay on your machine, when you want free, unlimited local experimentation, when you work offline, or when you need a quick local model for a prototype, internal tool or learning. Also asked as: when to use ollama · can i use ollama in vscode Good fits: Building and testing RAG pipelines without API costs. Processing private documents that cannot go to cloud services. Coding help in your editor with a local model. Automations with simple language tasks, such as classification or extraction. Teaching and learning how LLMs behave. Poor fits: hard reasoning and complex coding, where frontier hosted models are much stronger, and high-traffic production APIs, where serving engines and managed services scale better. Should I use Ollama or vLLM? Use Ollama for simplicity on a single machine: easy installs, model management and a friendly API. Use vLLM when serving a model to many concurrent users on GPUs, where its continuous batching and memory management give far higher throughput. A common pattern is Ollama during development and vLLM, or a managed provider, in production. vLLM exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so code written against OpenAI-style endpoints moves between them easily. vLLM needs more setup, a capable GPU and attention to model formats, while Ollama runs on laptops and CPUs. Benchmark your real workload: requests per second, latency at your concurrency, and memory use. Can I use Ollama in production? Yes, for modest workloads such as internal tools, small teams or low-traffic features, if you add authentication, monitoring and fixed model versions. For high concurrency or strict latency targets, a serving engine or managed API is usually better. Production checklist for Ollama: Put an authenticated proxy in front; the API has no login. Pin model versions and test before updating. Set concurrency and queue limits for your hardware. Keep models loaded to avoid cold starts. Log requests, latency and errors; alert on failures. Have a fallback provider for outages. Multi-provider fallback, which RAG.NextUpgrad uses, keeps users served when one model server struggles. Which Ollama model should I use? Choose by task and hardware: a 7B to 8B instruction model for general chat on a 16 GB laptop, a coding-tuned model for programming, a small 1B to 4B model for fast simple tasks or weak hardware, and an embedding model for search and RAG. Also asked as: which ollama model to use How to decide: List your task: chat, coding, extraction, classification, embeddings. Check memory: model file size plus room for context. Shortlist two or three from recent, reputable families in the Ollama library. Test on ten real prompts and compare quality and speed. Re-check every few months; open models improve quickly, and a newer small model often beats an older larger one. Can I use Ollama in VS Code? Yes. Several VS Code extensions connect to Ollama's local API for chat, code explanation and autocomplete, and VS Code's own AI chat can use Ollama models through its language model settings. Configure the extension with the Ollama URL and model name. For coding, choose a coding-tuned model that fits your GPU, and a small fast model for inline completions, since completions need low latency. Expect local models to be weaker than frontier hosted models on complex refactors, but useful for explanations, boilerplate and private codebases. Keep Ollama running in the background, and check ollama ps if responses are slow. How can I use Ollama models in GitHub Copilot? In VS Code, Copilot Chat lets you add models from other providers, including local models served by Ollama, through its model management settings, so you can chat with a local model in the Copilot interface. Availability depends on your Copilot plan, VS Code version and organisation policies. Steps generally involve opening the model picker in Copilot Chat, choosing to manage models, selecting Ollama as a provider, and picking an installed model. Local models will not match the hosted premium models on hard tasks, but they keep code on your machine and do not use premium request allowances. Organisations may disable bring-your-own-model options, so check policies at work. How do I use Ollama in n8n? Add n8n's Ollama chat model or embeddings node, set the credentials to your Ollama base URL, usually http://localhost:11434, or http://host.docker.internal:11434 if n8n runs in Docker, and connect it to an AI Agent or chain node. Also asked as: how to use ollama in n8n Typical uses: classify incoming emails, extract fields from form submissions into JSON, summarise documents, or answer questions over a vector store, all without sending data to external APIs. Keep prompts strict and outputs structured, validate them with an IF or Code node, and route uncertain results to a person. If n8n and Ollama run on different machines, secure the connection; never expose Ollama's port publicly. How do I use Ollama with LlamaIndex? Install LlamaIndex's Ollama integrations for the LLM and embeddings, set them as the defaults in LlamaIndex settings, then build an index and query engine as usual. Also asked as: how to use ollama with llamaindex # pip install llama-index llama-index-llms-ollama llama-index-embeddings-ollama from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader, Settings from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama from llama_index.embeddings.ollama import OllamaEmbedding Settings.llm = Ollama(model=&quot;llama3.2&quot;, request_timeout=120) Settings.embed_model = OllamaEmbedding(model_name=&quot;nomic-embed-text&quot;) index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(SimpleDirectoryReader(&quot;notes&quot;).load_data()) print(index.as_query_engine().query(&quot;What is paging?&quot;)) Raise timeouts for slower hardware, and evaluate retrieval with a few known questions before trusting answers. Can you use Gemini with Ollama? No. Gemini models are proprietary and only available through Google's apps and APIs, so they cannot run in Ollama. Google's open-weight Gemma models, which share research with Gemini, are available in Ollama. If you want Gemini, call the Gemini API, which has a free tier through Google AI Studio. If you want a local Google model, run Gemma with Ollama, choosing a size that fits your hardware. Many applications combine both: Gemma locally for private or high-volume simple tasks, and Gemini or another hosted model for harder ones, behind a common interface so switching is a configuration change. Will Ollama use my NPU? Generally not. Mainline Ollama runs models on CPUs and on supported GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD and Apple Silicon; neural processing units in recent laptops are not its main target. Some vendors provide their own tools or builds for running models on their NPUs. Copilot+ PCs and other laptops with NPUs use them mainly for Windows AI features and vendor-optimised runtimes. If NPU acceleration matters to you, look at the chip vendor's AI toolkits and check whether they support the models you want. For most users, a GPU or a strong CPU with enough RAM is what determines Ollama performance, so check ollama ps to see where your model runs.

# Where do Copilot files go? Uploads, downloads, chat history and limits
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/where-do-copilot-files-go/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Where Copilot files go depends on the account. With a work or school account, files you upload to Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat and documents it creates are usually stored in your OneDrive. With a personal account, files stay attached to the conversation and generated files are offered as a download link. This page explains Copilot versus Copilot Chat, where uploads, downloads and exports end up, what to do when Copilot will not produce a file, whether it reads Excel, how long it keeps history, why it has limits, and how it compares with ChatGPT.

## Copilot vs Copilot Chat: what is the difference?

Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat is the chat assistant included for work and school accounts, grounded in the web and the files you give it. Microsoft 365 Copilot is the paid add-on that also reads your organisation's emails, files and meetings and works inside the Office apps.

The practical difference is reach. Copilot Chat answers from public web content and from documents you upload or open, under enterprise data protection. The full Microsoft 365 Copilot can answer "what did my manager say about the launch?" by searching your mailbox, Teams chats and SharePoint, within your permissions, and it adds features such as meeting recaps in Teams and analysis in Excel. Consumer Copilot, for personal Microsoft accounts, is a third product with its own app and limits. Check the Copilot icon and the account shown in the corner to know which one you are using.

## Where do Copilot files go?

On work and school accounts, files that Copilot Chat receives or creates are generally saved to your OneDrive, in a folder created for Copilot. On personal accounts, they stay with the conversation and you download what you need.

The quickest way to find a file is the link in Copilot's reply: open it, then use "open file location" or check the file's path in OneDrive. Documents created inside Word, Excel or PowerPoint with Copilot are ordinary files and save wherever you save them, usually OneDrive or SharePoint. Copilot Pages, the shareable canvas for Copilot responses, are stored in Microsoft's cloud and appear in your Microsoft 365 app. Exact folder names and behaviour have changed over time, so search OneDrive for the file name if the link does not show it.

## Where does Copilot save files?

Copilot saves files where the surrounding app saves them. In Word, Excel and PowerPoint it is your chosen location, usually OneDrive or SharePoint. In Copilot Chat on a work account it is your OneDrive. In consumer Copilot it is your browser's download folder once you download.

This matters for two reasons. First, Copilot in Excel and Word works best on files saved to OneDrive or SharePoint, because it relies on the cloud copy; local files can limit features. Second, saved files follow normal sharing rules: a file in your OneDrive is private until you share it, and a file in a team SharePoint site is visible to that team. Rename generated files straight away, because default names such as "Document 3" are hard to find later.

## Where do files uploaded to Copilot go?

On a work or school account, a file you upload to Copilot Chat is generally stored in your OneDrive so Copilot can read it, and it stays covered by your organisation's security and compliance policies. On a personal account, it is kept with that conversation.

Uploading a file does not make it public or share it with colleagues. For work accounts, Microsoft states that prompts, responses and uploaded content are not used to train the foundation models and remain inside the Microsoft 365 service boundary. Even so, follow your college or company's data policy: do not upload documents you are not allowed to process with AI tools, such as other people's personal data. If you upload sensitive drafts often, clean up the OneDrive folder now and then.

## Where do Copilot files export to?

Exports go to the app or folder you choose. Copilot responses can be copied, exported to Word or turned into a Copilot Page; downloaded files go to your browser's downloads folder; and Office documents save to OneDrive or SharePoint by default.

If you want a response as a document, ask Copilot to create a Word document or use the export option under the response, then open it and save it under a proper name. For tables, ask for an Excel file or copy the table into Excel directly; formatting usually survives the paste. On phones, downloads go to the system's download location or the Files app. If an export link expires, which can happen with generated files, ask Copilot to regenerate the file in the same conversation.

## Why is Copilot not giving downloadable files?

Usually because the product or plan you are using cannot create that file type in chat, the request did not trigger file creation, or the download link expired. Asking explicitly for a named file type often fixes it.

Try these in order:

- Ask clearly: "Create a Word document named report.docx with this content."
- Ask for the content as text or a table in the chat, then paste it into Word or Excel yourself.
- Use Copilot inside the target app instead: Copilot in Word for documents, in Excel for spreadsheets, in PowerPoint for decks.
- Start a new conversation if the old one is long; long chats behave less reliably.
- Check whether your organisation has disabled file generation.

Copying the content is always the fallback, and it is often faster than fighting the download.

## Can Copilot read Excel files?

Yes. You can upload an Excel file to Copilot Chat and ask questions about it, and Copilot inside Excel analyses the open workbook directly: summaries, formulas, charts, PivotTables and trends.

For the best results inside Excel, format the data as a table with Ctrl+T, give each column a clear header, remove merged cells and blank rows, and save the file to OneDrive or SharePoint. Then ask specific questions, such as "which product had the largest month-on-month drop?". In chat, very large workbooks may be summarised rather than read in full, so share a focused sheet. Check any formula Copilot writes on a few rows by hand before trusting the totals.

## How long does Copilot keep chat history?

Consumer Copilot keeps your conversations until you delete them, either one by one or all at once in privacy settings. Work and school accounts keep Copilot interactions according to your organisation's retention policies, which admins set.

On work accounts, Copilot interactions are stored within the organisation's Microsoft 365 environment so they can be covered by compliance features such as retention and eDiscovery, the same way email is. Deleting a conversation from your view may not remove the organisation's record if a retention policy applies. On personal accounts you control the history yourself. Either way, assume anything you type may be kept and read later, and keep passwords, keys and personal identity numbers out of every chat.

## Why does Copilot have a chat limit?

Limits keep the service affordable and reliable. Every reply costs computing time, very long conversations exceed what the model can hold in context, and long chats tend to drift and give worse answers.

A model can only consider a fixed amount of text at once, its context window. In a long chat, older messages are dropped or summarised, so Copilot can forget instructions you gave at the start. Limits on turns per conversation or requests per day also protect the service at busy times and differ by account type. Work with the limits rather than against them: one conversation per task, a short summary of the important facts when you start a new chat, and the key instructions repeated in your first message.

## How does Copilot compare to ChatGPT?

Both are capable assistants, and Copilot uses OpenAI's GPT models for much of its work. The difference is integration: Copilot is built into Windows, Edge and Microsoft 365, while ChatGPT is a standalone app with its own tools.

Choose Copilot if your work happens in Outlook, Word, Excel and Teams, or your organisation provides it with enterprise data protection, because it can see the documents you are working on. Choose ChatGPT if you want one broad assistant with strong voice mode, image generation, custom GPTs and many third-party apps. Many people use both: Copilot for work documents, ChatGPT for learning and side projects. Test both on the same real task before deciding, because model updates change the balance every few months.

# Whisper in Python: install, audio arrays, timestamps, speakers, and self-hosting
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/whisper-ai-python-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Whisper in Python usually means `openai-whisper`, the open-source package for OpenAI's speech recognition model: install it, load a model and call `transcribe` on an audio file to get text with timestamps. This page is a developer's guide: setup and Python versions, feeding audio as NumPy arrays, word-level timestamps, adding speaker labels, choosing between self-hosted Whisper and a hosted API, apps built on Whisper, and safety. Speech-to-text is part of my OCR & Speech Workspace, so the advice comes from building with it.

## What is Whisper in Python?

In Python, Whisper is the `openai-whisper` library, which runs OpenAI's open-source Whisper speech recognition models locally. It transcribes audio in many languages, can translate speech into English, and returns segments with start and end times.

It depends on PyTorch for the model and ffmpeg for reading audio files. Model sizes range from tiny to large, trading speed for accuracy. Faster community implementations, such as faster-whisper and whisper.cpp, run the same models more efficiently and are popular in production. The Hugging Face Transformers library also provides Whisper models through its speech recognition pipeline, which is convenient if you already use Transformers.

## How do I use Whisper AI in Python?

Install ffmpeg on your system, install the package, load a model and transcribe.

```bash
pip install -U openai-whisper
```

```python
import whisper
model = whisper.load_model("small")             # tiny, base, small, medium, large
result = model.transcribe("lecture.mp3", language="en")
print(result["text"])
for seg in result["segments"][:3]:
    print(f'{seg["start"]:.1f}-{seg["end"]:.1f}s: {seg["text"]}')
```

Set the language when you know it, to avoid misdetection on short clips. Use a GPU if available; on CPU, start with `small` or try faster-whisper. For translation into English, pass `task="translate"`. The result also includes the detected language and segment timings, which you can turn into SRT subtitles with a few lines of code. For very long recordings on limited memory, split the audio into parts of a few minutes, transcribe each, and keep the offsets so every line still points to the right moment in the original file.

## Does Whisper AI work with Python 3.13?

It depends on whether PyTorch and Whisper's other dependencies provide packages for your Python version on your platform. If installation fails on a very new Python, create a virtual environment with a Python version that PyTorch officially supports and install there.

Check PyTorch's installation page for the supported Python versions and your operating system and GPU combination, then install the matching PyTorch build before installing Whisper. Most problems on new Python releases come from compiled dependencies not yet published as wheels, which makes pip try to build from source and fail. Using tools such as `pyenv` or `uv` to manage several Python versions side by side avoids breaking your system Python.

## How do I convert any audio file to a NumPy array for Whisper?

Whisper expects mono audio sampled at 16 kHz as a float32 NumPy array with values between -1 and 1. Use `whisper.load_audio`, which calls ffmpeg, or a library such as librosa, then pass the array to `transcribe`.

```python
import whisper, librosa
audio = whisper.load_audio("call.m4a")                       # float32, 16 kHz mono via ffmpeg
# or: audio, _ = librosa.load("call.m4a", sr=16000, mono=True)
result = whisper.load_model("base").transcribe(audio)
```

If your audio arrives as raw bytes from a microphone or stream, convert integer samples to float32 by dividing by 32768 for 16-bit audio, and resample to 16 kHz. Wrong sample rates produce garbled or sped-up transcripts, a common bug.

## How do I use whisper_timestamped in Python?

`whisper_timestamped` is an open-source extension of Whisper that adds word-level timestamps and confidence scores. Install it, load a model through it, and call its `transcribe` function; each segment then includes a list of words with start and end times.

```python
import whisper_timestamped as wt
audio = wt.load_audio("talk.mp3")
model = wt.load_model("small")
out = wt.transcribe(model, audio, language="en")
for w in out["segments"][0]["words"][:5]:
    print(w["text"], w["start"], w["end"], w["confidence"])
```

Word timestamps help with subtitles, karaoke-style highlighting and aligning transcripts with slides. Alternatives include WhisperX, which aligns words with a separate model, and the word timestamp option in faster-whisper. Check each project's README for current usage.

## Does Whisper do speaker diarisation, and how do I add it?

No. Whisper transcribes what was said but does not label who said it. To add speakers, run a diarisation model, such as pyannote.audio, to find speaker turns, then assign each transcript segment or word to the speaker active at that time. WhisperX combines these steps.

The pipeline: transcribe with Whisper and get timestamps; run diarisation to get segments like "Speaker 1 from 0.0 to 12.3 seconds"; align by overlapping times; merge consecutive segments from the same speaker. Diarisation works best with clear audio and distinct voices, and struggles with overlapping speech. Some diarisation models require accepting terms and a Hugging Face token. For meetings, many cloud speech services provide diarisation built in.

## AssemblyAI vs Whisper large-v3: which should you ship?

Ship self-hosted Whisper large-v3 when you need privacy, control and low cost at high volume, and can run GPUs. Ship a hosted speech API such as AssemblyAI when you need fast integration, streaming, diarisation and other features out of the box, and accept per-minute pricing and sending audio to a provider.

Decide with a test: transcribe 20 to 50 of your real recordings with both, compute word error rate against reference transcripts, and check names, numbers and speaker labels. Also compare latency, uptime commitments, data retention terms and total cost, including your engineering time for GPUs, scaling and monitoring. Accuracy differences vary by accent, domain and audio quality, so public benchmarks are only a starting point.

## When should I stop self-hosting Whisper?

Consider moving to a hosted API when GPU costs and maintenance time exceed API costs, when you need real-time streaming at scale, when reliability requirements outgrow your setup, or when you need features such as diarisation and custom vocabulary without building them.

Keep self-hosting when privacy or data residency rules require audio to stay on your infrastructure, when volume is high enough that GPUs are cheaper per minute, or when you need full control over models and versions. A useful middle path is a hybrid: self-host batch transcription of sensitive recordings and use an API for live features. Track cost per audio hour and engineer hours monthly to make the decision with numbers.

## Does Whisper AI have an app?

OpenAI does not ship Whisper as a standalone consumer app; Whisper is a model and open-source library. Many third-party apps use Whisper for transcription on desktop and mobile, and OpenAI's own products use speech recognition in features such as voice input.

If you want an app, look for transcription apps that state they run Whisper on the device, which keeps audio private, or that use a cloud API, which is faster on weak hardware. Check reviews, privacy policies and whether recordings are uploaded. For developers, a simple personal app is easy to build: a small web page that uploads audio to your own Whisper backend and returns a transcript.

## Is Whisper AI safe?

Whisper itself is safe to use: it is open-source software from OpenAI, and running it locally keeps audio on your machine. Safety concerns come from how you use it and which apps or services wrap it.

Points to watch: third-party apps may upload your recordings, so read their privacy policies; Whisper can occasionally produce text that was never spoken, especially during silence or music, which matters for medical, legal or accessibility uses; and recording people requires their consent. Download Whisper and models from official sources, keep dependencies updated, and review transcripts for important decisions.

# Who is a prompt engineer? Role, job description, and is it a real job?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/who-is-a-prompt-engineer/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

A prompt engineer is someone who designs, tests and refines the instructions, examples and context given to AI models so that they produce accurate, consistent and useful output for a specific product or task. The skill is real and valuable, but most people who do it hold broader titles, such as AI engineer, GenAI developer or conversation designer. This page covers the role and a typical job description, whether it is a real, lasting and technical job, certifications and pay, and how to prompt-engineer LLMs and AI systems well. Who is a prompt engineer? A prompt engineer is a specialist in getting reliable behaviour from AI models through prompts: system instructions, task instructions, examples, output formats and the context supplied, often inside a software product. Also asked as: how to prompt engineer ai They typically sit between product, engineering and domain experts: understanding what users need, translating it into precise instructions, and proving with tests that the model behaves correctly across many inputs. In practice, many are software engineers, data scientists, writers or domain experts who developed strong prompting and evaluation skills. The job title is less common than the skill, which has become part of everyday AI engineering. What is the role of a prompt engineer? The role is to make AI features reliable: write and maintain system prompts, design structured outputs, write tool descriptions for agents, build test sets, measure quality, analyse failures and improve prompts and context until results meet the bar. Also asked as: what is the role of prompt engineer Day-to-day tasks: Turning product requirements into clear model instructions. Creating evaluation sets of real and adversarial examples. Comparing models and prompt versions with metrics. Working with retrieval to supply the right context. Guarding against prompt injection and unsafe outputs. Documenting prompts and versioning them like code. The role overlaps heavily with AI engineering, which adds building the surrounding software. What is a prompt engineer job description? A typical job description asks for designing and optimising prompts for LLM-powered features, building evaluation frameworks, collaborating with engineers and product teams, and staying current with model capabilities, along with experience using LLM APIs and often Python. Common requirements in listings: Experience with LLM APIs from providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic or Google. Python for scripting evaluations and integrations. Understanding of retrieval-augmented generation and structured outputs. Strong writing and analytical thinking. Ability to design tests and interpret metrics. Domain knowledge for specialised roles, such as legal, health or education. When you read a listing, check whether it is really an AI engineering role in disguise; most are. Is prompt engineer a real job? Yes, the work is real: companies building AI products need people who can make models behave reliably. But dedicated "prompt engineer" titles are relatively uncommon, and most of this work is done by AI engineers, ML engineers, product specialists and domain experts. Early hype suggested prompt engineering would be a large standalone profession. In practice, as models became better at following plain instructions, the work shifted from clever wording to specification, context design and evaluation, which fit naturally into engineering and product roles. For students, the safest path is to learn prompting as part of a broader skill set rather than betting on the title alone. Is prompt engineer still a job? The skill is more important than ever, but it is increasingly part of other roles. Job listings now more often ask for "experience with prompt engineering" within AI engineer, GenAI developer, solutions engineer or content roles than for standalone prompt engineers. What has grown is the surrounding work: building agents, writing tool descriptions, designing retrieval, evaluating outputs and handling safety. Those are prompt engineering in a wider sense. If you enjoy the work, aim for roles such as AI engineer or applied AI specialist, where prompting is a daily tool and you also build the systems around it. Is prompt engineer a technical job? It can be either, but the most valuable version is technical. Strong prompt engineers use APIs, write Python to run evaluations, design JSON schemas, work with retrieval systems and understand model behaviour, tokens, context limits and costs. Less technical versions exist in content, marketing and education, where the focus is writing prompts for tools such as ChatGPT to produce material. Those roles value writing skill and domain knowledge. For long-term career growth in tech, build the technical side: being able to build and measure an AI feature end to end is far more valuable than writing good prompts in a chat window. What is a certified prompt engineer? A "certified prompt engineer" usually means someone who completed a prompt engineering course that issues a certificate. There is no widely recognised industry licence or official certification body for prompt engineering. Certificates from reputable course providers show you studied the topic, which may help a little on a CV. Employers care more about evidence: a project with measurable improvements, such as raising extraction accuracy on a test set by redesigning prompts and adding validation. Be cautious of expensive certifications that promise jobs. Free official guides from model providers, plus a portfolio project, are a better investment. What is the salary of a prompt engineer? Pay depends on the actual role, company, location and experience rather than the title, and listings vary widely. Because standalone prompt engineer roles are uncommon, there is no reliable single figure, especially in India. Also asked as: what is the salary of prompt engineer To understand current pay for the roles you target, compare listings on job portals and company career pages for AI engineer and GenAI developer positions, and talk to people in those roles. Technical roles that combine prompting with software engineering, retrieval and evaluation are generally valued more than prompt-writing alone. Focus on building the skills those higher-value roles require. How do I prompt-engineer an LLM? Treat prompts like code: define the task precisely, write a clear system prompt, specify the output format, add examples where format matters, supply the right context, then test against a set of real inputs and iterate based on failures. Also asked as: how to prompt engineer llm A practical loop: Write a test set of 30 to 50 real inputs with expected outputs. Draft the prompt with role, rules, context and output schema. Run all tests, score results and read failures. Fix one thing at a time: instruction, example, context or schema. Re-run and keep the version only if scores improve. Use structured outputs for anything parsed by code, and keep prompts in version control. How do I prompt-engineer AI systems beyond a single model? For AI systems, prompt engineering extends to context design and tools: deciding what information to retrieve, how to describe tools so agents use them correctly, when the model should ask for help, and how to evaluate the whole pipeline, not just one prompt. In a RAG system, most quality comes from retrieval: good chunks, hybrid search and reranking, then a prompt that requires citations and permits "I don't know". In agents, tool names and descriptions are the most influential prompts. Evaluate end to end with task success rates and faithfulness scores. That system-level view is what separates prompt engineering in production from prompting in a chat window, and it is how I approach systems like RAG.NextUpgrad.

# Why does Copilot not work? Fixes, offline use, saved chats and credits
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/why-copilot-not-working/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Copilot usually stops working because of a sign-in or licence problem, an outdated app, a network or firewall block, a policy set by your organisation, or an outage at Microsoft. It also needs an internet connection, since its models run in the cloud. This page walks through fixes for constant and intermittent failures, what works offline, how long Copilot and Claude keep your chats, and how Copilot credits and Copilot Studio work.

## Why does Copilot not work?

The most common causes are being signed in with the wrong account, a missing licence for the feature you want, an outdated Windows, Edge or Office version, a network that blocks Copilot, or a policy that disables it on work devices.

A checklist that fixes most cases:

- Confirm which account is signed in, personal or work, and that it has the feature.
- Update Windows, Edge and the Microsoft 365 apps.
- Sign out completely and sign back in.
- Try copilot.microsoft.com in a browser to isolate app problems.
- Switch networks, for example to mobile data, to rule out a firewall or VPN.
- Ask IT whether Copilot is enabled for your account and device.

If nothing works, check Microsoft's service status for an incident.

## Why does Copilot sometimes not work?

Intermittent failures usually come from temporary service load, an expiring sign-in session, unstable network connections, very long conversations, or hitting a usage limit for a feature such as image creation.

Patterns and fixes:

- **Fails at busy times**: wait a few minutes or retry; heavy load causes timeouts.
- **Fails after a long chat**: start a new conversation with a short summary.
- **Fails on one feature only**: you may have reached that feature's limit.
- **Fails on campus or office Wi-Fi only**: the network may filter some endpoints.
- **Fails after waking the laptop**: sign-in tokens may need refreshing; restart the app.

Note the time and what you were doing when it fails; patterns point to the cause quickly.

## Does Copilot work offline?

No. Copilot's chat runs on large models in Microsoft's cloud, so it needs an internet connection. Without one, the app cannot send your prompt or receive an answer.

Some AI features on Copilot+ PCs run locally on the laptop's neural processing unit, such as certain camera effects, live captions and some image tools, and those can work offline. They are Windows features, not the Copilot chat assistant. If you need an assistant without internet, for example while travelling, you can run a small open-weight model locally with a tool such as Ollama, accepting much lower capability than Copilot or other cloud assistants.

## Does Copilot work without internet?

The Copilot assistant does not work without internet, but you can prepare for offline time: export or copy answers you need, save documents locally, and use on-device Windows features that do not need the cloud.

Practical tips for poor connectivity, common on trains and in hostels: draft prompts offline and send them when connected; keep conversations short so they load quickly on slow networks; use the mobile app on mobile data if Wi-Fi is unreliable; and save important outputs as files rather than relying on chat history. GitHub Copilot in your code editor also needs a connection for suggestions, so download documentation you will need for offline coding.

## Do Copilot chats save?

Yes. Consumer Copilot saves your conversations in your account so you can return to them, until you delete them. Work and school accounts store Copilot interactions within the organisation's Microsoft 365 environment.

On a personal account, open your conversation history in the Copilot app or website to revisit, rename or delete chats, and use your Microsoft privacy settings to manage stored data. On a work account, your history may be visible to you in Copilot Chat, and the organisation can retain and search interactions for compliance, like email. If you do not want something stored, do not type it into any assistant. GitHub Copilot keeps chat history in your editor session.

## How long are Copilot chats saved?

On personal accounts, chats are kept until you delete them or clear your history. On work and school accounts, the organisation's retention policies decide how long Copilot interactions are kept, which can range from short periods to several years.

Deleting a chat on a work account removes it from your view, but a retention policy may keep a copy for compliance. Admins configure these policies in Microsoft Purview, often matching the rules for Teams chats and email. If you need to know your organisation's rules, ask IT or check your company's data policy. For personal accounts, review the privacy dashboard periodically and delete conversations you no longer need.

## Do Copilot chats expire?

Generally no, on personal accounts: conversations stay in your history until you delete them. On work accounts, an organisation's retention policy can delete them automatically after a set time.

Some temporary content does expire: generated download links for files can stop working after a while, and very old features or conversation formats can change when Microsoft updates the app. If a chat contains something you will need later, such as code, a plan or an important explanation, copy it into a document or notes app. Chat history is a convenience, not a reliable archive.

## Does Claude AI save chats?

Yes. Claude saves your conversations in your Anthropic account so they sync across the web, desktop and mobile apps, until you delete them. Projects keep their files and instructions as well.

You can delete individual chats, and your privacy settings control whether your conversations may be used to improve Anthropic's models; review that setting and choose deliberately. Deleted conversations are removed from your history and deleted from Anthropic's systems after a period described in its privacy policy. Incognito-style chats that are not saved to history are available too. As with any assistant, keep passwords, keys and identity documents out of your chats.

## How do Copilot credits work?

In Copilot Studio, agent usage is measured in Copilot Credits: each interaction or action an agent performs consumes credits from your organisation's capacity, with more complex actions, such as generative answers or autonomous runs, costing more. Consumer Microsoft 365 plans use a separate allowance of AI credits for Copilot in apps.

For organisations, admins buy capacity and assign it to environments, then monitor consumption in the Power Platform admin centre. Agents used by licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot users inside Microsoft 365 may be billed differently from public website agents. Because Microsoft adjusts rates and names, check the current Copilot Studio licensing guide before estimating costs. Designing agents with focused knowledge and fewer unnecessary actions reduces consumption.

## How does Copilot Studio work?

Copilot Studio is a low-code tool where you build an agent from instructions, knowledge sources and actions, test it in a chat pane, then publish it to channels such as Teams, websites and Microsoft 365 Copilot. A language model orchestrates which knowledge and actions to use for each message.

The building blocks are knowledge such as websites, SharePoint and uploaded files; actions such as connectors, Power Automate flows and APIs; topics for fixed conversation paths; and triggers for agents that run on events or schedules. Analytics show conversations, success rates and where users get stuck. Agents live in Power Platform environments, so development, testing and production can be separated and governed. Start with one narrow use case and expand after reviewing real conversations.
