# Why vector embeddings? How they work, creation, storage, inversion and GraphRAG
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/why-vector-embeddings/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Vector embeddings exist because computers cannot compare meaning directly: an embedding model converts text, images or audio into a list of numbers where similar meanings sit close together, so software can search, cluster and recommend by similarity instead of exact words. They are the retrieval engine of RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad and the identity layer of FaceVision. This page covers why they matter, how they work and are created, storage, inversion, GraphRAG, quantization, and when to use them. Why do we use vector embeddings? We use vector embeddings because they let software measure similarity of meaning. Keyword matching fails when people use different words; embeddings recognise that "reset password" and "forgot my login" are related, enabling semantic search, recommendations and retrieval. They also compress complex data into compact numbers that standard algorithms can process: clustering similar documents, detecting duplicates, classifying text with little training data, and finding similar images or faces. In FaceVision, a face becomes an embedding, and recognition compares embeddings rather than storing or comparing photos. One representation powers many tasks, which is why embeddings became foundational in modern AI systems. What are embeddings in vector search? In vector search, embeddings are the vectors stored in the index and the vector made from the query. The search returns stored items whose embeddings are closest to the query embedding, usually by cosine similarity. Also asked as: why vector embeddings Both sides must come from the same model so they share one vector space. The index uses approximate nearest-neighbour structures such as HNSW to search millions of vectors quickly. Results carry IDs and metadata so the application can show documents, products or images. In RAG, the top chunks then go to a language model. Adding keyword search alongside, in hybrid search, covers exact identifiers that embeddings can blur. How do vector embeddings work? An embedding model maps each input to a point in a high-dimensional space, typically hundreds to thousands of dimensions. Training arranges this space so that related inputs are close and unrelated ones are far apart, letting distance stand in for similarity. Each dimension is not a single human-readable feature; meaning is spread across all of them. Directions in the space can encode relationships, as the classic word2vec example of king and queen showed. Modern models use transformers that read whole sentences, so the same word in different contexts gives different vectors. Similarity is computed with cosine similarity or dot product, which are cheap enough to compare at scale. How are vector embeddings created? They are created by passing data through a trained embedding model: text through a text encoder, images through an image encoder. The model outputs a fixed-length vector for each input. Models are trained on large datasets to place related pairs close together. Common training uses contrastive learning: the model sees pairs that should match, such as a question and its answer, or an image and its caption, and pairs that should not, and adjusts so matches score higher. You rarely train your own; you choose a pretrained model from open-source libraries or an API provider, chunk your data sensibly, and embed it in batches. Fine-tuning an embedding model on your domain can help when general models miss specialised vocabulary. How do I create vector embeddings with Sentence Transformers? Install the library, load a pretrained model, and call encode on a list of texts. Normalise embeddings so dot product equals cosine similarity. Also asked as: how to create vector embeddings using sentencetransformers from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer model = SentenceTransformer(&quot;all-MiniLM-L6-v2&quot;) emb = model.encode([&quot;How do I reset my password?&quot;, &quot;Steps to change your login&quot;], normalize_embeddings=True) print(emb.shape) # (2, 384) print(emb[0] @ emb[1]) # cosine similarity Run pip install sentence-transformers first. Encode in batches for large datasets and use a GPU if available. Choose a model by testing on your own queries; multilingual models exist for Hindi and other languages. Where are vector embeddings stored? Embeddings are stored in vector databases, vector extensions of existing databases such as pgvector for PostgreSQL, search engines with vector support, or in-memory libraries such as FAISS. Each embedding is saved with an ID and metadata linking it to its source. Choose by scale and existing stack: if you already run PostgreSQL and have up to a few million vectors, pgvector keeps everything in one database. Dedicated vector databases suit larger scale or heavy filtering. Libraries suit offline experiments. Whatever the store, keep the original source data, so you can re-embed when you change models, and record which model and version created each vector. Can vector embeddings be reversed? Partly, yes. Research has shown that text embeddings can be inverted to reconstruct much of the original text: a 2023 study recovered a large share of short inputs exactly from their embeddings using an iterative method. So embeddings are not anonymised data. Treat embeddings as sensitive as their source: encrypt them at rest, control access, and avoid sharing them with untrusted parties. Face embeddings are biometric data under many privacy laws, which is why FaceVision stores embeddings only, never images, behind authenticated APIs, and still treats those embeddings as sensitive. Techniques such as adding noise or using private models reduce inversion risk but can reduce search quality. Does GraphRAG use vector embeddings? Yes. Microsoft's GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph by having a language model extract entities and relationships from text, then summarises communities of related entities. Its local search uses embeddings to find entities related to a question, then gathers connected graph information. Its global search answers broad questions using community summaries rather than vector retrieval alone. So GraphRAG combines graphs and embeddings rather than replacing embeddings. It shines for questions that span many documents, such as themes across a corpus, but costs more to build because of extensive model calls during indexing. For straightforward factual questions, standard hybrid RAG is usually cheaper and sufficient. Are vector distances still relevant with the same model but different quantization? Mostly yes: embeddings from the same model at different precisions, such as float32 and int8, or a quantised version of the model, usually stay close enough that distances remain meaningful, though rankings can shift slightly. Embeddings from different models are never comparable. Also asked as: are vector distances still relevant if embeddings are created with the same model but different quantization Practical guidance: embed your whole corpus and your queries with the same model version and precision where possible. If you quantise stored vectors for memory savings, use the database's supported scheme and rescore top results with full-precision vectors. If you switch to a quantised model for serving, measure retrieval recall on an evaluation set; if it drops, re-embed the corpus with the new model. When should I use vector embeddings? Use embeddings when you need similarity by meaning: semantic search over documents, RAG, recommendations, duplicate detection, clustering and classification with little labelled data. Skip them when exact matching or structured queries solve the problem. Also asked as: when to use vector embeddings Exact lookups such as order numbers, filters such as price ranges, and reports with SQL do not need embeddings. Many real systems combine both: keyword search for exact terms, embeddings for meaning, and filters for structure. Start simple, measure whether embeddings improve results on real queries, and add them where they help. Remember the costs: embedding computation, storage, and re-embedding when models change.

# Word embeddings explained: meaning, how they are made, dimensions and cosine
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/word-embeddings-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Yes, "embeddings" is a word: the plural of "embedding", meaning something fixed firmly into a surrounding mass. In machine learning, an embedding is a vector of numbers representing an item, and word embeddings represent words so that similar meanings sit close together. They underpin search, recommendations and the retrieval in RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad. This page explains what word embeddings mean, how they are created and help, their dimensions, word order, cosine similarity, fine-tuning, which to choose, and how to learn them. Is "embeddings" a word? Yes. "Embedding" is a standard English noun derived from the verb "embed", and "embeddings" is its plural. Dictionaries define embedding as the act of fixing something within a surrounding mass, or the thing embedded. Also asked as: is embeddings a word In mathematics, an embedding is a way of placing one structure inside another while preserving its properties. Machine learning borrowed the term for mapping words, sentences, images or users into a vector space where geometry reflects relationships. So "word embeddings", "sentence embeddings" and "image embeddings" are all correct technical terms, and spell checkers that flag "embeddings" are simply missing technical vocabulary. What does "word embeddings" mean? Word embeddings are dense vectors of real numbers that represent words, learned so that words appearing in similar contexts have similar vectors. "Doctor" and "physician" end up close together; "doctor" and "bicycle" far apart. Also asked as: what does word embeddings mean Unlike one-hot encoding, where each word is an isolated position in a huge sparse vector, embeddings capture relationships compactly. Famous examples show directions with meaning: the vector from "man" to "woman" resembles the one from "king" to "queen". Classic word embeddings give each word one fixed vector. Modern contextual embeddings from transformers give a word different vectors depending on its sentence, so "bank" in "river bank" and "bank loan" differ. How are word embeddings created? Word embeddings are learned from large amounts of text by training a model to predict words from their contexts, or contexts from words, so the vectors that make predictions work become the embeddings. Word2vec, GloVe and fastText are the classic methods. Word2vec, from Google in 2013, trains a shallow network with either CBOW, predicting a word from neighbours, or skip-gram, predicting neighbours from a word. GloVe, from Stanford, factorises global word co-occurrence statistics. FastText adds character n-grams so it can build vectors for rare and misspelled words. In transformers, an embedding layer is learned along with the whole model, and contextual vectors come from later layers. How do word embeddings help? Word embeddings help models understand that different words can mean similar things, which improves search, classification, recommendations and translation. They give neural networks meaningful, compact inputs instead of arbitrary word IDs. Practical benefits: semantic search finds "cheap flights" for "low-cost airfare"; classifiers generalise from fewer labelled examples because similar words share information; spelling variants and synonyms are handled better; and vectors can be compared, clustered and visualised. In RAG systems, embeddings of chunks and questions drive retrieval, though combining them with keyword search catches exact names and codes that embeddings can blur. How many dimensions do word embeddings have? Classic word embeddings typically use 50 to 300 dimensions; 300 was common for word2vec and GloVe. Modern sentence and document embeddings range from 384 to around 4,096 dimensions, depending on the model. Also asked as: how many dimensions are word embeddings More dimensions can capture finer distinctions but cost more memory and compute, and returns diminish. For search over millions of chunks, a 384 or 768-dimension model is often a good balance; some models support truncating vectors to fewer dimensions with little quality loss. Each dimension is not individually interpretable as a single meaning; information is spread across them. Whatever you choose, the index must use the same dimension as the model's output. Can word embeddings ignore the order of words? Static word embeddings themselves carry no order information; each word has one vector regardless of position. Simple methods that average word vectors into a sentence vector do ignore order, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look identical. Models that need order add it: recurrent networks read words in sequence, convolutional networks see local windows, and transformers add positional encodings to word embeddings before attention. Modern sentence embedding models are transformer-based, so they distinguish most order-dependent meanings, though subtle differences can still produce very similar vectors. Test with examples that matter for your application, such as negations. Why is cosine distance used to measure similarity between word embeddings? Cosine similarity compares the direction of two vectors, ignoring their length. For embeddings, direction carries meaning while length often reflects word frequency or other factors, so cosine gives a more reliable measure of semantic similarity than raw distance. Also asked as: why is the cosine distance used to measure the similatiry between word embeddings Cosine similarity is the dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their lengths, ranging from minus one to one. Cosine distance is one minus that value. Many embedding models are trained with cosine-based objectives, so cosine matches how they were optimised. If vectors are normalised to unit length, cosine similarity equals the dot product, and ranking by Euclidean distance gives the same order, which is why vector databases often normalise vectors. Are word embeddings updated during training for document classification? They can be either. You can freeze pretrained embeddings, keeping them fixed while training the classifier, or fine-tune them along with the model. Fine-tuning often helps with enough data; freezing is safer with small datasets. Also asked as: are word embeddings further updated during training for document classification With few labelled examples, updating embeddings can overfit and distort words that appear rarely in training. With larger datasets, fine-tuning adapts vectors to domain meanings, such as "positive" in medical reports. A common strategy is to freeze at first, then unfreeze later with a lower learning rate. With transformers, the standard approach is fine-tuning the whole model, or using adapters such as LoRA, rather than separate word vectors. What is the point of word embeddings, and which should I use? The point is to represent meaning numerically so software can compare, search and learn from text. For most new projects, use a modern sentence embedding model rather than classic word vectors, because it captures context and works directly on sentences and passages. Also asked as: what&#x27;s the point of word embeddings? and which one should i use for my project Guidance: Semantic search or RAG: a sentence-transformers model or a hosted embedding API, chosen by testing on your queries. Multilingual content: a multilingual embedding model. Low resources or offline: small sentence models, or fastText for word-level work. Teaching and analysis: word2vec or GloVe, which are easy to explore. Evaluate two or three models on your own data before committing. Is there a good word embeddings tutorial? Yes. TensorFlow's word embeddings guide trains embeddings in a classification model, the Gensim library has word2vec tutorials, Stanford's CS224N lectures cover the theory, and the Sentence Transformers documentation teaches modern sentence embeddings for search. A learning path: Train word2vec with Gensim on a small corpus and explore nearest neighbours. Visualise vectors with PCA or the TensorFlow Embedding Projector. Build a classifier with an embedding layer. Switch to Sentence Transformers and build semantic search over your own notes. Compare cosine results with keyword search on the same questions. Building something small end to end teaches more than reading theory alone.
